Rule 3, read with rule 6, of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - General - Period April, 2004 to March, 2005 - Whether trading activity merely involves purchases and sales and cannot be considered as a service/exempted service - Held, yes - Whether in cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of purview of both Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994 and, thus, assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor an excisable goods - Held, yes - Whether, in such a case, once in a quarter or once in a six months, quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities was to be deducted according to standard accounting principles and balance only will be availed for purpose of payment of service tax of output service - Held, yes [Para 8]

Rule 2(1), read with Rule 2(d) and Rules 2(e) and 6, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Commission Agent's Services - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on commission in respect of procurement of orders in respect of 'manufacturing activity' as well as 'trading activity' - Department allowed credit in respect of commission relating to manufacturing activity but denied credit of commission relating to 'trading activity' on ground that it was ineligible for credit - HELD : Assessee availed credit on commission in respect of trading goods, which is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products and therefore, assessee is not eligible to avail credit on commission paid on trading goods - Activities not integrally connected with business of manufacture of final products would not qualify as input service - Hence, credit was rightly denied [Paras 5 to 9] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat Credit : Service tax paid on commission in respect of trading goods, which is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products, is not eligible for input service credit

Rule 6  of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Common imputs and input services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Assessment year 2008-09 - During year 2008-09, assessee provided taxable as well as exempted services - Adjudicating Authority having found that assessee had not maintained separate accounts, as required under rule 6(2), confirmed demand as per provisions of rule 6(3)(i) on value of exempted services - Commissioner (Appeals) having noticed that assessee had reversed proportionate credit on value of exempted services subsequently with interest held that assessee had satisfied conditions in view of retrospective amendment carried out to provisions of rule 6 by Finance Act, 2010 and accordingly set aside impugned order - Against impugned order, revenue filed appeal and assessee filed cross objections - Whether in view of fact that Commissioner (Appeals) had already allowed benefit and further in view of complexity of nature, as a special case, assessee would be eligible to reverse proportionate credit attributable to clearances to Jammu  Kashmir State alone for year 2008-09 subject to condition that it would file a letter rectifying deficiencies in letter of option given by it earlier as contemplated in rule 6(3A) - Held, yes [Paras 17 and 18][In favour of assessee]CENVAT: Where assessee, during year 2008-09, provided taxable as well as exempted services and Adjudicating Authority having noticed that it had not maintained separate accounts confirmed demand on value of exempted services and further Appellate Authority having noticed that assessee had reversed proportionate credit on value of exempted services subsequently with interest, set aside impugned order, assessee would be eligible to reverse proportionate credit attributable to clearances to Jammu  Kashmir State alone

Rule 3 ,  read with rules 2(d), 2(e) and rule 6  of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - General - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee was manufacturing as well as trading in cars - Department denied credit of common input services used for trading in ratio of turnover of manufactured and traded cars - Assessee made reversal as per formula under rule 6(3A) effective from 1-4-2011 - Tribunal held that : (a) prior to 1-4-2011, trading was not exempted service' (b) formula under rule 6(3A) taking value of trading services at '10 per cent of cost or actual margin, whichever is higher' was 'encouraging trading' and was inapplicable as introduced only from 1-4-2011; (c) hence, credit was reversible in ratio of sales value of manufactured and traded cars - HELD : Tribunal's observation that 'introduction of revised formula from 1-4-2011, intended to encourage trading' was misdirected - Since Tribunal failed to consider fixation of proportionate credit formula on merits, matter was remanded back for decision afresh [Paras 19 to 28] [Matter remanded]Cenvat Credit : Where, for period prior to 1-4-2011, Tribunal directed credit reversal on 'full sales value' of trading activity observing that formula introduced from 1-4-2011 was intended to encourage trading vis-à-vis manufacturing, High Court set aside said observations and directed Tribunal to decide matter afresh

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Input service - For period prior to 1-4-2011, trading is not a service and hence services used in trading cannot be considered as input services and therefore, credit taken on common input services has to be disallowed/reversed based upon trading turnover and manufacturing turnover [In favour of revenue]

Rule 6, read with rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Stay order - Assessee, a constituent of a company, entered into an agreement for sale of telecommunication equipments - Invoice for telecommunication equipments was issued from Corporate Office and invoice for services was issued from assessee-branch office - Assessee took (i) Cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in provisions of taxable output services as also (ii) cenvat credit distributed/allotted by Corporate Office i.e., Input service distributor (ISD) - Commissioner took a view that sale of telecommunication equipments from Corporate Office was a trading activity and not a taxable service, hence, exempted within meaning of rule 2(e); Commissioner held that assessee had to avail Cenvat credit only to extent of 20 per cent of amount of service tax payable and, resultantly, excess credit taken by assessee was to be recovered - However, there was no finding that assessee had provided taxable as well as exempted services - Whether, prima facie, trading activity of selling telecommunication equipments did not constitute exempted services for assessee to come within mischief of rule 6(3)(c) and, therefore, demand raised by Commissioner in that regard, prima facie, was not sustainable - Held, yes - Whether further, prima facie, adjudicating authority had no jurisdiction to raise question of admissibility or otherwise of impugned credit allotted by input service distributor and availed of by assessee, as eligibility or otherwise of service tax credit has to be examined at end of ISD only - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, there would be total waiver of pre-deposit requirement - Held, yes [Stay granted]

Section 73 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 read with rule 14 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Demands and recovery -  Appellant a manufacture of excisable goods availed Cenvat Credit of service tax paid on various services - These services were used both for manufacture of excisable goods and trading of non-excisable goods, but no separate accounts were maintained for credit availed by them in respect of taxable activities and non-taxable activities - However, since, appellant also did not declare to department, availment of credit on non-taxable trading activities, Adjudicating authority issued notice for recovery of ineligible service tax credit under section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Appellant submitted that Cenvat credit was availed on common inputs services used for trading activities in their capacity of an output service provider and therefore, notice for recovery of ineligible service tax credit should have been made under provisions of Rule 14 of CCR read with section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 and not under section 11A - Whether since appellant is a manufacture of excisable goods and credit taken on input services has been utilized for payment of duty on excisable goods, correct provision for recovery of wrongly availed credit is rule 14 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Held, yes - Whether, wrongly availed credit has to be recovered from person who has availed credit and not from person who has distributed credit - Held, yes [Para 5.1]GST/EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where appellant is a manufacture of excisable goods and credit taken on input services has been utilized for payment of duty on excisable goods, correct provision for recovery of wrongly availed credit is rule 14 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944   GST/EXCISE/ST/VAT: Manufacturer of excisable goods could not have taken any credit on common input services used in manufacture of excisable goods and traded goods prior to 1-4-2011 when trading was not a taxable service to extent it is attributable to traded goods

Rule 2(1), read with rules 2(d), 2(e), and 6, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Commission Agent's Services - Assessee procured contract of Rs. 41.5 crore to supply pre-heaters to DC out of which goods valuing Rs. 5.5 crore were supplied out of own manufacture and balance were supplied out of purchases from market - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on commission in respect of procurement of said contract - Department allowed credit in respect of commission relating to manufacturing activity of Rs. 5.5 crore but denied credit of commission relating to 'trading activity' of Rs. 36 crore - HELD : Assessee availed credit on commission in respect of trading goods, which is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products and therefore, assessee is not eligible to avail credit on commission paid on trading goods - Hence, denial of credit relating to Rs. 36 crore was in consonance with rule 2(l) [Para 10] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat Credit : Service tax paid on commission in respect of trading goods is not eligible for credit because same is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products  Cenvat Credit : Where credit is taken in respect of trading activity and said fact was not disclosed by assessee, same can be denied invoking extended period

Section 16 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit -  Whether unless there is a nexus between input/input services on which credit is taken and output/output services, CENVAT credit cannot be taken - Held, yes - Whether therefore, appellant manufacturer of excisable goods could not have taken any credit on common input services used in manufacture of excisable goods and traded goods prior to 1-4-2011 when trading was not a taxable service to extent it was attributable to traded goods - Held, yes [Para 5.4]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Period 2012-17 - Appellant was providing Commercial Training and Coaching Services and they had also invested in mutual funds and have earned profit during years 2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17 which they have shown as under head 'other income' - Department considered investment in mutual fund as trading in mutual funds and issued a notice on presumption that appellant is providing exempted services which is trading in mutual funds and has not maintained separate records for common input services availed in providing output services and exempted activity i.e. trading and hence liable to pay 6 per cent/7 per cent of amount of exempted services - However, it is found that 'trading' has not been defined under service Tax but in context of securities,'trading' means an activity where a person is engaged in selling goods and occupy for purpose of making profit but certainly trading is different from redemption of mutual fund units - In instant case appellant cannot transfer mutual fund units to third party and give only by redemption to mutual fund because appellant is not permitted to trade mutual fund unit in absence of a license from SEBI - There is a restriction on right to transfer unit and appellant cannot transfer units to any other person - Further, appellant cannot be termed as service provider because he only makes an investment in mutual fund and earn profit from it which is shown in Books of Account under head 'other income' - Whether therefore, question of invoking Rule 6 did not arise and Department had wrongly invoked provisions of Rule 6(3) demanding reversal of credit on exempted service - Held, yes [Para 5]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where appellant only made investments in mutual fund and earned profit from it which was shown in Books of Account under head 'other income', he could not have been termed as 'service provider', hence, department had wrongly invoked provisions of rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 demanding reversal of credit on exempted services

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Appellant had entered into a business solutions agreement and another business promotion agreement with Amazon as per which appellant had to store various merchandizes in Amazon warehouse and facilitate dispatch of goods - Service tax was collected from appellant by Amazon for warehousing services provided to appellant - As per business promotion agreement entered with Amazon, appellant had to sell different products at prices fixed by Amazon through various promotion sales - Appellant was engaged not only in trading but also providing taxable service - Appellant utilized input services provided by Amazon for engaging in trading as well as providing taxable service - Appellant availed input tax credit for period commencing from April 2014 and took credit upto October 2015 on service tax collected from it by Amazon on business support service and storage and warehousing services - Since appellant had utilized input services for trading (exempted services) as well as taxable output services, it opted for reversal of proportionate credit as provided under rule 6(3A)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 and as credit reversed was in excess of proportionate credit to be reversed, it had filed refund claim being balance of credit wrongly reversed (paid in cash) by it - Original authority rejected refund claim entirely - Commissioner (Appeals) held that appellant had to reverse/pay credit along with interest as per rule 6(3A)(i) at rate of 7 per cent of value of exempted services and, therefore, was eligible for refund of only part of amount - Whether view taken by Commissioner (Appeals) that appellant had to reverse credit as per rule 6(3)(i) was against provisions of law - Held, yes - Whether appellant would be eligible for refund after reversal/paying of proportionate credit on exempted services by applying rule 6(3)(i) - Held, yes [Para 5]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where Amazon was providing BSS and warehousing services to appellant and appellant having utilized input services for trading (exempted services) as well as taxable output services, it opted for reversal of proportionate credit as provided under rule 6(3A)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, appellant would be eligible for refund after reversal/paying of proportionate credit on exempted services by applying rule 6(3)(i)

Section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Invocation of Extended Period of Limitation - Assessee's contention that 'treating trading as exempt service was a bona fide interpretational error' cannot be accepted - Till fiction was introduced from 1-4-2011 that trading is an exempted service, 'trading', being sale of goods covered by sales tax law, could not have been considered as a service (taxable or exempted) - There is no scope for any interpretational misconception on this aspect - Extended period is, therefore, invocable [Para 13] [In favour of revenue]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Position prior to 1-3-2008 - Assessee, a provider of both exempted service and taxable service, did not maintain separate accounts in respect of credit attributable to input and input services used in providing such taxable and exempted output services - Assessee utilised credit of inputs and input services only up to 20 per cent of service tax payable on output services as per rule 6(3)(c) - Department alleged that as credit of capital goods and inputs/input services was not separately shown by assessee, assessee had violated provisions of rule 6(3)(c) - HELD : In view of judgment in assessees own case in Idea Cellular Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 19 STT 423 (New Delhi - CESTAT) in Idea Cellular Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 19 STT 423 (New Delhi - CESTAT), credit of capital goods was not hit by restriction under rule 6(3)(c) - As prima facie case was in favour of assessee, requirement of pre-deposit waived [Paras 4 and 5] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 2(e), read with rule 2(l) and rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 35F of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted service - Stay Order - Assessee, a dealer of motor vehicles, took credit of rent paid on premises used for trading purposes - Assessee was also engaged in repair, maintenance and servicing of motor vehicles - In some cases, premises were exclusively used for repair, maintenance and servicing only - Department sought reversal of credit pertaining to trading activity - Tribunal opined, prima facie, that amendment in rule 2(e) with effect from 1-4-2011 covering trading activity as exempted service was clarificatory and retrospective - Tribunal also did not consider aspect of invocation of extended period of limitation and ordered pre-deposit of entire demand with interest - HELD : Adjudicating authority had raised demand based on pro rata credit pertaining to trading activity in ratio of value of trading services as determined as per rule 6 and value of taxable services - One of various issues that was involved was whether said formula was applicable or some other basis could be applied, which was more just, fair or equitable - Keeping in view said position, requirement of pre-deposit was reduced to half of CENVAT credit reversal sought (without interest) [Paras 7 to 10] [Partly in favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : A dealer of motor vehicle is not entitled to credit of rent paid for building used for trading purposes; but, in case of services used for both trading activity and taxable services, reversal of credit may be sought on pro rata basis in ratio of value of two activities or on some other just, fair and equitable basis

I. Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Period from April 2000 to March 2007 - Department denied credit on ground that assessee did not maintain separate accounts for input services used for taxable and exempted services and input service tax credit had been availed/utilised in excess of 20 per cent of credit taken in contravention of rule 6(3)(c) - HELD : Cap of 20 per cent was applicable on service tax payable and not on service tax credit actually availed - What was restricted was only utilisation of credit and not taking credit per se; credit taken could be carried forward - When cap was removed on 1-4-2008, assessee was eligible to utilise credit also - Further, utilising credit in excess of limit would attract only interest liability; entire service tax itself could not be denied to assessee - Hence, matter was remanded back to adjudicating authority to re-examine matter in light of CBEC circular dated 21-11-2008 [Para 5.1] [In favour of assessee]ST : Utilising Cenvat credit in excess of limit fixed under rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 would attract only interest liability; entire credit itself cannot be denied to assessee  ST : Break bulk fee and freight rebate are not, prima facie, liable to service tax under Custom House Agent's services and Business Auxiliary Services respectively  ST : Commission and incentive received from airlines for booking of cargo space is, prima facie, liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary services  ST : CCX fee received from foreign principal for purpose of delivering documents to customers in India, to collect and remit freight charges due to overseas company is liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary services  ST : Cenvat Credit cannot be denied for procedural violations

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Period 2005-06 and 2006-07 - Assessee under a contract with State Government laid pipelines for a canal pipeline project - Assessee by considering said service as falling under category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’ paid service tax on same after availing benefit of Modvat credit - Revenue viewed that above service was not taxable and therefore held that in view of provisions of rule 6(3)(c) assessee was entitled to avail Cenvat credit to extent of 20 per cent only as it was not maintaining separate accounts for inputs and input services used for both exempted and taxable services - However, it was found that Cenvat credit accounts were being maintained separately by assessee on basis of various projects being handled by it - In fact, total amount of credit availed in respect of project of laying down of pipelines had been taken by revenue from Cenvat credit accounts maintained by assessee - Whether, in view of above, question of invocation of provisions of rule 6(3)(c) did not arise - Held, yes [Para 10]

Section 11A, of the Central Excise Act, 1944, read with section 73, of the Finance Act, 1994 and Section 28, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Invocation of Extended Period of Limitation - Assessee took credit relating to services used in 'trading activity' - Department invoked extended period of limitation citing suppression of facts - HELD : Assessee had not disclosed availment of input service credit on commission in respect of trading activities and said facts came to knowledge of department only on verification of documents such as contract agreements, commission agreements etc. - Hence, invocation of extended period was valid [Para 7] [In favour of revenue]

Section 11A, of the Central Excise Act, 1944, read with section 73, of the Finance Act, 1994 and Section 28, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Invocation of Extended Period of Limitation - Assessee took credit relating to services used in 'trading activity' - Department invoked extended period of limitation citing suppression of facts - HELD : It was found by lower authorities and Tribunal that assessee had not disclosed availment of input service credit on commission in respect of trading activities and said facts came to knowledge of department only on verification of documents such as contract agreements, commission agreements etc. - Hence, invocation of extended period was valid [Para 7] [In favour of revenue]

Input tax credit - Common credit - Applicant is engaged in trading of both taxable and exempted goods - Advance ruling was sought on how much percentage of ITC is to be availed in view of fact that supply involves both taxable and exempted supplies - HELD: As applicant is involved in supply of both taxable and exempted supplies, ITC is to be availed proportionately in terms of procedure provided for in sections 16 and 17 of CGST Act, read with rule 42 of CGST Rules [Section 16, read with section 17, of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Rule 42 of Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017] [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]  Advance ruling - Maintainability of - Whether an advance ruling can be sought on question of GST consequences if goods are purchased from unregistered and composition dealers - HELD: Said question sought for advance ruling is not covered under issues referred to in section 97(2) of CGST Act on which Authority for Advance Ruling can pass an advance ruling [Section 97 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 10] [In favour of revenue]

Section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Power to grant exemption from service tax -  Period prior to 7-12-2008 - In view of clarification by Director (Drawback) that service tax on foreign commission agency had not factored in All Industry Rates of Drawback and, further because, foreign commission agent's services were not input services so as to be eligible for drawback, assessee could not be denied refund in respect of said services under Notification No. 41/2007-ST - Refund could not be denied even if assessee had made exports under drawback shipping bills and clause (e) of proviso to said notification had barred exemption by way of refund in cases where drawback had been claimed - Moreover, since rate of refund thereunder had increased from 2 per cent to 10 per cent of FOB with effect from 7-12-2008, said increased rate was eligible to assessee filing claim of refund on or after 7-12-2008 [Paras 5.4  5.5] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Air travel agent - Period September 2003 to 2004 - Assessee, air travel agent, received commission in two categories, i.e., ‘standard commission’ and ‘supplementary commission’ and paid service tax voluntarily only on ‘standard commission’ and contended that ‘supplementary commission’ was, in fact, a trade discount - Whether since both commissions were charge on airfare, for claiming this exemption, appellant had to show that ‘supplementary commission’ was an amount received in excess of commission envisaged in Notification No. 22/97-ST, dated 26-6-1997 - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had not been able to establish that, it was not entitled to waiver of pre-deposit and stay of recovery - Held, yes [Para 4] Circulars and Notifications : Notification No. 22/97-ST, dated 26-6-1997

II. Rule 6, read with rule 2(1), of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Stay Order - Period from November 2006 to March 2011 - Assessee, a manufacturer, was engaged in manufacture as well as trading of goods and took credit of input services used for both, manufacture and trading - Assessee argued that since duty on traded goods was paid by concerned manufacturer, hence, they were entitled to take credit of input services used in trading - HELD : Assessee is not entitled to credit of input services in respect of non-dutiable goods - Hence, since 90 per cent of turnover related to traded goods, proportionate pre-deposit of Rs. 1 crore was upheld as against total demand of Rs. 1.27 crores [Paras 5 to 8] [In favour of revenue]

III. Rule 2(l), read with rule 3, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Commission agent's services - Period September 2005 - Assessee availed credit of service tax paid under reverse charge on services received from agent located abroad - Department denied credit on ground that said services were not chargeable to service tax and hence, credit could not be allowed - HELD : During relevant time, revenue was of view that Service Tax was to be paid on said services - Hence, in absence of any dispute that said services were input services, credit taken could not be denied for reason that later it was decided that assessee need not have paid Service Tax - Hence, credit was allowed [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer or producer of final products and provider of taxable service - Whether where assessee was providing taxable services as well as exempted services, inasmuch as it had not maintained separate accounts of input services and capital goods used in above two types of services, it was entitled to utilise only 20 per cent of input service credit; however, no such restriction is put in respect of use of service tax availed on capital goods - Held, yes [Para 3] [Matter remanded]

Input tax credit - Common credit - Applicant is engaged in trading of both taxable and exempted goods - Advance ruling was sought on how much percentage of ITC is to be availed in view of fact that supply involves both taxable and exempted supplies - HELD: As applicant is involved in supply of both taxable and exempted supplies, ITC is to be availed proportionately in terms of procedure provided for in sections 16 and 17 of CGST Act, read with rule 42 of CGST Rules [Section 16, read with section 17, of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Rule 42 of Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017] [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where a taxpayer is engaged in supply of both taxable and exempted supplies, ITC is to be proportionately availed    GST : Advance ruling cannot be sought on question of GST consequences in case goods are purchased from unregistered and composition dealers as it is not covered under issues on which an application for advance ruling is maintainable

Section 65(25), read with section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Taxable services - Clearing and Forwarding Agent's Services - Period from April 2001 to March 2004 - Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with work of clearing and forwarding of goods, service would not be a taxable service under Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services - Said service is appropriately classifiable under Business Auxiliary Services and is exempt for period from 1-7-2003 to 9-7-2004 under Notification No. 13/2003-ST [Paras 2 to 8] [In favour of assessee]Service Tax : Where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with work of clearing and forwarding of goods, service would not be a taxable service under Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services

Section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 read with rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Charge of service tax on services rendered from outside India - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee, a manufacturer of excisable goods, exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it - It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A - Whether as per reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and it had wrongly taken cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods - Held, yes [Paras 2 and 6] [In favour of revenue]Service Tax : Where assessee exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it and availed credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, it was not eligible to avail cenvat of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services for trading of imported goods

Rule 2(p) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Output service - Assessee took Cenvat credit of service tax paid on GTA service and utilized same for payment of service tax on commission paid to its foreign agent for procurement of export orders, under head business auxiliary services - Adjudicating authority held that service tax paid on GTA service could not be taken as credit by assessee as it was not paying any excise duty on its final product and also was not providing any output service - Commissioner (Appeals) held that prior to omission of Explanation to rule 2(P) with effect from 18-4-2006, not only credit can be taken by a person who is liable to pay service tax but also same can be utilized for payment of excise duty/service tax - However, revenue contended that in view of decision of Tribunal in ITC Ltd. v. CCE [2011] 31 STT 463/11 taxmann.com 166 (Bang - CESTAT), even prior to 19-4-2006 assessee was required to pay service tax on GTA service received by him in cash but not through Cenvat credit - Whether matter was to be remanded to Commissioner (Appeals) for fresh decision - Held, yes [Para 5] [Matter remanded]

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Period April, 2006 to January, 2007 - Assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax on commission paid to commission agent for receiving services of latter - Revenue denied credit on ground that benefit was liable to be restricted to procurement of purchase orders by commission agents and was not admissible insofar as collection of sale price of goods was concerned - Whether bifurcating commission agents’ function into pre-clearance and post-clearance of goods as done by lower authorities is clearly not permissible inasmuch as commission agents’ service is one integrated service and, therefore, assessee was entitled to benefit of Cenvat credit on entire amount of commission paid by it to commission agent - Held, yes [Para 3]

Cenvat credit of Service Tax - Reversal of credit on common input services - Appellant availed Cenvat credit on common input services used for providing both taxable service and exempt service and not maintained separate accounts/records for receipt and use of common input services issue as to entitlement of credit stands decided at the level of first Appellate Authority - Further Tribunal upheld entitlement of petitioner for reversal after computing proportionate credit by applying Rule 6(3)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Matter remanded by Tribunal only for limited purpose of quantification of amount eligible for refund - Hence show cause notice purporting to reopen question of entitlement to credit, is bad in law - Revenue authorities directed to issue fresh show cause notice limiting scope of examination to quantification of input service alone [Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 18 and 28]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with section 35F of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Commission agents - Appellants submitted that their activity as commission agents was not covered under service tax statute at relevant point of time and subsequently it had been brought under statute but exempted - Whether since there was prima facie merit in submission of appellants, pre-deposit of amount was required to be waived - Held, yes

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Period 2013-2017 - Assessee was registered and holding service tax registration certificate for provider/recipient of work contract, Design Services, Business Support Services etc., and were availing the credit of the tax paid on "input services" under provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Revenue having noticed that assessee was also engaged in trading of mutual fund units and same being exempted services, raised demand of 6% of value of exempted services - Whether assessee was not engaged in business of trading in securities (Mutual Funds) but investment in Mutual Fund was an investment activity and gain from return of Mutual Fund was taxed as capital gain and not as business income and, therefore, Rule 6(3) was not applicable; impugned demand of 6% of value of exempted services was not sustainable - Held, yes [Para 5] [ In favour of assessee]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where assessee was not engaged in business of trading in securities (Mutual Funds) but investment in Mutual Fund was an investment activity and gain from return of Mutual Fund was taxed as capital gain and not as business income, Rule 6(3) was not applicable

Rule 7 ,  read with rule 6  of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Manner of Distribution of Credit by Input Service Distributor - Period prior to 1-4-2012 - Department raised demand on ground that credit pertaining to one unit was distributed to another unit for purpose of enabling it to use credit - HELD : During relevant period, only conditions in rule 7 for distribution of credit were : (a) credit could not exceed tax paid; and (b) credit exclusively of exempted units could not be distributed - Since both conditions had been fulfilled, credit cannot be denied - Condition as to pro rata distribution of credit under rule 7(d) was introduced only from 1-4-2012 - Demand cannot be raised even by applying rule 6, as assessee had not provided 'taxable as well as exempt' services - Hence, demand was set aside [Paras 4 to 6] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Requirement of registration is procedural; hence, credit cannot be denied to input service distributor even if it is unregistered, provided assessee has maintained all records for verification by revenue

Cenvat credit of Service Tax - Reversal of credit on common input services - Appellant availed Cenvat credit on common input services used for providing both taxable service and exempt service and not maintained separate accounts/records for receipt and use of common input services issue as to entitlement of credit stands decided at the level of first Appellate Authority - Further Tribunal upheld entitlement of petitioner for reversal after computing proportionate credit by applying Rule 6(3)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Matter remanded by Tribunal only for limited purpose of quantification of amount eligible for refund - Hence show cause notice purporting to reopen question of entitlement to credit, is bad in law - Revenue authorities directed to issue fresh show cause notice limiting scope of examination to quantification of input service alone [Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 18 and 28]ST/Cenvat : Matter was remanded by Tribunal only for limited purpose of quantification of amount eligible for refund, hence show cause notice purporting to reopen question of entitlement to credit, is bad in law; revenue authorities will issue fresh show cause notice limiting scope of examination to quantification of input service alone

Section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 - Charge of service tax on services received from outside India - Period 9-7-2004 to 30-9-2006 - Assessees engaged foreign agents for identifying prospective customers and marketing their services - Assessees paid commission to those foreign agents in foreign currency - Revenue demanded service tax from assessees in category of ‘Business auxiliary service’ - High Court in Indian National Shipowners Association v. Union of India [2009] 18 STT 212 (Bom.) held that it was only after enactment of section 66A on 18-4-2006 that taxable services received from abroad by a person belonging to India are taxable in hands of Indian residents - Whether since assessees had received business auxiliary services from commission agents based abroad mostly prior to 18-4-2006 and there is no provision in Act to tax assessees for those services, demands on that account for period prior to 18-4-2006 had to fail - Held, yes [Para 4.3] Circulars & Notifications : CBEC Circular No. F. No. 36/4/2001, dated 8-10-2001

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Periods 2008-09 to 2009-10 - Assessee provided dutiable and exempted services and also availed Cenvat credit on certain common input services - It opted for payment at prescribed percentage on value of exempted services and also paid amounts for earlier periods - Revenue held that assessee could not exercise option retrospectively for earlier period and hence credit taken was improper - Whether there is no bar for making payments as per prescribed percentages for prior period as it may not be feasible to segregate quantum of input service credit pertaining to dutiable and exempted services and, therefore, assessee's actions of paying amounts for past period was justified - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]CENVAT: There is no bar for making as per prescribed percentage payment on value of exempted services for prior period where it may not be feasible to segregate quantum of input services pertaining to dutiable  exempted services

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Input service - Travelling services - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee was providing Management Consultancy and Insurance Auxiliary Services - Assessee took input service credit of Rent-a-cab and Air Travel Agent Service - Department denied credit on ground that both these services are used for employees' benefit - Assessee argued that : (a) Rent-a-cab service is expressly excluded from input service from 1-4-2011, but, for present case relating to period prior to 1-4-2011, credit is allowed; (b) air travel agent's services were availed for travel of employees for business purposes - HELD : Rent-a-cab and Air Travel Agent services, though used by employees, are for performance of assessee's business - Hence, both services are input service - Further, expenses towards both services was booked as expenditure in profit and loss account - Rent-a-cab service was not excluded from definition of input service; hence, prior to 1-4-2011, credit was admissible [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Rent-a-cab service is expressly excluded from input service from 1-4-2011, but, for period prior to 1-4-2011, said service availed for employees for business purposes, is eligible for credit; similarly, air travel agent's services availed for travel of employees for business purposes is also eligible for credit

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, read with section 86 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Cenvat Credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted service - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of both dutiable and exempted products - Commissioner on finding that assessee was not maintaining separate accounts in respect of input duty credit and input service tax credit vis-a-vis dutiable final product and exempted final product, demanded reversal of credit utilized for payment of duty on dutiable products - However, Commissioner prematurely quantified an amount of ‘excess credit’ for reversal by assessee inasmuch as amount of input service tax credit to be denied or allowed under separate show-cause notice covering some input services, was yet to be determined by adjudicating authority - Whether in view of above, there would be waiver of pre-deposit and stay on recovery in respect of amount of credit prematurely demanded by Commissioner as also in respect of interest sought to be charged on such amount - Held, yes [Para 3]

Section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Business auxiliary service - Period 14-9-2004 to 31-3-2007 - Assessee was engaged in providing business auxiliary service as a commission agent - During 1-7-2003 to 8-7-2004 service of commission agent was exempted from service tax vide Notification No. 13/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003 which was subsequently amended by making same liable to service tax with effect from 9-7-2004 - After that amendment, a show-cause notice was issued to assessee demanding service tax for relevant period which was confirmed by adjudicating authority - Assessee contended that said demand included amount which was outstanding as on 9-7-2004 for service provided prior to 9-7-2004 - Whether since taxable service was provided prior to 9-7-2004, even though payment was received on or after 9-7-2004, no service tax can be charged - Held, yes [Para 3]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Assessee-company was hired under a contract for canvassing and advancing sale of principal’s products and procuring orders - Assessee was to receive commission - Authorities held that services provided by assessee were covered under category of clearing and forwarding service and demanded duty for period 1997-2003 - Whether, in view of nature of service provided by assessee, it was to be held as commission agent rather than consignment agent - Held, yes - Whether, since services as commission agent were made liable to tax under category of business auxiliary service with effect from 1-7-2003 and period in instant appeal was prior to said date, assessee was not liable to pay any tax during period in question - Held, yes [Para 3] Circular and Notification - Board Circular No. 59/8/2003, dated 20-6-2003

Cenvat credit - Reversal of - Common inputs/input services used for both taxable and exempted final products services - Position prior to 1-4-2016 - Assessee was rendering services to BCCI for organizing IPL T-20 cricket matches under a franchise agreement - Revenue generated from stadium gate receipt/sale of ticket, prize money received from BCCI-IPL and in-stadium sale i.e. stadium revenue could not be considered towards rendering of any services hence no Cenvat credit was required to be reversed - Moreover, prior to amendment to Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from 1-4-2016, there was no requirement to reverse Cenvat credit on input/input services used in an activity that was not a service [Rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 5, 5.5 and 5.6] [In favour assessee]

Section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 - Charge of service tax on services received from outside India - Period prior to 18-4-2006 - Whether service of foreign based commission agent rendered prior to 18-4-2006 is not taxable under category of ‘Business auxiliary service’ which includes commission agent - Held, yes [Para 2]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Common input and inputs services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Cenvat credit - And amending Notification No. 27/2005-CE (NT) dt. 16.5.2005 - Amendment by way of addition of Explanation III to Rule 6 (3) vide notification is effective from 16.5.2005 - Prior to 16.5.2005 a manufacturer producing both dutiable as well as exempted final product and paying 8% or 10% amount on exempted final product, was entitled to take credit on all inputs whether common to both final products or exclusively used in manufacture of exempted goods only (Para 32)

facts.text:
Assessee was manufacturing TV, washing machines, AC, etc. and was also importing said goods for resale.

Assessee took credit of input services pro rata based on turnover ratio attributable to manufacturing business.

Department argued that since 'imported goods' were 'exempted goods', assessee was liable to pay 10 per cent 5 per cent 6 per cent of value of said exempted goods. Department issued notice dated 7-10-2011 invoking extended period to seek demand.

Assessee argued that —

since he was not taking credit relating to 'trading business', rule 6(2) or rule 6(3) were inapplicable ;

since credit as per formula under Rule 6(3A) was merely Rs. 16 lakh, which was not taken; demand of Rs. 297 crore was invalid ;

its procedure of taking credit only on dutiable goods based on turnover ratio was known to department when audit was conducted in 2008 and furthermore, for earlier period, proceedings on same ground had been initiated and were pending before Tribunal; therefore, allegation of suppression was invalid.

Revenue argued that activity of trading could be considered as services and since during material time, it was not a taxable service, it should be construed as 'exempted service'. Since assessee has not maintained any separate account in respect of the dutiable/taxable goods/services and exempted goods/services, payment at 10 per cent/ 5 per cent of the value of the exempted services was to be made under rule 6(3).

Assessee argued that trading was deemed as exempted service only from 1-4-2011; hence, demand for period prior thereto cannot be made on that count.

Facts

The assessee is a trader in personal computers, photocopiers, telecom products and mobile phones etc. and had provided taxable services like Maintenance and Repair; Commissioning and Installation; Leased Circuit; Online Information and Data Processing and Business Auxiliary Services.

Assessee -

availed credit on service tax paid on input services utilized for its trading activities;

utilized credit to an extent not exceeding 35 per cent up to 09-09-2004 and to an extent of 20 per cent thereafter, of the Service tax payable on its taxable output services,

in terms of Rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 and Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004,

treating trading as an exempted service.

The show-cause notice dated 11-10-2006 alleged that as trading of goods is not a service, this cannot be considered as an exempted service and provisions of the Act and rules thereunder do not apply to trading activities.

The assessee reversed credit availed on service tax incurred by the assessee on sales commission, brokerage, travel agent service, warehouse charges, freight and courier charges, being input services for its trading activities.

The assessee neither responded to the show-cause notice nor attended personal hearing. Hence, the impugned order was passed ex parte.

Revenue's Arguments

Services utilized for trading of computers etc. would not amount to services utilized/consumed in the rendition of output services, since output services were provided after culmination of trading activities i.e. sale and delivery of computers etc. to customers. Input services in respect of which cenvat credit was taken stood utilized prior to delivery of computers and cannot be said to have been consumed/used in relation to rendition of output services;

Since trading is neither a service nor amounts to an exempted service, cenvat credit earned on an input services of trading-cannot be considered as credit earned on exempted service;

Consequently, cenvat credit taken in respect of input services of trading is liable to be reversed in toto and the inadmissible cenvat credit utilized for payment of service tax on taxable output services liable to be recovered, along with interest and penalty;

Since the assessee deliberately availed to disclose availment of cenvat credit on services which were not an input services for its output services, assessee contravened Rules 3 and 4 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 and the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, with an intent to evade payment of Service tax and therefore the extended period is invocable and interest and penalty also leviable.

Assessee's Arguments

The assessee submitted that -

all taxable services were provided by the assessee only in relation to computers, photocopiers etc. sold to various customers;

commissioning, installation, maintenance and repair services etc. were also services provided in relation to these traded goods;

Rule 2(b) of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 defines 'Input Services' as any service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service;

transportation of goods and the other services utilized for despatching goods to customers premises, is integral to the post-trading rendition of taxable services such as installation, commissioning, repair, maintenance etc.; and

thus, credit taken is unexceptionable.

The assessee alternatively claimed that since credit was utilized only to the extent of 35 per cent or 20 per cent of the payable service tax, as the case may be, interest should be calculated only on amount of credit actually utilized; that there is a distinction between taking of credit and utilization of credit and it is utilization alone that results in lesser remittance of tax in cash to Government and not taking of credit in assessee's books. Therefore, interest should be calculated only on the amount actually utilized, if wrongly utilized, but not on the gross credit wrongly availed.

No penalty should be imposed since availment of credit on the assumption that trading is an exempted activity was on account of interpretation and penalty is leviable only for wilful and deliberate conduct and not where availment of credit is on the basis of a mistaken but plausible interpretation of relevant provisions.

Issue Involved

Whether credit was rightly claimed and reversed ?

The revenue issued on the assessee a show cause notice alleging that it was utilizing the input service for providing output taxable service of clearing and forwarding agent service as well as for trading and proposed to raise demand upon it.

The Adjudicating Authority dropped the demand proposed in the show cause notice. He held that to be an exempted service, it must be a taxable service under the Finance Act, 1994. He further held that the trading activity was a non-taxable service. Therefore, it could not be an exempted service.

The Revisional Authority opined that as per rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 'exempted services' means taxable services which are exempt from the whole of the service tax leviable thereon, and includes services on which no service tax is leviable under section 66 of the Finance Act. Therefore, service on which no service tax was leviable under section 66 could be termed as 'exempted service'.

On appeal to Tribunal:

The appellant was engaged in trading activities as well as in commission business. The appellant obtained centralized registration with the service tax department under the category "Business Ancillary Services".

Evidently, the appellant's records were examined by the internal audit party of the department. The audit carried out revealed that the appellant had been claiming credit of service tax on various common input services which were used both for its trading activity and its business of commission agent.

As far as the commission agency business was concerned, service tax was paid by the appellant, while no service tax was paid for trading activity. Thus, the audit party came to the conclusion that excess credit of service tax had been claimed by the assessee.

The stand taken by the appellant was that during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax. It was alleged that due to an incorrect audit objection to the alleged utilization of cenvat credit qua the exempted services, the appellant had paid up the purportedly excess amount, which was, otherwise not payable.

The Adjudicating Authority, however, was not impressed with the stand taken by the appellant and, therefore, proceeded to reject its claim for refund.

The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order passed by Adjudicating Authority.

On appeal to the High Court:

The assessee was registered with the Department for providing taxable services falling under the categories of Consulting Engineer, Maintenance or Repair Services and, Erection, Commissioning and Installation Services. It had entered into a contract with ‘B’ for supply and installation of BTS, Microcell and other Microwave equipments for telecommunication network. The invoice for the supply of telecommunication equipment was issued from its corporate office and the invoice for service portion was issued from its branches. The assessee was taking the Cenvat credit of tax paid on the input services used in the provision of taxable output services as well as the Cenvat credit distributed by its Corporate Office (i.e., input service distributor). It was noticed that the Cenvat credit distributed by the corporate office also pertaining to the input services used exclusively for the procurement of telecommunication equipments. The revenue took a view that the assessee was engaged in the sale of telecommunication equipments from its Corporate Office which was a trading activity and a non-taxable service outside the scope of the Act. Therefore, the trading activity fell within the meaning of exempted services as defined under rule 2(e). According to the revenue as the assessee had not maintained separate records at its Corporate Office for the input services commonly used in the taxable output services provided from the branches or in the exempted services provided from the Corporate Office, it was liable to utilize the Cenvat credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding twenty per cent of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services in terms of rule 6(3)(c). However, the assessee had utilized the entire Cenvat credit available with it towards the discharge of service tax liability on the taxable output services. Thus, the Commissioner confirmed the demand on the ground that the assessee had utilized excess Cenvat credit which was liable to be recovered from it. Besides that, the Commissioner also confirmed the demand on the ground that the assessee had wrongly availed of the Cenvat credit on insurance service, foreign consultancy service, etc., which were used exclusively in the provision of exempted services and, were utilized towards payment of service tax. The Commissioner also confirmed the demand disallowing the Cenvat credit on the services, viz., flower arrangements, garden maintenance, outdoor catering, real estate agent’s services for residential accommodation of its employees distributed by its Corporate Office on the ground that same could not be termed as input services defined under rule 2(l).

On application :

The appellant was engaged in providing maintenance and repair services and commissioning and installation service of RO systems. It was observed that the appellants were availing the credit on advertising, security, courier, telephone and banking services which were not entirely used in providing ‘maintenance and repair’ services, but also used in trading activity and, therefore, credit of input services which were entirely used in trading activity was not available to the appellants for payment of service tax. The amounts of service tax payable for two half-yearly period were Rs. 34,143 and Rs. 27,315. Total Cenvat credit available to the appellants was Rs. 6,828, i.e., 20 per cent of Rs. 34,143 as per rule 6(3) and Rs. 8,877, i.e., 35 per cent of Rs. 25,363 as per rule 3(5). The balance amount was to be paid by the appellants in cash only.

The appellants had adjusted the service tax amount fully from Cenvat credit and wrongly availed Cenvat credit of Rs. 43,801.

The lower authorities claimed that appellant should have maintained separate accounts in respect of input services used for trading activity which were liable to service tax and the Cenvat credit availed by the appellant was demanded.

Facts

Assessee, a firm of Chartered Accountants, was providing both taxable as well as exempted services.

Assessee did not maintain separate accounts for services used in providing taxable and exempted services as required under rule 6(2) and also did not opt for pro rata reversal of the Cenvat Credit under rule 6(3A). Hence, department raised demand of 8 per cent/6 per cent of value of exempted services.

It was also noticed that they had availed and utilised Cenvat credit on input services of insurance and maintenance of motor vehicles which were not in the name of the firm.

Assessee's Arguments

They had paid proportionate of Cenvat credit as required under rule 6(3)(ii) before the issue of show cause notice. Further, the provisions of rule 6(3A) are technical in nature and there is no time limit prescribed for giving option to avail rule 6(3A).

Rule 6(3A) was amended from 1-4-2008 and he was ignorant about these provisions and continued to follow the old provision which restricted utilisation of Cenvat credit to the extent of 20 per cent.

Input services of insurance and car are used for business and expenses are reflected in the profit & loss account of the firm.

Order-in-Original and Order-in-Appeal travelled beyond the show-cause notice to the extent that the show-cause notice only sought to deny credit on the bills which were not in the name of the firm.

Extended period of limitation cannot be invoked in the absence of mens rea.

The assessee-firm acted as a commission agent on behalf of agriculturists. Under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, if the assessee proved that it was acting on behalf of the agriculturist principals, such goods were exempted from sales tax. The assessee maintained mercantile system of accounting and its books of account indicated all details of agriculturist principals, purchasers, the quantity of goods sold, the sale proceeds and also sales tax collected from the purchasers. The sales tax collected was credited to the sales tax account and the sales tax account was debited with the payments made to Government as and when assessments were completed. At the end of the year, when the assessment was completed, if it was established that the assessee was only acting for the agriculturist principals, and if each of the agriculturist principal's turnover was less than Rs. 10,000, the amounts paid during the course of the year were refunded. The assessee, while debiting the sales tax account with the said amount of refund, credited the same to separate sales tax refund account. The assessee also maintained debtors ledger wherein each agriculturist principal's account was credited with the amount of sales tax refundable to him, so that the total of the credits given in the separate debtors ledger accounts was equal to the total of the credits standing in the refund account in the main ledger account.

The assessee claimed that the refunded sales tax amount should not be treated as trading receipt and, therefore, it should not be included in the assessee's income as it had to be made over to the agriculturist principals. The ITO, however, included the impugned amount. The Tribunal upheld the assessee's claim.

On reference :

Facts

The assessee was a Property Trading and Development Company having business of acquisition, asset management or development and subsequent disposal of commercial properties in UK as well as Scotland.

With a mind to raise capital and secure a quotation for its shares on Alternative Investment Market of London Stock Exchange (AIM), assessee availed services of nominated advisor, reporting accountants, auditors, a broker, a portfolio valuer and the services of solicitors as well as registrars and receiving bankers viz.

Admission & Placing;

Admission, Placing and other Legal Advice;

Admission, Placing and Annual Accounts Valuation;

Admission, Placing and work related to Production of Annual Accounts;

Admission, Placing and Corporate Identity Matters.

There were two distinct objects in the mind of the assessee : one to raise capital and the second to establish their position as a quoted company and so acquire and retain benefits for the future.

The assessee took input credit of VAT paid on aforesaid services.

The informed that listing was in part for the general business purposes and was not an essential element of the issue of shares.

The Department denied credit on ground that said services were only linked to an issue of shares, an exempt supply.

Statutory Provisions

UK Value Added Tax Act, 1994, sections 25 and 26 : Section 25 provides that a taxable person is entitled to credit for so much of his input tax as is allowable under section 26. Section 26(1) provides that the amount of any input tax to which a taxable person is entitled to credit is so much of the input tax allowable by regulations made for this purpose as is attributable to taxable (and not exempt) supplies. Section 26(3) provides that the Commissioners shall make regulations for securing a fair and reasonable attribution of input tax as between taxable and exempt supplies.

UK Value Added Tax Act, 1994, section 31(1) : A supply is an exempt supply if it is of a description specified in schedule 9. Group 5 of Schedule 9 is headed "Finance". Item 6 specifies as exempt supplies (inter alia): "The issue, transfer or receipt of, or any dealing with, any security or secondary security being (a) shares, stocks, bonds, notes (other than promissory notes), debentures, debenture stock or shares in an oil royalty;…."

UK Value Added Tax Regulations 1995, Regulation 101 :

(1) Subject to regulation 102, the amount of input tax which a taxable person shall be entitled to deduct provisionally shall be that amount which is attributable to taxable supplies in accordance with this regulation.

(2) In respect of each prescribed accounting period

(a)

… goods or services supplied to the taxable person in the period shall be identified,

(b)

there shall be attributed to taxable supplies the whole of the input tax on such of those goods or services as are used or to be used by him exclusively in making taxable supplies,

(c)

no part of the input tax on such of those goods or services as are used or to be used by him exclusively in making exempt supplies, or in carrying on any activity other than the making of taxable supplies, shall be attributed to taxable supplies, and

(d)

there shall be attributed to taxable supplies such proportion of the input tax on such of those goods or services as are used or to be used by him in making both taxable and exempt supplies as bears the same ratio to the total of such input tax as the value of taxable supplies made by him bears to the value of all supplies made by him in the period.

(3) In calculating the proportion under paragraph (2)(d) above, there shall be excluded…(b)…(v) any supply which falls within Group 5 of schedule 9 to the Act …

(4) The ratio calculated for the purpose of paragraph (2)(d) above shall be expressed as a percentage and, if that percentage is not a whole number, it shall be rounded up to the next whole number.

Issue Involved

Were input supplies used exclusively for the purposes of the exempt transaction or partly for an exempt transaction and partly for the general purpose of the business?

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of both, dutiable and exempted bulk drugs. It had opted for not maintaining separate accounts for dutiable and exempted goods as envisaged under rule 6(3). It took credit of duty paid on all the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods, including exclusive inputs (other than common inputs) and paid 10 per cent on the sale price of exempted goods cleared in domestic market. By the Notification No. 27/2005, dated 16-5-2005 rule 6(3) was amended by inserting Explanation III clarifying that credit shall not be allowed on inputs and input services used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted service. Pursuant to the above amendment show-cause notices were issued to the assessee demanding the Cenvat credit relatable to (i) the exclusive inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods which were cleared on payment at 10 per cent of the sale price of the exempted goods; (ii) the exclusive inputs removed as such; (iii) the exclusive inputs used in the finished goods exported; (iv) the exclusive inputs used in the finished goods removed to 100 per cent EOU; (v) the exclusive inputs lying in stock; (vi) the exclusive inputs used in the finished goods lying in the stock. The demands were confirmed by the Commissioner.

On appeal :

The assessee, a service provider, had three departments. The department 'A' provided taxable service. The department 'B' provided exempted service. The department 'C' received the input service.

The assessee allocated the cenvat credit of service tax paid on input service availed by the department 'C' to the department 'A' to the extent of Rs. 1.11 crores and the department 'B' to the extent of Rs. 6.66 lakhs on the ratio of the turnover.

The Adjudicating Authority disallowed the entire cenvat credit allocated to the department 'A' on the ground that the department 'B', which provided exempted service, availed part of the cenvat credit.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal the revenue submitted that when the manufacturer or the service provider provides taxable service as well as exempted service, he comes under rule 6(2) to maintain record for verification by revenue. Once the assessee comes under rule 6(2), in that circumstance, application of rule 6(2) and rule 6(3) simultaneously is not possible. The assessee failed to comply with the condition prescribed by rule 6(3) read with rule 6(3A). Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has rightly denied the entire cenvat credit of Rs. 1.11 crores allocated to the department 'A'.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. During the year 2011-12, it had exported final products manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it. It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on import of services received from one 'C' under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A.

The Adjudicating Authority having discovered that the assessee had availed service tax credit on marketing consultancy services for traded goods (exempted goods) rendered by 'C' opined that the assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and the cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods was erroneous and recoverable in terms of rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

Thereupon the assessee reversed the cenvat credit to the extent of service tax attributable to trading of imported goods and also paid interest. It asserted that it was eligible for the cenvat credit in respect of market consultancy services.

The Adjudicating Authority confirmed the demand of service tax and interest and also imposed equal penalty on the assessee under rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 11AC of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order-in-original.

On second appeal:

The assessee was engaged in providing various output services. The Commissioner confirmed service tax demand for relevant period on the assessee on the ground that it had availed Cenvat credit in respect of services which were used for providing services in J&K State and SEZ which were exempted during relevant time, and while paying the service tax, it was required to utilize only 20 per cent of the credit available for payment of service tax on the input service in accordance with the provisions of rule 6(3)(c ). On appeal, the assessee contended that rule 6(3)(c) was not applicable to instant case since it had not at all taken the credit in respect of ten common services which were utilized by it. The assessee also contended that once it had not taken credit on the common services, question of maintenance of separate records also did not arise.

The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacturing tractors, tractor engines and part thereof. The assessee had availed Cenvat Credit, amounting to Rs.72 lakh as it had paid service tax on the basis of reverse charge mechanism qua services rendered by a non-resident service provider. The assessee had paid sales commissions to the said service provider. The services rendered by the service provider were taxable under the category 'Business Auxiliary Service'. Since, it was an input service, service tax was paid by the assessee qua which Cenvat Credit was claimed.

It was a common ground that the goods manufactured by the assessee, for which services of the said sales commission agent were utilized were exempted from payment of excise duty, by virtue of notification no 6/2006/CE dated 1-3-2006.

The revenue, however, took exception to the Cenvat Credit claimed by the assessee and, accordingly, issued a show-cause notice. Statutory Provisions, Sixth Council Directive 77/388/EEC of 17 May, 1977

Article 17 : The taxable person is entitled to deduct only "in so far as the goods and services are used for the purposes of his taxable transactions". As regards goods and services to be used by a taxable person both for transactions in respect of which value added tax is deductible and transactions in respect of which value added tax is not deductible, it is provided that only such proportion of the tax shall be deductible as is attributable to the taxable transactions.

Article 19 : This article lays down the following rules for calculating that proportion. Paragraph 2 of that article provides: "By way of derogation from the provisions of paragraph 1, there shall be excluded from the calculation of the deductible proportion, amounts of turnover attributable to the supplies of capital goods used by the taxable person for the purposes of his business. Statutory Provisions, Sixth Council Directive 77/388/EEC of 17 May, 1977

Article 2(1) : Supply of goods or services effected for consideration within the territory of the country by a taxable person acting as such is subject to VAT.

Article 4 : Any person who independently carries out any economic activity specified in Article 4(2) is a taxable person. Economic activities are defined in Article 4(2) as comprising all activities of producers, traders and persons supplying services including the exploitation of tangible or intangible property for the purpose of obtaining income therefrom on a continuing basis.

Article 13B(d)(5) : Without prejudice to other Community provisions, Member States shall exempt … the following transactions: … transactions, including negotiation, excluding management and safekeeping, in shares, interests in companies or associations, debentures and other securities, excluding:

-

documents establishing title to goods,

-

the rights or securities referred to in Article 5(3).

Article 17 : In so far as the goods and services are used for the purposes of his taxable transactions, the taxable person shall be entitled to deduct from the tax which he is liable to pay ... value added tax due or paid in respect of goods or services supplied or to be supplied to him by another taxable person.

As regards goods and services used by a taxable person both for transactions in respect of which VAT is deductible and for transactions in respect of which it is not deductible, the first sub-paragraph of Article 17(5) of the Sixth Directive provides that only such proportion of the value added tax shall be deductible as is attributable to the former transactions. The second sub-paragraph of Article 17(5) states that this proportion shall be determined, in accordance with Article 19, for all the transactions carried out by the taxable person.

Article 19 : 1. The proportion deductible under the first sub-paragraph of Article 17(5) shall be made up of a fraction having:

-

as numerator, the total amount, exclusive of value added tax, of turnover per year attributable to transactions in respect of which value added tax is deductible under Article 17(2) and (3).

-

as denominator, the total amount, exclusive of value added tax, of turnover per year attributable to transactions included in the numerator and to transactions in respect of which value added tax is not deductible. The Member States may also include in the denominator the amount of subsidies, other than those specified in Article 11A(1)(a).

The proportion shall be determined on an annual basis, fixed as a percentage and rounded up to a figure not exceeding the next unit.

2. …there shall be excluded from the calculation of the deductible proportion, amounts of turnover attributable to …transactions specified in Article 13B(d), in so far as these are incidental transactions, and to incidental real estate and financial transactions. ...

HELD (PER TECHNICAL MEMBER) It is seen that rule 6(1) specifically prohibits Cenvat credit being allowed on such quantity of inputs as used in the manufacture of exempted goods. It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Facts

ONGC availed of services at the area of operation, viz., at the well-heads, well platforms, process platforms, pipelines, vessels, at the Uran plant and at the administrative offices at Mumbai.

The Department denied Cenvat Credit of input services on ground that :
