digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 16 of the Central Goods And Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit - Period April 2006 to 2008 - Whether it could not be contended that since definition of Rule 2(e) underwent amendment with effect from 1-4-2011, whereby, it was indicated that trading activity would fall in category of services, therefore rule 6(3)(c) could apply to trading activity only after 1.4.2011 - Held, yes - During relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax - Appellant company acted as a commission agent was also engaged in trading activities - Whether since appellant was not paying service tax on trading activity, credit of tax paid on services vis-a-vis input services could only be taken on a pro-rata basis as per formula stipulated in Rule 6(3)(c) - Held, yes - Whether however, since no separate accounts were maintained by appellant with regard to taxable and non-taxable services, apportionment as provided in Rule 6(3)(c) would triggered - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in denying credit of service tax - Held, yes [Para 12][In favour of revenue]GST/Cenvat Credit: Where during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax, if appellant engaged in activities of trading and commission agency did not maintain separate accounts regarding taxable and non-taxable services, it would not be entitled to credit of service tax

FACT: The appellant was engaged in trading activities as well as in commission business. The appellant obtained centralized registration with the service tax department under the category "Business Ancillary Services".

Evidently, the appellant's records were examined by the internal audit party of the department. The audit carried out revealed that the appellant had been claiming credit of service tax on various common input services which were used both for its trading activity and its business of commission agent.

As far as the commission agency business was concerned, service tax was paid by the appellant, while no service tax was paid for trading activity. Thus, the audit party came to the conclusion that excess credit of service tax had been claimed by the assessee.

The stand taken by the appellant was that during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax. It was alleged that due to an incorrect audit objection to the alleged utilization of cenvat credit qua the exempted services, the appellant had paid up the purportedly excess amount, which was, otherwise not payable.

The Adjudicating Authority, however, was not impressed with the stand taken by the appellant and, therefore, proceeded to reject its claim for refund.

The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order passed by Adjudicating Authority.

On appeal to the High Court:

HELD: Clearly, during the period in issue, i.e., 2006-07 and 2007-08, trading activity, which was one of the businesses, carried out by the appellant was not amenable to service tax. The amendment to rule 2(e), stated that there was no liability to pay service tax of trading activity, during the relevant period. [Para 9]

In this context, it may also be relevant to note, how exempted services was defined in rule 2(e) of the 2004 rules till 31-3-2011 and thereafter.

Both before and after amendment, 'exempted services' meant those taxable services, which were exempt from whole of service tax and, included those services on which service tax was not leviable, under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.2]

Therefore, given the rule position, what would govern the matter would be the determination of the issue as to whether or not, a particular service is amenable to service tax under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.3]

Since, the trading activity was not amenable service tax at the relevant period, surely, the apportionment as provided in rule 6(3)(c) would get triggered. [Para 10.4]

Having regard to the rule position and given the admitted fact that no separate accounts were maintained by the appellant, with regard to the taxable and non-taxable services, clause (c) of sub-rule 3 of rule 6 of 2004 rules would apply. [Para 11]

For the foregoing reasons, there was interference is called for with the order of the Tribunal. Accordingly, the questions of law framed are answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. [Para 12]

; therefore, allegation of suppression was invalid.

Revenue argued that activity of trading could be considered as services and since during material time, it was not a taxable service, it should be construed as 'exempted service'. Since assessee has not maintained any separate account in respect of the dutiable/taxable goods/services and exempted goods/services, payment at 10 per cent/ 5 per cent of the value of the exempted services was to be made under rule 6(3). Assessee argued that trading was deemed as exempted service only from 1-4-2011; hence, demand for period prior thereto cannot be made on that count.

HELD: The goods which the assessee had traded are imported goods. As per the definition of exempted goods under rule 2(d) of CCR exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-C.E., dated 1-3-2011 is availed.

Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods. By no stretch of imagination imported goods which are traded can be considered as exempted goods. If that be so, the question of invoking the provisions of rule 6(2) and 6(3) for payment of a sum at the rate of 10 per cent/5 per cent on the value of the exempted goods would not arise at all. On this ground alone the impugned notice and the order is not sustainable in law. [Para 5.2]

Secondly, as per rule 6(2) maintenance of separate accounts is envisaged only when a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT credit. In the present case, the assessee has not availed any CENVAT credit at all in respect of input services relating to the traded goods. Therefore, question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise at all. Consequently provision of sub-rule (3) of the said rule 6 mandating payment of an amount equal to 10 per cent/5 per cent of the value of the exempted goods and exempted service would also not apply.

Even assuming but not admitting that the assessee has availed input service credit on both dutiable/exempted goods and taxable/exempted service, rule 6(3A) which came into force w.e.f. 1-4-2008 provides for reversal of credit on the input service attributable to exempted goods/services on a proportionate basis based on the turnover. In the present case, the assessee has precisely done that ab initio and has not taken any credit in respect of input services attributable to the traded goods. Calculation done by the assessee has not been disputed by the revenue and the revenue has not shown that the credit taken by the assessee in respect of input services in relation to manufactured goods was in excess of what was eligible to be taken. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence led by Revenue proving that the assessee has taken ineligible credit, the question of assessee violating the provisions of Rule 6 of the CCR, 2004 would not arise at all. [Para 5.3]

If the assessee reversed input service tax credit attributable to trading activities according to standard accounting principles, the same would suffice for satisfying the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 6. [Para 5.4]

As regards the wrong availment of credit during the period 2005-08, another show-cause notice has already been issued to the assessee which has been adjudicated and pending before Tribunal. Thus, the department was fully aware of the practices followed by the assessee and has also approved of the same. In view of the above, invocation of the extended period of time to demand service tax is also not sustainable in law. [Para 5.5]

service only from 1-4-2011

Provisions of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, which came into force with effect from 16-08-2002 govern the entitlement to availment and utilization of cenvat credit up to 9-09-2004, on which date the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force. The 2004 Rules govern the field since 10-09-2004. [Para 5] Under the Credit Rules, 2002 input service is defined in rule 2(c) as any taxable service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service. Rule 3(1) provided that an output service provider shall be allowed to take credit (service tax credit) of the service tax paid on input service, in the enumerated manner. Sub-clause (a) of this Rule provides that where an input service falls in the same category of taxable service as the output service, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 16-08-2002; sub-clause (b) stipulates that in any other case, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 14-05-2003. Sub rule (2) of Rule 3 provides that for the purpose of these rules, two services shall be deemed to be falling in the same category of taxable service, if the input service or output service fall in the same sub-clause of clause (105) of Section 65 of the Act.

Sub-rule (4) of rule 3 states that where a service provider avails credit on any input service and renders output services which are chargeable to service tax as well as exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be, he shall maintain separate accounts for receipt and consumption of input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of taxable output services and input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be. Sub-rule (5) of rule 3 enacts that where a service provider opts not to maintain separate accounts, as stipulated in sub-rule (4), he shall be allowed to utilize service tax credit for payment of service tax on any output service only to an extent of an amount not exceeding 35 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on such output services. [Para 6]

On a true and fair construction of the relevant provisions of the Credit Rules, 2002, it is apparent that credit could be taken on an input service falling in the same category of taxable service as the output service in respect of which the service tax liability arises and discharged from the available credit. It is axiomatic that trading in goods is neither a taxable service and could not, in the absence of a legislative/statutory fiction provided, capable of being construed as an exempted service. [Para 7]

Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, 2004 sets out the obligations of a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) provides that no cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or exempted services except in circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). Sub-rule (2) enjoins maintenance of separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input or input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service; and the quantity of input spent for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and authorizes taking of cenvat credit only on that quantity of input or input services which are intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing taxable output services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 carves out specified exclusions to the requirements set out in sub-rule (2). Sub-clause (c) of rule 6(3) stipulates that the provider of an output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

The 2004 Credit Rules were amended with effect from 01-04-2011, by Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT). To the extent relevant for this lis, by an Explanation added to Rule 2 of the 2004 Rules, it was clarified by this amendment that 'exempted services' include 'trading'. [Para 9]

From the provisions of both, the Credit Rules, 2002 and the Credit Rules, 2004 it is clear that trading is neither a service nor an exempted service. Therefore no credit of the service tax paid on taxable input services used for trading could be taken and utilized for remittance of service tax on taxable services provided by the assessee, even for discharging a percentage (35 per cent or 20 per cent, as a case may be) of the service tax liability on the taxable service provided.

envat credit, it would be not liable to pay interest on such credit reversed before utilisation - Only that when assessee had utilized credit, i.e. if it had not paid tax which is legally due to Government by utilising such Cenvat credit, Government would sustain loss and liability to pay interest from date amount became due arises - Hence, matter was remanded for computation of interest in terms of said observations [Paras 16  17] [In favour of assessee] FACT: Facts

The assessee is a trader in personal computers, photocopiers, telecom products and mobile phones etc. and had provided taxable services like Maintenance and Repair; Commissioning and Installation; Leased Circuit; Online Information and Data Processing and Business Auxiliary Services.

Assessee -

availed credit on service tax paid on input services utilized for its trading activities;

utilized credit to an extent not exceeding 35 per cent up to 09-09-2004 and to an extent of 20 per cent thereafter, of the Service tax payable on its taxable output services,

in terms of Rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 and Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004,

treating trading as an exempted service.

The show-cause notice dated 11-10-2006 alleged that as trading of goods is not a service, this cannot be considered as an exempted service and provisions of the Act and rules thereunder do not apply to trading activities.

The assessee reversed credit availed on service tax incurred by the assessee on sales commission, brokerage, travel agent service, warehouse charges, freight and courier charges, being input services for its trading activities.

The assessee neither responded to the show-cause notice nor attended personal hearing. Hence, the impugned order was passed ex parte.

Revenue's Arguments

Services utilized for trading of computers etc. would not amount to services utilized/consumed in the rendition of output services, since output services were provided after culmination of trading activities i.e. sale and delivery of computers etc. to customers. Input services in respect of which cenvat credit was taken stood utilized prior to delivery of computers and cannot be said to have been consumed/used in relation to rendition of output services;

Since trading is neither a service nor amounts to an exempted service, cenvat credit earned on an input services of trading-cannot be considered as credit earned on exempted service;

Consequently, cenvat credit taken in respect of input services of trading is liable to be reversed in toto and the inadmissible cenvat credit utilized for payment of service tax on taxable output services liable to be recovered, along with interest and penalty;

Since the assessee deliberately availed to disclose availment of cenvat credit on services which were not an input services for its output services, assessee contravened Rules 3 and 4 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 and the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, with an intent to evade payment of Service tax and therefore the extended period is invocable and interest and penalty also leviable.

Assessee's Arguments

The assessee submitted that -

all taxable services were provided by the assessee only in relation to computers, photocopiers etc. sold to various customers;

commissioning, installation, maintenance and repair services etc. were also services provided in relation to these traded goods;

Rule 2(b) of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 defines 'Input Services' as any service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service;

transportation of goods and the other services utilized for despatching goods to customers premises, is integral to the post-trading rendition of taxable services such as installation, commissioning, repair, maintenance etc.; and

thus, credit taken is unexceptionable.

The assessee alternatively claimed that since credit was utilized only to the extent of 35 per cent or 20 per cent of the payable service tax, as the case may be, interest should be calculated only on amount of credit actually utilized; that there is a distinction between taking of credit and utilization of credit and it is utilization alone that results in lesser remittance of tax in cash to Government and not taking of credit in assessee's books. Therefore, interest should be calculated only on the amount actually utilized, if wrongly utilized, but not on the gross credit wrongly availed.

No penalty should be imposed since availment of credit on the assumption that trading is an exempted activity was on account of interpretation and penalty is leviable only for wilful and deliberate conduct and not where availment of credit is on the basis of a mistaken but plausible interpretation of relevant provisions.

Issue Involved

Whether credit was rightly claimed and reversed ?

HELD: I. Trading an exempted service only from 1-4-2011

Provisions of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, which came into force with effect from 16-08-2002 govern the entitlement to availment and utilization of cenvat credit up to 9-09-2004, on which date the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force. The 2004 Rules govern the field since 10-09-2004. [Para 5]

when the output service provider is providing services which are chargeable to service tax and as well as exempted services. Similar is the situation in rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. Both these rules clearly speak of exempted services. Rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules also covers non-taxable services. Since trading activity was not at all a service, it is not correct to apply these provisions. [Para 7]

Eligibility for availing input service tax credit In cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994. Therefore, there arises a situation where an assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable goods. There is no provision to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture. In such a situation the only correct legal position appears to be that the appellant choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what will be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to service tax. The only obvious solution which would be legally correct appeared to be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles was deducted and the balance only will be availed for the purpose of payment of service tax of output service. This proposition was not against the law in view of the fact the there were several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal, wherein a view had been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit. [Para 8]

Uday Joshi for the Appellant. J.S. Negi for the Respondent.

FACT: The revenue issued on the assessee a show cause notice alleging that it was utilizing the input service for providing output taxable service of clearing and forwarding agent service as well as for trading and proposed to raise demand upon it.

The Adjudicating Authority dropped the demand proposed in the show cause notice. He held that to be an exempted service, it must be a taxable service under the Finance Act, 1994. He further held that the trading activity was a non-taxable service. Therefore, it could not be an exempted service.

The Revisional Authority opined that as per rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 'exempted services' means taxable services which are exempt from the whole of the service tax leviable thereon, and includes services on which no service tax is leviable under section 66 of the Finance Act. Therefore, service on which no service tax was leviable under section 66 could be termed as 'exempted service'.

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: To be an exempted service, the activity should be a service. Without any statute categorizing the trading as a service, it cannot be held that it is an 'exempted service'. Therefore, the order-in-revision was not sustainable. [Para 2b]

HEADNOTE: Rule 6, read with rules 2(d), 2(e), 2(l) and rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, and Rule 3, of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 - CENVAT Credit -  Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Period from July, 2003 to March, 2006 - Assessee was engaged in trading of computers, photocopiers, telecom products and mobile phones etc. and was also providing services of Maintenance and Repair; Commissioning and Installation; Business Auxiliary Services, etc. - Assessee took credit of input services used in trading and complied with procedure specified in rule 6 arguing that 'trading' is an exempt service - Department argued that trading became exempt service only from 1-4-2011 and, therefore, during relevant period, services used for trading were ineligible for credit in toto - HELD : Trading is neither a service nor an exempted service; therefore, no credit of the service tax paid on taxable input services used for trading could be taken and utilized even if procedure contemplated in Rule 6 ibid is followed - Explanation added in rule 2(e), though stated to be clarificatory, can have only a prospective effect since Finance Act does not authorize rules to be made with retrospective effect - Therefore, trading would be comprehended as exempted service only with effect from 1-4-2011 - Hence, entire credit of services used for trading was reversible [Paras 5 to 11] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat Credit : Trading would be comprehended as exempted service only with effect from 1-4-2011 when explanation was inserted below rule 2(e); hence, in case of services used for trading, entire credit is reversible and extended period invocable to sustain this demand  Cenvat Credit : Even for period prior to 1-3-2011, interest is not leviable if wrongly taken cenvat credit is reversed before utilization

Section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Invocation of Extended Period of Limitation - Assessee's contention that 'treating trading as exempt service was a bona fide interpretational error' cannot be accepted - Till fiction was introduced from 1-4-2011 that trading is an exempted service, 'trading', being sale of goods covered by sales tax law, could not have been considered as a service (taxable or exempted) - There is no scope for any interpretational misconception on this aspect - Extended period is, therefore, invocable [Para 13] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: The appellant was engaged in providing maintenance and repair services and commissioning and installation service of RO systems. It was observed that the appellants were availing the credit on advertising, security, courier, telephone and banking services which were not entirely used in providing ‘maintenance and repair’ services, but also used in trading activity and, therefore, credit of input services which were entirely used in trading activity was not available to the appellants for payment of service tax. The amounts of service tax payable for two half-yearly period were Rs. 34,143 and Rs. 27,315. Total Cenvat credit available to the appellants was Rs. 6,828, i.e., 20 per cent of Rs. 34,143 as per rule 6(3) and Rs. 8,877, i.e., 35 per cent of Rs. 25,363 as per rule 3(5). The balance amount was to be paid by the appellants in cash only.

The appellants had adjusted the service tax amount fully from Cenvat credit and wrongly availed Cenvat credit of Rs. 43,801.

The lower authorities claimed that appellant should have maintained separate accounts in respect of input services used for trading activity which were liable to service tax and the Cenvat credit availed by the appellant was demanded.

HELD: Trading activity - Whether a service

As regards the issue as to whether trading activity can be called a service, it is quite clear that since trading activity is nothing but purchase and sales and is covered under Sales Tax Law, it may not be appropriate to call it a service. Trading activity cannot be called a service and, therefore, it cannot be considered as an exempted service also. [Para 5]

Applicability of Cenvat Credit Rules (and Service Tax Credit Rules) on trading activity

Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 provides that where output service provider does not maintain separate account, he is to follow the procedure or avail the options available under that rule. Rule 6 is applicable only when the output service provider is providing services which are chargeable to service tax and as well as exempted services. Similar is the situation in rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. Both these rules clearly speak of exempted services. Rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules also covers non-taxable services. Since trading activity was not at all a service, it is not correct to apply these provisions. [Para 7]

FACT: Assessee was manufacturing TV, washing machines, AC, etc. and was also importing said goods for resale.

Assessee took credit of input services pro rata based on turnover ratio attributable to manufacturing business.

Department argued that since 'imported goods' were 'exempted goods', assessee was liable to pay 10 per cent 5 per cent 6 per cent of value of said exempted goods. Department issued notice dated 7-10-2011 invoking extended period to seek demand.

Assessee argued that —

since he was not taking credit relating to 'trading business', rule 6(2) or rule 6(3) were inapplicable ;

since credit as per formula under Rule 6(3A) was merely Rs. 16 lakh, which was not taken; demand of Rs. 297 crore was invalid ;

its procedure of taking credit only on dutiable goods based on turnover ratio was known to department when audit was conducted in 2008 and furthermore, for earlier period, proceedings on same ground had been initiated and were pending before Tribunal; therefore, allegation of suppression was invalid.

Revenue argued that activity of trading could be considered as services and since during material time, it was not a taxable service, it should be construed as 'exempted service'. Since assessee has not maintained any separate account in respect of the dutiable/taxable goods/services and exempted goods/services, payment at 10 per cent/ 5 per cent of the value of the exempted services was to be made under rule 6(3).

both, the Credit Rules, 2002 and the Credit Rules, 2004 it is clear that trading is neither a service nor an exempted service. Therefore no credit of the service tax paid on taxable input services used for trading could be taken and utilized for remittance of service tax on taxable services provided by the assessee, even for discharging a percentage (35 per cent or 20 per cent, as a case may be) of the service tax liability on the taxable service provided. The Explanation added in 2011 though stated to be clarificatory in character can have only a prospective effect since the Finance Act does not authorize rules to be made with retrospective effect. Therefore, trading would be comprehended within the scope of an exempted service only with effect from 01.04.2011, the date of coming into force of the Explanation added to rule 2 of the 2004 Credit Rules. [Para 10]

The assessee not only availed cenvat credit of input services used/ consumed for its trading, by debiting in its cenvat credit account to that extent but had also utilized the credit for discharging its service tax liability for having provided taxable services, to the extent of 35 per cent up to 10-09-2004 and 20 per cent thereafter of the service tax payable on such taxable services, clearly contrary to the provisions of the 2002 Credit Rules and the 2004 Credit Rules, as the case may be. [Para 11]

II. Invocation of extended period valid :

Show-cause notices in both cases were issued invoking the extended period of limitation on the ground that the assessee had deliberately failed to disclose availment of cenvat credit utilized for trading which clearly does not amount to input service used for providing taxable or exempted services; and since trading would not in any event be considered an exempted service. The assessee's contention that 'this is a bona fide interpretational error on the part of the assessee and therefore invocation of the extended period is not justifiable' does not merit acceptance. Till the fiction was introduced that trading is an exempted service, by the Explanation introduced with effect from 01-04-2011 in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, trading which is a sale of goods could not have been considered as a service, a taxable service or an exempted service. The input services (on which cenvat credit was earned by the assessee) were consumed for its trading activities and could not have been availed or taken for discharging service tax on the services provided by the assessee, after the trading activity. There is no scope for any interpretational misconception on this aspect. Invocation of the extended period is therefore without error. Trading is purchase and sale of goods, covered by sales tax law and cannot be considered a service or an exempted service. [Para 13]

III. Option to pay penalty at 25 per cent of duty/tax granted, as said option was not granted by lower authorities

An Adjudication Authority should explicitly specify the option available to the assessee under section 11AC of the Act (which is similar to the option available under Section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994). In view of Board Circular dated 22-5-2008, all cases where penalty under section 11AC of the Central Excise Act is imposed, provisions contained in the first and second proviso of this Section should be mandatorily mentioned in the adjudication order. [Para 14]

Hence, the assessee was required to be provided an option to remit 25 per cent of the penalties imposed under rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994, within thirty days from the date of the adjudication order, along with interest and the amount of cenvat credit disallowed, after taking credit for the service tax and interest if any already remitted. It requires to be noted that the total amount of disallowed cenvat credit was already remitted by the assessee in respect of both the adjudication orders impugned in these appeals, even prior to issue of the respective show-cause notices. If no such option was indicated in an adjudication order, the Tribunal must provide such option from the date of its order. [Para 15]

IV. Interest not leviable, if credit availed not utilized

Where credit was taken or utilised and the mistake is brought to assessee's notice; an assessee corrects the mistake and immediately reverses the entry, the assessee cannot be said to have been taken benefit of the wrong entry in the account books; and if the assessee had not taken the benefit of Cenvat credit it would be not liable to pay interest i.e. when credit taken is reversed before utilisation of the credit; once the entry was reversed it is as if that Cenvat credit was not available. Only that when assessee had taken the credit, i.e. if it had not paid the duty which is legally due to Government by utilising such Cenvat credit, the Government would sustain loss; the liability to pay interest from the date the amount became due arises; and Government would be entitled to be compensated for deprivation of the unpaid/under paid duty. [Para 16]

However, for the period prior to 1-4-2016, does this mean that a service provider can take and retain full credit on input services received even after receipt of Completion Certificate. The situation will be governed by rule 3 till such time, i.e., till the time rule 6 was specifically made applicable by virtue of the deeming fiction created. [Para 7] It is trite law and in terms of rule 3, cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used to provide output service is eligible. In fact, the Bombay High Court in the case of Mercedes Benz India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2016] 66 taxmann.com 332/54 GST 367 held, qua 'trading activity' vis-à-vis rule 6 mechanism, that it could not have been the intention of the Government to encourage trading by allowing full credit prior to 1-4-2011 and that the 'value' of exempt supply in nature of trading as provided after 1-4-2011 in law for complying with proportionate credit requirements should be made applicable to the period prior to 1-4-2011 as well. In the instant case, it is evident that the assessee had started taking only proportionate credit after receipt of Completion Certificate which was after due intimation to the revenue and also certified by independent CA. It is the case of the assessee that rule 6 in toto cannot apply prior to 1-4-2016 to the instant case, since sale of immovable property is not exempt service at all. In the light of the provisions of rule 3, the assessee cannot avail full cenvat credit on input services received after obtaining Completion Certificate. However, the assessee cannot be expected to pay an amount equal to 8%/10% of sale price of immovable property after obtaining such Completion Certificate where no service tax is paid as if it is sale of immovable property, since rule 6 per se does not apply to the instant case until 1-4-2016 at all. Even after 1-4-2016, since the assessee had availed only proportionate credit, it is not legally required to pay 8%/10% amount under rule 6(3), since it can be said to have maintained separate accounts as required under rule 6(2). [Para 9]

Having taken only proportionate credit of service tax paid on input services after receipt of Completion Certificate, duly backed by CA certificate and certified work sheets for the proportionate credits availed after Completion Certificate and also demonstrated on sample basis during the course of hearing, the assessee has fulfilled its obligation under rule 3 read with rule 6 and as such it is not liable to pay an amount equal to 8%/10% of the 'sale price of immovable property' after receipt of completion certificate under rule 6. The next question for consideration would arise as to whether the assessee was also required to reverse proportionate credit, out of the valid input service credits availed by it during the period 2010 till obtaining Completion Certificate, i.e., availing during the time when whole of output service of construction of residential complex was taxable. [Para 12]

While the law does not intend to allow any undue benefit to a service provider in terms of cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in providing non-taxable output activity, cenvat credit is a vested right. Once it is legally and validly availed, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific provisions exist for the same. [Para 13]

It has been a consistent judicial view that credit entitlement is on the date of receipt of inputs when the output activity was wholly dutiable. Merely because the finished goods eventually became exempt later on, the credit availed on inputs which were contained in semi-finished/finished goods form was held as not deniable. [Para 14]

In fact, in order to overcome such legal position, transitional provisions were introduced in the Cenvat Credit Rules. Rule 11, as it existed during the material period, provides that where any inputs are contained in semi-finished or finished goods form, as on date when the finished goods become exempt or output services become exempt, such credit will have to be reversed. As clarified vide Clarification No.334/1/2007-TRU, dated 28-2-2007 and also taken note of by the Madras High Court in the case of Tractor And Farm Equipment Ltd. v. CCE [2015] 54 taxmann.com 122/50 GST 68 and eventually upheld by the Apex Court, such embargo applies only to inputs and not to input services at all. Admittedly, in the instant case, the dispute is limited to credits availed on input services during a time when output service was wholly taxable. However, portion thereof became non-taxable on account of receipt of Completion Certificate later on. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Period 1-9-2004 to 29-2-2008 - Assessee was engaged in providing various output services - Service tax was demanded from assessee on ground that it had availed Cenvat credit in respect of services which were used for providing services in J&K State and SEZ which were exempted during relevant time, and while paying service tax it was required to utilize only 20 per cent of credit available for payment of service tax on input service in accordance with provisions of rule 6(3)(c) - Assessee contended that rule 6(3)(c) was not applicable to instant case as it had not taken credit of service tax paid on all common input services - However, no verification had been conducted with respect to claim made by assessee - Whether matter was to be remitted to Commissioner for fresh consideration - Held, yes [Para 5]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in providing various output services. The Commissioner confirmed service tax demand for relevant period on the assessee on the ground that it had availed Cenvat credit in respect of services which were used for providing services in J&K State and SEZ which were exempted during relevant time, and while paying the service tax, it was required to utilize only 20 per cent of the credit available for payment of service tax on the input service in accordance with the provisions of rule 6(3)(c ). On appeal, the assessee contended that rule 6(3)(c) was not applicable to instant case since it had not at all taken the credit in respect of ten common services which were utilized by it. The assessee also contended that once it had not taken credit on the common services, question of maintenance of separate records also did not arise.

HELD: There was considerable force in the argument of the assessee that once service tax paid on input services had not been taken at all, the provisions of rule 6(3)(c ) would not be applicable. However, it was found that even though the assessee submitted a list of ten services and the credit available thereon which was not taken, yet no verification had been conducted to check whether the claim made by the assessee that it had not taken Cenvat credit in respect of the common services and, therefore, it would not be required to maintain separate accounts, was correct. In fact, the Commissioner’s view that even if Cenvat credit on common input services was not taken, the assessee was required to maintain separate accounts, could not be accepted. [Para 4]

The very beginning of the rule 6(2) shows that only where a provider of output service avails Cenvat credit in respect of input services and uses the same and he is engaged in providing exempted as well as taxable services, then only he is required to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and utilization of input services. There was no detailed discussion on applicability of the rule and the requirement of maintenance of separate accounts by the Commissioner in the impugned order. However, in view of this provision, unless the department showed that the assessee had availed credit of input services which had also been used for providing any of the exempted services, the demand could not be sustained. For this purpose, there was a need for verification of the claim made by the assessee that it had not taken credit of service tax paid on all the common input services and their number was only ten. Even though all the other points were arguable, yet if it was found that the claim made by the assessee in respect of those ten services was correct and, in such a case, the whole case made out by the department would not be sustainable, it would be appropriate to send the matter back to the Commissioner so that he could get this verified properly and thereafter consider the matter afresh. In view of the above discussion, the requirement of pre-deposit of service tax demanded, interest thereon, penalties, etc., was to be waived and the stay petition was to be allowed and the matter was to be remanded to the Commissioner for fresh adjudication. [Para 5]

Admittedly, in the instant case, the dispute is limited to credits availed on input services during a time when output service was wholly taxable. However, portion thereof became non-taxable on account of receipt of Completion Certificate later on. [Para 15] This being the case, a harmonious reading of rule 3 read with rules 6 and 11 will suggest that eligibility/entitlement to credit has to be examined only at the time of receipt of input service and once it is found to be availed at a time when output service is wholly taxable and the said credit is availed legitimately, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific machinery provisions are made in this regard. As per TRU Clarification dated 28-2-2007, even if one assumed sale of immovable property after completion certificate to be 'exempt service', there is no legal requirement to reverse any credit availed on 'input services' in the past (prior to obtaining Completion Certificate) at all. [Para 16]

In the instant case, before obtaining the Completion Certificate, the service of the assessee was very much taxable during which period the assessee received input service.

From a bare reading of rule 4(7), it is clear that the assessee is not required to wait till output service is sold to the service recipient. The assessee can take the credit immediately after the day on which bill/challan of input service is received. In the instant case, there is no dispute that the assessee has availed the credit after receipt of bill, challan in respect of input service. Therefore, the assessee was legally entitled to take the credit on the date after the receipt of service bills/challans. Therefore, the availment of cenvat credit by the assessee is absolutely legal and correct in accordance with rule 4(7). At the time of taking credit, there is no existence of any exempted service. Therefore, there is no application of rule 6. The part of the service was exempted only after obtaining completion certificate. Thereafter the assessee was not required to avail the cenvat credit on the input service, if any, received after obtaining the Completion Certificate. In the instant case, the assessee has either not availed the cenvat credit in respect of the services received after obtaining the Completion Certificate in respect of exempted service or availed proportionate credit attributed to the taxable output service. For this reason also rule 6 has no application for the period after obtaining the Completion Certificate.

In case of service becomes exempted at a later stage, unlike the provision for manufactured goods provided under rule 11(1)(2) and (3), there is no such provision in respect of the service. The only provision for the service is provided under sub-rule (4) of rule 11. From a reading of sub-rule(4) of rule 11, it can be seen that even if an output service provider avail the credit and output service becomes exempted; in such case the credit only in respect of inputs lying in stock or is contained in taxable service is required to be paid, whereas there is no provision for payment of cenvat credit equivalent to the input services used in respect of exempted service. Therefore, the cenvat credit availed in respect of input service is not required to be paid back under any circumstances. [Para 18]

Therefore, the assessee was not legally required to reverse any credit which was availed by it during the period 2010 till obtaining Completion Certificate, i.e., during the period when output service was wholly taxable in its hands, merely because later on some portion of the property was converted into immovable property on account of receipt of Completion Certificate and on which no service tax would be paid in future. [Para 19]

It is the case of the revenue that by demanding 8%/10% amount of sale of immovable property after obtaining Completion Certificate, the credits availed in the past are ipso facto regularized. It should, however, be appreciated that payment of 8%/10% is only an option or rather a mechanism to seek credit reversal on lump sum basis, where the assessee cannot maintain separate accounts/reverse proportionate credit on turnover basis or in cases where the assessee himself so chooses to follow such option. In other words, it is a substitute to regularise credit instead of accepting proportionate credit availed during the time when output service was exempt. Since the credits availed when output service was wholly taxable cannot be called into question, it cannot be said that such 8%/10% amount of sale of immovable property is to regularise not only credits availed after completion certificate but also availed during 2010 till the time completion certificate was obtained. In that sense, rule 6, if invoked, can deal with only prospective credits availed after output activity becoming exempt and not credits availed before the output activity become exempt. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Rule 6, read with rules 2(d), 2(e), 14 and 15, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Assessee, a CA firm, neither maintained separate accounts for exempt services, nor opted for pro rata reversal under rule 6(3A) - Department demanded 8 per cent/6 per cent of value of exempt services viz. Rs. 26,487 invoking extended period - Assessee made pro rata reversal of Rs. 927 even before issuance of notice and claimed that demand be dropped - HELD : Rule 6(3A) requires that option should be exercised in writing and credit attributable to exempted services must be paid provisionally for every month, which was not done by assessee - It would be too harsh to enforce payment of Rs. 26,487 for non-payment of mere Rs. 927 - It could not be said that there was mens rea to evade payment of Rs. 927 - Hence, demand, alongwith penalties under rule 15(3), were set aside [Para 6] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Credit of insurance/repair of motorcar is available to assessee-firm even if car is in name of partner, provided car is shown as assets in books of firm and depreciation and other expenditure thereon is incurred/borne by firm  Cenvat Credit : Where assessee did not opt for reversal of pro rata credit under rule 6(3A) but made such reversal of mere Rs. 927 before issuance of notice, he cannot be asked to pay Rs. 26,487 towards 8 per cent/6 per cent of value of exempt services, as same would be too harsh

Rule 2(l), read with rules 3 and 9, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - General - Assessee took input service credit of insurance and maintenance services of motor car - Department denied credit on ground that motor car was not in name of 'firm' but one of partners - HELD : It was found that : (a) motor car was considered as an asset in books of account of firm; (b) depreciation thereon was claimed in firm's books proving that it was used for business of partnership firm; (c) insurance/repairs and maintenance bills, which were issued in name of partner, were also taken into books of account, treating it as expenditure to firm - Hence, credit in question was eligible as expenditure was incurred by firm [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944, read with section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 and section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Scope of show-cause notice - Allegation in show cause notice that 'services on which credit is availed appears to be not input services and therefore credit is inadmissible' is neither definitive nor substantiated in any manner - In any case, in absence of allegation in notice that 'vehicles are not used for providing output services', credit cannot be denied on that count [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: Facts

Assessee, a firm of Chartered Accountants, was providing both taxable as well as exempted services.

Assessee did not maintain separate accounts for services used in providing taxable and exempted services as required under rule 6(2) and also did not opt for pro rata reversal of the Cenvat Credit under rule 6(3A). Hence, department raised demand of 8 per cent/6 per cent of value of exempted services.

It was also noticed that they had availed and utilised Cenvat credit on input services of insurance and maintenance of motor vehicles which were not in the name of the firm.

Assessee's Arguments

They had paid proportionate of Cenvat credit as required under rule 6(3)(ii) before the issue of show cause notice. Further, the provisions of rule 6(3A) are technical in nature and there is no time limit prescribed for giving option to avail rule 6(3A).

Rule 6(3A) was amended from 1-4-2008 and he was ignorant about these provisions and continued to follow the old provision which restricted utilisation of Cenvat credit to the extent of 20 per cent.

Input services of insurance and car are used for business and expenses are reflected in the profit & loss account of the firm.

the vendors as per B’s orders. ‘B’ was the recipient of the service. FW had Research & Development facilities and assisted ‘B’ to decide the designs of the garments. The services rendered to ‘B’ and ‘DSI’ were correctly treated by the Commissioner as not exempt as exports during the material period. Only on 1-3-2007, such services when delivered and used outside India by a recipient located outside India, were extended the exemption. [Para 4] The assessees, had rendered services to the companies in terms of their contracts with them. They assisted in procurring of purchase orders by the vendors. They monitored progress and timely execution of the export orders placed by the companies. There was no contract between the assessees and their respective vendors. The assessees admittedly rendered the services described in the show-cause notices as evaluation of prospective customers for the companies, processing of purchase orders, customer management, processing of transactions, information and tracking of delivery schedules, operational assistance for marketing, formulation of customer service and pricing policies, managing distribution and logistics. The services rendered to the vendors and the foreign companies by the assessees, conformed to the statutory definition of ‘Support service of business or commerce’ (SSBC). The services rendered to the foreign companies and vendors were, therefore, classifiable under ‘SSBC’ and not under ‘BAS’. Levy on SSBC was introduced with effect from 1-5-2006. Therefore, the demands of service tax on those services, categorizing them as BAS for the period prior to 1-5-2006, from the assessees were not sustainable. [Para 4.1]

As regards BAS received by the assessees from foreign agents, the CBEC had clarified the jurisdiction where the Act operated in the territory of India in its Circular F.No. 36/4/2001, dated 8-10-2001. [Para 4.2]

As clarified by the Bombay High Court, in the case of Indian National Shipowners Association v. Union of India [2009] 18 STT 212, it was only after enactment of section 66A on 18-4-2006 that taxable services received from abroad by a person belonging to India are taxed in the hands of the Indian residents. The assessees, in the instant case, had received BAS from commission agents based abroad mostly prior to 18-4-2006. There is no provision in the Act to tax the assessees for these services. Therefore, demands on this account for the period prior to 18-4-2006 had to fail. [Para 4.3]

As the demands failed, no penalty could be imposed. In the circumstances, demand of tax, interest and penalties imposed in the impugned orders was liable to be set aside except for an amount paid by the assessee-FA for the period from April, 2006 to September, 2006, under reverse charge method as Indian recipient of services of foreign commission agents. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1972-73 - Whether commission received by assessee on account of dharmada, gaushala and pathshala could not be treated as part of its trading receipts - Held, yes  Section 37(2A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Entertainment expenditure -  Assessment year 1972-73 - ITO allowed assessee's claim in respect of messing expenses for its constituents, to extent of half-Tribunal allowed assessee's claim in full on ground that such expenses were necessitated by nature of trade carried on by assessee - Whether in view of amended provisions of section 37(2A) during relevant assessment year, no amount was admissible under head 'Entertainment expenses' - Held, yes - Whether, in said view, normally entire amount claimed by assessee would be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether, however, since department had not gone in appeal either to Commissioner or to Tribunal, half which had been allowed by ITO could not be touched - Held, yes - Whether, in result, ultimately ITO's order was to be restored - Held, yes

Section 37(2A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Entertainment expenditure -  Assessment year 1972-73 - ITO allowed assessee's claim in respect of messing expenses for its constituents, to extent of half-Tribunal allowed assessee's claim in full on ground that such expenses were necessitated by nature of trade carried on by assessee - Whether in view of amended provisions of section 37(2A) during relevant assessment year, no amount was admissible under head 'Entertainment expenses' - Held, yes - Whether, in said view, normally entire amount claimed by assessee would be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether, however, since department had not gone in appeal either to Commissioner or to Tribunal, half which had been allowed by ITO could not be touched - Held, yes - Whether, in result, ultimately ITO's order was to be restored - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a commission agent, claimed deduction on account of dharmada, gaushala and pathshala expenses. He also claimed deduction on account of messing expenses for his constituents. The ITO disallowed the first claim in toto but allowed the claim in respect of messing expenses to the extent of half. On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the assessee's claim in respect of dharmada, etc. In regard to the claim for messing expenses for the constituents it held, it did not involve any element of entertainment. These expenses were necessitated by the nature of the trade carried on by the assessee. The constituents, who came from outlying agencies, had to stay on for lunch or dinner and for that purpose the assessee provided them with meals. It accordingly allowed the claim of the assessee in full.

On reference :

HELD: Following the decision in Thakur Das Shyam Sunder v. Addl. CIT [1974] 93 ITR 27 (All.), the Tribunal was justified in holding that the receipts on account of dharmada, gaushala and pathshala could not be treated as part of the trading receipts of the assessee.

As regards the allowability of messing expenses in the case of Brij Raman Dass & Sons v. CIT [1976] 104 ITR 541 (All.), it was held that the phrase 'entertainment expenses' occurring in section 37(2A) includes all expenses incurred in connection with the business of the entertainment of customers and constituents and the entertainment may consist of providing refreshments or it may consist of providing some other form of entertainment. For the assessment year 1972-73, the relevant provisions of section 37(2A) were amended and no amount was admissible under the head 'Entertainment expenses'. In this view normally the entire amount claimed by the assessee would be disallowed but it was found that half of the amount was allowed by the ITO. The department had not gone in appeal either to the Commissioner or to the Tribunal. This part of the allowance could not be touched. The half which had been allowed by the ITO was outside the purview of the appeal in the Tribunal. The result would be that ultimately the ITO's order stood restored.

Note : The decision was partly in favour of assessee and partly in favour of revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 65(104c) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Business support services - Period 1-7-2003 to 18-4-2006 - Assessees were sourcing agents of foreign companies which were importers of readymade garments - Assessees identified Indian vendors for procurement and supply of garments to said companies - They also provided operational assistance to vendors to ensure supply of goods to foreign companies and also to ensure payments by foreign companies to vendors - They also co-ordinated with vendors for production, logistics and shipments of goods ordered by foreign companies - Whether services rendered to vendors and foreign companies by assessees conformed to statutory definition of ‘Support services of business or commerce (SSBC)’ and not ‘Business auxiliary service’ (BAS) and since levy on SSBC was introduced with effect from 1-5-2006, demands of service tax on those services, categorizing them as BAS for period prior to 1-5-2006, from assessees, were not sustainable - Held, yes [Para 4.1]

Section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 - Charge of service tax on services received from outside India - Period 9-7-2004 to 30-9-2006 - Assessees engaged foreign agents for identifying prospective customers and marketing their services - Assessees paid commission to those foreign agents in foreign currency - Revenue demanded service tax from assessees in category of ‘Business auxiliary service’ - High Court in Indian National Shipowners Association v. Union of India [2009] 18 STT 212 (Bom.) held that it was only after enactment of section 66A on 18-4-2006 that taxable services received from abroad by a person belonging to India are taxable in hands of Indian residents - Whether since assessees had received business auxiliary services from commission agents based abroad mostly prior to 18-4-2006 and there is no provision in Act to tax assessees for those services, demands on that account for period prior to 18-4-2006 had to fail - Held, yes [Para 4.3] Circulars & Notifications : CBEC Circular No. F. No. 36/4/2001, dated 8-10-2001

FACT: The assessees, namely, FA and FW, were sourcing agents of two foreign companies, ‘DSI’ and ‘B’ which were importers of readymade garments. The assessees identified vendors (garment manufacturers) in India for procurement and supply of garments to said companies. They also provided operational assistance to vendors to ensure supply of goods to foreign companies as per terms and conditions of purchase orders and ensured payment by foreign companies to them. Besides that the assessees also engaged services of foreign commission agents for identifying customers and rendering marketing services on their behalf. For the above activities, namely, (i) service provided to foreign companies, (ii) operational assistance provided to Indian vendors and (iii) services received from foreign commission agents, the Commissioner confirmed demand of service tax under the category of ‘Business auxiliary service’ and also imposed penalties.

On appeal :

HELD: The assessees rendered services of the same description to the vendors. The assessee-FA rendered services to DSI by identifying the vendors in India for procurement and supply of garments. They co-ordinated with vendors for production, logistics and shipment of goods ordered, to DSI. FA rendered services to vendors by attending to the processing of purchase orders placed by DSI, by giving necessary operational assistance in the execution and ensuring the receipt of sale proceeds. These services were rendered without a contract with the vendors and were incidental to services rendered to DSI. Similarly the assessee-FW had rendered services to the foreign company-B by monitoring production and export of garments by the vendors as per B’s orders. ‘B’ was the recipient of the service. FW had Research & Development facilities and assisted ‘B’ to decide the designs of the garments. The services rendered to ‘B’ and ‘DSI’ were correctly treated by the Commissioner as not exempt as exports during the material period. Only on 1-3-2007, such services when delivered and used outside India by a recipient located outside India, were extended the exemption. [Para 4]

HEADNOTE: Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Business auxiliary service - Assessee rendered commission agent’s service for period prior to 1-7-2003 - Service tax was demanded - However, commission agent’s service was covered in ‘Business auxiliary service’ only on 1-7-2003 - Whether assessee had made out a prima facie case against demand of service tax - Held, yes [Para 2]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Assessee used to receive goods from principal, store them in its godown, clear them to buyers, collect payment for sale and transmit sale proceeds to principal after taking commission - Whether services of appellant were of a consignment agent which was included in definition of ‘clearing and forwarding agent’s service’ - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, appellant had no prima facie case against demand of service tax - Held, yes [Para 3]

FACT: In instant appeal, the dispute arose as to whether the assessee could be said to have rendered services of ‘consignment agent’ or ‘commission agent’ to their customers.

HELD: In case of the first assessee, the assessee identified buyers for their principals, collected purchase orders, completed the sale transactions, collected payments and transmitted thereof to the principal. Thus, it had functioned as commission agent. The service of a commission agent was expressly covered under ‘Business auxiliary service’ which was introduced into the statute book only on 1-7-2003. The period of dispute in the appeal was prior to that date. The assessee had made out a prima facie case against the demand of service tax and, accordingly, waiver of pre-deposit and stay of recovery in respect of the amount of tax and penalties were to be granted. [Para 2]

In case of other two assessees the assessees were, admittedly, physically dealing with excisable goods. It used to receive such goods from its principal, store them in their godown, clear them to buyers, collect payments for the sale and transmit the same to the principal after taking commission. That activity would attract the definition of ‘clearing and forwarding agent’, which includes consignment agent. Apparently, therefore, the assessees seemed to have rendered service of a consignment agent to it customers during the respective periods. Such service was taxable during the period of dispute. Hence, there seemed to be no prima facie case for the assessees against the demand of service tax. Accordingly, it was directed to pre-deposit the tax amounts. [Para 3]

65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 and the same was fully exempt from service tax during the period of dispute in terms of exemption Notification no. 8/2003-S.T., If the assessee is providing a taxable service, although exempt by way of notification, but which had been exported, the assessee would be entitled to take Cenvat input credit in terms of rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Para 8] As regards the question of eligibility for Cenvat credit in respect of input services used in or in relation to providing of BPO service, the position is different. This service, as held above, is covered by the definition of 'Business Support Service' which became taxable with effect from 1-5-2006 and hence, during the period prior to 1-5-2006, the same cannot be treated as taxable under any other entry and as such, has to be treated as a non-taxable service. Rule 5 is applicable when any input or input service has been used in providing output service which is exported. The term 'output service' as defined in rule 2(p) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2005 during the period of dispute, means any taxable service provided by the provider of taxable service to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder or any other person, as the case may be, and the expression 'provider' and 'provided' shall be construed accordingly. In terms of Explanation to rule 2(p), if a person liable for paying service tax does not provide any taxable service or does not manufacture final products, the service tax for which he is liable to pay service tax shall be deemed to be the output service. Thus, in terms of definition of 'output service' in rule 2(p) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the 'output service' has to be a 'taxable service'. A 'taxable service' is the one in respect of which, in terms of the provisions of section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994, the tax at the prescribed rate is required to be paid and these services are those services which are specified in various clauses of section 65(105). A service which is not specified in any of the clauses of section 65(105) of the Finance Act, 1994, could not be treated as a 'taxable service' during the period of dispute. Since BPO service which was provided by the assessee to their offshore client and which involved transaction processing and the processing of mediclaims, etc. was not a taxable service during the period of dispute and it became taxable as "Support Service for business of Commerce" with effect from 1-5-2006 under section 65(105)(zzzq) read with section 65(104c) ibid, during the period of dispute, this service would not be covered by the provisions of rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 and accordingly, the Cenvat credit would not be available in respect of inputs or input services used in or in relation to providing of this service, whether for offshore clients or for domestic clients. Therefore, the assessee were not entitled for Cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in or in relation to providing of the BPO service during the period of dispute, even if the same had been exported. [Para 9]

While the Cenvat credit demand is for the period from 1-4-2005 to 28-2-2006, the show cause notice had been issued on 23-10-2009. Assessee's submission is that while in the service tax return for the six monthly period ending September, 2006 submitted by them on 25-10-2006, they had not disclosed the information pertaining to export of services and availment of Cenvat credit in respect of input services but in a subsequent letter dated 9-3-2007 addressed to the concerned Superintendent, the information regarding export of service and Cenvat credit in respect of the input services for the same had been furnished. The fact of the assessee intimating the department in respect of their return for the six monthly Period ending September, regarding export of services and availment of Cenvat credit in respect of the same under their letter dated 9-3-2007 has been accepted by the department but the Commissioner has observed that the same cannot be accepted as voluntary disclosure, as there is no provision for filing of revised return. When the department accepts that the assessee under their letter dated 9-3-2007 had submitted the required information about export of service and availment of Cenvat credit in respect of the input service during the period of dispute, they cannot be accused of having suppressed this information from the department with intent to evade service tax by wrongly availing the Cenvat credit. The ST-3 returns filed by an assessee are, after all, required to be scrutinized by the concerned range officers/Asstt. Commissioner. Hence, longer limitation period would not be applicable to the department and as such, the entire demand for wrongly availed Cenvat credit would be time-barred. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 read with rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Charge of service tax on services rendered from outside India - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee, a manufacturer of excisable goods, exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it - It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A - Whether as per reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and it had wrongly taken cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods - Held, yes [Paras 2 and 6] [In favour of revenue]Service Tax : Where assessee exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it and availed credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, it was not eligible to avail cenvat of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services for trading of imported goods

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. During the year 2011-12, it had exported final products manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it. It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on import of services received from one 'C' under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A.

The Adjudicating Authority having discovered that the assessee had availed service tax credit on marketing consultancy services for traded goods (exempted goods) rendered by 'C' opined that the assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and the cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods was erroneous and recoverable in terms of rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

Thereupon the assessee reversed the cenvat credit to the extent of service tax attributable to trading of imported goods and also paid interest. It asserted that it was eligible for the cenvat credit in respect of market consultancy services.

The Adjudicating Authority confirmed the demand of service tax and interest and also imposed equal penalty on the assessee under rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 11AC of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order-in-original.

On second appeal:

HELD: The Adjudicating Authority discovered that the assessee has availed service tax credit on marketing consultancy service on traded goods rendered by 'C' and as per the reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, the assessee has wrongly taken the proportionate cenvat credit to the extent of service tax attributable to trading activity. Further the cenvat credit has been reversed on being pointed out by the Adjudicating Authority. In the impugned order, the Commissioner (Appeals) has discussed the whole issue with cogent reasoning and has rightly rejected the appeal of the assessee. Therefore, as far as confirmation of demand and interest is concerned, there is no infirmity in the impugned order.

As far as the levy of penalty is concerned, unless and until there is a finding that there was suppression of fact and irregular availement of credit, the question of levying penalty under rule 15(2) does not arise. Moreover, in the instant case, the assessee reversed the duty along with interest on being pointed out by the Adjudicating Authority and there was no intention to evade payment of duty as is required under rule 15 read with section 11AC. Therefore, the penalty levied upon the assessee was liable to be set aside. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Business auxiliary service - Period 14-9-2004 to 31-3-2007 - Assessee was engaged in providing business auxiliary service as a commission agent - During 1-7-2003 to 8-7-2004 service of commission agent was exempted from service tax vide Notification No. 13/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003 which was subsequently amended by making same liable to service tax with effect from 9-7-2004 - After that amendment, a show-cause notice was issued to assessee demanding service tax for relevant period which was confirmed by adjudicating authority - Assessee contended that said demand included amount which was outstanding as on 9-7-2004 for service provided prior to 9-7-2004 - Whether since taxable service was provided prior to 9-7-2004, even though payment was received on or after 9-7-2004, no service tax can be charged - Held, yes [Para 3]

Rule 6 of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 - Payment of service tax - Period 14-9-2004 to 31-3-2006 - Whether service tax can be charged only on amount received and not on billed amount - Held, yes [Para 3.1] Circulars & Notifications : Notification No. 13/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003

FACT: The assessee was providing business auxiliary service as commission agent. During the period from 1-7-2003 to 8-7-2004, the service of commission agent was exempted from service tax under Notification No. 13/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003 and this notification was amended only with effect from 9-7-2004 so as to make the assessee liable for payment of service tax. The assessee was issued with a SCN for recovery of service tax for the period from 14-9-2004 to 31-3-2007. Though the assessee pleaded that the value of taxable service, for the period from 14-9-2004 to 31-3-2007, as determined by the Department also included amount which was outstanding as on 9-7-2004 for service provided during period prior to 9-7-2004 and also the amount of receivables for the period of demand which had not been received, the Assistant Commissioner did not accept the assessee’s contention and confirmed the entire demand along with interest and penalties. The Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld that order.

On appeal :

HEADNOTE: Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Period June 2005 to October 2006 - Assessee, a manufacturer, was registered as an ‘input service distributor’ - It received various services and distributed same to various factories - It utilized input service credit availed at various factories for payment of excise duty liability of various factories on final products manufactured by them - Revenue denied said credit on ground that though input service credit was availed by assessee for duty paid as well as exempted final products, but it had not maintained separate records for inputs used in manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods - Whether since assessee had not maintained, separate accounts of input service separately for dutiable as well as non-dutiable exempted goods, in view of rule 6 only option left with assessee was either to reverse proportionate input service credit or to reverse 10 per cent of value of exempted final product at time of clearance - Held, yes - Whether assessee was not entitled to avail input service credit in full but it had to reverse input service credit proportionately availed for exempted final product - Held, yes [Paras 15 &16]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. It also imported finished goods on payment of duty. During the course of the business, it availed a number of services which were used in relation to the manufacture of final products as well as in relation to selling and marketing of final products, etc. As the assessee was having its head office situated in Mumbai which was registered as ‘Input service distributor’, the assessee received various services which it distributed to various factories as an input service distributor by issue of invoice in terms of rule 4A(2). The credit so distributed and availed by the assessee at various factories was utilized to discharge the excise duty liability of various factories on various final products manufactured by them. The revenue, however, denied said input service credit taken by the assessee on ground that said credit was availed for duty paid final products as well as exempted final products and, hence, it was not entitled to input service credit as per rule 6(2), as it was not maintaining separate account of input service for dutiable as well as exempted goods. Accordingly, demand was confirmed on assessee along with penalties.

On appeal :

HELD: As per the provisions of rule 6, the assessee has to maintain separate accounts of input/input services for both dutiable as well as non-dutiable exempted goods. In case assessee fails to maintain separate accounts for input/output services, then he shall pay an amount equal to 10 per cent of total price excluding sale tax and other taxes, if any, paid on such goods of the exempted final product charged by the manufacturer for sale of such goods at the time of such clearances from the factory. [Para 13]
