HEADNOTE: Section 65(25), read with section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Taxable services - Clearing and Forwarding Agent's Services - Period from April 2001 to March 2004 - Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with work of clearing and forwarding of goods, service would not be a taxable service under Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services - Said service is appropriately classifiable under Business Auxiliary Services and is exempt for period from 1-7-2003 to 9-7-2004 under Notification No. 13/2003-ST [Paras 2 to 8] [In favour of assessee]Service Tax : Where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with work of clearing and forwarding of goods, service would not be a taxable service under Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services

FACT: Facts

The assessee gets TV sets manufactured by three manufacturers.

Three manufacturers of TV sets place orders on manufacturers of picture tubes.

The picture tubes are directly supplied by the picture tube manufacturers and payments are received from the manufacturers of TV sets directly.

The rates of picture tubes are however settled by the assessee with the supplier/manufacturers of picture tubes.

After receiving payment from the manufacturers of TV sets, manufacturers/suppliers of picture tubes pay agreed amounts as commission, to the assessee.

Department sought levy of service tax on this commission under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services'.

Issue Involved

Whether commission earned by assessee was liable to service tax under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' ?

HELD: Commission on purchase not covered under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' :

The conjunctive 'and' between the words 'clearing' and 'forwarding' indicate and mean that where clearing operations are separate from forwarding operations, levy of tax would not be attracted i.e. there would be no charge of tax if the transaction involved only one of the two components of the conjuncted service namely 'clearing' and 'forwarding'. The expression a clearing and forwarding agent in relation to clearing and forwarding operations, in any manner' contemplates only one person operating both as the clearing and the forwarding agent; and if a person has rendered service as forwarding agent without rendering any service as 'clearing agent' he could not be considered to have rendered both services as a 'clearing and forwarding agent'. [Para 2]

'Clearing and forwarding operations' would be various activities having a bearing on clearance of goods and would normally involve documentary processes and arrangements for transfer of goods to their destination; and may also involve clearance at subsequent stages during forwarding operations. A clearing and forwarding agent normally undertakes the following activities :-

(a)

Receiving goods from the factories or premises of the principal or his agents;

(b)

Warehousing these goods;

(c)

Receiving despatch orders from the principal;

(d)

Arranging despatch of goods as per the directions of the principal by engaging transport on his own or through the authorised transporters of the principal;

(e)

Maintaining records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; and

(f)

Preparing invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 3]

Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for the vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of the enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with the work of clearing and forwarding of goods, the service would not be a taxable service as defined in section 65(105)(j) read with section 65(25) which defines a clearing and forwarding agent. [Para 4]

In this case, assessee neither receives goods from the factory premises of the principal; warehouses such goods; receives despatch orders from the principal; arranges despatch of goods as per directions of the principal by engaging a transport on its own or through authorised transporters of the principal; nor maintains records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; nor even prepares invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 5]

FACT: • During the course of the audit of the records, it was found that the assessee had availed credit of service tax paid on manpower supply service and security service during the period 2005-06 and 2006-07 up to January 2007.

• It was found that even though the invoices issued by the service providers charged service tax but no service tax was paid to the Government.

• Subsequent investigations revealed that the premises given in the invoice and the registration number were found to be wrong and no service tax had been paid by the service providers.

• The assessee pleaded that it was not aware that the firms were non-existent and they were not paying the service tax.

• The assessee objected to invocation of extended period of limitation and imposition of personal penalty on its employee.

• The assessee had also availed credit of telephone services and not made reversal required under rule 6 though it was engaged in trading activity and manufacture of exempted goods.

Assessee's contentions

• They had received the service during the relevant period.

• Since the registration number and the address were available and service was being received, they had a bona fide belief that service tax paid by them to the service providers was in turn paid to the Government of India.

• They had taken all reasonable steps that an ordinary person could have taken.

Revenue's contentions

• The employee of the assessee had clearly stated that they were receiving the services from the two service providers and the service provider suddenly disappeared in January 2007.

• He also admitted that the company had not verified the existence of the service providers and service providers had come to the factory and collected the cheques.

• Thus, it cannot be said that the assessee were not aware of the fraud played by the two service providers.

• Thus, credit was deniable invoking extended period of limitation.

Issue involved

• Whether credit was available ?

• Whether personal penalty could be imposed upon assessee ?

HELD: Assessee failed to take proper steps before availing credit

• The assessee aware of the disappearance of the service provider after January 2007. They did not put any effort to find out even at that stage as to whether the service providers were in existence and whether they had paid service tax collected from them to the Government.

• It was strange that appellants received, services from a service provider whose existence they knew only because he used to come to collect the cheque and they did not even bother to verify whether the office premises in the invoice was in existence or not.

• Since the service provider was located in Vapi itself (place of assessee) would also go against the assessee since it cannot even be their case that ascertaining the existence or otherwise of the service provider was a difficult task.

• The fact that appellant did not make any efforts to locate the service provider nor did they make any effort to intimate the department nor did they debit the amount of credit taken goes against the appellants and therefore it has to be held that the invocation of extended time-limit for demand in this case is sustainable.

• Further, for the same reasons, the assessee is liable to penalty also. [Para 9]

Credit was reversible as assessee was engaged in trading activity/ exempted goods

• The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of animal feed which is exempted and was also engaged in trading activity.

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacturing tractors, tractor engines and part thereof. The assessee had availed Cenvat Credit, amounting to Rs.72 lakh as it had paid service tax on the basis of reverse charge mechanism qua services rendered by a non-resident service provider. The assessee had paid sales commissions to the said service provider. The services rendered by the service provider were taxable under the category 'Business Auxiliary Service'. Since, it was an input service, service tax was paid by the assessee qua which Cenvat Credit was claimed.

It was a common ground that the goods manufactured by the assessee, for which services of the said sales commission agent were utilized were exempted from payment of excise duty, by virtue of notification no 6/2006/CE dated 1-3-2006.

The revenue, however, took exception to the Cenvat Credit claimed by the assessee and, accordingly, issued a show-cause notice. By virtue of said show-cause notice, the assessee was called upon to show-cause as to why input service credit ought not to be recovered with interest under rule 14 of the Cenvat credit rules, 2004 read with section 11A and 11B. Furthermore, the assessee was also called upon to show cause, as to why penalty under rule 15(3) ought not to be imposed.

The assessee contended that reliance was placed on rule 6(1), which, apparently, prohibited Cenvat Credit being taken qua exempted goods, had to be read along with rule 6(6).

The adjudicating authority was not persuaded by the stand taken by the assessee and, accordingly, proceeded to pass impugned order, whereby the demand raised was confirmed.

Being aggrieved, the assessee preferred an appeal with the Tribunal. The Tribunal reversed the view of the adjudicating authority.

On appeal to the High Court:

HELD: A plain reading of rule 6(1), would show that Cenvat Credit is not allowed, inter alia, qua such input service, which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods, except in circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). Sub-rule (2) is not relevant for the purposes of this case. [Para 12]

In so far as of rule 6(6) is concerned, it clearly states that provisions of sub-rules (1), (2), (3) and (4) shall not be applicable, in case of excisable goods, are removed without payment of duty, inter alia, under circumstance adverted to in clause (v). In other words, in a situation where goods are cleared for export, under bond, in terms of the provisions of the Central Excise Rules,2002. [Para 12.1]

There is no dispute that, in the instant case, as indicated above, the assessee's goods were cleared for export, albeit under bond. [Para 12.2]

Therefore, the question, which arises is, would rule (6)(6), would trump in the instant case, the provisions of rule 6(1). [Para 12.3]

It is no one's case that the goods manufactured by the assessee were not excisable. Though the goods were excisable, the only reason, that Central Excise duty was not paid or was not payable, was, on account of the provisions of the 2006 notification. Therefore, upon executing the bond, the assessee removed what were otherwise excisable goods without payment of duty. [Para 13]

One of the exceptions to rule 6(1) is a circumstance, where excisable goods are exported pursuant to the execution of bond, in terms of Central Excise Rules 2002. [Para 13.1]

HEADNOTE: Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - General - Assessee, with a view to raise capital and secure a quotation for its shares on Stock Exchange, availed services of nominated advisor, reporting accountants, auditors, a broker, a portfolio valuer and services of solicitors as well as registrars and receiving bankers - Assessee had two objects in mind : to raise capital and to establish their position as a quoted company and so acquire and retain benefits for future - Assessee took input credit of tax paid on aforesaid services, which was denied on ground that said services were only linked to an issue of shares, which was itself not liable to tax - HELD : Assessee could have raised capital from private sources without listing itself on stock exchange - Moreover, for general business purposes of assessee, desirability of stock-exchange quotation was reflected in making their shares tradable, providing business credibility, raising their business profile and enabling future acquisition of assets, in addition to facilitating raising of capital - Said services were, therefore, in relation to "accounting, auditing, financing, …share registry", which are specifically listed in inclusive part of rule 2(l) of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and were, accordingly, eligible as input services [Para 32] [In favour of assessee]ST/UK VAT : Services of nominated advisor, reporting accountants, auditors, broker, portfolio valuer, solicitors, registrars and receiving bankers with a view to raise capital and secure a quotation for assessee's shares on Stock Exchange are 'input services'

HEADNOTE: Section 65(27) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Taxable services - Commercial Training or Coaching Services - Period from 1-7-2004 to 31-3-2006 - Technology based training for employment skill development and training courses for medical transcription, insurance agents etc. are vocational course which enable persons receiving such training to get direct employment or get self-employed - Therefore, these training courses, though imparted with aid of computers, cannot be treated as computer training courses - Being vocational courses, same were exempt under Notification No. 24/2004-ST [Para 6] [In favour of assessee]Service Tax : Technology based training for employment skill development and training courses for medical transcription, insurance agents etc. are vocational course and are exempt from service tax

FACT: Facts

The assessee was a commercial coaching and training centre providing the service of Computer Training and Technology Based Training (TBT) for skill development, and training for medical transcription; insurance agents etc. to their clients.

The assessee claimed exemption from service tax treating itself as vocational training institute.

The Department denied said exemption. Further, department found that

Cenvat credit had been taken on the basis of the service provider's invoices which were not in the name of the assessee; and

The assessee was using common inputs and input services in or in relation to providing dutiable taxable services as well as exempt services, but, they were not maintaining separate account of the inputs/input services meant for exempt services and taxable services and were not complying with rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

The demand was confirmed accordingly.

Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed demand with interest but set aside penalty under section 76.

Assessee's Arguments

The assessee was not a computer training institute as they were not exclusively providing coaching or training relating to computer software and hardware.

On undergoing, technology based training for skill development, training for medical transcription, insurance agents etc., a person can get direct employment and get self-employed and hence these training courses are vocational training courses which would be exempt from service tax.

Provisions of rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules are not applicable in the assessee's case, as the assessee had maintained separate account of the inputs/input services meant for exempt services and taxable services.

Further, Cenvat credit taken on the basis of invoices which were not in the name of the assessee has already been deposited alongwith interest.

Revenue's Arguments

TBT Courses and training courses for medical transcription, insurance agent etc. are not vocational training courses listed in National Council for Vocational Training (NCVT) and hence this activity could not be said to be vocational training and has to be treated as computer training, which was not exempt.

The assessee have not maintained separate account and inventory in respect inputs/input services used for exempted services and taxable services.

Issue Involved

Whether demands were prima facie valid ?

HELD: Technology based training for employment skill development, the training courses for medical transcription, insurance agents etc. are vocational course which enable the persons receiving such training to get direct employment or get self-employed. Therefore these training courses though imparted with the aid to computers cannot be treated as computer training courses and, hence, would be eligible for exemption under Notification No. 24/2004-ST. [Para 6]

Though the assessee plead that they were maintaining separate account of inputs/input services, prima facie no evidence in this regard has been produced. Therefore, on this count, the assessee have not established prima facie case in their favour. [Para 7]

Hence, pre-deposit was ordered in part. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Common inputs and input services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Period 1-4-2008 to 15-5-2008 - Assessee, a service provider, had three departments, namely, 'A', 'B' and 'C' - Department 'A' provided taxable service - Department 'B' provided exempted service - Department 'C' received input service - Assessee allocated cenvat credit of service tax paid on input service availed by department 'C' to department 'A' to extent of Rs. 1.11 crores and department 'B' to extent of Rs. 6.66 lakhs on ratio of turnover - Adjudicating Authority disallowed entire cenvat credit allocated to department 'A' on ground that department 'B', which provided exempted service, availed part of cenvat credit - Whether disallowance of credit allocated to department 'A' was contrary to principle of proportionately - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee/Matter remanded]Excise  Customs : Where cenvat credit of service tax paid by department providing input service was allocated to other two departments, one providing taxable service while other exempted service, cenvat credit allocated to department providing taxable service could not be disallowed on plea that department providing exempt service availed cenvat credit

FACT: The assessee, a service provider, had three departments. The department 'A' provided taxable service. The department 'B' provided exempted service. The department 'C' received the input service.

The assessee allocated the cenvat credit of service tax paid on input service availed by the department 'C' to the department 'A' to the extent of Rs. 1.11 crores and the department 'B' to the extent of Rs. 6.66 lakhs on the ratio of the turnover.

The Adjudicating Authority disallowed the entire cenvat credit allocated to the department 'A' on the ground that the department 'B', which provided exempted service, availed part of the cenvat credit.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal the revenue submitted that when the manufacturer or the service provider provides taxable service as well as exempted service, he comes under rule 6(2) to maintain record for verification by revenue. Once the assessee comes under rule 6(2), in that circumstance, application of rule 6(2) and rule 6(3) simultaneously is not possible. The assessee failed to comply with the condition prescribed by rule 6(3) read with rule 6(3A). Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has rightly denied the entire cenvat credit of Rs. 1.11 crores allocated to the department 'A'.

HELD: A bare reading of sub-rule (2) and sub-rule (3) of rule 6 makes clear that sub-rule (3) contains overriding provision which is independent in its nature irrespective of anything stated in sub-rule (1) and sub-rule (2) of rule 6. When sub-rule (2) is read, that throws light that the assessee has chosen a way of maintaining its record which enabled it to substantially allocate the cenvat credit of service tax suffered by the department 'C' to the department 'A' and partly to the department 'B', it has complied to the provisions of sub-rule (2) of rule 6. Once the conduct of the assessee is very clear because of the proportionality of the credit allocated, due to its division of the department and maintenance of records, there cannot be any presumption by revenue that the assessee's case falls under rule 6(3).

It is also apparent from record that the order passed by the Adjudicating Authority is unreasonable for the reason that as against credit of Rs. 6.66 lakh allocated to the department 'B' which provided exempted service, disallowance of entire credit of Rs. 1.11 crores allocated to department 'A' providing taxable service is contrary to the principle of proportionality. Therefore, the entire disallowance does not call for any decision in favour of revenue. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Recovery of service tax not levied or paid or short-levied or short-paid or erroneously refunded Period 2005-06 and 2006-07 - Assessee was awarded a contract by State Government for laying pipelines for a canal project - Assessee by considering said service as falling under category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’ paid service tax on same after availing benefit of Modvat credit - However, revenue took view that services provided by assessee were non-taxable services and assessee was not entitled to credit; and, therefore, invoking extended period of limitation it confirmed demand - Whether since assessee was admittedly paying service tax on services and filing returns, and audits were taking place during relevant period raising objections and subsequently dropping same, any suppression or mis-statement could not be attributed to assessee with mala fide intention so as to invoke longer period of limitation - Held, yes - Whether therefore demand raised beyond period of limitation was barred - Held, yes [Para 8]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Period 2005-06 and 2006-07 - Assessee under a contract with State Government laid pipelines for a canal pipeline project - Assessee by considering said service as falling under category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’ paid service tax on same after availing benefit of Modvat credit - Revenue viewed that above service was not taxable and therefore held that in view of provisions of rule 6(3)(c) assessee was entitled to avail Cenvat credit to extent of 20 per cent only as it was not maintaining separate accounts for inputs and input services used for both exempted and taxable services - However, it was found that Cenvat credit accounts were being maintained separately by assessee on basis of various projects being handled by it - In fact, total amount of credit availed in respect of project of laying down of pipelines had been taken by revenue from Cenvat credit accounts maintained by assessee - Whether, in view of above, question of invocation of provisions of rule 6(3)(c) did not arise - Held, yes [Para 10]

FACT: The assessee was awarded a contract by the State Government under the Sujalam Sufalam Spreading Canal Pipe Line Project for laying pipelines. The assessee by considering the said service as falling under the category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’ paid the service tax on the same after availing the benefit of Modvat credit and filed due service tax returns with the department. Based upon the enquiries conducted and investigations made, the revenue entertained a view that the above laying down of pipelines did not amount to providing services under the category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’, and the service being non-taxable, the assessee was not entitled to avail the Cenvat credit. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee raising demand by invoking the provisions of rule 6(3)(c), which provide for restriction for utilizing of Cenvat credit to the extent of 20 per cent only, in the event of non-maintenance of separate accounts for inputs and input services used for both exempted and taxable services. On adjudication, the Commissioner held that inasmuch the services of laying down pipelines had been held to be a non-taxable service, the same could not be equated with exempted services and, as such, rule 6(3)(c) could not be invoked. He further held that as the assessee had maintained separate Cenvat credit accounts project wise, the allegation of maintenance of a common credit account was incorrect and, as such, rule 6(3)(c) had no applicability. He, accordingly, dropped the demand. Though in the instant appeal the assessee did not dispute service tax liability, yet challenged impugned order on ground of limitation.

HELD: It was noticed that in all the earlier matters, the revenue had strongly contended before the Tribunal that the activity of laying down pipelines under the contract awarded to the assessee by the State Government under the Sujalam Sufalam Water Scheme was liable to service tax under the Commercial or Industrial Construction Services. It was only, in the instant case, the reverse stand was taken by the revenue. All the other assessees similarly situate were not paying any service tax on the identical activities and proceedings were initiated against them by the revenue, on the ground that such services being provided by them were taxable. It was only when the matter reached to the Tribunal, a view was taken that such services were not taxable. [Para 7]

or payment of service tax on taxable output service. In fact, for the persons of category (a ), the taxable service received by them, even if the duty liability on the same is required to be discharged by them, would be their input service, in respect of which they can avail of the Cenvat credit and use the same for payment of duty on their final products being manufactured by them or for paying service tax on taxable output service being provided by them. [Para 8.1] As regards the persons of category (b ) to which the assessee belongs, to even though prior to 19-4-2006, by virtue of the Explanation to rule 2(p), the service received by them, on which they are liable to pay tax under rule 2(1)(d ) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994, is deemed to be their ‘output service’, yet they cannot take service tax credit in respect of other taxable services received or input duty credit in respect of duty paid goods received, as they are not manufacturing any dutiable final products or providing any taxable services. In terms of provisions of rule 3(1), credit of service tax paid on ‘input services’ received and/or of central excise duty paid on inputs/capital goods received can be taken only if the input services received and inputs and capital goods received are used in or in relation to manufacture of final products or providing of taxable output services. For the persons of category (b ), in respect of their deemed output ‘service’, which is the service received by them on which they are liable to pay the tax, other taxable services received by them cannot be deemed to be the input services, as for this another legal fiction will be required, which is not there in the rules. In the instant case, since the assessee was not manufacturing any final product or providing any taxable services, the services of telephone, security services, repair and maintenance services, scientific or technical consultancy services, etc., cannot be treated as the input services for their ‘deemed output service’, i.e., the GTA services received by them. Therefore, in respect of GTA service received by the assessee, there was no question of payment of service tax through the Cenvat credit account and the same had to be paid in cash. [Para 8.1.1]

Thus, prior to 19-4-2006 irrespective of whether a person provided taxable service and/or manufactured dutiable final products or did not provide any taxable service or manufactured any dutiable final product, he was required to pay the service tax on the GTA service received by him in cash, not through the Cenvat credit. [Para 8.2]

As regards the period with effect from 19-4-2006, ‘output service’, as defined in rule 2(p) during this period, means any taxable service provided by the ‘provider of taxable service’ to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder, or to any other person and the terms ‘provided’ and ‘provider’ shall be construed accordingly. During this period the Explanation to rule 2(p ) had been deleted. Thus, during this period only the service actually being provided by an assessee could be treated as his ‘output service’ and the service received by him, on which he was liable to pay service tax as service recipient by the provision of section 68(2) of the Finance Act, 1994, read with rule 2(1)(d ) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994, could not be treated as his ‘output service’. Thus, with effect from 19-4-2006, irrespective of whether the assessee was providing any taxable output service or manufacturing some final products or was not manufacturing any final products or providing any taxable output service, in respect of the GTA service received by it, it was required to pay service tax in cash, not through the credit account. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - General - Assessee was a manufacturer of transmission towers and provider of services in relation to such towers - Assessee availed credit on inputs, capital goods and input services - Department denied credit contending that assessee was not maintaining a separate account in respect of input/input services utilized in manufacture of final product and used in providing output services - HELD : Assessee had availed credit which was available to them - There is no provision in CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, for segregation of CENVAT credit for payment of excise duty and for payment of service tax - There is no requirement for one to one correlation of CENVAT credit availed on input services towards payment of output services - Hence, CENVAT Credit was admissible to assessee [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ♦ The assessee was a manufacturer of transmission towers and was also providing services of erection, commissioning & installation, management, maintenance or repair, testing, inspection of such towers.

♦ For their activity of manufacturing and providing the above services, the assessee availed CENVAT credit on inputs, capital goods and input services.

♦ The department was of the view that since the assessee appellants are not maintaining a separate account in respect of input/input services utilized in the manufacture of final product and used in providing the output services therefore, they were not entitled for input service credit availed by them.

ISSUE INVOLED

♦ Whether separate CENVAT Credit account is required to be maintained for input/input services utilized in the manufacture of final product and used in providing the output services ?

HELD: ♦ Rule 3(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 permits utilization of CENVAT Credit for payment of service tax and excise duty. [Para 5]

♦ There is no provision for segregation of CENVAT credit for payment of excise duty and for payment of service tax. There is no requirement for one to one correlation of CENVAT credit availed on input services towards payment of output services. [Para 6]

♦ Hence, assessee was eligible for CENVAT Credit. [Para 7]

EDITOR'S NOTE

♦ A question of day-to-day importance stands raised in this judgment.

♦ The requirement to maintain separate accounts exists under Rule 6 only in case where a manufacturer is engaged in manufacture of dutiable and exempt goods or a provider of output services is engaged in provision of taxable and exempt services.

♦ Though CENVAT Credit Rules contain separate provision in respect of manufacturer of excisable goods and provider of services, it must be noted that once CENVAT Credit is validly availed, there is no restriction on its utilization except as stated in Rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

has a wide import. The service, in other words, need not be a service which is directly used by the manufacturer in the manufacture of a final product. The definition of "input service" comprehends within its sweep a service which is used by the manufacturer even indirectly, and in or in relation to the manufacture of a final product.

Where the legislature or its delegate uses the expression "in or in relation to", its object and purpose is to widen the scope and purview of the entitlement. When the words "directly or indirectly" and "in or in relation to the manufacture of final products" are used in conjunction that is indicative of the comprehensive sweep and ambit of the statutory provision. [Para 13]

Effect of rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 :

Rule 6(1) stipulates that no Cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or for provision of exempted services, save in the circumstances which are mentioned in rule 6(2).

Rule 6(2) deals with a situation where inter alia a manufacturer manufactures both dutiable final products as well as exempted goods. In such a situation, in order to avail of Cenvat credit, the manufacturer is required to maintain separate accounts for the receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs and input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products and the quantity of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods. Rule 6(2) stipulates that a manufacturer can take Cenvat credit only on that quantity of input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. In other words, Cenvat credit is not admissible on that quantity of input or input service which is not intended for use and is not used in the manufacture of dutiable goods.

Rule 6(5) confers an option to follow one of two courses of action to a manufacturer not opting to maintain separate accounts. Under rule 6(5), which has a non obstante provision overriding sub-rules (1), (2) and (3) credit of the whole of the service tax paid on taxable services of a specified description is allowable unless such a service is used exclusively in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services. In other words, where a service is of the description which is specified in rule 6(5), the manufacturer is entitled to credit of the whole of the service tax unless the service is used exclusively, that is to say solely in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods or any provision of exempted services. [Para 13]

Services used in manufacture of exempted intermediate product are eligible for credit if such intermediate product is used in dutiable final product :

Merely because the assessee manufactures exempted goods, that would be no justification to disallow to it the benefit of availing of Cenvat credit on that quantity of input service which is utilised in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products.

The definition of the expression "input service" is cast in broad terms. The expression "input service" means any service used by the manufacture, whether directly or indirectly or in or in relation to the manufacture of final products.

It is impossible to accept the hypothesis that would assert, that input services that are utilized by the assessee in or in relation to the process of manufacture that takes place at Mumbai Offshore is not a service that is used by the manufacturer in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products. The dutiable final products that are manufactured by the assessee at its Uran plant are fundamentally premised upon the manufacturing process which commences at Mumbai Offshore.

There can be no manner of doubt that the input services which go into the process of production at Mumbai Offshore meet the description of services that are utilized by the manufacturer directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products. The manufacture of the dutiable final products cannot take place without the process in question.

The words "used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products" fulfil the statutory object and purpose of preventing a cascading effect and burden of duty. They must be given their plain and natural meaning.

However, it would be necessary to clarify that Cenvat credit can be availed of only on that quantity of input service which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 14]

Conclusion :

The Tribunal judgment holding that assessee was disentitled to the benefit of Cenvat credit in respect of the input services used in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products on the ground that crude oil which is subject to a further process of manufacture at the Uran plant for the production of dutiable final products is exempted from central excise duty, was set aside.

ONGC admittedly also produces dutiable final products. The production of those dutiable products is possible only on the continuous supply of crude oil. However, it was clarified that as a manufacturer of both dutiable and exempted goods, the assessee would be required to comply with the discipline and rigour of rule 6 and would be entitled to take Cenvat credit only on that quantity of input service which is used in the manufacture of the ultimate dutiable product. [Para 17]

The service tax was to be restricted to the tax on discounted price at which the mobile operator was "selling" the card. [Para 15] [See Editor's Note] In this case, BSNL was paying tax on full MRP instead of actual value :

Suppose, BSNL issues SIM cards costing Rs. 500 plus service tax of Rs. 50/- to the distributor as per terms of an agreement against appropriate security. Distributor sells the card to the customer, collects Rs. 550 from customer by cheque in the name of BSNL and deposits it with BSNL. BSNL pays service tax of Rs. 50 to Govt. Out of the remaining Rs. 500 constituting the value of service rendered by BSNL, Rs. 15 is paid to the distributor. Revenue is asking service tax on this Rs. 15 from the distributor considering it as consideration for business auxiliary service rendered by distributor to BSNL in marketing the service of BSNL. [Para 16]

Thus, BSNL was paying service tax on MRP of the cards and paying commission to distributors out of MRP realized. In such a situation, collecting service tax on MRP of SIM card from BSNL and collecting service tax again on that part of the amount paid by BSNL to the distributor out of MRP realized, puts the parties to these transactions at a doubly disadvantageous position as compared to service tax actually payable on the discounted price of the card. [Para 17]

Double taxation plea not permissible in case of VAT chain :

The argument that tax should not be demanded in situations where somebody else has paid tax on the taxable value of a service is not an argument that can be accepted normally. If this argument is adopted, a taxpayer "X" in a VAT chain can argue that the next person "Y" who uses the service as input will be paying tax and X need not pay tax. In a VAT chain it is difficult to identify who is the ultimate consumer who is not paying further tax.

Taking the case of telecommunication service if the customer is a person who does not pay service tax on any of his activities, a telecom operator cannot adopt this argument. But if the customer is an industrialist he is eligible for credit of service tax to be paid by him. So a telecom operator can adopt the argument in respect of services rendered to such customers. Such logic will make any VAT system for collecting tax unworkable. [Para 21]

Scheme of taxation of services provided by sub-contractors was changed w.e.f. 23-8-2007 :

During the initial phase of levying service tax when the Cenvat credit scheme was not extended to service tax, this concept that a sub-contractor need not pay tax if the main service provider was paying tax on the value inclusive of the value of service provided by the sub-contractor was initially supported by various CBEC Circulars. [Para 21]

But this approach was changed with effect from 23-8-2007 when Circular No. 96/7/2007-S.T., dated 23-8-2007 was issued and it was clarified that sub-contractors would also be liable to service tax subject to credit availability. [Para 22]

Transaction herein was a single transaction and tax on full value was paid prior to payment of commission, which could be easily verified :

The argument of the distributors in the present case is not as unreasonable as illustrated in the example discussed above. [Para 23]

This is not a case where the distributor is doing a service, billing for it, collecting the charges for the service and then BSNL charging for the services to the customers through a separate process. On the contrary this is a case where BSNL sells the cards through the distributor and collects money from customers through the distributor and then pays to the distributor out of consideration received by them from their customers on which consideration service tax is first discharged by BSNL. That is to say, the transactions of both the parties are essentially one and payment on the full value of service occurs earlier than payment of commission to the distributor. Further payment of tax on full value of service rendered by the principal i.e., BSNL, is easily verifiable unlike in the case of services rendered by many other sub-contractors for other type of services. [Para 23]

Some services which are on similar footing as sale of SIM cards or recharge coupons by distributors are services provided by,-

Section 16 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit -  Whether unless there is a nexus between input/input services on which credit is taken and output/output services, CENVAT credit cannot be taken - Held, yes - Whether therefore, appellant manufacturer of excisable goods could not have taken any credit on common input services used in manufacture of excisable goods and traded goods prior to 1-4-2011 when trading was not a taxable service to extent it was attributable to traded goods - Held, yes [Para 5.4]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Period 2012-17 - Appellant was providing Commercial Training and Coaching Services and they had also invested in mutual funds and have earned profit during years 2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17 which they have shown as under head 'other income' - Department considered investment in mutual fund as trading in mutual funds and issued a notice on presumption that appellant is providing exempted services which is trading in mutual funds and has not maintained separate records for common input services availed in providing output services and exempted activity i.e. trading and hence liable to pay 6 per cent/7 per cent of amount of exempted services - However, it is found that 'trading' has not been defined under service Tax but in context of securities,'trading' means an activity where a person is engaged in selling goods and occupy for purpose of making profit but certainly trading is different from redemption of mutual fund units - In instant case appellant cannot transfer mutual fund units to third party and give only by redemption to mutual fund because appellant is not permitted to trade mutual fund unit in absence of a license from SEBI - There is a restriction on right to transfer unit and appellant cannot transfer units to any other person - Further, appellant cannot be termed as service provider because he only makes an investment in mutual fund and earn profit from it which is shown in Books of Account under head 'other income' - Whether therefore, question of invoking Rule 6 did not arise and Department had wrongly invoked provisions of Rule 6(3) demanding reversal of credit on exempted service - Held, yes [Para 5]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where appellant only made investments in mutual fund and earned profit from it which was shown in Books of Account under head 'other income', he could not have been termed as 'service provider', hence, department had wrongly invoked provisions of rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 demanding reversal of credit on exempted services

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Appellant had entered into a business solutions agreement and another business promotion agreement with Amazon as per which appellant had to store various merchandizes in Amazon warehouse and facilitate dispatch of goods - Service tax was collected from appellant by Amazon for warehousing services provided to appellant - As per business promotion agreement entered with Amazon, appellant had to sell different products at prices fixed by Amazon through various promotion sales - Appellant was engaged not only in trading but also providing taxable service - Appellant utilized input services provided by Amazon for engaging in trading as well as providing taxable service - Appellant availed input tax credit for period commencing from April 2014 and took credit upto October 2015 on service tax collected from it by Amazon on business support service and storage and warehousing services - Since appellant had utilized input services for trading (exempted services) as well as taxable output services, it opted for reversal of proportionate credit as provided under rule 6(3A)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 and as credit reversed was in excess of proportionate credit to be reversed, it had filed refund claim being balance of credit wrongly reversed (paid in cash) by it - Original authority rejected refund claim entirely - Commissioner (Appeals) held that appellant had to reverse/pay credit along with interest as per rule 6(3A)(i) at rate of 7 per cent of value of exempted services and, therefore, was eligible for refund of only part of amount - Whether view taken by Commissioner (Appeals) that appellant had to reverse credit as per rule 6(3)(i) was against provisions of law - Held, yes - Whether appellant would be eligible for refund after reversal/paying of proportionate credit on exempted services by applying rule 6(3)(i) - Held, yes [Para 5]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where Amazon was providing BSS and warehousing services to appellant and appellant having utilized input services for trading (exempted services) as well as taxable output services, it opted for reversal of proportionate credit as provided under rule 6(3A)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, appellant would be eligible for refund after reversal/paying of proportionate credit on exempted services by applying rule 6(3)(i)

Section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Invocation of Extended Period of Limitation - Assessee's contention that 'treating trading as exempt service was a bona fide interpretational error' cannot be accepted - Till fiction was introduced from 1-4-2011 that trading is an exempted service, 'trading', being sale of goods covered by sales tax law, could not have been considered as a service (taxable or exempted) - There is no scope for any interpretational misconception on this aspect - Extended period is, therefore, invocable [Para 13] [In favour of revenue]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Position prior to 1-3-2008 - Assessee, a provider of both exempted service and taxable service, did not maintain separate accounts in respect of credit attributable to input and input services used in providing such taxable and exempted output services - Assessee utilised credit of inputs and input services only up to 20 per cent of service tax payable on output services as per rule 6(3)(c) - Department alleged that as credit of capital goods and inputs/input services was not separately shown by assessee, assessee had violated provisions of rule 6(3)(c) - HELD : In view of judgment in assessees own case in Idea Cellular Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 19 STT 423 (New Delhi - CESTAT) in Idea Cellular Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 19 STT 423 (New Delhi - CESTAT), credit of capital goods was not hit by restriction under rule 6(3)(c) - As prima facie case was in favour of assessee, requirement of pre-deposit waived [Paras 4 and 5] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 2(e), read with rule 2(l) and rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 35F of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted service - Stay Order - Assessee, a dealer of motor vehicles, took credit of rent paid on premises used for trading purposes - Assessee was also engaged in repair, maintenance and servicing of motor vehicles - In some cases, premises were exclusively used for repair, maintenance and servicing only - Department sought reversal of credit pertaining to trading activity - Tribunal opined, prima facie, that amendment in rule 2(e) with effect from 1-4-2011 covering trading activity as exempted service was clarificatory and retrospective - Tribunal also did not consider aspect of invocation of extended period of limitation and ordered pre-deposit of entire demand with interest - HELD : Adjudicating authority had raised demand based on pro rata credit pertaining to trading activity in ratio of value of trading services as determined as per rule 6 and value of taxable services - One of various issues that was involved was whether said formula was applicable or some other basis could be applied, which was more just, fair or equitable - Keeping in view said position, requirement of pre-deposit was reduced to half of CENVAT credit reversal sought (without interest) [Paras 7 to 10] [Partly in favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : A dealer of motor vehicle is not entitled to credit of rent paid for building used for trading purposes; but, in case of services used for both trading activity and taxable services, reversal of credit may be sought on pro rata basis in ratio of value of two activities or on some other just, fair and equitable basis

I. Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Period from April 2000 to March 2007 - Department denied credit on ground that assessee did not maintain separate accounts for input services used for taxable and exempted services and input service tax credit had been availed/utilised in excess of 20 per cent of credit taken in contravention of rule 6(3)(c) - HELD : Cap of 20 per cent was applicable on service tax payable and not on service tax credit actually availed - What was restricted was only utilisation of credit and not taking credit per se; credit taken could be carried forward - When cap was removed on 1-4-2008, assessee was eligible to utilise credit also - Further, utilising credit in excess of limit would attract only interest liability; entire service tax itself could not be denied to assessee - Hence, matter was remanded back to adjudicating authority to re-examine matter in light of CBEC circular dated 21-11-2008 [Para 5.1] [In favour of assessee]ST : Utilising Cenvat credit in excess of limit fixed under rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 would attract only interest liability; entire credit itself cannot be denied to assessee  ST : Break bulk fee and freight rebate are not, prima facie, liable to service tax under Custom House Agent's services and Business Auxiliary Services respectively  ST : Commission and incentive received from airlines for booking of cargo space is, prima facie, liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary services  ST : CCX fee received from foreign principal for purpose of delivering documents to customers in India, to collect and remit freight charges due to overseas company is liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary services  ST : Cenvat Credit cannot be denied for procedural violations

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Period 2005-06 and 2006-07 - Assessee under a contract with State Government laid pipelines for a canal pipeline project - Assessee by considering said service as falling under category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’ paid service tax on same after availing benefit of Modvat credit - Revenue viewed that above service was not taxable and therefore held that in view of provisions of rule 6(3)(c) assessee was entitled to avail Cenvat credit to extent of 20 per cent only as it was not maintaining separate accounts for inputs and input services used for both exempted and taxable services - However, it was found that Cenvat credit accounts were being maintained separately by assessee on basis of various projects being handled by it - In fact, total amount of credit availed in respect of project of laying down of pipelines had been taken by revenue from Cenvat credit accounts maintained by assessee - Whether, in view of above, question of invocation of provisions of rule 6(3)(c) did not arise - Held, yes [Para 10]

Section 11A, of the Central Excise Act, 1944, read with section 73, of the Finance Act, 1994 and Section 28, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Invocation of Extended Period of Limitation - Assessee took credit relating to services used in 'trading activity' - Department invoked extended period of limitation citing suppression of facts - HELD : Assessee had not disclosed availment of input service credit on commission in respect of trading activities and said facts came to knowledge of department only on verification of documents such as contract agreements, commission agreements etc. - Hence, invocation of extended period was valid [Para 7] [In favour of revenue]

Section 11A, of the Central Excise Act, 1944, read with section 73, of the Finance Act, 1994 and Section 28, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Invocation of Extended Period of Limitation - Assessee took credit relating to services used in 'trading activity' - Department invoked extended period of limitation citing suppression of facts - HELD : It was found by lower authorities and Tribunal that assessee had not disclosed availment of input service credit on commission in respect of trading activities and said facts came to knowledge of department only on verification of documents such as contract agreements, commission agreements etc. - Hence, invocation of extended period was valid [Para 7] [In favour of revenue]

Input tax credit - Common credit - Applicant is engaged in trading of both taxable and exempted goods - Advance ruling was sought on how much percentage of ITC is to be availed in view of fact that supply involves both taxable and exempted supplies - HELD: As applicant is involved in supply of both taxable and exempted supplies, ITC is to be availed proportionately in terms of procedure provided for in sections 16 and 17 of CGST Act, read with rule 42 of CGST Rules [Section 16, read with section 17, of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Rule 42 of Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017] [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]  Advance ruling - Maintainability of - Whether an advance ruling can be sought on question of GST consequences if goods are purchased from unregistered and composition dealers - HELD: Said question sought for advance ruling is not covered under issues referred to in section 97(2) of CGST Act on which Authority for Advance Ruling can pass an advance ruling [Section 97 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 10] [In favour of revenue]

Section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Power to grant exemption from service tax -  Period prior to 7-12-2008 - In view of clarification by Director (Drawback) that service tax on foreign commission agency had not factored in All Industry Rates of Drawback and, further because, foreign commission agent's services were not input services so as to be eligible for drawback, assessee could not be denied refund in respect of said services under Notification No. 41/2007-ST - Refund could not be denied even if assessee had made exports under drawback shipping bills and clause (e) of proviso to said notification had barred exemption by way of refund in cases where drawback had been claimed - Moreover, since rate of refund thereunder had increased from 2 per cent to 10 per cent of FOB with effect from 7-12-2008, said increased rate was eligible to assessee filing claim of refund on or after 7-12-2008 [Paras 5.4  5.5] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Air travel agent - Period September 2003 to 2004 - Assessee, air travel agent, received commission in two categories, i.e., ‘standard commission’ and ‘supplementary commission’ and paid service tax voluntarily only on ‘standard commission’ and contended that ‘supplementary commission’ was, in fact, a trade discount - Whether since both commissions were charge on airfare, for claiming this exemption, appellant had to show that ‘supplementary commission’ was an amount received in excess of commission envisaged in Notification No. 22/97-ST, dated 26-6-1997 - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had not been able to establish that, it was not entitled to waiver of pre-deposit and stay of recovery - Held, yes [Para 4] Circulars and Notifications : Notification No. 22/97-ST, dated 26-6-1997

II. Rule 6, read with rule 2(1), of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Stay Order - Period from November 2006 to March 2011 - Assessee, a manufacturer, was engaged in manufacture as well as trading of goods and took credit of input services used for both, manufacture and trading - Assessee argued that since duty on traded goods was paid by concerned manufacturer, hence, they were entitled to take credit of input services used in trading - HELD : Assessee is not entitled to credit of input services in respect of non-dutiable goods - Hence, since 90 per cent of turnover related to traded goods, proportionate pre-deposit of Rs. 1 crore was upheld as against total demand of Rs. 1.27 crores [Paras 5 to 8] [In favour of revenue]

III. Rule 2(l), read with rule 3, of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Commission agent's services - Period September 2005 - Assessee availed credit of service tax paid under reverse charge on services received from agent located abroad - Department denied credit on ground that said services were not chargeable to service tax and hence, credit could not be allowed - HELD : During relevant time, revenue was of view that Service Tax was to be paid on said services - Hence, in absence of any dispute that said services were input services, credit taken could not be denied for reason that later it was decided that assessee need not have paid Service Tax - Hence, credit was allowed [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer or producer of final products and provider of taxable service - Whether where assessee was providing taxable services as well as exempted services, inasmuch as it had not maintained separate accounts of input services and capital goods used in above two types of services, it was entitled to utilise only 20 per cent of input service credit; however, no such restriction is put in respect of use of service tax availed on capital goods - Held, yes [Para 3] [Matter remanded]

Input tax credit - Common credit - Applicant is engaged in trading of both taxable and exempted goods - Advance ruling was sought on how much percentage of ITC is to be availed in view of fact that supply involves both taxable and exempted supplies - HELD: As applicant is involved in supply of both taxable and exempted supplies, ITC is to be availed proportionately in terms of procedure provided for in sections 16 and 17 of CGST Act, read with rule 42 of CGST Rules [Section 16, read with section 17, of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Rule 42 of Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017] [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where a taxpayer is engaged in supply of both taxable and exempted supplies, ITC is to be proportionately availed    GST : Advance ruling cannot be sought on question of GST consequences in case goods are purchased from unregistered and composition dealers as it is not covered under issues on which an application for advance ruling is maintainable

Section 65(25), read with section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Taxable services - Clearing and Forwarding Agent's Services - Period from April 2001 to March 2004 - Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with work of clearing and forwarding of goods, service would not be a taxable service under Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services - Said service is appropriately classifiable under Business Auxiliary Services and is exempt for period from 1-7-2003 to 9-7-2004 under Notification No. 13/2003-ST [Paras 2 to 8] [In favour of assessee]Service Tax : Where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with work of clearing and forwarding of goods, service would not be a taxable service under Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services

Section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 read with rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Charge of service tax on services rendered from outside India - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee, a manufacturer of excisable goods, exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it - It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A - Whether as per reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and it had wrongly taken cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods - Held, yes [Paras 2 and 6] [In favour of revenue]Service Tax : Where assessee exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it and availed credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, it was not eligible to avail cenvat of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services for trading of imported goods

Rule 2(p) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Output service - Assessee took Cenvat credit of service tax paid on GTA service and utilized same for payment of service tax on commission paid to its foreign agent for procurement of export orders, under head business auxiliary services - Adjudicating authority held that service tax paid on GTA service could not be taken as credit by assessee as it was not paying any excise duty on its final product and also was not providing any output service - Commissioner (Appeals) held that prior to omission of Explanation to rule 2(P) with effect from 18-4-2006, not only credit can be taken by a person who is liable to pay service tax but also same can be utilized for payment of excise duty/service tax - However, revenue contended that in view of decision of Tribunal in ITC Ltd. v. CCE [2011] 31 STT 463/11 taxmann.com 166 (Bang - CESTAT), even prior to 19-4-2006 assessee was required to pay service tax on GTA service received by him in cash but not through Cenvat credit - Whether matter was to be remanded to Commissioner (Appeals) for fresh decision - Held, yes [Para 5] [Matter remanded]

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Period April, 2006 to January, 2007 - Assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax on commission paid to commission agent for receiving services of latter - Revenue denied credit on ground that benefit was liable to be restricted to procurement of purchase orders by commission agents and was not admissible insofar as collection of sale price of goods was concerned - Whether bifurcating commission agents’ function into pre-clearance and post-clearance of goods as done by lower authorities is clearly not permissible inasmuch as commission agents’ service is one integrated service and, therefore, assessee was entitled to benefit of Cenvat credit on entire amount of commission paid by it to commission agent - Held, yes [Para 3]

Cenvat credit of Service Tax - Reversal of credit on common input services - Appellant availed Cenvat credit on common input services used for providing both taxable service and exempt service and not maintained separate accounts/records for receipt and use of common input services issue as to entitlement of credit stands decided at the level of first Appellate Authority - Further Tribunal upheld entitlement of petitioner for reversal after computing proportionate credit by applying Rule 6(3)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Matter remanded by Tribunal only for limited purpose of quantification of amount eligible for refund - Hence show cause notice purporting to reopen question of entitlement to credit, is bad in law - Revenue authorities directed to issue fresh show cause notice limiting scope of examination to quantification of input service alone [Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 18 and 28]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with section 35F of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Commission agents - Appellants submitted that their activity as commission agents was not covered under service tax statute at relevant point of time and subsequently it had been brought under statute but exempted - Whether since there was prima facie merit in submission of appellants, pre-deposit of amount was required to be waived - Held, yes

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Period 2013-2017 - Assessee was registered and holding service tax registration certificate for provider/recipient of work contract, Design Services, Business Support Services etc., and were availing the credit of the tax paid on "input services" under provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Revenue having noticed that assessee was also engaged in trading of mutual fund units and same being exempted services, raised demand of 6% of value of exempted services - Whether assessee was not engaged in business of trading in securities (Mutual Funds) but investment in Mutual Fund was an investment activity and gain from return of Mutual Fund was taxed as capital gain and not as business income and, therefore, Rule 6(3) was not applicable; impugned demand of 6% of value of exempted services was not sustainable - Held, yes [Para 5] [ In favour of assessee]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where assessee was not engaged in business of trading in securities (Mutual Funds) but investment in Mutual Fund was an investment activity and gain from return of Mutual Fund was taxed as capital gain and not as business income, Rule 6(3) was not applicable

Rule 7 ,  read with rule 6  of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Manner of Distribution of Credit by Input Service Distributor - Period prior to 1-4-2012 - Department raised demand on ground that credit pertaining to one unit was distributed to another unit for purpose of enabling it to use credit - HELD : During relevant period, only conditions in rule 7 for distribution of credit were : (a) credit could not exceed tax paid; and (b) credit exclusively of exempted units could not be distributed - Since both conditions had been fulfilled, credit cannot be denied - Condition as to pro rata distribution of credit under rule 7(d) was introduced only from 1-4-2012 - Demand cannot be raised even by applying rule 6, as assessee had not provided 'taxable as well as exempt' services - Hence, demand was set aside [Paras 4 to 6] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Requirement of registration is procedural; hence, credit cannot be denied to input service distributor even if it is unregistered, provided assessee has maintained all records for verification by revenue

Cenvat credit of Service Tax - Reversal of credit on common input services - Appellant availed Cenvat credit on common input services used for providing both taxable service and exempt service and not maintained separate accounts/records for receipt and use of common input services issue as to entitlement of credit stands decided at the level of first Appellate Authority - Further Tribunal upheld entitlement of petitioner for reversal after computing proportionate credit by applying Rule 6(3)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Matter remanded by Tribunal only for limited purpose of quantification of amount eligible for refund - Hence show cause notice purporting to reopen question of entitlement to credit, is bad in law - Revenue authorities directed to issue fresh show cause notice limiting scope of examination to quantification of input service alone [Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 18 and 28]ST/Cenvat : Matter was remanded by Tribunal only for limited purpose of quantification of amount eligible for refund, hence show cause notice purporting to reopen question of entitlement to credit, is bad in law; revenue authorities will issue fresh show cause notice limiting scope of examination to quantification of input service alone

Section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 - Charge of service tax on services received from outside India - Period 9-7-2004 to 30-9-2006 - Assessees engaged foreign agents for identifying prospective customers and marketing their services - Assessees paid commission to those foreign agents in foreign currency - Revenue demanded service tax from assessees in category of ‘Business auxiliary service’ - High Court in Indian National Shipowners Association v. Union of India [2009] 18 STT 212 (Bom.) held that it was only after enactment of section 66A on 18-4-2006 that taxable services received from abroad by a person belonging to India are taxable in hands of Indian residents - Whether since assessees had received business auxiliary services from commission agents based abroad mostly prior to 18-4-2006 and there is no provision in Act to tax assessees for those services, demands on that account for period prior to 18-4-2006 had to fail - Held, yes [Para 4.3] Circulars & Notifications : CBEC Circular No. F. No. 36/4/2001, dated 8-10-2001

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Periods 2008-09 to 2009-10 - Assessee provided dutiable and exempted services and also availed Cenvat credit on certain common input services - It opted for payment at prescribed percentage on value of exempted services and also paid amounts for earlier periods - Revenue held that assessee could not exercise option retrospectively for earlier period and hence credit taken was improper - Whether there is no bar for making payments as per prescribed percentages for prior period as it may not be feasible to segregate quantum of input service credit pertaining to dutiable and exempted services and, therefore, assessee's actions of paying amounts for past period was justified - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]CENVAT: There is no bar for making as per prescribed percentage payment on value of exempted services for prior period where it may not be feasible to segregate quantum of input services pertaining to dutiable  exempted services

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Input service - Travelling services - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee was providing Management Consultancy and Insurance Auxiliary Services - Assessee took input service credit of Rent-a-cab and Air Travel Agent Service - Department denied credit on ground that both these services are used for employees' benefit - Assessee argued that : (a) Rent-a-cab service is expressly excluded from input service from 1-4-2011, but, for present case relating to period prior to 1-4-2011, credit is allowed; (b) air travel agent's services were availed for travel of employees for business purposes - HELD : Rent-a-cab and Air Travel Agent services, though used by employees, are for performance of assessee's business - Hence, both services are input service - Further, expenses towards both services was booked as expenditure in profit and loss account - Rent-a-cab service was not excluded from definition of input service; hence, prior to 1-4-2011, credit was admissible [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Rent-a-cab service is expressly excluded from input service from 1-4-2011, but, for period prior to 1-4-2011, said service availed for employees for business purposes, is eligible for credit; similarly, air travel agent's services availed for travel of employees for business purposes is also eligible for credit

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, read with section 86 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Cenvat Credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted service - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of both dutiable and exempted products - Commissioner on finding that assessee was not maintaining separate accounts in respect of input duty credit and input service tax credit vis-a-vis dutiable final product and exempted final product, demanded reversal of credit utilized for payment of duty on dutiable products - However, Commissioner prematurely quantified an amount of ‘excess credit’ for reversal by assessee inasmuch as amount of input service tax credit to be denied or allowed under separate show-cause notice covering some input services, was yet to be determined by adjudicating authority - Whether in view of above, there would be waiver of pre-deposit and stay on recovery in respect of amount of credit prematurely demanded by Commissioner as also in respect of interest sought to be charged on such amount - Held, yes [Para 3]

Section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Business auxiliary service - Period 14-9-2004 to 31-3-2007 - Assessee was engaged in providing business auxiliary service as a commission agent - During 1-7-2003 to 8-7-2004 service of commission agent was exempted from service tax vide Notification No. 13/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003 which was subsequently amended by making same liable to service tax with effect from 9-7-2004 - After that amendment, a show-cause notice was issued to assessee demanding service tax for relevant period which was confirmed by adjudicating authority - Assessee contended that said demand included amount which was outstanding as on 9-7-2004 for service provided prior to 9-7-2004 - Whether since taxable service was provided prior to 9-7-2004, even though payment was received on or after 9-7-2004, no service tax can be charged - Held, yes [Para 3]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Assessee-company was hired under a contract for canvassing and advancing sale of principal’s products and procuring orders - Assessee was to receive commission - Authorities held that services provided by assessee were covered under category of clearing and forwarding service and demanded duty for period 1997-2003 - Whether, in view of nature of service provided by assessee, it was to be held as commission agent rather than consignment agent - Held, yes - Whether, since services as commission agent were made liable to tax under category of business auxiliary service with effect from 1-7-2003 and period in instant appeal was prior to said date, assessee was not liable to pay any tax during period in question - Held, yes [Para 3] Circular and Notification - Board Circular No. 59/8/2003, dated 20-6-2003

Cenvat credit - Reversal of - Common inputs/input services used for both taxable and exempted final products services - Position prior to 1-4-2016 - Assessee was rendering services to BCCI for organizing IPL T-20 cricket matches under a franchise agreement - Revenue generated from stadium gate receipt/sale of ticket, prize money received from BCCI-IPL and in-stadium sale i.e. stadium revenue could not be considered towards rendering of any services hence no Cenvat credit was required to be reversed - Moreover, prior to amendment to Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from 1-4-2016, there was no requirement to reverse Cenvat credit on input/input services used in an activity that was not a service [Rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 5, 5.5 and 5.6] [In favour assessee]

Section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 - Charge of service tax on services received from outside India - Period prior to 18-4-2006 - Whether service of foreign based commission agent rendered prior to 18-4-2006 is not taxable under category of ‘Business auxiliary service’ which includes commission agent - Held, yes [Para 2]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Common input and inputs services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Cenvat credit - And amending Notification No. 27/2005-CE (NT) dt. 16.5.2005 - Amendment by way of addition of Explanation III to Rule 6 (3) vide notification is effective from 16.5.2005 - Prior to 16.5.2005 a manufacturer producing both dutiable as well as exempted final product and paying 8% or 10% amount on exempted final product, was entitled to take credit on all inputs whether common to both final products or exclusively used in manufacture of exempted goods only (Para 32)

facts.text:
Assessee was manufacturing TV, washing machines, AC, etc. and was also importing said goods for resale.

Assessee took credit of input services pro rata based on turnover ratio attributable to manufacturing business.

Department argued that since 'imported goods' were 'exempted goods', assessee was liable to pay 10 per cent 5 per cent 6 per cent of value of said exempted goods. Department issued notice dated 7-10-2011 invoking extended period to seek demand.

Assessee argued that —

since he was not taking credit relating to 'trading business', rule 6(2) or rule 6(3) were inapplicable ;
