Statutory Provisions

UK Value Added Tax Act, 1994, sections 25 and 26 : Section 25 provides that a taxable person is entitled to credit for so much of his input tax as is allowable under section 26. Section 26(1) provides that the amount of any input tax to which a taxable person is entitled to credit is so much of the input tax allowable by regulations made for this purpose as is attributable to taxable (and not exempt) supplies. Section 26(3) provides that the Commissioners shall make regulations for securing a fair and reasonable attribution of input tax as between taxable and exempt supplies.

UK Value Added Tax Act, 1994, section 31(1) : A supply is an exempt supply if it is of a description specified in schedule 9. Group 5 of Schedule 9 is headed "Finance". Item 6 specifies as exempt supplies (inter alia): "The issue, transfer or receipt of, or any dealing with, any security or secondary security being (a) shares, stocks, bonds, notes (other than promissory notes), debentures, debenture stock or shares in an oil royalty;…."

UK Value Added Tax Regulations 1995, Regulation 101 :

(1) Subject to regulation 102, the amount of input tax which a taxable person shall be entitled to deduct provisionally shall be that amount which is attributable to taxable supplies in accordance with this regulation.

(2) In respect of each prescribed accounting period

(a)

… goods or services supplied to the taxable person in the period shall be identified,

(b)

there shall be attributed to taxable supplies the whole of the input tax on such of those goods or services as are used or to be used by him exclusively in making taxable supplies,

(c)

no part of the input tax on such of those goods or services as are used or to be used by him exclusively in making exempt supplies, or in carrying on any activity other than the making of taxable supplies, shall be attributed to taxable supplies, and

(d)

there shall be attributed to taxable supplies such proportion of the input tax on such of those goods or services as are used or to be used by him in making both taxable and exempt supplies as bears the same ratio to the total of such input tax as the value of taxable supplies made by him bears to the value of all supplies made by him in the period.

(3) In calculating the proportion under paragraph (2)(d) above, there shall be excluded…(b)…(v) any supply which falls within Group 5 of schedule 9 to the Act …

(4) The ratio calculated for the purpose of paragraph (2)(d) above shall be expressed as a percentage and, if that percentage is not a whole number, it shall be rounded up to the next whole number.

In view of the above reasoning, it could be held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are not applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. HELD (PER TECHNICAL MEMBER) It is seen that rule 6(1) specifically prohibits Cenvat credit being allowed on such quantity of inputs as used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Therefore, there is no authority in law for availing Cenvat credit on the quantity of inputs intended or used for the manufacture of exempted goods except in terms of rule 6(2), which allows the manufacturer to avail the Cenvat credit only in respect of that particular quantity of inputs, which is intended to be used in the manufacture of dutiable goods subject to their maintaining separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of final products. But if separate accounts are not maintained, though Cenvat credit is availed, then sub-rule 3 of rule 6 provides for payment of amount equal to Cenvat credit on dutiable inputs for cases covered under sub-rule (3)(a ) and in respect of all other inputs, sub-rule (3)(b) of rule 6 provides for payment of an amount of 8 per cent or 10 per cent of total price (excluding sales tax and other taxes, if any, paid on such goods), of the exempted final products charged by the manufacturer for the sale of such goods at the time of their clearance from the factory. Thus, reversal of the credit taken or availed under rule 6 is not contemplated by the rules. [Para 15]

If the interpretation put by the majority order is held to be correct, it will render the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) ibid providing for payment of an amount equal to 8 per cent or 10 per cent rather otiose. This militates against an interpretation, which renders it superfluous and is of no significance. [Para 16]

It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacturer of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts had to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. There is no provision for giving retrospective effect to this amendment. It cannot be given, as the amount of reversal of credit has to be worked out in a manner prescribed in the Rules. There was no such prescription prior to the amendment. This decision of the majority will make the amendment superfluous. Such interpretation has to be avoided. [Para 23]

In the light of the aforesaid discussions, it was held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. [Para 26]

The assessee had not maintained any books of account regarding the expenses incurred by him in respect of the agency business done by him. In view of the modified instruction issued by the Board contained in Circular dated 6-6-1984 he claimed deduction from the commission received by him from LIC to the extent of 50 per cent. The Assessing Officer accepted the claim and allowed the deduction of 50 per cent from the commission earned by the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the said order and restricted the said deduction after interpreting the said circular. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to get 50 per cent of the deduction out of the commission received up to Rs. 60,000.

On reference :

Facts

The assessee, M/s. ONGC, operated a large number of oil wells and ten process platforms which were situated in different oilfields at Mumbai Offshore.

The gas oil mix extracted through each oil well of ONGC was transported to one of the process platforms through sub-sea high pressure pipelines.

ONGC had set up a plant at Uran, to make full economic use of the crude oil and associated natural gas extracted from the oil wells.

The process platforms at Mumbai Offshore were integrated with the Uran plant through a network of Oil Trunk Pipelines. These pipelines were designed for transportation of gases and liquids at high pressures.

ONGC was manufacturing both dutiable and exempted goods.

ONGC availed of services at the area of operation, viz., at the well-heads, well platforms, process platforms, pipelines, vessels, at the Uran plant and at the administrative offices at Mumbai.

ONGC availed of Cenvat credit of input services, as distributed by the Input Service Distributors under the provisions of the Cenvat Credit Rules.

The Department denied Cenvat Credit of input services on ground that :

Cenvat credit distributed by the Input Service Distributors (ISD) pertained to input services availed of and used exclusively at the oilfields of Mumbai Offshore, whose final products viz. crude oil and natural gas were exempted from excise duty.

I.S.D. was required to take registration within 30 days from the date of commencement of business. As the ISDs of the assessee had obtained registration in the first quarter of 2009, the credit availed on tax paid prior to registration as ISD was inadmissible under rule 3(1).

Further, since units of ONGC were located at separate locations and in separate jurisdictions, it could not be held that services used at one unit would constitute input services for other.

Issue Involved

Whether the Cenvat credit in question was available ?

held.text:
I. Trading an exempted service only from 1-4-2011

Provisions of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, which came into force with effect from 16-08-2002 govern the entitlement to availment and utilization of cenvat credit up to 9-09-2004, on which date the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force. The 2004 Rules govern the field since 10-09-2004. [Para 5]

Under the Credit Rules, 2002 input service is defined in rule 2(c) as any taxable service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service. Rule 3(1) provided that an output service provider shall be allowed to take credit (service tax credit) of the service tax paid on input service, in the enumerated manner. Sub-clause (a) of this Rule provides that where an input service falls in the same category of taxable service as the output service, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 16-08-2002; sub-clause (b) stipulates that in any other case, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 14-05-2003. Sub rule (2) of Rule 3 provides that for the purpose of these rules, two services shall be deemed to be falling in the same category of taxable service, if the input service or output service fall in the same sub-clause of clause (105) of Section 65 of the Act.

Sub-rule (4) of rule 3 states that where a service provider avails credit on any input service and renders output services which are chargeable to service tax as well as exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be, he shall maintain separate accounts for receipt and consumption of input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of taxable output services and input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be. Sub-rule (5) of rule 3 enacts that where a service provider opts not to maintain separate accounts, as stipulated in sub-rule (4), he shall be allowed to utilize service tax credit for payment of service tax on any output service only to an extent of an amount not exceeding 35 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on such output services. [Para 6]

On a true and fair construction of the relevant provisions of the Credit Rules, 2002, it is apparent that credit could be taken on an input service falling in the same category of taxable service as the output service in respect of which the service tax liability arises and discharged from the available credit. It is axiomatic that trading in goods is neither a taxable service and could not, in the absence of a legislative/statutory fiction provided, capable of being construed as an exempted service. [Para 7]

Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, 2004 sets out the obligations of a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) provides that no cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or exempted services except in circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). Sub-rule (2) enjoins maintenance of separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input or input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service; and the quantity of input spent for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and authorizes taking of cenvat credit only on that quantity of input or input services which are intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing taxable output services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 carves out specified exclusions to the requirements set out in sub-rule (2). Sub-clause (c) of rule 6(3) stipulates that the provider of an output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

The 2004 Credit Rules were amended with effect from 01-04-2011, by Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT). To the extent relevant for this lis, by an Explanation added to Rule 2 of the 2004 Rules, it was clarified by this amendment that 'exempted services' include 'trading'. [Para 9]

Clearly, during the period in issue, i.e., 2006-07 and 2007-08, trading activity, which was one of the businesses, carried out by the appellant was not amenable to service tax. The amendment to rule 2(e), stated that there was no liability to pay service tax of trading activity, during the relevant period. [Para 9]

In this context, it may also be relevant to note, how exempted services was defined in rule 2(e) of the 2004 rules till 31-3-2011 and thereafter.

Both before and after amendment, 'exempted services' meant those taxable services, which were exempt from whole of service tax and, included those services on which service tax was not leviable, under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.2]

Therefore, given the rule position, what would govern the matter would be the determination of the issue as to whether or not, a particular service is amenable to service tax under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.3]

Since, the trading activity was not amenable service tax at the relevant period, surely, the apportionment as provided in rule 6(3)(c) would get triggered. [Para 10.4]

Having regard to the rule position and given the admitted fact that no separate accounts were maintained by the appellant, with regard to the taxable and non-taxable services, clause (c) of sub-rule 3 of rule 6 of 2004 rules would apply. [Para 11]

For the foregoing reasons, there was interference is called for with the order of the Tribunal. Accordingly, the questions of law framed are answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. [Para 12]

The goods which the assessee had traded are imported goods. As per the definition of exempted goods under rule 2(d) of CCR exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-C.E., dated 1-3-2011 is availed.

Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods. By no stretch of imagination imported goods which are traded can be considered as exempted goods. If that be so, the question of invoking the provisions of rule 6(2) and 6(3) for payment of a sum at the rate of 10 per cent/5 per cent on the value of the exempted goods would not arise at all. On this ground alone the impugned notice and the order is not sustainable in law. [Para 5.2]

Secondly, as per rule 6(2) maintenance of separate accounts is envisaged only when a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT credit. In the present case, the assessee has not availed any CENVAT credit at all in respect of input services relating to the traded goods. Therefore, question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise at all. Consequently provision of sub-rule (3) of the said rule 6 mandating payment of an amount equal to 10 per cent/5 per cent of the value of the exempted goods and exempted service would also not apply.

Even assuming but not admitting that the assessee has availed input service credit on both dutiable/exempted goods and taxable/exempted service, rule 6(3A) which came into force w.e.f. 1-4-2008 provides for reversal of credit on the input service attributable to exempted goods/services on a proportionate basis based on the turnover. In the present case, the assessee has precisely done that ab initio and has not taken any credit in respect of input services attributable to the traded goods. Calculation done by the assessee has not been disputed by the revenue and the revenue has not shown that the credit taken by the assessee in respect of input services in relation to manufactured goods was in excess of what was eligible to be taken. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence led by Revenue proving that the assessee has taken ineligible credit, the question of assessee violating the provisions of Rule 6 of the CCR, 2004 would not arise at all. [Para 5.3]

If the assessee reversed input service tax credit attributable to trading activities according to standard accounting principles, the same would suffice for satisfying the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 6. [Para 5.4]

As regards the wrong availment of credit during the period 2005-08, another show-cause notice has already been issued to the assessee which has been adjudicated and pending before Tribunal. Thus, the department was fully aware of the practices followed by the assessee and has also approved of the same. In view of the above, invocation of the extended period of time to demand service tax is also not sustainable in law. [Para 5.5]

Trading activity - Whether a service

As regards the issue as to whether trading activity can be called a service, it is quite clear that since trading activity is nothing but purchase and sales and is covered under Sales Tax Law, it may not be appropriate to call it a service. Trading activity cannot be called a service and, therefore, it cannot be considered as an exempted service also. [Para 5]

Applicability of Cenvat Credit Rules (and Service Tax Credit Rules) on trading activity

Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 provides that where output service provider does not maintain separate account, he is to follow the procedure or avail the options available under that rule. Rule 6 is applicable only when the output service provider is providing services which are chargeable to service tax and as well as exempted services. Similar is the situation in rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. Both these rules clearly speak of exempted services. Rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules also covers non-taxable services. Since trading activity was not at all a service, it is not correct to apply these provisions. [Para 7]

Eligibility for availing input service tax credit

In cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994. Therefore, there arises a situation where an assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable goods. There is no provision to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture. In such a situation the only correct legal position appears to be that the appellant choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what will be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to service tax. The only obvious solution which would be legally correct appeared to be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles was deducted and the balance only will be availed for the purpose of payment of service tax of output service. This proposition was not against the law in view of the fact the there were several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal, wherein a view had been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit. [Para 8]

Uday Joshi for the Appellant. J.S. Negi for the Respondent.

20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

The 2004 Credit Rules were amended with effect from 01-04-2011, by Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT). To the extent relevant for this lis, by an Explanation added to Rule 2 of the 2004 Rules, it was clarified by this amendment that 'exempted services' include 'trading'. [Para 9] From the provisions of both, the Credit Rules, 2002 and the Credit Rules, 2004 it is clear that trading is neither a service nor an exempted service. Therefore no credit of the service tax paid on taxable input services used for trading could be taken and utilized for remittance of service tax on taxable services provided by the assessee, even for discharging a percentage (35 per cent or 20 per cent, as a case may be) of the service tax liability on the taxable service provided.

The Explanation added in 2011 though stated to be clarificatory in character can have only a prospective effect since the Finance Act does not authorize rules to be made with retrospective effect. Therefore, trading would be comprehended within the scope of an exempted service only with effect from 01.04.2011, the date of coming into force of the Explanation added to rule 2 of the 2004 Credit Rules. [Para 10]

The assessee not only availed cenvat credit of input services used/ consumed for its trading, by debiting in its cenvat credit account to that extent but had also utilized the credit for discharging its service tax liability for having provided taxable services, to the extent of 35 per cent up to 10-09-2004 and 20 per cent thereafter of the service tax payable on such taxable services, clearly contrary to the provisions of the 2002 Credit Rules and the 2004 Credit Rules, as the case may be. [Para 11]

II. Invocation of extended period valid :

Show-cause notices in both cases were issued invoking the extended period of limitation on the ground that the assessee had deliberately failed to disclose availment of cenvat credit utilized for trading which clearly does not amount to input service used for providing taxable or exempted services; and since trading would not in any event be considered an exempted service. The assessee's contention that 'this is a bona fide interpretational error on the part of the assessee and therefore invocation of the extended period is not justifiable' does not merit acceptance. Till the fiction was introduced that trading is an exempted service, by the Explanation introduced with effect from 01-04-2011 in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, trading which is a sale of goods could not have been considered as a service, a taxable service or an exempted service. The input services (on which cenvat credit was earned by the assessee) were consumed for its trading activities and could not have been availed or taken for discharging service tax on the services provided by the assessee, after the trading activity. There is no scope for any interpretational misconception on this aspect. Invocation of the extended period is therefore without error. Trading is purchase and sale of goods, covered by sales tax law and cannot be considered a service or an exempted service. [Para 13]

III. Option to pay penalty at 25 per cent of duty/tax granted, as said option was not granted by lower authorities

An Adjudication Authority should explicitly specify the option available to the assessee under section 11AC of the Act (which is similar to the option available under Section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994). In view of Board Circular dated 22-5-2008, all cases where penalty under section 11AC of the Central Excise Act is imposed, provisions contained in the first and second proviso of this Section should be mandatorily mentioned in the adjudication order. [Para 14]

Hence, the assessee was required to be provided an option to remit 25 per cent of the penalties imposed under rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994, within thirty days from the date of the adjudication order, along with interest and the amount of cenvat credit disallowed, after taking credit for the service tax and interest if any already remitted. It requires to be noted that the total amount of disallowed cenvat credit was already remitted by the assessee in respect of both the adjudication orders impugned in these appeals, even prior to issue of the respective show-cause notices. If no such option was indicated in an adjudication order, the Tribunal must provide such option from the date of its order. [Para 15]

IV. Interest not leviable, if credit availed not utilized

held, qua 'trading activity' vis-à-vis rule 6 mechanism, that it could not have been the intention of the Government to encourage trading by allowing full credit prior to 1-4-2011 and that the 'value' of exempt supply in nature of trading as provided after 1-4-2011 in law for complying with proportionate credit requirements should be made applicable to the period prior to 1-4-2011 as well. [Para 8] In the instant case, it is evident that the assessee had started taking only proportionate credit after receipt of Completion Certificate which was after due intimation to the revenue and also certified by independent CA. It is the case of the assessee that rule 6 in toto cannot apply prior to 1-4-2016 to the instant case, since sale of immovable property is not exempt service at all. In the light of the provisions of rule 3, the assessee cannot avail full cenvat credit on input services received after obtaining Completion Certificate. However, the assessee cannot be expected to pay an amount equal to 8%/10% of sale price of immovable property after obtaining such Completion Certificate where no service tax is paid as if it is sale of immovable property, since rule 6 per se does not apply to the instant case until 1-4-2016 at all. Even after 1-4-2016, since the assessee had availed only proportionate credit, it is not legally required to pay 8%/10% amount under rule 6(3), since it can be said to have maintained separate accounts as required under rule 6(2). [Para 9]

Having taken only proportionate credit of service tax paid on input services after receipt of Completion Certificate, duly backed by CA certificate and certified work sheets for the proportionate credits availed after Completion Certificate and also demonstrated on sample basis during the course of hearing, the assessee has fulfilled its obligation under rule 3 read with rule 6 and as such it is not liable to pay an amount equal to 8%/10% of the 'sale price of immovable property' after receipt of completion certificate under rule 6. [Para 11]

The next question for consideration would arise as to whether the assessee was also required to reverse proportionate credit, out of the valid input service credits availed by it during the period 2010 till obtaining Completion Certificate, i.e., availing during the time when whole of output service of construction of residential complex was taxable. [Para 12]

While the law does not intend to allow any undue benefit to a service provider in terms of cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in providing non-taxable output activity, cenvat credit is a vested right. Once it is legally and validly availed, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific provisions exist for the same. [Para 13]

It has been a consistent judicial view that credit entitlement is on the date of receipt of inputs when the output activity was wholly dutiable. Merely because the finished goods eventually became exempt later on, the credit availed on inputs which were contained in semi-finished/finished goods form was held as not deniable. [Para 14]

In fact, in order to overcome such legal position, transitional provisions were introduced in the Cenvat Credit Rules. Rule 11, as it existed during the material period, provides that where any inputs are contained in semi-finished or finished goods form, as on date when the finished goods become exempt or output services become exempt, such credit will have to be reversed. As clarified vide Clarification No.334/1/2007-TRU, dated 28-2-2007 and also taken note of by the Madras High Court in the case of Tractor And Farm Equipment Ltd. v. CCE [2015] 54 taxmann.com 122/50 GST 68 and eventually upheld by the Apex Court, such embargo applies only to inputs and not to input services at all. Admittedly, in the instant case, the dispute is limited to credits availed on input services during a time when output service was wholly taxable. However, portion thereof became non-taxable on account of receipt of Completion Certificate later on. [Para 15]

This being the case, a harmonious reading of rule 3 read with rules 6 and 11 will suggest that eligibility/entitlement to credit has to be examined only at the time of receipt of input service and once it is found to be availed at a time when output service is wholly taxable and the said credit is availed legitimately, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific machinery provisions are made in this regard. As per TRU Clarification dated 28-2-2007, even if one assumed sale of immovable property after completion certificate to be 'exempt service', there is no legal requirement to reverse any credit availed on 'input services' in the past (prior to obtaining Completion Certificate) at all. [Para 16]

In the instant case, before obtaining the Completion Certificate, the service of the assessee was very much taxable during which period the assessee received input service.

The assessee utilized the credit of service tax paid on input services and the credit allotted to it by its Corporate Office as ISD (Input service distributor). There was no allegation or finding that the assessee had provided taxable and exempted services. The assessee was one of the constituents of a company engaged in trading of telecommunication equipments. The Corporate Office of the company raised invoices for sale of the equipment. The Department had treated it as a provision of exempt services relying on definition of exempted services under rule 2(e ). [Para 4]

In the case of Bhel-Ge Turbine Service (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2010] 27 STT 214 (Bang. - CESTAT) it was held that exempted services mentioned in rule 2(e ) covered only services which were notified and, prima facie, could not be interpreted to include the services on which no tax was levied under section 66. Therefore, prima facie, the trading activity involved did not constitute exempted services for the assessee to come within the mischief of rule 6(3)(c). Therefore, prima facie, the demand of service tax in that regard was not sustainable. [Para 5]

Credit of service tax to the tune of Rs. 15,12,673 transferred by the Corporate Office as ISD, was found to be inadmissible, as the same pertained to supply of telecommunication equipments which constituted exempted services. Similarly, part of the credit to the extent of Rs. 1,53,30,380 received by the assessee on transfer by the ISD was held to be not admissible for the reason that the Corporate Office had failed to follow provisions of rule 6(3)(c). Credit of Rs. 87,111 was found relatable to input services, such as flower arrangement, garden maintenance, outdoor catering, real estate etc. distributed by the Corporate Office, found to be not admissible input services. [Para 6]

The basis of those demands was that the credit transferred by the Corporate Office was not admissible either as it did not qualify as an input service or as the Corporate Office had not fulfilled the conditions of rule 6(3)(c). The Corporate Office registered with the service tax department could not be held to have rendered the taxable and exempted services for the reason that it was engaged in trading activity. Therefore, these demands were, prima facie, not sustainable. [Para 6.1]

The Tribunal in the case of CST v. Godfrey Philips India (P.) Ltd. [2009] 22 STT 259 (Ahd. - CESTAT), held that the eligibility or otherwise of service tax credit has to be examined at end of ISD only . Therefore, prima facie, adjudicating authority had no jurisdiction to raise question of admissibility or otherwise of impugned credit allotted by ISD and availed of by the assessee. In the circumstances, there was to be total waiver of pre-deposit requirement of the dues adjudged against the assessee and recovery thereof was to be stayed. [Para 7]

There was considerable force in the argument of the assessee that once service tax paid on input services had not been taken at all, the provisions of rule 6(3)(c ) would not be applicable. However, it was found that even though the assessee submitted a list of ten services and the credit available thereon which was not taken, yet no verification had been conducted to check whether the claim made by the assessee that it had not taken Cenvat credit in respect of the common services and, therefore, it would not be required to maintain separate accounts, was correct. In fact, the Commissioner’s view that even if Cenvat credit on common input services was not taken, the assessee was required to maintain separate accounts, could not be accepted. [Para 4]

The very beginning of the rule 6(2) shows that only where a provider of output service avails Cenvat credit in respect of input services and uses the same and he is engaged in providing exempted as well as taxable services, then only he is required to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and utilization of input services. There was no detailed discussion on applicability of the rule and the requirement of maintenance of separate accounts by the Commissioner in the impugned order. However, in view of this provision, unless the department showed that the assessee had availed credit of input services which had also been used for providing any of the exempted services, the demand could not be sustained. For this purpose, there was a need for verification of the claim made by the assessee that it had not taken credit of service tax paid on all the common input services and their number was only ten. Even though all the other points were arguable, yet if it was found that the claim made by the assessee in respect of those ten services was correct and, in such a case, the whole case made out by the department would not be sustainable, it would be appropriate to send the matter back to the Commissioner so that he could get this verified properly and thereafter consider the matter afresh. In view of the above discussion, the requirement of pre-deposit of service tax demanded, interest thereon, penalties, etc., was to be waived and the stay petition was to be allowed and the matter was to be remanded to the Commissioner for fresh adjudication. [Para 5]

Assessee failed to take proper steps before availing credit

• The assessee aware of the disappearance of the service provider after January 2007. They did not put any effort to find out even at that stage as to whether the service providers were in existence and whether they had paid service tax collected from them to the Government.

• It was strange that appellants received, services from a service provider whose existence they knew only because he used to come to collect the cheque and they did not even bother to verify whether the office premises in the invoice was in existence or not.

• Since the service provider was located in Vapi itself (place of assessee) would also go against the assessee since it cannot even be their case that ascertaining the existence or otherwise of the service provider was a difficult task.

• The fact that appellant did not make any efforts to locate the service provider nor did they make any effort to intimate the department nor did they debit the amount of credit taken goes against the appellants and therefore it has to be held that the invocation of extended time-limit for demand in this case is sustainable.

• Further, for the same reasons, the assessee is liable to penalty also. [Para 9]

Credit was reversible as assessee was engaged in trading activity/ exempted goods

• The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of animal feed which is exempted and was also engaged in trading activity.

• If that is the case in respect of trading activity, the credit attributable to trading activity, is not admissible and is required to be reversed.

• The principle of self assessment and submission of only the results of self assessment in the form of return would show that it is the responsibility of the assessee to assess the goods correctly and pay the taxes correctly.

• In this case it cannot be said that the assessee was not aware that for trading activity credit is not admissible.

• Once the assessee is considered to be aware of statutory provisions relating to availment of credit and his activities, the normal conclusion of a ordinary prudent person is that the assessee had deliberately avoided reversing the credit attributable to trading activity and thereby suppressing/misdeclaring the fact of availment of credit to the department.

• Therefore the demand with interest and imposition of penalty has to be upheld. [Para 10]

Personal penalty not leviable on employee

• It cannot be said that the employee derived any extra benefit because of the lapses.

• It has not been shown that there was any motive on his part.

• Since penalty has been imposed on the assessee, penalty imposed employee has to be set aside. [Para 12]

As per the provisions of rule 6, the assessee has to maintain separate accounts of input/input services for both dutiable as well as non-dutiable exempted goods. In case assessee fails to maintain separate accounts for input/output services, then he shall pay an amount equal to 10 per cent of total price excluding sale tax and other taxes, if any, paid on such goods of the exempted final product charged by the manufacturer for sale of such goods at the time of such clearances from the factory. [Para 13]

In the instant case, undoubtedly the assessee had not maintained separate accounts of input service credit separately for dutiable as well as non-dutiable exempted goods. The only option left with the assessee was either to reverse proportionate input service credit or to reverse 10 per cent of the value of the exempted final product at the time of clearance. [Para 14]

In assessee’s own case, the Commissioner vide order No. 15/MI/2008, dated 31-7-2008 had held that assessee had to reverse the input service credit proportionately. The same view would be taken and it was to be held that assessee was not entitled to avail input service credit in full but it had to reverse input service credit proportionately, which is the intent of the law. [Para 15]

In view of the above discussion, requantification of the amount of reversal was required to be made to ascertain the proportionate inadmissible input service credit availed by the assessee for exempted final product. For the said purpose, the matter was sent back to the adjudicating authority to requantify the amount of inadmissible input service credit as discussed above. As issue involved in this case was a matter of interpretation of the admissibility of input service credit, no penalty was warranted in these appeals. Hence the penalties were dropped. [Para 16]

To be an exempted service, the activity should be a service. Without any statute categorizing the trading as a service, it cannot be held that it is an 'exempted service'. Therefore, the order-in-revision was not sustainable. [Para 2b]

So a telecom operator can adopt the argument in respect of services rendered to such customers. Such logic will make any VAT system for collecting tax unworkable. [Para 21]

Scheme of taxation of services provided by sub-contractors was changed w.e.f. 23-8-2007 : During the initial phase of levying service tax when the Cenvat credit scheme was not extended to service tax, this concept that a sub-contractor need not pay tax if the main service provider was paying tax on the value inclusive of the value of service provided by the sub-contractor was initially supported by various CBEC Circulars. [Para 21]

But this approach was changed with effect from 23-8-2007 when Circular No. 96/7/2007-S.T., dated 23-8-2007 was issued and it was clarified that sub-contractors would also be liable to service tax subject to credit availability. [Para 22]

Transaction herein was a single transaction and tax on full value was paid prior to payment of commission, which could be easily verified :

The argument of the distributors in the present case is not as unreasonable as illustrated in the example discussed above. [Para 23]

This is not a case where the distributor is doing a service, billing for it, collecting the charges for the service and then BSNL charging for the services to the customers through a separate process. On the contrary this is a case where BSNL sells the cards through the distributor and collects money from customers through the distributor and then pays to the distributor out of consideration received by them from their customers on which consideration service tax is first discharged by BSNL. That is to say, the transactions of both the parties are essentially one and payment on the full value of service occurs earlier than payment of commission to the distributor. Further payment of tax on full value of service rendered by the principal i.e., BSNL, is easily verifiable unlike in the case of services rendered by many other sub-contractors for other type of services. [Para 23]

On a plain reading of the provisions of section 80HHC, it is evident that it applies to the assessee engaged in the business of export out of India including trading of goods. The expression 'business of export' must be given its due meaning. It not only speaks of export out of India, but also includes 'trading of goods'. [Para 7]

Indisputably, the CBDT issued a Circular No. 621, dated 19-12-1991 by way of explanatory notes to the provisions of section 80HHC. Said circular provided for modification of provisions relating to exemption of income from exports. The amendment by inserting sub-section (3) in the said provision was carried out so as to compensate the exporter from the comparative disadvantages faced by him in the international market. The formula, as was existing prior to 1991 as stated in the circular, often used to provide a distorted figure of export profits when receipts like interest commission, etc., which did not have an element of turnover were included in the profit and loss account and, thus, it was clarified that 'profits of the business' for the said provision would not include receipt by way of brokerage, commission, interest or any other receipt of a similar nature. It was, however, categorically stated that as some expenditure might be incurred in earning these incomes, which in the generality of cases is part of common expenses, ad hoc 10 per cent deduction from such incomes is provided to account for these expenses. The amendments in no uncertain terms were to take effect from 1-4-1992, i.e., for the assessment year 1992-93, and subsequent assessment years.

The aforementioned circular dated 19-12-1991 issued by the CBDT was binding on the Department. [Para 8]

Once it was held that the amendment carried out in 1991 by reason of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1991 was prospective in nature, ex facie the High Court committed a serious error in opining that the same being clarificatory in character would apply to the assessment year 1990-91. By reason of the purported clarification issued by the CBDT in terms of the said Circular, the area of exemption had not been widened, it has in effect and substance been curtailed.

By reason of such amendment, the Parliament did not intend that the income derived by way of brokerage/commission by the assessee should not be reckoned for the purpose of computing profit or loss earned by a person engaged in the business of export but by reason thereof the deduction to the extent of 10 per cent was held to be allowable thereby. [Para 9]

Section 80HHC was incorporated in the Act for providing incentive to export houses. It is now a well-settled principle of law that although the exemption provisions are to be construed strictly as regards the applicability thereof to the case of the assessee, but once it is found that the same is applicable, the same are required to be interpreted liberally. [Para 10]

It is also trite law that an exemption is to be granted unless it is expressly taken away. [Para 11]

The expression 'income arising out of business of export' brings within its sweep not only the export of any goods or merchandise manufactured or possessed by the assessee but also of trading goods. The Parliament, therefore, intended to provide incentive when a positive profit is earned by an exporter. [Para 12]

Resultantly, the judgment of the High Court could not be sustained and it was to be held that income derived by the assessee towards commission/brokerage for procuring orders of export for other exporters would be eligible to exemption from tax under section 80HHC.[Para 16]

In view of the aforesaid, the assessee is not liable to pay 8%/10% amount of value of service became exempted after receipt of Completion Certificate under rule 6. The assessee is eligible to seek refund of the amount paid under protest towards credit availed from 2010 till receipt of completion certificate. [Para 24]

In the instant case, the assessee had availed cenvat credit in the course of constructing the real estate projects developed by it, in terms of rule 3. The dispute is limited to whether the assessee is required to reverse any portion of the cenvat credit availed by it after date of receipt of Completion Certificate for the projects, since thereafter it will not be discharging service tax liability on properties sold, where no advance was received prior to receipt of Completion Certificate at all. The assessee, however, was paying service tax in case of properties which were not yet sold by way of sale deed even after obtaining Completion Certificate, where advances were received for such properties prior to the date of obtaining such Completion Certificate. [Para 4]

The assessee submitted that it availed only proportionate cenvat credit determined on scientific basis by it (considering square foot area where service tax was paid and balance area where service tax will not be paid after completion certificate). It had not only given due intimation in this regard at the time of obtaining Completion Certificate but also produced CA certificate to support its case in this regard.

The instant appeal involves the following legal questions:

(a)

Whether receipt of consideration for residential units sold as immovable property after receipt of Completion Certificate amounts to providing exempted service and rule 6 is applicable in such case and as such whether the assessee is liable to pay 8%/10% amount of exempted value under rule 6.

(b)

Whether credit can be allowed to the assessee under rule 3 in such circumstances.

(c)

Whether the assessee can be said to have 'maintained proper separate accounts' as required under rule 6.

(d)

Whether the assessee is required to reverse cenvat credit availed during the period when output service was taxable before receipt of completion certificate, since such services were availed to construct entire property and portion of such property did not attract service tax after receipt of completion certificate.

(e)

Connected to the question (d), whether the assessee is eligible to seek refund of the amount paid under protest towards credit availed from 2010 till receipt of Completion Certificate based on CERA audit objection, wherein such credit was sought to be reversed based on considering square foot area where service tax was paid and balance area where service tax will not be paid after Completion Certificate. [Para 5]

There is merit in the submission of the assessee that for the purpose of invoking provisions of rule 6, in the present set of facts and circumstances, the output service must first be exempt service. Upon receipt of Completion Certificate for the projects, the output activity of sale of residential units becomes 'non-service' as per provisions of section 65B of the Finance Act, 1994 read with definition of the term 'exempt service' under rule 2(e). This is further supported by specific amendment carried out in rule 6(1), whereby with effect from 1-4-2016, Explanation 3 was inserted specifically dealing with a situation as in the instant case, where a deeming fiction was created that for the purposes of rule 6 exempted services as defined in clause (e) of rule 2 shall include an activity, which is not a 'service' as defined in section 65B(44) provided that such activity has used inputs or input services. There was no such stipulation prior to 1-4-2016 in law and prima facie such situation was not to be treated as exempt service and did not attract the mischief created under rule 6. [Para 6]

However, for the period prior to 1-4-2016, does this mean that a service provider can take and retain full credit on input services received even after receipt of Completion Certificate. The situation will be governed by rule 3 till such time, i.e., till the time rule 6 was specifically made applicable by virtue of the deeming fiction created. [Para 7]

It is trite law and in terms of rule 3, cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used to provide output service is eligible. In fact, the Bombay High Court in the case of Mercedes Benz India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2016] 66 taxmann.com 332/54 GST 367 held, qua 'trading activity' vis-à-vis rule 6 mechanism, that it could not have been the intention of the Government to encourage trading by allowing full credit prior to 1-4-2011 and that the 'value' of exempt supply in nature of trading as provided after 1-4-2011 in law for complying with proportionate credit requirements should be made applicable to the period prior to 1-4-2011 as well. [Para 8]

So far as the Call Centre Service is concerned, there is no dispute that this being a service provided on behalf of the clients is covered by the definition of Business Auxiliary Service as given in section 65(105)(zzb) read with section 65(19). As regards the BPO service, the same involved processing of mediclaims and transaction processing for the assessee's clients. These activities are specifically covered by the definition of Business Support Service as given in section 65(105)(zzzq) read with section 65(104c) of the Finance Act, 1994 which came into force with effect from 1-5-2006. It is well settled law that when a new service is brought within tax net by introducing a new clause in section 65(105) of the Finance Act, 1994, it has to be presumed that that service was not covered by any other clauses of section 65(105). Therefore, BPO service involving transaction processing and processing of mediclaims etc. became taxable with effect from 1-5-2006 and as such, the same was not taxable during the period of dispute. [Para 7]

So far as the Call Centre Service (Business Auxiliary Service) provided to overseas clients is concerned, there is no dispute that this is taxable service under section 65(105)(zzb) read with section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 and the same was fully exempt from service tax during the period of dispute in terms of exemption Notification no. 8/2003-S.T., If the assessee is providing a taxable service, although exempt by way of notification, but which had been exported, the assessee would be entitled to take Cenvat input credit in terms of rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Para 8]

The Larger Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE [2006] 4 STT 231 (New Delhi - CESTAT) had examined a similar issue and held that an agent engaged only for procuring purchase orders for the vendors on commission basis does not engage in any of the activities enumerated in the para 2.2 of Trade Notice No. 87/97 of Madurai Commissionerate (Equivalent to CBEC Circular, dated 11-7-1997), directly or indirectly. The commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with the work of clearing and forwarding of the goods would be a person, who in the ordinary course of business, makes contract for sale or purchase of the goods for others. The definition of ‘Commission Agent’ under section 2(aaa ) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 would apply in or in relation to service tax as it applies to duty of excise by virtue of clause (2) of section 65. Services of commission agents were included in the definition of ‘Business auxiliary service’ under clause (19) of section 65 with effect from 2003, which included service of the commission agent. The activity of mere procurement of purchase order for the principal on commission basis of a commission agent was treated separately by the Parliament from the activities of the C&F agent. In the instant case, the Commissioner (Appeals) found that the marketing agents appointed by the assessee did not carry out any activity other than procuring orders for the assessee’s goods. This activity was brought under the tax net with effect from 1-7-2003 when business auxiliary service was introduced. Business auxiliary service, inter alia, covers promotion of marketing or sale of goods. Therefore, the service involved was correctly classifiable under business auxiliary service with effect from 1-7-2003. Same services could not be classified under ‘Clearing & forward agent’s service’ for any previous period as the scope of clearing and forwarding agent’s service was not modified when business auxiliary service was introduced in the Act. Prabhat Zarda Factory (India) Ltd.’s case (supra) relied on by the revenue was overruled by the Larger Bench decision of the Tribunal in Larsen & Toubro Ltd.’s case (supra). In the circumstances, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be sustained and the appeal filed by the revenue was liable to be rejected.

As is clear from Board Circular No. 59/8/2003 dated 20-6-2003, there is difference between commission agent and consignment agent. Consignment agent actually deals with the goods, when he receives the same from the principal and dispatches them on the direction of the principal to the ultimate customer. Consignment agent may not even be associated with the procurement of orders or does not directly deal with the self-purchase. He is acting on behalf of the principal and deals with the movement of the goods as per the direction of the principal. On the other hand, commission agent is only concerned with the procurement of orders, for which he may receive the fixed amount along with some percentage amount. In the instant case, as per the terms of the agreement, the appellants were hired for canvassing and advancing the sale of the principal products and also to procure orders for the same. In such a scenario, they had to be held as commission agent rather than consignment agent. The services as commission agent were levied to tax under the category of business auxiliary service with effect from 1-7-2003 and period in instant appeal was prior to the said date. As such, they were not liable to pay any tax during the said period. [Para 3]

Further, inasmuch as the issue stands decided by the Larger Bench decision of the Tribunal, in Kotdwar Steels Ltd. v. CCE [2006] TIOL 814 (CESTAT - Delhi)(LB), the impugned order was to be set aside and the appeal was to be allowed, with consequential relief to the appellants. [Para 4]

♦ Rule 3(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 permits utilization of CENVAT Credit for payment of service tax and excise duty. [Para 5]

♦ There is no provision for segregation of CENVAT credit for payment of excise duty and for payment of service tax. There is no requirement for one to one correlation of CENVAT credit availed on input services towards payment of output services. [Para 6]

♦ Hence, assessee was eligible for CENVAT Credit. [Para 7]

EDITOR'S NOTE

♦ A question of day-to-day importance stands raised in this judgment.

♦ The requirement to maintain separate accounts exists under Rule 6 only in case where a manufacturer is engaged in manufacture of dutiable and exempt goods or a provider of output services is engaged in provision of taxable and exempt services.

♦ Though CENVAT Credit Rules contain separate provision in respect of manufacturer of excisable goods and provider of services, it must be noted that once CENVAT Credit is validly availed, there is no restriction on its utilization except as stated in Rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Rule 6 speaks about obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) of rule 6 states that cenvat credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input or input services which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or for providing exempted services. Sub-rule (2) of rule 6 states that in case the manufacture or service provider uses common inputs/input services, then such manufacturer or service provider has to maintain separate accounts and credit is to be taken only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for manufacture of dutiable goods or providing taxable services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 speaks about the situation when such manufacturer or service provider does not maintain separate accounts. It provides for two options. It was amended vide Notification No. 10/2008-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2008 with effect from 1-4-2008. As per the new sub-rule (3) of rule 6, the manufacturer/service provider opting not to maintain separate account has to follow either of the following two options:-

A manufacturer shall pay 10 per cent (5 per cent with effect from 7-7-2009) of sale price of the exempted goods and an output service provider shall pay 8 per cent (6 per cent with effect from 7-7-2009) of the value of the exempted services; or

Reverse the credit on inputs and input services pertaining to exempted goods and exempted services as per the procedure and conditions prescribed in rule 6(3A). [Para 5]

The rule 6(3A) states that while exercising the option, the manufacturer of goods or the provider of output service shall intimate in writing the department regarding the option exercised. In the instant case, admittedly there is no intimation given by the assessee informing its exercise of option. The contention of the department is that when the assessee has not intimated its option in writing then the assessee is bound to pay the duty amount calculated under the first option. The said rule does not say that on failure to intimate, the manufacturer/service provider would lose his choice to avail second option of reversing the proportionate credit. Rule 6(3A) is nothing but a procedure contemplated for application of rule 6(3). Therefore, the argument of the revenue that the requirement to intimate the department about the option exercised is mandatory and on failure the assessee has no other option but to accept and comply rule 6(3)(i) and make payment of 5 per cent/10 per cent of sale price of exempted goods/value of exempted services is not acceptable or convincing. The rule 6(3A) does not lay down any such restriction. The procedure and conditions laid in rule 6(3A) is intended to make rule 6(3)workable and not to take away the option available to the assessee. In any case, at no stretch of imagination can it be said that on failure to intimate the department, rule 6(3)(i) would automatically come into application. [Para 6]

Therefore, the impugned demand raised against the assessee was not legal and proper. [Para 7]

The assessees rendered services of the same description to the vendors. The assessee-FA rendered services to DSI by identifying the vendors in India for procurement and supply of garments. They co-ordinated with vendors for production, logistics and shipment of goods ordered, to DSI. FA rendered services to vendors by attending to the processing of purchase orders placed by DSI, by giving necessary operational assistance in the execution and ensuring the receipt of sale proceeds. These services were rendered without a contract with the vendors and were incidental to services rendered to DSI. Similarly the assessee-FW had rendered services to the foreign company-B by monitoring production and export of garments by the vendors as per B’s orders. ‘B’ was the recipient of the service. FW had Research & Development facilities and assisted ‘B’ to decide the designs of the garments. The services rendered to ‘B’ and ‘DSI’ were correctly treated by the Commissioner as not exempt as exports during the material period. Only on 1-3-2007, such services when delivered and used outside India by a recipient located outside India, were extended the exemption. [Para 4]

The assessees, had rendered services to the companies in terms of their contracts with them. They assisted in procurring of purchase orders by the vendors. They monitored progress and timely execution of the export orders placed by the companies. There was no contract between the assessees and their respective vendors. The assessees admittedly rendered the services described in the show-cause notices as evaluation of prospective customers for the companies, processing of purchase orders, customer management, processing of transactions, information and tracking of delivery schedules, operational assistance for marketing, formulation of customer service and pricing policies, managing distribution and logistics. The services rendered to the vendors and the foreign companies by the assessees, conformed to the statutory definition of ‘Support service of business or commerce’ (SSBC). The services rendered to the foreign companies and vendors were, therefore, classifiable under ‘SSBC’ and not under ‘BAS’. Levy on SSBC was introduced with effect from 1-5-2006. Therefore, the demands of service tax on those services, categorizing them as BAS for the period prior to 1-5-2006, from the assessees were not sustainable. [Para 4.1]

As regards BAS received by the assessees from foreign agents, the CBEC had clarified the jurisdiction where the Act operated in the territory of India in its Circular F.No. 36/4/2001, dated 8-10-2001. [Para 4.2]

As clarified by the Bombay High Court, in the case of Indian National Shipowners Association v. Union of India [2009] 18 STT 212, it was only after enactment of section 66A on 18-4-2006 that taxable services received from abroad by a person belonging to India are taxed in the hands of the Indian residents. The assessees, in the instant case, had received BAS from commission agents based abroad mostly prior to 18-4-2006. There is no provision in the Act to tax the assessees for these services. Therefore, demands on this account for the period prior to 18-4-2006 had to fail. [Para 4.3]

As the demands failed, no penalty could be imposed. In the circumstances, demand of tax, interest and penalties imposed in the impugned orders was liable to be set aside except for an amount paid by the assessee-FA for the period from April, 2006 to September, 2006, under reverse charge method as Indian recipient of services of foreign commission agents. Since the assessee has considered only commission income as its income and, after relevant expenditure, offered net profit for taxation, it claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders in terms of sections 194Q and 194A. In total, the Assessing Officer allowed proportionate credit for TDS on the ground that the assessee has offered only the part of the income, whereas it claimed TDS on the entire sales value. It is found that, once the assessee is operating as a commission agent, then the income of the assessee is net commission income received from the farmers, but not the total sales value of the farmers. Since the law provides for TDS under section 194Q on total sales value, and further, the assessee has raised sales invoices in its name, the traders have deducted TDS on the entire sales value, but the fact remains that, the assessee has considered the total income accrued on the total sales value being commission received from the farmers, as its income. Therefore, the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A, has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee and thus, the provisions of section 199 read with rule 37BA(2) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 are complied with. Therefore, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) that Assessing Officer has rightly allowed proportionate credit as per section 199 read with rule 37BA(2), is incorrect, going by the facts, because, there is no finding from the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) that, the income on which TDS has been deducted under sections 194Q and 194A has not suffered tax in the hands of the assessee. Since the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194A and 194Q has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee, the assessee has righty claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders and reported in Form 26AS. The Assessing Officer, without appreciating relevant facts, allowed proportionate credit for TDS, even though the assessee is entitled for credit for the entire TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A. The Commissioner (Appeals), without appreciating relevant facts, simply sustained additions made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 8]

. As per TRU Clarification dated 28-2-2007, even if one assumed sale of immovable property after completion certificate to be 'exempt service', there is no legal requirement to reverse any credit availed on 'input services' in the past (prior to obtaining Completion Certificate) at all. [Para 16]

In the instant case, before obtaining the Completion Certificate, the service of the assessee was very much taxable during which period the assessee received input service. From a bare reading of rule 4(7), it is clear that the assessee is not required to wait till output service is sold to the service recipient. The assessee can take the credit immediately after the day on which bill/challan of input service is received. In the instant case, there is no dispute that the assessee has availed the credit after receipt of bill, challan in respect of input service. Therefore, the assessee was legally entitled to take the credit on the date after the receipt of service bills/challans. Therefore, the availment of cenvat credit by the assessee is absolutely legal and correct in accordance with rule 4(7). At the time of taking credit, there is no existence of any exempted service. Therefore, there is no application of rule 6. The part of the service was exempted only after obtaining completion certificate. Thereafter the assessee was not required to avail the cenvat credit on the input service, if any, received after obtaining the Completion Certificate. In the instant case, the assessee has either not availed the cenvat credit in respect of the services received after obtaining the Completion Certificate in respect of exempted service or availed proportionate credit attributed to the taxable output service. For this reason also rule 6 has no application for the period after obtaining the Completion Certificate.

In case of service becomes exempted at a later stage, unlike the provision for manufactured goods provided under rule 11(1)(2) and (3), there is no such provision in respect of the service. The only provision for the service is provided under sub-rule (4) of rule 11. From a reading of sub-rule(4) of rule 11, it can be seen that even if an output service provider avail the credit and output service becomes exempted; in such case the credit only in respect of inputs lying in stock or is contained in taxable service is required to be paid, whereas there is no provision for payment of cenvat credit equivalent to the input services used in respect of exempted service. Therefore, the cenvat credit availed in respect of input service is not required to be paid back under any circumstances. [Para 18]

Therefore, the assessee was not legally required to reverse any credit which was availed by it during the period 2010 till obtaining Completion Certificate, i.e., during the period when output service was wholly taxable in its hands, merely because later on some portion of the property was converted into immovable property on account of receipt of Completion Certificate and on which no service tax would be paid in future. [Para 19]

It is the case of the revenue that by demanding 8%/10% amount of sale of immovable property after obtaining Completion Certificate, the credits availed in the past are ipso facto regularized. It should, however, be appreciated that payment of 8%/10% is only an option or rather a mechanism to seek credit reversal on lump sum basis, where the assessee cannot maintain separate accounts/reverse proportionate credit on turnover basis or in cases where the assessee himself so chooses to follow such option. In other words, it is a substitute to regularise credit instead of accepting proportionate credit availed during the time when output service was exempt. Since the credits availed when output service was wholly taxable cannot be called into question, it cannot be said that such 8%/10% amount of sale of immovable property is to regularise not only credits availed after completion certificate but also availed during 2010 till the time completion certificate was obtained. In that sense, rule 6, if invoked, can deal with only prospective credits availed after output activity becoming exempt and not credits availed before the output activity become exempt. [Para 21]

As submitted by the assessee, even CERA authorities, while raising objection and making the assessee reverse cenvat credit availed during 2010 till obtaining of Completion Certificate, adopted the same basis of square feet area which attracted service tax as compared to square feet area which was converted into immovable property after receipt of Completion Certificate. This basis is, therefore, acceptable to revenue authorities. It was such basis which was adopted by the assessee in availing only proportionate credit after receipt of Completion Certificate. [Para 22]

Since the assessee is not required to reverse any credit availed by it on valid input services availed during the period 2010 till obtaining of completion certificate, the said amount reversed by it under protest cannot be retained by the revenue authorities and has to be returned to the assessee. [Para 23]

In view of the aforesaid, the assessee is not liable to pay 8%/10% amount of value of service became exempted after receipt of Completion Certificate under rule 6.

There was no dispute by either side that when an application is made by a person for registration as a sub-broker or a person registered as such under the SEBI Act, 1992 read with the regulations made thereunder, he shall be called as a stock broker. So also, there is no dispute that in terms of section 65(105)(a) services provided to any person by a sub-broker or stock broker in connection with the sale or purchase of securities listed on a recognized stock exchange shall be taxable services from 10-9-2004. So also, a sub-broker who is registered or has made an application for registration as such under the SEBI Act, 1992, is permitted to provide similar service as provided by a stock broker. The service so provided becomes taxable service under the Act with effect from 10-9-2004. [Para 8]

It is true that there is no provision under the Act for double taxation. The scheme of service tax law suggests that it is a single point tax law without being a multiple taxation legislation. In the absence of any statutory provision to the contrary, providing of service being event of levy, self-same service provided shall not be doubly taxable. If service tax is paid by a sub-broker in respect of same taxable service provided by the stock broker, the stock broker is entitled to the credit of the tax so paid on such service if entire chain of identity of sub-broker and stock broker is established and transactions are provided to be one and the same. In other words, if the main stock broker is subjected to levy of service tax on the self-same taxable service provided by sub-broker to the stock broker and the sub-broker has paid service tax on such service, the stock broker shall be entitled to the credit of service tax. Such a proposition finds support from the basic rule of Cenvat credit and service of a sub-broker may be input service provided for a stock broker if there is an integrity between the services. Tax paid by a sub-broker may not be denied to be set off against ultimate service tax liability of the stock broker if the stock broker is made liable to pay service tax for the self-same transaction. Such set off depends on the facts and circumstances of each case and subject to verification of evidence as well as rules made under the law with effect from 10-9-2004. No set off is permissible prior to this date when a sub-broker was not within the fold of law during that period. [Para 9]

Therefore, the matter was sent back to the original authority to verify as to whether the stock brokers had paid service tax on behalf of the sub-brokers and, if so, reduce the demand on sub-brokers to that extent and pass fresh orders. All the appeals were allowed by way of remand. [Para 10]

Ramsarup [1962] 45 ITR 248 , the Full Bench held that on atrue interpretation of section 10 and sub-section (1) of section 24 and the first proviso thereto, an assessee is not entitled to claim a set-off of the loss suffered by him in speculation business against the profits of the assessee in a business other than a business consisting of speculative transactions. Following the above decision, if the speculation transactions were separate and distinct from the commission agency business, the losses arising from speculative transactions had been properly disallowed and carried forward. Further, the Tribunal was right in its conclusion that the true profit and loss of a transaction could only be worked out after allowing the commission paid in that transaction and, therefore, the speculative profits and losses could only be worked out after debiting the commission paid. Therefore the commission payment made on the assessee's speculative transactions, formed a direct charge and, therefore, rightly loaded against speculative transactions.

As regards the period with effect from 19-4-2006, ‘output service’, as defined in rule 2(p) during this period, means any taxable service provided by the ‘provider of taxable service’ to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder, or to any other person and the terms ‘provided’ and ‘provider’ shall be construed accordingly. During this period the Explanation to rule 2(p ) had been deleted. Thus, during this period only the service actually being provided by an assessee could be treated as his ‘output service’ and the service received by him, on which he was liable to pay service tax as service recipient by the provision of section 68(2) of the Finance Act, 1994, read with rule 2(1)(d ) of the Service Tax Rules, 1994, could not be treated as his ‘output service’.
