[2008] 12 STT 19 (MAG)

MY COLUMN/YOUR QUERIES

V. S. DATEY

YOUR QUERIES

Service tax query board is a forum where you can send your queries relating to service tax to us for reply. Queries should be sent to st_query@taxmann.com. Reply will be sent by e-mail. If the query is of general nature, it will be published in this column, without disclosing name of the person sending the query. The replies will be sent after due consideration, but without any legal responsibility.

CENVAT CREDIT WHEN BOTH TAXABLE AND EXEMPT SERVICES PROVIDED

We are telecom service providers. We are not in a position to maintain separate set of books for exempted and taxable services, even when we are providing both. We have availed Cenvat Credit at regular rates of capital goods and service tax.

The scrutiny of the documents by Excise Auditor was made from October 2004 and notice was issued as follows – As per Rule 6(3) (b) & (c) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002, "the provider of output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding twenty percent of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services. However, if company has utilised more than this limit, then the excess credit utilised needs to be recovered with interest as provided in Rule 14 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002."

In view of the above, you are requested to guide on the solution to save taxes and interest if (A) The above matter relates exclusively to Capital Goods, (B) The above matter relates exclusively to Inputs/input Services (C) The above matter has combine problem of Capital Goods as well as Inputs/Input Services. Please arrange to reply at the earliest as AC (Audit) has given only two days to make payment.

Firstly, note that the ‘two day time for making payment’ is a pressure tactic. You should not fall prey to such pressures.

Secondly, the provision of 20% does not apply to Cenvat credit of capital goods. Thus, you can avail full Cenvat credit of capital goods plus 20% of credit of inputs and input services.

Thirdly, in case of 16 specified input services, restriction of 20% does not apply. See if some of input services fall in that category.

Finally, find what is the ratio of exempt services and taxable services. If (say) exempt services are 20% and if you forego 20% of credit of inputs and input services, what situation emerges? Of course, here is no provision to reverse credit on proportionate basis; but in Ballarpur Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (201) ELT 146 [2007] 11 STT 321 Mumbai CESTAT, it was held that if Cenvat credit is reversed on pro rata basis, it means Cenvat credit has not been availed – relying upon Mayur Colours Ltd. v. CCE 2001(136) ELT 1111 (Tri-Mumbai). System of taking credit on proportionate basis has been accepted by the department in case of textile manufacturers/processors, where maintenance of separate account is not practically possible – CBE&C Circular No. 845/03/2006-CX dated 1-2-2007. Rule 6(3)(d) of the Cenvat Credit Rules also accepts principle of proportionate reversal in case of general insurance companies.

It can be argued that this principle should apply in all the cases.

Our company is a member of Bombay Stock Exchange and is registered with service tax authorities under the category of Stock Broker. In addition to that we are also trading in shares in our own account. To expand our business, we have appointed Franchisees to whom we are paying service tax. Since commission paid to them has direct relation with the brokerage earned by us, we are claiming the same in total (100%) as Cenvat credit against service tax payable on brokerage.

In addition, we are also claiming Cenvat credit in total on common services like Telephone, Insurance, Bank charges, etc., since we are of the opinion that own trading is not a service and we are only providing taxable service of stock broker. According to our interpretation, restriction given in rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 is not applicable in our case.

During the course of Service Tax audit of our company, officials are considering own trading as a service and, therefore, they are forcing us to claim whole Cenvat credit restricted up to 20% of total liability and to pay the balance amount in cash. My query is

1.Whether own trading can be considered as non-taxable service

The backdrop for some of these changes seems to be certain judgments on the term ‘input services’ such as Coca Cola India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 130 (Bom.), CCE v. GTC Industries Ltd. [2008] 17 STT 63 (Mum. - CESTAT). Definition of ‘Exempted service’ - ‘Exempted service’ will include ‘trading’ and services which are partially exempt (i.e., services on which abatement is available). Further, value of exempted services in case of ‘trading’ is the difference between sale price and purchase price of the goods traded. The reason for this proposed amendment seems to be the certain judgments on implications of ‘trading activity’ on cenvat credit such as Orion Appliances Ltd. v. CST [2010] 27 STT 319 (Ahd. - CESTAT), Faber Heatcraft Industries Ltd., In re [Appeal No. PIII/PAP/130 of 2008, dated 28-2-2008, Metro Shoes (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 14 STT 280 (Mum. - CESTAT).

’ were replaced by ‘or developing of computer software’ by the Finance Act, 2006, w.e.f. 1-5-2006].

Clauses (iv), (v) and (vi ) were inserted and clause (vii) expanded, vide the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004, w.e.f. 10-9-2004. Scope was further expanded by amendments which have become effective from 16-6-2005. Ancillary service taxable only when main service is taxable - Really, services in clause (vii) of Business Auxiliary Services are taxable only if they are incidental or ancillary to services specified in clauses (i) to (vi) of definition of Business Auxiliary Service. Thus, unless the service provider provides any service as specified in clauses (i) to (vi), the service cannot be taxed under clause (vii) alone.

Though the Air Cargo Agent gets commission from Airlines, yet he is not tied to any particular airline. In my view, the Air Cargo Agent can come within the broad definition of ‘commission agent’ as inserted w.e.f.16-6-2005. However, it is doubtful if he could come within that definition prior to that date. In any case, the service would come within definition of ‘Business Support Service’ and would be taxable from 1-5-2006. Thus, dispute seems to be restricted to the period between 9-7-2004 (when exemption to services of commission agent was withdrawn) and 16-6-2005.

It is highly doubtful if they were subject to service tax during 1-7-2003 to 9-7-2004.

CREDIT OF INPUT SERVICE TAX USED AS COMMON SERVICES

A manufacturing company manufactures twisted and texturising yarn. It pays excise duty on such yarn. It is also appointed dealer of POY/PFY of a Ltd. Co. Some quantity of above yarn (raw-material yarn) is consumed in manufacture of excisable yarn and he does trading for rest of the quantity. He receives commission on whole quantity of yarn purchased as a dealer. Service tax is paid on commission received on whole lot of yarn received as a dealer. The same company also manufactures machines for own use and for public sale. Excise duty is paid on manufacturing of final machines. It pays service tax on job charges paid in manufacture of making machines and also on repairs and maintenance on machines. The company is registered under excise and service tax provisions. Query - (a) Whether service tax paid on (input services) relating to job work and R and M can be set-off against service tax payable by company on output service tax on yarn commission? (b) It is said that with Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, across the board sectorial credit can be enjoyed by manufacturer-cum-service provider? (c) What are restrictions for a manufacturer-cum-service tax provider in Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004?

Basically, Cenvat provisions do not require one to one relationship. Cenvat is a common pool of credit of all duties as specified in rule 3(1). This credit can be utilised for payment of any duty or tax, as specified in rule 3(4), subject to restrictions as specified in rule 3(7). Thus, except restrictions under rule 3(7), the credit is completely inter-changeable.

Moreover, definition of input service is very wide. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’. Any relation with manufacture or provision of service is not required. Hence, in my view, Cenvat credit of any input service is available for payment of service tax on any output service.

Of course, department may not easily agree to this but I think legal position is quite clear.

A manufacturer engaged in manufacture of plastic bottles is also rendering services of a commission agent (sales agent) which is taxable as ‘business auxiliary service’. He avails credit of duties paid on various ‘inputs’ used exclusively for manufacture of excisable goods, ‘Capital Goods’ used exclusively for manufacture of excisable goods, ‘Input Services’ used for manufacture as well as for providing the service. Is he entitled to utilise Credit of the duties paid on ‘inputs’ or ‘capital goods’ for paying the service tax?

The question is raised only in light of the fact that the inputs/capital goods have no relationship at all with rendering of the service of Commission Agent.

The principle discussed above will apply here also.

for the mechanism for availment of Cenvat credit by a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and providers of taxable and exempted services. Let us try to analyse and see whether traded goods can be considered as exempted goods or exempted services.

Rule 2(d) defines ‘exempted goods’, as excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to ‘nil’ rate of duty. In order to get classified as ‘exempted goods’, the goods should be first excisable goods, i.e., excise duty should be leviable on the same and then there should be an exemption from payment of excise duty or it should be chargeable at nil rate of duty. Obviously, the excise duty is not leviable on the traded goods and, hence, traded goods would not fall under the category of ‘Exempted goods’.

Rule 2(e) defines ‘exempted service’ as taxable service which is exempt from whole of the service tax leviable thereon, and includes services on which no service tax is leviable under section 66 of the Finance Act.

Bare reading of the above definition shows that the definition is wide and even covers all the services on which service tax is not leviable. However, trading activity on which VAT/CST is charged cannot be called service and, therefore, cannot be considered as an exempted service also.

Concerned case-laws

3. On a perusal of above definition, it is clear that traded goods would neither fall under the category of dutiable/exempted goods or taxable/exempt services and, hence, rule 6 would not apply in determining the eligibility of Cenvat credit in respect of common input services used in providing dutiable goods/taxable services and traded goods.

Hon’ble CESTAT in the case of ABB Ltd. v. CCE&ST [2009] 21 STT 77 (Bang. - CESTAT)(LB) has held that the term ‘activities relating to business’ in the inclusive part of the definition of input service is a term of wide import and credit would be available in respect of all ‘Input services’ related to the business activities. Hence, based on this, one view can be taken that Cenvat credit in respect of common input services used in providing dutiable goods/taxable services and traded goods, would be available by treating them as services related to business activities.

However, such an interpretation would not be fair on account of the following reasons :

(i)Services referred to in the inclusive definition of ‘Input services’ under rule 2(l ) are required to be used in or in relation to the manufacture of final product or provision of taxable services and inclusive definition only suggests that some services which may seemingly not appear to be used in relation to the manufacture of final product would nevertheless be deemed to be so used [Prima facie view in the case of Colgate Palmolive (I) Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 12 STT 269 (Mum. - CESTAT)].

(ii)In case the assessee undertakes an activity, which cannot be called service or cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the scope/purview of the Excise Act as well as the Finance Act and, hence, to interpret that service tax credit will be allowed in respect of common input services utilized for providing one activity covered under the Act and another outside the ambit of the Act would not be fair.

(iii)Even on the grounds of equity, in case an assessee undertakes 100 per cent of this business activity as trading, he would not be entitled to credit of any input services. Hence, merely because the assessee also provides dutiable goods/taxable services, in addition to trading activity, he should not be entitled to full credit of service tax credit in respect of common inputs without the express authority of law.

Hon’ble CESTAT in the case of Orion Appliances Ltd. v. CST [2010] 27 STT 319 (Ahd. - CESTAT), while dealing with this issue, has held as under :

(i)Trading activity is nothing but purchase and sales and is covered under sales tax law; it cannot be called a service and, hence, cannot be considered as an exempted service also.

(ii)Since trading activity is not an exempted service, it is not correct to apply rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules as well as rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules.

(iii)In cases where an assessee is undertaking activity which cannot be called a service or manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both the Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994.

(iv)An assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable good.

(v)There are no provisions in the law to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture.

(vi)In such a situation, the only correct legal position appears to be that it is for the appellant to choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit.

CENVAT CREDIT – OPTION TO MAINTAIN SEPARATE ACCOUNTS

1. We are providing works contract services and job-work services where both services are liable for service tax one is at full rate and another is at abatement rate with reverse charge. We are taking Input of all input service and capital goods. Now we are doing some trading activity in same firm. Since we cannot separate common service like audit fees, accounting consultancy, bank charges etc. so we will be maintaining separate accounts. Whether this would be sufficient and if not, then, whether we have to give reverse 7% on trading turnover ?

Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, as it stood before 1-4-2016, mandated maintenance of separate books of account for taxable and exempted activities, failing which credit was liable to be reversed as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 (viz. 6 or 7 per cent; or pro rata).

Now, the requirement to maintain separate accounts has been done away within. In case of exempted as well as taxable activities, the credit cannot be taken for exempted activities and said credit is to be computed as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The said rule provides for percentage-based payment or pro rata reversal, as opted for by the assessee.

Hence, you have options :

Do not take credit of common inputs and input services

If credit is taken of common inputs and input services, then, —

either opt for percentage-based reversal or

opt for pro rata reversal.

CENVAT CREDIT – REVERSAL ON DISCOUNT RECEIVED ON INPUT SERVICES

2. One of my client has availed CENVAT credit on input service on the entire amount of the bill. Subsequently service provider has given the discount on the bill. Whether proportionate CENVAT credit to be reversed on the portion of the amount of discount received ?

Assuming no reverse charge case, credit can be taken on receipt of invoice. Further, payment of value of service and service tax should be made to the service provider within 3 months of date of invoice, failing which credit has to be reversed and can be re-taken only after full such payment.

As regards Part/Discounted Payment, it is provided in Circular No. 122/3/2010-S.T., dated 30-4-2010 that, in cases where receiver of service makes part/discounted payment only after 3 months, then, he is entitled to take full or pro rata credit provided he has also paid the amount of service tax, (whether proportionately reduced or the original amount) to the service provider.

Going by the Circular, if original amount of service tax is paid to the service provider, then, credit would not be touched. Accordingly, we opine as under :

[a]

If service tax amount is not changed and only value is reduced/negotiated, then, full credit may be taken [full and final settlement towards value would amount to 'payment of value' and would suffice requirements of rule 4(7)].

[b]

Alternatively, if service tax amount is also changed [say, original service tax is Rs. 14 and service tax as per revised value is Rs. 9.8], then, service provider may take benefit of rule 6(3) [credit of Rs. 4.2 may be taken by service provider] and service receiver may take credit of Rs. 9.8.

SERVICE TAX – GOVERNMENT/LOCAL AUTHORITY CAN BE BUSINESS ENTITY

3. Can Government/Local Authority be Business Entity for the purpose of section 65B of the Finance Act, 1994 ?

All services by government or local authority to any business entity are liable to service tax. Business Entity [Section 65B(17)]means any person ordinarily carrying out any activity relating to industry, commerce or any other business or profession. Since even government or local authority can be carrying out any activity relating to industry, commerce or any other business or profession, hence, they can also be business entity. Accordingly, the services might be liable to service tax.

However, by virtue of Entry 54 of Mega Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012, services provided —

by Government or a local authority

to another Government or local authority

falling under section 66D(a)(iv),

are exempt from service tax.

Hence, even if government or local authority is business entity, services availed by it from another government or local authority falling under section 66D(a)(iv) are exempt.

SERVICE TAX - SMALL SERVICE PROVIDER EXEMPTION - CLUBBING OF PARTNER'S RECEIPTS WITH THAT OF FIRM

1. Our partnership is registered under service tax and has been paying service tax under commercial coaching services. Now, the partners are also individually providing the same services however their receipts are less then Rs. 9 Lakhs. Please clarify whether partners are liable to pay service tax on the basis of their relation with firm and whether partners' receipts can be clubbed with that of the firm ?

As per definition of 'person' under section 65B(37), person is defined to include firm as a separate category of persons. Therefore, for purpose of service tax, firm is a separate person from its partners and same view would apply in respect of claim of small service provider's exemption.

However, creation of bogus entities or bogus separation of receipts in order to claim SSI-exemption has been held to be impermissible under Central Excise and same attracts clubbing of turnover.

SERVICE TAX - COMMISSION FROM FOREIGN COMPANIES - LIABILITY TO SERVICE TAX

2. We are providing services of commission agent to Singapore based foreign company for the sale of iron ore. The commission is received in foreign exchange. Please clarify whether this would be liable to service tax ? Can there be any tax planning ?

As per rule 2(f) of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012, intermediary is defined to mean "intermediary" means a broker, an agent or any other person, by whatever name called, who arranges or facilitates a provision of a service (hereinafter called the 'main' service) or a supply of goods, between two or more persons, but does not include a person who provides the main service or supplies the goods on his account. As per rule 9(c), the Place of Provision of services of an intermediary would be location of such intermediary (w.e.f. 1-10-2014).

In view of definition under Rule 2(f), commission agents and other agents, or the like would be liable to service tax on their location basis. Accordingly, Indian commission agents of foreign companies are liable to service tax w.e.f. 1-10-2014, even if the commission is earned by them in the foreign exchange.

Hence, it appears that your services are liable to service tax. We would suggest of any tax planning in view of very wide words used.

Nevertheless, if it can be shown that the services being provided are consultancy services, not relatable to supply/sale of goods, then only, rule 9(c) read with rule 2(f) would not apply.

CENVAT CREDIT - WORKS CONTRACT SERVICES v. TRADING SERVICE

3. We are having 2 divisions : trading division and service division (works contract services). Can we take credit of input services received from sub-contractor which is used exclusively to provide works contract service ?

Since trading activity is also an exempted service under rule 2(e) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004; hence, you become provided for taxable as well as exempt service and have to comply with the provisions of rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Therefore, you should either maintain separate accounts and, if not, pay 7% (6% up to 18-5-2015) of the value of exempted services of trading as per rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

The provisions of rule 6 override provisions of all other rules.

4. We are distributors of products of Johnson & Johnson. The following is the procedure :

J&J supplies to us @ Rs. 100 (invoiced) ;

We sells to our customer @ Rs. 100 ;

Bad debts, if any, are borne by us ;

We raise a debit note of Rs. 10 towards profit margin on sales ;

On confirmation J & J raises credit note of Rs. 10 on us.

CENVAT CREDIT

We are providing both taxable and exempt services. Taxable services are to the tune of Rs. 45 lakhs and exempt services are Rs. 30 lakhs. Total input service tax paid is Rs. 3,00,000 which includes Rs. 1,00,000 which is directly related to taxable services. Balance Rs. two lakhs relates to common input services like telephone, rent, etc. We would like to know whether provision of proportionate credit under rule 6(3) applies to entire input credit of Rs. three lakhs or whether we can take full credit of Rs. one lakh and apply ratio to balance credit of Rs. two lakhs ?

Basic issue is whether rule 6(2) and 6(3) are mutually exclusive or whether they are complimentary. Of course, applying the ratio to entire credit is a safer option and in second case, some litigation is possible and, hence, it should be taken only after disclosing all details to the Department and after considering possible cost of litigation (after making full disclosure). However, my views are as follows—

Rule 6(2) and 6(3) should be taken as complimentary and not mutually exclusive. The words used in rule 6(3) are ‘notwithstanding anything contained in rule 6(1) and 6(2), the manufacturer of goods or provider of output service, opting not to maintain separate accounts, shall follow either of the following options as applicable to him’.

This sub-rule can be interpreted to mean that the assessee can follow rule 6(2) for inputs and input services for which he can maintain separate records and accounts and follow rule 6(3) in respect of inputs and input services for which the assessees opts not to maintain separate accounts.

In my view, fair interpretation is that rule 6(3) should apply to cases of common inputs and common input services where the assessee is not in a position to maintain separate accounts. Thus, rule 6(2) and 6(3) are complimentary.

In costing, there are concepts of ‘allocation’ and ‘apportionment’. The costs which can be allocated directly to a particular product should be so allocated, while costs which cannot be directly allocated to any particular product/service, should be apportioned on a reasonable basis. This principle can be applied here.

The input goods/services which can be directly allocated to taxable goods/services and exempt goods/services should be allocated under rule 6(2). Full credit should be allowed of the Cenvat credit allocable to taxable goods/services and no credit should be allowed for the Cenvat credit allocable to exempt goods/services. The remaining input credit/input services should be apportioned between taxable goods/services and exempt goods/services on the basis of formulae given in rule 6(3A). This should give best possible and most fair results. Of course, this should be done after making full disclosure to the Department, to avoid charge of suppression of facts.

INPUT SERVICES USED FOR SELF-MANUFACTURED AS WELL AS TRADED GOODS

We are manufacturers of engineering products. We also are traders of those products, i.e., we procure these goods under our brand name and sale. We have appointed selling agents for sale of our products (both self-manufactured and traded). We pay selling commission to our indenting agents. The selling agents charge service tax on the commission. We avail Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission paid by us on traded goods as well as self-manufactured goods, and utilise the same for payment of excise duty on our self-manufactured products. Department has issued a show-cause notice to us, informing that we are not eligible for service tax paid by us on commission attributable to traded goods. Please advise.

You are eligible for Cenvat credit of service tax paid both on self-manufactured goods and traded goods, for the following reasons -

(1)Definition of ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is very wide. As per inclusive part of the definition, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’, since the words used are ‘such as’ and not ‘viz.’.

(2)The inclusive part of definition clearly covers ‘sales promotion’. The inclusive part of definition does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’.

(3)Cenvat Credit Rules do not require any one to one relation between input and output.

(4)Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not require distribution of Cenvat credit in any particular ratio. Entire credit of service tax at HO or depot or branch offices can be transferred to any unit without any restriction. The rule makes no distinction between services used for manufacture and services used for other activities like trading, financing, etc.

(5)The Finance Minister in para 148 of his Budget Speech on 8-7-2004 has stated as follows, "I propose to take a major step towards integrating tax on goods and services. Accordingly, I propose to extend credit of service tax and excise duty across goods and services".

(6)Thus, the Cenvat Credit Rules have to be interpreted keeping this goal in mind and, hence, cannot be interpreted narrowly. As per doctrine of purposive interpretation, an interpretation which advances purpose of the Statute should be preferred over an interpretation which defeats the purpose.

(7)It is clear that after introduction of the Cenvat Credit Rules, the whole company is treated as one single entity for Cenvat credit. The definition of ‘input service’ and ‘input service distributor’ has abolished distinction between ‘goods’, ‘manufacture’ and ‘services’. Entire company is treated as one unit for purpose of Cenvat credit, as is the position under ‘Goods and Service Tax’ (GST) which has been set as the goal. Even concept of ‘LTU’ (Large Taxpayer Unit) is a step in that direction.

(8)Even assuming that there is some ambiguity (though really there is none), it is well-settled principle that the benefit of doubt goes to assessee.

Thus, Cenvat credit availed by you is legally correct.

However, you must keep in mind that current decisions of Tribunal are highly conservative and, hence, ultimate result is uncertain. You should be mentally prepared to pay interest @ 13%, if final decision goes against you.

VALUATION FOR ADVERTISING SERVICES

We are advertising agents. We have been paying service tax on the selling agency commission paid by us and not on cost of advertisement space. This is on the basis of MF(DR) letter F No. 341/43/96-TRU dated 31-10-1996 and Mumbai II Commissionerate TN 114/96 dated 1-11-1996. Audit department of Central Excise has stated that as per TRU Circular No. B1/4/2006-TRU dated 19-4-2006, all earlier circulars relating to valuation have been withdrawn. Hence, audit department of excise is of the view that service tax is payable on the entire amount received by us from our clients, which includes cost of advertisement space also. Actually, we collect advertisement charges and pay net amount to print media after deducting our commission. Please advise whether department’s view is correct.

Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016 and amended w.e.f. 13-4-2016.

Meaning of 'if such activity has used inputs or input services' – In my view, activities like interest, dividend, deposits, loans etc. do not use inputs or input services in real sense of the term. Hence, these should not be treated as 'exempted service'. Thus, trading of goods, transactions in immovable property, transaction in money and services provided by employee to employer will be 'exempted service' [The provision that service provided by employee to employer is 'exempted service for rule 6(1) does not seem to make sense, as really in that case, assessee (employer) is service receiver and not service provider at all] - Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Value of such activity shall be invoice value. If such invoice value is not available, then it will be determined by reasonable means - Explanation 4 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

4.1 Trading of goods or securities is 'exempted service' - A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods or immovable property. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods or immovable property. The sale may be within India or outside.

For example, authorised service station of automobiles is also selling spare parts. A brand name owner manufactures some goods and also gets similar goods manufactured from ancillary units.

A Builder/Developer may also be trading in land or other immovable property.

Obviously, there will be many common input services.

As per section 66D(e) of Finance Act, 1994, trading of goods has been specified as service in negative list.

Thus, trading of goods is 'exempted service' for purpose of rule 6.

In case of traded goods, the value of exempt service shall be the difference between the sale price and the cost of goods sold (determined as per the generally accepted accounting principles without including the expenses incurred towards the purchases) or ten percent of the cost of goods sold, whichever is more [Explanation I(c) after rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2011].

Thus, if the sale price is Rs. 100 and the purchase cost is Rs. 60, the difference of Rs. 40 will be considered as value of 'exempted service'. If purchase price is Rs. 95, value of exempted service will be Rs. 10 (difference or 10% whichever is more).

Inputs or capital goods removed as such or after use are traded goods and hence 'exempted service' – Cenvat Credit Rules 3(5) and 3(5A) allow removal of Inputs or capital goods as such or after use. These are to be treated as traded goods and hence it is 'exempted service'. Such removal cannot be treated as removal of 'exempted goods'.

'Value' in case of trading of securities - In case of trading in securities, the value of exempt service shall be the difference between the sale price and the purchase price of the securities traded on one percent of the purchase price of the securities, whichever is more [Explanation I(d) after rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012].

4.2 Sale of immovable property is 'exempted service' - 'Exempted service' shall include an activity which has been defined as 'not service' under section 65(44) of Finance Act, 1994, if such activity has used inputs or input services - Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016 and amended w.e.f. 13-4-2016.

Thus, transfer of immovable property will be 'exempted service' for purposes of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Value of exempted service in case of immovable property - Though rule makes provision only in respect of traded goods, in my view, the same principle will apply to trading of immovable property also.

4.3 Services on which service tax paid under some conditional abatement/composition scheme are 'exempted services' - The definition of 'exempted service' has been expanded w.e.f. 1-4-2011, by providing that taxable service whose part of value is exempt on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services used in providing such taxable service has been taken, shall be 'exempted service'.

The word used is 'and' and not 'or'. In case of some services, Cenvat credit of input services is available though not of inputs (input goods). Such services will not be treated as 'exempted services'.

If these are taken in dividend (above the line), it will amount to reversal of Cenvat credit attributable to these services, which certainly is illogical.

3.2 Calculation of value of common inputs in case of exempted final products - The formulae as given in rule 6(3A) are only in respect of Cenvat credit attributable to (a ) inputs used for provision of exempted services and (b) input services used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services.

There is no formula to calculate Cenvat credit attributable to value of inputs used in manufacture of exempted final product, when inputs are common. In any case, consumables, fuel, dies, toolings, etc., will be ‘common inputs’ in most of the cases.

In absence of any formula, the only option with the assessee is to calculate the same either on basis of input-output ratio, or on the basis of formula similar to the one applicable for calculation of inputs used for provision of exempted services.

3.3 Treatment of traded goods - A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods. The sale may be within India or outside. Obviously, there will be many common input services. Now, traded goods are not ‘exempt goods’. It is also not ‘service’, since one is not providing services to anyone else. Further, one cannot provide service to oneself.

Including the entire value of turnover of traded goods into dividend (above line) will be highly unfair to the assessee since the services attributable to such traded goods will certainly not be proportional to value of the traded goods, in cases where the assessee is both manufacturer as well as trader.

As the formulae stand today, turnover of traded goods can neither be included in divisor (below the line) nor the dividend (above the line). This would give higher Cenvat credit to the assessee. It would be fair to provide some percentage of turnover of traded goods (by way of rules), which should be added to dividend (above the line) to give fair results.

If no such provision is made in rules, there is a strong case to argue that it is not includible in divisor as well as dividend at all, since it is neither exempted goods nor exempted service (rather it is not ‘service’ at all).

3.4 Supplies to EOU, SEZ, etc. - Rule 6(6) states that provisions of rules 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply in case of excisable goods removed to SEZ, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting.

According to strict interpretation, this turnover shall not come either in denominator or in dividend. This would be unfair. It will give absurd results, particularly when sales to SEZ, EOU, etc., are large, as amount to be reversed will be very heavy. Sales to SEZ, EOU, etc., should appear in denominator, as per correct VAT principles.

3.5 Services specified in rule 6(5) - As per rule 6(5) in case of specified 16 services, full Cenvat credit of input service is available even if these services are partly used in manufacture of exempted final product/output services. This rule has not been amended even if rule 6(3) has been recast with effect from April 1, 2008. Cenvat credit in relation to these services should be outside the calculations made as per rule 6(3A) and entire credit will be available, without any reversal.

3.6 Treatment of opening balance - An assessee always tries to utilise Cenvat credit first and then pay through PLA/GAR-7. However, despite his efforts, some opening balance is possible, particularly in initial stages of production/provision of services.

Principally, the formula should apply to opening balances also.

3.7 Service tax paid under reverse charge method - In cases where service tax is paid under reverse charge method (particularly GTA services and sponsorship services), what would be the treatment ? As per amended rules, in case of GTA service, this amount should be paid by GAR-7 challan and not by cash with effect from March 1, 2008. However, this is not ‘output service’ as per amended rule 2(p). Hence, it appears that this amount is ‘input service’ and will be ‘service tax paid’. It will neither appear in divisor nor in dividend, but proportional reversal will have to be made.

The author here explains the concerned provisions and relevant case-laws on the subject. ‘Specifically’ he makes a pointer to the decision of CESTAT in Orion Appliances Ltd. v. CST [2010] 27 STT 319 (Ahd. - CESTAT) and opines that the said decision deserves kudos because the CESTAT has preferred a very well-reasoned and fair judgment on an issue, which has wide ramifications to majority of the assessees across the country as well as for the department.

And he suggests that as this issue has been discussed and litigated over a period of time since the introduction of Cenvat credit in respect of service tax, it is high time that CBEC realizes the need for providing a clarification on the same so as to ensure that the litigation on the same is put to rest.

Introduction

1. There are a number of assessees who are engaged in provision of taxable services as well as sale of traded goods or are engaged in the manufacture of dutiable goods as well as sale of traded goods. In case of such assessees, there would be input services specifically pertaining to traded goods as well common input services that are used both for duitable goods/taxable services and for traded goods.

The question that arises in such cases is whether the assessee is entitled to take credit in respect of input services that are specifically pertaining to traded goods as well as common input services that are used both for dutiable goods/taxable services and for traded goods?

Some relevant provisions

2. Section 37 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 94 of the Finance Act, 1994 provide powers to the Central Government to make rules to provide for credit of duty or service tax paid/deemed to have been paid on the goods used in, or in relation to manufacture of excisable goods or provision of taxable services. In exercise of these powers, the Central Government has made Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules provides that a manufacturer of final product or provider of taxable service shall be allowed to take credit (Cenvat credit) in respect of any input service received by the manufacturer of final product or by provider of output service.

Rule 2(l) defines ‘input service’ to mean any service;—

"(i )used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service; or

(ii )used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products, up to the place of removal,

and includes services used in relation to setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, advertisement or sales promotion, market research, storage up to the place of removal, procurement of inputs, activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security, inward transportation of inputs or capital goods and outward transportation up to the place of removal;"

Above definition makes it clear that input services would mean only those services which are used by a provider of taxable service for providing output service or used by a manufacturer in or in relation to manufacture. Hence, any services exclusively used for traded goods would not get covered under the definition of ‘input service’ and Cenvat credit would not be available for the same.

Rule 6 provides for the mechanism for availment of Cenvat credit by a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and providers of taxable and exempted services. Let us try to analyse and see whether traded goods can be considered as exempted goods or exempted services.

Introduction

1. The basic principle of any VAT system is that credit of duty or tax paid on the input goods or service can be availed only for payment of duty on final products or output services. As a natural corollary, if no duty/tax is payable on final product or output services, credit of duty/tax paid on inputs or input services cannot be availed.

Rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 is framed to ensure that the above principle is applied while allowing the CENVAT credit of excise duty/service tax to the manufacturers/service providers.

The fundamental principles of rule 6 are as follows :

No credit shall be allowed on inputs/input services used exclusively in the manufacture of goods/provision of services on which no duty/tax is being paid.

Full credit shall be allowed on the inputs/input services used exclusively in the manufacture of dutiable goods/taxable services.

Credit on common inputs/input services shall be allowed only to the extent of attributable to dutiable goods/taxable services.

However, owing to the drafting errors and complications in combining the above cited principles, practical implementation & understanding of above rule thrown many challenges/issues. And some of these issues are settled and some are unsettled.

In this budget 2016, the entire rule 6 was redrafted with view to simplify & rationalize ensuring the above principles. In this article, an attempt is made to articulate the issues faced previously and how the redrafted rule 6 addresses or not addresses the issues.

Non-taxable items are 'Exempted' items

2. The first issue was whether "non-excisable" are to be considered as "exempted goods" and similarly, whether "non-service activities" are to be considered as "exempted services" ? The following is the discussion in this regard :

a.

Rule 6 makes a reference to the words 'exempted goods'. Now the issue which was prevailing was whether the expression 'exempted goods' (excisable but exemption given) shall be interpreted to include 'non-excisable goods'? Non-excisable goods are those goods, which do not find place in the Central Excise Tariff like alcohol etc.

b.

Judiciary expressed the view in case of Commissioner v. Kesar Enterprises Ltd. — 2001 (130) E.L.T. 93 (Tribunal) wherein it was held that reversal under rule 57CC (now rule 6) is not applicable. However partly differing with the said view in Sahni Strips & Wires Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner — 2012 (283) E.L.T. 418 (Tribunal), Tribunal held that non-excisable goods are not covered within the definition of 'exempted goods' but credit attributable to these non-excisable goods are ineligible.

c.

Similar on the issue of the any activity not being a service there was a decision of the Tribunal in case of Orion Appliances Ltd. v. CST [2010] 27 STT 319 (Ahd - Cestat) wherein it was held that the activity of trading is not a service at all; therefore the same cannot be a exempted service, however it held that CENVAT attributable to trading has to be restricted.

d.

However, an amendment was made w.e.f. 1-3-2015, wherein an Explanation was inserted to provide that exempted goods shall include 'non-excisable goods'. Consequently, credit of duties/tax paid on inputs/input services used in manufacture of non-excisable goods are ineligible and rule 6 would apply for reversal of ineligible credit.

e.

Another issue that remained unsettled is 'what is the treatment in case of non-service activities (activity is not a service at all)' and whether definition of 'exempted service' shall be interpreted to include said non-service activity ? For instance, flats booked after receipt of completion certificate was a transaction of sale of immovable property and not a service. Once the same is not a service, the doubt arises whether same shall be treated as exempted services?

f.

To bring clarity to this issue, present amendment videnotification 13/2016-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2016 inserts an Explanation to provide that activity, which is not a service at all is also covered within the ambit of exempted service, if any inputs/input services were used for said non-service activity. Consequently credit of duties/tax paid on inputs/input services used in an activity which is not at all service becomes ineligible.

With the above changes & developments, the principle that no credit shall be availed if output is not taxed appears to be achieved and settled.

This article examines as to under what circumstances the provisions of rule 6(3)(c) can be applied restricting the service provider to utilize only 20 per cent of credit, especially with reference to the phrase ‘exempted services’.

Introduction

1. Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 (the CCR), assigns an obligation on the manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods as well as the provider of taxable and exempted service, as stipulated therein. In terms of rule 6(2), the provider of output service who avails cenvat credit in respect of any input or input service has to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption, and inventory of input and input service meant for use in providing output service on which service tax is payable. In other words, the service provider is to maintain records separately for receipt, consumption, inventory of each of the input/input service which are (a) relatable to taxable output service and (b) exempted service. If for any reason such maintenance of accounts is neither possible nor feasible, in terms of provisions of rule 6(3)(c), the provider of output service shall utilize credit only to extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the service tax payable on taxable input service. On the contrary, the credit can be utilized fully under the following circumstances :

uIf the entire services are taxable service on which service tax is paid (no exempted service) (or)

uIf separate accounts are maintained as above.

New Cenvat Credit Rules

2. In the Budget 2004-05, credit of service tax and excise duty was extended across goods and services. The concept of inter-sectoral credit or credit across goods and services was brought into force, followed by introduction of new Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

As per rule 2(e) of the CCR, ‘exempted service’ means taxable services which are exempt from the whole of duty leviable thereon and includes services on which no service tax is leviable under section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994.

As per rule 2(d), ‘exempted goods’ means excisable goods which are exempt from whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to ‘NIL’ rate of duty.

The definitions are similar except that in respect of ‘exempted goods’ it includes goods which are chargeable to ‘NIL’ rate of duty for the reason that duty as per section 3 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 shall be levied on all excisable goods manufactured or produced in India at the rates set forth in the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985, and for some goods the tariff rate itself is ‘NIL’, while in respect of taxable services charge of service tax at 12 per cent is as per the provisions of section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994.

In terms of rule 6(1) of the CCR, the CENVAT credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input service which is used in ‘exempted services’ except under circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2) . Therefore, a service provider who provides ‘taxable service’ and ‘exempted service’ but does not maintain separate set of accounts in terms of rule 6 (2), is permitted to utilize the input credit only to the tune of 20 per cent of service tax payable in view of the embargo in rule 6(3)(c).

Rule 3 of the ESR contains provisions relating to export of services which have to be fulfilled to deem such services as export of services. Further, as per rule 4 of the ESR, any service which is taxable under clause (105) of section 65 of the Act, may be exported without payment of tax.

CLASSIFICATION OF TAXABLE SERVICES

6. Taxable services are defined separately under clause (105) of section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994. Services are supplied as a single composite service by bundling number of different services or disaggregating a single supply into different components. Tax liability may vary depending upon the treatment of the transaction either as a single composite service or multiple supply of service. For the purpose of levy of service tax, a single composite service is to be classified under any one of the specified taxable services.

For the purpose of classification of a service covering number of separate services, a view has to be taken as to whether an individual service is merely a component of the overall supply or is itself a distinct and independent supply i.e., whether the component is merely ancillary to the principal supply or the component can be considered as separate taxable service in its own right. A service, which does not constitute for a customer an aim in itself but a means of better enjoying the principal supply, is considered as a supply ancillary to the principal supply.

Section 65A states the principles for classification of taxable services. Classification of a composite service is based on that component of the service which gives the essential character. There is a need to determine whether a given transaction is the one containing major and ancillary elements or the one containing multiple and separate major elements. In the case of a transaction containing a major and ancillary elements, classification is to be determined based on the essential features or the dominant element of the transaction. A supply which comprises a single supply from an economic point of view should not be artificially split. The method of charging or invoicing does not in itself determine whether the service provided is a single service or multiple services. Single price normally suggests a single supply though not decisive. The real nature and substance of the transaction and not merely the form of the transaction should be the guiding factor for deciding the classification.

Seven new services are being separately defined as taxable services. Specifying a service separately as a taxable service does not necessarily mean or suggest that services falling within the scope of newly specified service were not earlier classifiable under any one of the existing taxable services. Grouping of services under a specific taxable service may change. The scope and coverage of a taxable service are to be determined strictly in accordance with the language of the relevant statutory provision existing during the material period.

Commission agents and service tax

Though service tax came into existence in the year 1994, the commission agents were brought under this tax only from 1-7-2003 under definition of ‘Business Auxiliary Service’. In this article, the author has analyzed the various aspects of service tax relating to commission agents such as ex-emption granted and thereafter withdrawn, import and export of service and other related issue

Levy of service tax

1. The business of commission agents is existing since time immemorial and most of the industrial/business activities depend upon the services of a commission agent. As the very name indicates, commission agents are authorized persons who act for or on behalf of another person, normally referred as ‘Principals’ and earn commission arising on fulfilment of the agreed terms and conditions.

Since the commission agents are rendering services to the principals, the service tax angle is inevitable. Though service tax started in the year 1994, yet only from July 1, 2003, the commission agents were brought under this tax net under definition of ‘Business Auxiliary Service’, which on the date of introduction read as under:

"(1a) ‘Business auxiliary service’ means any service in relation to,—

(i )promotion or marketing or sale of goods produced or provided by or belonging to the client; or

(ii )promotion or marketing of service provided by the client; or

(iii )any customer care service provided on behalf of the client; or

(iv )any incidental or auxiliary support service such as billing, collection or recovery of cheques, accounts and remittance, evaluation of prospective customer and public relation services,

and includes services as a commission agent, but does not include any information technology service."

Exemption from service tax

2. As can be seen from the definition given above, the service of a commission agent is included in the Business Auxiliary Service. However, fortunately Notification No. 13/2003-ST, dated June 20, 2003 was issued granting unconditional exemption to commission agents from payment of service tax. To make sure that the exemption is granted in the intended manner, the term ‘Commission Agent’ was defined by way of Explanation under the above Notification which read as under:

"Commission Agent means a person who causes sale or purchase of goods on behalf of another person for a consideration which is based on the quantum of such sale or purchase."

Though commission agents were shocked to know about the coverage of their services under the net of Service Tax, yet they had a sigh of relief in view of the exemption granted to their services.

Withdrawal of exemption

3. The happiness of the commission agents did not last long when the exemption was quietly withdrawn vide Notification No. 8/2004, dated July 9, 2004, which has amended Notification No. 13/2003 and the restricted exemption was extended only to commission agents in relation to sale or purchase of agricultural produce. Thus, effectively from July 9, 2004, the commission agents came under the net of service tax. There was initial resistance in payment of service tax, but it took sometime for them to realize that it is a helpless situation of grin and bear it and, hence, they started complying with the provisions of service tax, starting from registration and ending with filing of half-yearly return.

General exemption of Rs. 4 lakhs

4. The only silver lining in the sky for commission agent is general exemption granted by Notification No. 6/2005-ST, dated March 1, 2005, though for a limited amount of Rs. 4 lakhs every year. This gives relief to small commission agents who were relieved from all procedural hassles but the organized commission agents are not eligible for the exemption in view of the limit of turnover of Rs. 4 lakhs only. To be eligible for the benefit under this exemption notification, the turnover of such commission agent should not have exceeded Rs. 4 lakhs in the preceding financial year. Under this clause, many commission agents became ineligible for the benefit of exemption.

Brief Background

1. Airlines sell tickets to IATA agent, IATA agent sells tickets to sub-agent, sub-agent sells the tickets to the ultimate customer.

Sub-agent is having two source of income- (i) Commission income which he gets from the IATA agent; & (ii) Profit charged from the customers by selling tickets at the amount higher than at what he gets tickets from the IATA agent.

The question that arises here for consideration is whether service tax is chargeable on the commission income only or on the amount of profit earned from the customers also ?

Analysis of Air Travel Agent's Service and commission under old law

2. In the regime to 1-7-2012 only those services where taxable which were prescribed in the list of 119 services. The service by way of booking of air tickets was taxed under the head 'Air Travel Agent's Service. According to this service only those persons were liable to be taxed who were receiving income directly from the airlines. The sub-agents who were not receiving the income from airlines were not liable to pay service tax in the earlier regime under this head of service. This contention was confirmed by the trade notice, Letter No. CE/20/ST/Air Travel/97, dated 27-8-1997 in which department had clarified that - sub-agents were not liable to pay service tax under the head of 'Air travel agent's service'. However, the commission income received by sub-agents fell under the head of 'Business Auxiliary Service'. The Business Auxiliary Service was introduced vide Notification No. 7/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003. The clause (vii) of said service covered the services of 'commission agent' in it. The commission agent for the said service meant as under—

"Commission Agent" means any person who acts on behalf of another person and causes sale or purchase of goods, or provision or receipt of services, for a consideration, and includes any person who, while acting on behalf of another person—

(i)

deals with goods or services or documents of title to such goods or services; or

(ii)

collects payment of sale price of such goods or services; or

(iii)

guarantees for collection or payment for such goods or services; or

(iv)

undertakes any activities relating to such sale or purchase of such goods or services;

Therefore, in the earlier regime the commission income earned by the sub-agents was liable to be taxed under the head of 'Business Auxiliary Service'.

Analysis of air travel agent's service and commission under new law

3. In the new regime, when the definition of service (section 65B(44)) was introduced under the Finance Act, 1994 each and every activity done or agreed to be done for a consideration from one person to another is a service and thereby, liable to service tax. Therefore, in the new regime also the commission income is liable to be taxed under the head of 'Business Auxiliary Service'.

Another important question which is to be answered is whether the profit earned on sale of such tickets is liable to service tax?

The definition of good is given under section 65B(25) of the Finance Act, 1994 as per which goods mean - every kind of movable property other than actionable claim and money; and includes securities, growing crops, grass, and things attached to or forming part of the land which are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale;

From the perusal of above definition it becomes amply clear that any movable property is goods. The ticket is 'goods'1 as it is a movable property. Now, the question which is to be determined is whether such profit is trading income or commission income?

There is very thin line of difference between the commission income and trading income. In the case of commission income, the commission agent gets the possession of goods but he does not get the ownership to those goods. He is entitled to sell those goods but he cannot claim those goods himself. On contrary, in the case of trading the title to goods is transferred. Where there is transfer of title in goods it is not liable to service tax as clause (e) of section 66D exempts the activity by way of - 'trading of goods'.

Conclusion

4. From the above discussion it can be concluded that where the title of goods is transferred in the name of sub-agent then the profit earned shall not be liable to service tax as it falls within the ambit of section 66D. Where the title to goods is not transferred, the profit earned shall be treated as commission income and shall be made liable to service tax under the head of 'Business Auxiliary Service'.

3.1.2. From April 2012 to March 2014

Due to amendment made in 2012, an additional restrictions have been introduced as regards the manner of allocation / distribution of credit to the credit recipient units viz.

(i)

credit of service tax attributable to service used wholly in a unit shall be distributed only to that unit; and

(ii)

credit of service tax attributable to service used in more than one unit shall be distributed pro rata on the basis of the turnover during the relevant period of the concerned unit to the sum total of the turnover of all the units to which the service relates during the same period.

The amended rule also incorporates provisions as regards the calculation of turnover values and relevant period to be considered for determination of credit distribution ratios.

3.1.3. From April 2014 to March 2016

From 1 April 2014, Rule 7 was further amended to provide that Turnover of previous month/quarter was replaced by the turnover of units in the preceding year and Turnover of only such units is to be considered which are operational in current year.

3.2. Predicaments in the vivid provisions prevailing till March 2016

3.2.1. The language of Rule 7 was producing doubt in the mind of manufacturers /Service provider as to whether the credit of common Input Service need to be distributed among all the units or to the units to which that service relates. 3.2.2. Applicability of Rule 6 to the ISD has been the debatable issue since long past. The dissenting views of the departments can be substantiated below:

CBEC circular of 2008 provides that "ISD does not provide any service and is like a trader. Hence question of either option as per Rule 6 of CCR does not arise."

In a Tribunal judgment of 2011 in case of Colgate Palmolive it was held that "assessee is required to reverse cenvat credit on proportionate basis while distributing credit if it is manufacturing both exempted as well as taxable goods."

A guidance note issued by CBEC in 2012 states that "credit is distributed on the strength of a challan issued by ISD and it shall be subject to Rule 6 of CCR"

Accordingly, it can be recapitulated that assessees were pinned between the ambiguity of loosely drafted provisions and its contradicting interpretation by adjudicating and appellate authorities.

3.3. Budget 2016- Problem Solver or Mystery in abundance?

3.3.1 Conquering the infirmity in the prevailing position, Budget 2016 came up with some extoling amendments provided below:

It was provided that Credit attributable to more than one unit but not all units should be distributed to only such units whereas earlier such credit could be distributed to all operational units.

Clearing and forwarding agent - This category also seeks to tax services of a commission agent. ‘Commission agent’ as per the Explanation to section 65(19) means any person who acts on behalf of another person and causes sale or purchase of goods, or provision or receipt of services, for a consideration, and includes any person who, while acting on behalf of another person—

(i )deals with goods or services or documents of title to such goods or services; or

(ii )collects payment of sale price of such goods or services; or

(iii )guarantees for collection or payment for such goods or services; or

It should be noted that commission agent is one who has to be differentiated from a clearing and forwarding agent (including a consignment agent) whose services would be taxed under the clearing and forwarding agent’s service. BUDGET 2008 - PRAGMATIC APPROACH TO EXEMPT SERVICES UNDER COMMON INPUT SERVICES

Budget 2008 proposes to amend rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 to provide two options to a provider of output services using common input or input services for providing taxable as well as exempt services and opting not to make separate accounts, i.e., he can either reverse the credit attributable to inputs and input services used for providing exempted services or pay 8 per cent amount of the value of the exempted services. The author opines that these two options appear to be simple and the service providers have been given a fair opportunity of choosing the option. The approach to the issue appears to be pragmatic.

Introduction

1. Permitting credit for inputs/tax on inputs while determining tax liability, is at the core of value added tax system. To the extent input credit is not permitted/denied, the very objective of value added system is defeated, leading to cascading of taxes. However, making provisions for input credit raises host of other issues as well. One of the major issues is to what extent input credit can be permitted when output service is partially exempt. Unlike tangible goods where identification of exempt goods manufactured and input thereof is possible, it may not be so in the case of rendering of services. Even in the case of manufacturing operations, identification of all the inputs and input services which go into manufacturing will not be possible. The case becomes more complex in the case of service provider. The Government cannot permit credit for input services going into rendering of exempt services as there will not be any tax revenue for the output services rendered. At the same time, denial of input credit totally will be unfair and will also pinch the service provider.

Existing Scenario

2. As per the provisions of rule 6(2) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, the Service Provider (SP) is required to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in rendering of exempted services and take CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in providing output service on which service tax is payable. Barring few cases, this is practically impossible. Apart from that even if one makes an attempt to do so, the ST Department will always include various services and higher proportion thereof for exempt services. All these are bound to lead to dispute.

In order to overcome this problem, CENVAT credit rule 6(3)(c ) contains provision under which CENVAT credit in respect of mixed output services is restricted to 20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output service. Although this may look simple at a glance, it has severe financial implications for the SP, particularly when output service forms a miniscule part of the total services. Let us examine its salient features and its implications.

(i)In the first stage the SP is required to compute total amount of service tax liability. This will not be inclusive of exempt services.

(ii)Secondly, the SP will have to compute CENVAT credit entitlement. Under the normal circumstances the whole of this amount will be permitted to be adjusted against the tax liability. Excess of credit, if any, will be carried forward to be adjusted against future tax liability.

(iii)In the case of exempt services, tax credit as computed above will be pertaining to exempt service as well. Since the SP is not paying any tax on such services, there cannot be any question of providing credit for the same. However, in view of practical difficulty, as per the provisions of rule 6(3)(c), the claim for credit is restricted to 20 per cent of the taxable output service.

(iv)In the case of CENVAT credit entitlement being more than tax liability on taxable output services, SP will be required to pay tax. This is despite the fact that substantial amount of credit may be available.

(v)It should be noted that excess amount of credit not adjusted against the tax liability will not lapse. The SP is entitled to carry forward and claim so in the next month/quarter. Thus, the right to claim credit is not lost forever, it only gets deferred.

During the intervening period, viz., March 1, 2003 to November 19, 2003, though there was no official notification granting exemption, reliance is placed on Circular No. 56/5/2003-ST, dated April 25, 2003 wherein it is clarified by the Board that service tax is destination based consumption tax and it is not applicable to export of services and that the export of service continued to remain tax free even after withdrawal of Notification.

With the above clarification from the Board, the commission agents, who were receiving their income in foreign exchange, remained out of the net of service tax and with the introduction of the Export of Services Rules, 2005, with effect from March 15, 2005, the commission agents are covered under the provisions of these rules and continue to enjoy the exemption by taking recourse to rule 4 of the Export of Services Rules, 2005.

Conditions to treat commission agents’ service as export of services

6. For the purpose of treating the services as export of services, all the services are divided into three categories, viz., property based services, performance based services and location of service recipient based. The Business Auxiliary Service, under which commission agents are covered, is covered under category 3 under rule 3(1)(iii) of the Export of Services Rules, 2005. Besides, the service recipient being outside India and amount being received in foreign exchange, one more condition was stipulated with effect from April 19, 2006 that the service should be delivered outside India and used outside India.

Though the commission agents do the ground work for canvassing the products, which results in obtaining the orders, unless the orders so procured are delivered to the foreign principal, yet it serves no purpose and on receipt of the orders from the commission agents from India, the foreign principals use the same for execution of the orders by exporting the goods to India. Based on the dispatch or based on the receipt of the goods in India or based on realization of the payment from Indian buyer, the commission agents are paid their commission as mutually agreed upon. In such situation, the commission so received is towards export of service, but since the service recipient is outside India, payment is being received in foreign exchange and the services of the commission agent are delivered outside India and used outside India, no service tax is payable on such transaction.

In the above situation, the commission agents are given the option either to pay service tax and claim rebate of the same under Rule 5 of the Export of Services Rules, 2005 or export of services without payment of service tax under rule 4 of the said Rules. Most of the commission agents certainly prefer rule 4 route, so that there is no question of payment of service tax at all.

Registration - A must

7. Many of the commission agents are under the impression that they are not required to obtain registration since they are representing foreign principals and such commission is not subject to service tax. It is, however, to be noted that the export of service is not exempt, per se, but permitted to be exported without payment of service tax. This is similar to rule 19 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002, which permits removal of goods for export without payment of duty though the very same goods are being cleared for home consumption on payment of duty. The service rendered being one of the notified taxable services under section 69 read with rule 4 of Service Tax Rules, 1994, registration is an important condition to be fulfilled by all service providers whose services are notified.

Issue : Whether the following transaction amounts to taxable service subject to service tax ?

(A) Jobbing : Transaction entered on principal-to-principal basis between member brokers of the same Stock Exchange.

(B) Own Trading : Transactions entered on their own account by the brokers.

(C) Arbitrage : Transactions entered into by two brokers of different stock exchanges in order to get profit from price difference between two markets. Clarification : (A) When the transaction is on principal-to-principal basis between brokers, no investor is involved and as such no taxable service is provided and, therefore, no service tax is chargeable. It will attract service tax with effect from September 10, 2004 in view of the changed definition of ‘taxable service’ under section 65(105)(a). This is because from such date, service provision to any person has been made taxable.

(B) Where a broker enters into a transaction on his own account with an investor who is non-member of the stock exchange, the service provided will be taxable service and subject to service tax.

(C) In case of arbitrage transaction, i.e., the transaction between two brokers of different stock exchanges, the service is provided by a broker, i.e., the member of a stock exchange to a non-member of that stock exchange even though the investor may be a member of another stock exchange. There being an investor involved in the transaction, the service so provided to the investor will be a taxable service subject to service tax.

Issue : Whether service tax is chargeable at both the ends, when an investor is provided with taxable service by two brokers of different stock exchanges by various quarters :

Example , if a Calcutta based investor buys a security quoted on the Bombay stock exchange through his broker in Calcutta, he ends up paying service tax twice first to the Bombay stock exchange broker and then to the Calcutta stock exchange broker through whom the initial order was placed. In a situation like this, it has been represented that, it amounts to double taxation on a transaction of one single security.

Clarification : In the situation pointed out above, the investor is provided with taxable service by two brokers. First by the Bombay stock exchange broker through the Calcutta stock exchange broker and then by the Calcutta stock exchange broker.

Since the commission/brokerage is charged at both the ends, the charge of service tax at both the ends is both conceptually and legally correct. The investor placed his order for buying a security quoted at the Bombay stock exchange for the reason that either it is not available at the Calcutta stock exchange or the price is more beneficial at the Bombay stock exchange. It is open to the investor to either place his order on the Bombay stock exchange broker or through his Calcutta stock exchange broker. In the former case, he would have to pay service tax only on the service provided by the Bombay stock exchange broker. In the latter case, he pays higher commission paid to him by the Calcutta stock exchange broker, which includes the brokerage of the Bombay stock exchange broker. It cannot, therefore, be said that the investor is paying service tax twice.

The investor, in fact, pays double commission for avoiding the hassles involved in going to the Bombay stock exchange broker direct.

The service tax being the percentage of the brokerage charged from the investor, there is no double taxation involved. Service tax charged is only incidental to the charging of the commission/brokerage charged by the brokers.

It is, therefore, clarified that charging of service tax from an investor who is provided with taxable service by two brokers of different stock exchanges does not amount to double taxation.
