Formula - Common credit to be used for Pro rata Calculations 3. Another issue is whether, for applying the prescribed formula to arrive the credit attributable to dutiable/taxable and exempted goods/services, one has to take the "total credit" or he has to restrict only to "common credit" ? The following is the discussion in this regard :

a.

Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2006 prescribes a formula to arrive the attributable credit to the dutiable goods/taxable services in cases involving use of common inputs/input services for manufacture of both dutiable and exempted goods (similarly for service provider rendering both taxable & exempted services).

b.

While applying the formula, an issue was raised as to whether total credit (including exclusively used for taxable) shall be taken or only common credit. For example, total credit availed is Rs. 60 lakh whereas credit availed on inputs/input services used for both taxable & exempted services/goods is Rs. 2 lakh. Here, the question raised is whether Rs. 2 lakh shall be considered for calculating proportionate credit or Rs. 60 lakh.

c.

Logical answer is common credit and same was confirmed in the interim order of tribunal in case of SIFY Technologies Ltd. v. CCE 2014-TIOL-60-CESTAT-MAD however complete contrary view was expressed in another interim order by tribunal in case of Thyssenkrupp Industries India Private Limited v. CCE 2014 (310) ELT 317 (Tri. - Mumbai) on the ground that words "total credit taken" was used and not the common credit. However the law has been settled in the final decision of SIFY Technologies Ltd . (unreported) which provides that the rule 6 formula needs to be applied only on common credits.

d.

Vide the latest amendment to rule 6, it is clearly provided that formula needs to be applied only on common credit while arriving the attributable credit for dutiable goods/taxable services.

Options available & Credit reversal can't exceed actual credit

4. Another issue was 'what are the options available to restrict the credit attributable to exempted goods or exempted service in case where separate books were not maintained' ?

Rule 6 (existing upto 31-3-2016) gave three options —

a.

Maintain separate books to identify the extent of common inputs/input services used for dutiable goods/taxable services

b.

Reverse the credit applying the prescribed formula. Intimation to department is required to be given.

c.

Pay @ 6/7% on value of exempted goods/services

If assessee is not maintaining separate books and reversed the credit adopting the prescribed formula (either voluntarily or during/after investigation) but intimation regarding exercise of this option was not given, Revenue authorities were raising demands adopting the third option (payment of 6/7% of exempted value) citing that procedure prescribed for pro rata reversal was not followed. As result of this, the amount payable was far more than the credit attributable to exempted services/goods and in some cases, credit actually availed. For example, exempted goods/services turnover is Rs. 40 lakh and taxable turnover is Rs. 50 lakh. Total credit taken is Rs. 1 lakh only. If analogy of revenue is accepted i.e. option of paying 7/6% on exempted value is adopted, then amount payable is around Rs. 2.8 lakh whereas total credit taken (including credit exclusively attributable to taxable services) is only Rs. 1 lakh. This practice was causing serious anomalies.

On this, various appellate forums consistently held that once the credit was reversed applying the prescribed formula there can be no further demand mainly on the following grounds:

a.

It is upto assessee to exercise the preferable option and revenue department cannot force to avail particular option

b.

There is no provision specifying that if assessee does not opt for any of first two options, then third option is automatic

c.

No time-limit provided to exercise option

d.

It is only intimation and not the prior intimation

e.

Failure in intimation can be condoned as it is only procedural lapse

Noted judgments are Mercedes Benz India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE Order No. A/2166/2075/ED, dated 16-7-2015 and Commissioner v. Himalaya Drug Company — 2011 (271) ELT 350 (Kar.).

Resting this anomaly, the restructured rule 6 provides that Central Excise Officer competent to adjudicate the case based on the amount of Cenvat credit involved, may allow the assessee to avail options of reversing credit adopting the prescribed formula and condoning the procedure lapse during the adjudication.

receipt, consumption and inventory of input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and take Cenvat Credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing output service on which service tax is payable."

Further, sub-rule (3)(c) of the above said rules reads as under : "notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1) and sub-rule (2), the manufacturer or the provider of output service opting not to maintain separate accounts shall follow either of the following conditions as applicable to him, namely :

The provider of output service shall utilize the credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services."

From the above-said provision, it is clear that where an output service provider is availing credit on inputs and input services and providing taxable as well as exempted services without opting to maintain separate account of inputs and input services received and used for the exempted services and refrains to avail Cenvat Credit on such inputs/input services, he has no other option but to use Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on the output services. Therefore, the intention of the law is, the assessee shall either maintain separate account of input and input services for exempted output services and not to avail Cenvat Credit thereon or to utilize Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the service tax payable on output services. Therefore, if the assessee decides to avail Cenvat Credit directly related to the taxable output services and utilizes the same fully for payment of service tax on output services and simultaneously avails Cenvat Credit on common inputs and input services without maintaining separate account and utilizing such credit only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable, it will defeat the intention of the legal provision which is explained in the example given below :

Let the input service credit availed on input services used exclusively for taxable output service is Rs. 10,000.

Common input services which are used partly for taxable and partly for exempted services, credit availed fully of Rs. 20,000.

Let service tax payable on the taxable output service be Rs. 50,000.

The correct way to utilize the Cenvat Credit for the above said situation would be 20% of Rs. 50,000, i.e., Rs. 10,000 which can be utilized out of the total credit of Rs. 30,000 (Rs. 10,000 related to the taxable output services and Rs. 20,000 credit on common input services used for taxable as well as exempted output service). Therefore, the balance amount, i.e., Rs. 50,000 minus Rs. 10,000 Cenvat Credit utilized = Rs. 40,000 has to be used as to be paid through TR-6 challan.

Had Cenvat Credit been utilized as explained in the query, the assessee can utilize the credit of Rs. 10,000 which is directly related to taxable output service plus another Rs. 10,000 i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 service tax payable on output service = Rs. 20,000 and the balance amount of Rs. 30,000 would have been paid through TR-6 challan.

However, it may be noted that the provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, do not provide for more than one set of Cenvat Credit record for input service credit i.e. one for the input service credit related to taxable output service and second common input services credit account which are partly used for taxable output service and party for exempted services nor this sort of arrangement is prohibited, but considering the practice followed under Central Excise, I am of the opinion, that under above stated example, the assessee can avail total credit on Rs. 30,000 (10,000 + 20,000), but utilization will be restricted to 10% of service tax payable i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 = Rs. 10,000 and balance amount of Cenvat Credit unutilized (Rs. 30,000 total Cenvat Credit minus Rs. 10,000 credit utilized = Rs. 20,000) will be carried forward to the next month. It is further clarified that the law does not restrict the assessee to take Cenvat Credit on common input service only to the extent of 20% of service tax paid.

In the above said example the common input service credit of entire Rs. 20,000 can be availed and it is not restricted for availment of credit upto 20% of Rs. 20,000 i.e. Rs. 4,000.

Opinion : In short, if the assessee does not opt for separate account as envisaged under Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, he can avail the credit on the common inputs services fully but he can utilize the total credit available at the end of the month not exceeding 20% of service tax payable.

The CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 were amended along with the Budget 2011 announcements vide Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT), dated 1-3-2011. A few changes were further effected vide Notification No. 13/2011-CE (NT), dated 31-3-2011. On a few issues trade has requested for clarity. Accordingly, the following clarifications are presented issue-wise in a tabular format :

| Sl. No. | Issue | Clarification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. | Can credit of capital goods be availed of when used in manufacture of dutiable goods on which benefit under Notification No. 1/2011-CE is availed or in provision of a service whose part of value is exempted on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services is taken? | As per rule 6(4) no credit can be availed on capital goods used exclusively in manufacture of exempted goods or in providing exempted service. Goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-CE, dated the 1st March, 2011 is availed are exempted goods [Rule 2(d)]. Taxable services whose part of value is exempted on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services, used for providing such taxable service, shall be taken, are exempted services [Rule 2(e)]. Hence credit of capital goods used exclusively in manufacture of such goods or in providing such service is not allowed. |
| 2. | Is the credit of only specified goods and services listed in the definition of inputs and input services not allowed such as goods used in a club, outdoor catering etc., or is the list only illustrative? | The list is only illustrative. The principle is that Cenvat credit is not allowed when any goods and services are used primarily for personal use or consumption of employees. |
| 3. | How is the "no relationship whatsoever with the manufacture of a final product" to be determined? | Credit of all goods used in the factory is allowed except insofar as it is specifically denied. The expression "no relationship whatsoever with the manufacture of a final pro-duct" must be interpreted and applied strictly and not loosely. The expression does not include any goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. Only credit of goods used in the factory but having absolutely no relationship with the manufacture of final product is not allowed. Goods such as furniture and stationery used in an office within the factory are goods used in the factory and are used in relation to the manufacturing business and hence the credit of same is allowed. |
| 4. | Is the credit of input services used for repair or renovation of factory or office available? | Credit of input services used for repair or renovation of factory or office is allowed. Services used in relation to renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, are specifically provided for in the inclusive part of the definition of input services. |
| 5. | Is the credit of Business Auxiliary Service (BAS) on account of sales commission now disallowed after the deletion of expression "activities related to business"? | The definition of input services allows all credit on services used for clearance of final products upto the place of removal. Moreover activity of sale promotion is specifically allowed and on many occasions the remuneration for same is linked to actual sale. Reading the provisions harmoniously it is clarified that credit is admissible on the services of sale of dutiable goods on commission basis. |
| 6. | Can the credit of input or input services used exclusively in trading, be availed? | Trading is an exempted service. Hence the credit of any inputs or input services used exclusively in trading cannot be availed. |
| 7. | What shall be the treatment of credit of input and input services used in trading before 1-4-2008? | Trading is an exempted service. Hence credit of any inputs or input services used exclusively in trading cannot be availed. | 8. | While calculating the value of trading what principle to follow- FIFO, LIFO or one to one correlation? | The method normally followed by the concern for its accounting purpose as per generally accepted accounting principles should be used. |
| 9. | Are the taxes and year end discounts to be included in the sale price and cost of goods sold while calculating the value of trading? | Generally accepted accounting principles need to be followed in this regard. All taxes for which set off or credit is available or are refundable/ refunded may not be included. Discounts are to be included. |

Rule 6(3) has been radically changed w.e.f. 1-4-2008. Provisions upto 31-3-2008 are summarised below.

If assessee opts not to maintain separate accounts in respect of inputs and input services utilised for exempted goods/exempted output services as required under rule 6(2), he has to pay ‘amount’ of 10% of total price (excluding taxes) of exempted final product [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

In case of output services, he could utilise credit only upto 20% of service tax on output services. [He could ‘take’ full credit of service tax on input services, but utilise only upto 20% of tax payable on output services].

The third option i.e. proportionate reversal of Cenvat credit was not available upto 31-3-2008.

Partial manufacture/provision of exempted products/services — Cenvat credit of inputs and input services is not available if final product/output service is exempt from excise duty/service tax. In case of manufacturer manufacturing both exempt and dutiable goods (or service provider providing taxable as well as exempt services), it may happen that same inputs/input services are used partly for manufacture of dutiable goods/output services and partly for exempted goods/services. In such cases, the manufacturer/service provider has two options — (a) Maintain separate inventory and accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services. In such cases, he should not avail Cenvat credit of the inputs and input services which are used in exempted final services at all — Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules (b) Pay 10% ‘amount’ if he does not maintain separate inventory and records, if he is a manufacturer — Rule 6(3)(b) [If he is service provider, his credit is restricted to 20% of tax payable, as explained later] [provision upto 31-3-2008]

‘Amount’ if separate inventory and records not maintained - If the manufacturer opts not to maintain such separate accounts, he has to pay an amount equal to 10% of the ‘price’ of such exempted goods. Such payment can be made by debit to Cenvat credit account or PLA [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

Reversal of Cenvat credit in case of some exempted goods - In case of some specified exempted goods, the manufacturer of these final products only has to reverse Cenvat credit they had taken on inputs and input services, which were used for manufacture of exempted final product. - Rule 6(3)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Cenvat credit on capital goods — If capital goods are partly used for exempted goods and party for dutiable final products, entire Cenvat credit of duty paid on capital goods is available. Cenvat credit of duty on capital goods is not allowable only when it is exclusively used for manufacture of final products [rule 6(4)] — confirmed in Idea Cellular v. CCE (2009) 19 STT 423 = 36 VST 217 (CESTAT).

No reversal or payment of amount in certain cases — If excisable goods are removed to SEZ unit, SEZ developer, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting, payment of 10% ‘amount’ is not required [rule 6(6)].

Cenvat credit of service tax in case of supplies made by DTA to EOU - Supplies from DTA to EOU are entitled to Cenvat credit of service tax paid — para 6.11(v) of FTP.

9.11-2 Credit of service tax limited if service provider does not maintain separate accounts

Till 31-3-2008, in case of output service, if he did not maintain separate accounts, he could utilise Cenvat only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable on final product. He could ‘take’ full credit of service tax on input services, but utilise only upto 20% of tax payable on output services [The limit was 35% upto 10-9-2004].

For example, assume that service tax payable on output service is Rs 100. Service tax paid on input service is Rs 15. These input services are used both for taxable output services and exempt/non-taxable output services. In such case, assessee can avail and utilise credit of entire Rs 15. However, if tax paid on input services is Rs 75, and these are used both for exempted and output services, then assessee can actually utilise credit of only Rs 20. He will have to pay balance in cash, even if credit of Rs 55 is still available in his books.

He may take credit of Rs 75 in his Service Tax (Receivable) Account, but can utilise credit of Rs 20.

The balance may remain in his Service Tax Credit Account. He can utilise it in future if opportunity arises.

In Mundra Port and Special Economic Zone Ltd. v. CCE (2011) 33 STT 364 = 15 taxmann.com 33 (CESTAT), it was held that this credit could be carried forward on 1-4-2008 and utilised later.

Note that this provision does not apply w.e.f. 1-4-2008.

9.11-3 Treatment of opening balance of Cenvat credit as on 1-4-2008

Assessee always tries to utilise Cenvat credit first and then pay through PLA/GAR-7. However, despite his efforts, some opening balance is possible particularly in initial stages of production/provision of services. In case of assessees utilising Cenvat credit only to the extent of 20% service tax payable on output services, balance credit remained unutilised.

Issue is eligibility of Cenvat credit of opening balance and whether provision of ‘proportionate Cenvat credit’ will apply to opening balance.

It is well settled that Cenvat credit is indefeasible. Credit once validly taken cannot be denied in absence of specific statutory provision (Even such statutory provision cannot be confiscatory in nature).

CBE&C, vide circular No. 137/72/2008-CX.4 dated 21-11-2008 [20 STT 19 (ST)] has clarified that the accumulated credit as on 1-4-2008 will not lapse and can be utilised as there is no provision of periodic lapse of Cenvat credit. This would apply to assessees who were availing entire Cenvat credit but utilising only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable on taxable output services.

Meaning of 'exempted services'

Rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules defines exempted service as follows.

"Exempted service" means a —

(1)

taxable service which is exempt from the whole of the service tax leviable thereon; or

(2)

service, on which no service tax is leviable under section 66B of the Finance Act; or

(3)

taxable service whose part of value is exempted on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services, used for providing such taxable service, shall be taken;

but shall not include a service

(a)

which is exported in terms of rule 6A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 or

(b)

by way of transportation of goods by a vessel from customs station of clearance in India to a place outside India [The words in italics are inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2016]

Services on which no tax is payable are also 'exempt services' - For purpose of the definition of 'exempted services', services on which no service tax is leviable are also 'exempted services'. Thus, if a particular service is not taxable under present provisions of Finance Act, 1994, it will be 'exempted service' for purpose of rule 6.

It has been clarified that export of service will not be treated as exempted service for rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules - para 6 of CBE&C Circular No. 868/6/2008-CX dated 9-5-2008.

Activity which is not 'service' is also 'exempted service' - 'Exempted service' shall include an activity which has been defined as 'not service' under section 65(44) of Finance Act, 1994, if such activity has used inputs or input services - Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016 and amended w.e.f. 13-4-2016.

Meaning of 'if such activity has used inputs or input services' - In my view, activities like interest, dividend, deposits, loans etc. do not use inputs or input services in real sense of the term. Hence, these should not be treated as 'exempted service'.

Thus, trading of goods, transactions in immovable property, transaction in money and services provided by employee to employer will be 'exempted service' [The provision that service provided by employee to employer is 'exempted service for rule 6(1) does not seem to make sense, as really in that case, assessee (employer) is service receiver and not service provider at all] - Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Value of such activity shall be invoice value. If such invoice value is not available, then it will be determined by reasonable means - Explanation 4 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

9.4-1 Trading of goods or securities is 'exempted service'

A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods or immovable property. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods or immovable property. The sale may be within India or outside.

For example, authorised service station of automobiles is also selling spare parts. A brand name owner manufactures some goods and also gets similar goods manufactured from ancillary units.

A Builder/Developer may also be trading in land or other immovable property.

Obviously, there will be many common input services.

As per section 66D(e) of Finance Act, 1994, trading of goods has been specified as service in negative list.

Thus, trading of goods is 'exempted service' for purpose of rule 6.

In case of traded goods, the value of exempt service shall be the difference between the sale price and the cost of goods sold (determined as per the generally accepted accounting principles without including the expenses incurred towards the purchases) or ten per cent of the cost of goods sold, whichever is more [Explanation I(c) after rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2011].

Thus, if the sale price is Rs. 100 and the purchase cost is Rs. 60, the difference of Rs. 40 will be considered as value of 'exempted service'. If purchase price is Rs. 95, value of exempted service will be Rs. 10 (difference or 10% whichever is more).

Case law relating to specific services

Some case law relating to definition of 'input service' has become inapplicable after amendment to definition of 'input service' w.e.f. 1-4-2011. However, major part of case law is still relevant. The case law, which in my view is still relevant, is given below.

5.4-1 Services of Commission agent

There were disputes about eligibility of Cenvat credit on services provided by commission agent. Hence, following explanation has been added to rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, w.e.f. 3-2-2016 after sub-clause (C) -

Explanation - For the purpose of this clause, sales promotion includes services by way of sale of dutiable goods on commission basis.

The drafting of the explanation is faulty. Firstly, it is not clear what is meant by 'this clause', since firstly, any of sub-clauses (A), (B) and (C) of definition of 'input service' has no relation with 'sales commission'. Secondly, commission agent really never sales the goods. He only 'facilitates' sales. Thirdly, the explanation only refers to sale of dutiable goods. What about commission agents of services like hotels, travel of passengers, food etc?

Be as it may, at least issue of eligibility of input service of commission agent of goods has been sorted out.

The explanation has retrospective effect - The amendment dated 3-2-2016 does not specifically state that it is retrospective. However, in my view, it does have retrospective effect, for reasons stated below.

Right from beginning, department has consistently held (as per circulars/instructions discussed below) that input service of service tax paid by commission agents is eligible 'input service'. Tribunal and one High Court (Punjab and Haryana HC) have also consistently held the same view. Problems were created only because one adverse decision of Gujarat High Court in case of Cadila Healthcare delivered in year 2013.

In Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare AIR 1989 SC 1247 = 40 ELT 257 = 1989(2) SCC 95 = 177 ITR 97 (SC), it was observed that a declaratory law can be retrospective - similar views in R Rajgopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan 79 Taxman 92 = (1995) 2 SCC 630 = 1995 AIR SCW 1422 = 213 ITR 340 = AIR 1996 SC 238 (SC - 3 member bench order). An amendment (proviso in this case) inserted to remedy unintended consequences, to make the provision workable and which supplies an obvious omission has to be given retrospective interpretation.

An exemption notification issued to correct an obvious mistake has to be treated as corrective/clarificatory and can have retrospective effect - Ralson (India) v. CCE (2015) 51 GST 224 = 57 taxmann.com 122 = 319 ELT 234 (SC).

If a statute is curative or merely declaratory of the previous law, retrospective operation is generally intended - Allied Motors v. CIT 224 ITR 677 = 91 Taxman 205 = (1997) 3 SCC 472 = 1997 AIR SCW 1473 = AIR 1997 SC 1361 (SC 3 member bench) - quoted with approval in CIT v. Suresh N. Gupta (2008) 166 Taxman 315 (SC) * CIT v. Alom Extrusions (2009) 185 Taxman 416 = 319 ITR 306 (SC) - similar view in Central Bank of India v. Their Workmen 1960 SCR 200 = (1959) 29 Comp Cas 367 = AIR 1960 SC 12.

5.2-3 Trading is not service

Trading of goods is not a taxable service - Clause (e) of Negative List of services as per section 66D of Finance Act, 1994.

The obvious reason is that sales tax/Vat on trading is imposed by State Government as it is covered in List II i.e. State List.

Deemed sale of goods as per Article 366(29A) of Constitution of India has been excluded from definition of 'service' itself - see section 65B(44)(a)(ii) of Finance Act, 1994 introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012.

Service tax is not leviable on a transaction treated as sale of goods and subjected to levy of sales tax/VAT - Ref Code 036.03/23.8.07 of CBE&C Circular No. 96/7/2007-ST dated 23-8-2007. Though the clarification is in respect of services of authorized service station, the principle should apply to all transactions.

Trading of goods has been defined as 'exempted service' as per rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules. However, that is only for purpose of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules (for proportionate reversal or payment of 'amount') and not for any other purpose.

Overlapping and duplication with definition of 'service' - Following have been excluded from definition of 'service' itself - (a) Mere Transfer of title in goods and immovable property by way of sale, gift or in any other manner (b) Transactions which are merely 'deemed sale of goods' under Article 366(29A) of Constitution. - - Thus, once these activities have been excluded from definition of 'service' itself, it is really not necessary to again add 'trading of goods' in negative list of services.

It seems this has been done as abundant precaution, but issue is, once an activity is excluded from definite of 'service' itself, really even rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules (of proportionate reversal or payment of 'amount') may not apply [In my view, though rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules may not be applicable, the service used in relation to such activity cannot come within the definition of 'input service' and hence not eligible for Cenvat credit under rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules. Hence, applicability or non-applicability of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules is irrelevant].

CLARIFICATION ON AMENDMENTS TO RULE 6 EFFECTED FROM 1-4-2008

In the Budget 2008-09, certain amendments have been carried out in the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 pertains to an assessee who manufactures dutiable and exempted goods and provision of taxable and exempted services. As a general principle, CENVAT credit is not allowed on input or input service used for the manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services [refer Rule 6(1)]. Exception to Rule 6(1) is contained in rule 6(3), 6(5) and 6(6).

Rule 6(2) : Provides facility to an assessee to maintain separate Cenvat credit account for dutiable and exempted goods or services (hereinafter referred to as outputs) and take credit only on inputs and input services meant for use in dutiable outputs.

Rule 6(3) : Pertains to an assessee opting not to maintain separate Cenvat credit accounts for dutiable and exempted outputs. Such assessee has to opt for one of the following two options :

(i)

Pay an amount equal to 10% of the value of the exempted goods or 8% of the value of the exempted services. Exempted service includes non-taxable service also.

OR

(ii)

Pay an amount equivalent to the CENVAT credit attributable to inputs and input services used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted goods or for provision of exempted services. Rule 6(3A) prescribes the conditions and procedure to determine the amount of CENVAT credit attributable to exempted outputs.

Schemes under rule 6(3) are optional and each individual scheme is comprehensive and self-contained. An assessee can exercise the option in relation to all his activities as an assessee and the option is not available only in relation to a part of his activity and the option once exercised cannot be withdrawn during the said financial year.

The judgment of Gujarat High Court in case of Cadila was discussed at the Central Excise Tariff Conference on Tariff Matters organized by CBE&C on 28 and 29 October 2015. Minutes of the conference and decisions taken have been circulated vide CBE&C instruction F No. 96/85/2015-CX.1 dated 7-12-2015.

As per Para B.30 of aforesaid instruction dated 7-12-2015, the conference noted that in case of Cadila, the sales commission agent was only trading in goods i.e. buying and selling the goods without undertaking any sales promotion or advertising. If activity of sales commission agent involves an element of sales promotion, Cenvat credit of service tax paid on commission agent is available.

Full extract of para B.30 of the CBE&C instruction dated 7-12-2015 is given below.

B.30 Meerut Zone - Cenvat Credit - Admissibility of Cenvat Credit on Service Tax Paid on Sales Agency Commission Service:

Issue - CBEC vide its Circular No. 943/4/2011-CX dated 29.04.2011 at point No.5 has clarified that credit of service tax paid on sales commission services (Business auxiliary services) used in 28 relation to manufacture/sale of finished goods is admissible under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. However, there are conflicting judgments of Hon'ble High Courts in this regard. Hon'ble High Court of Gujarat in case of Cadila Health Care [2013 (30) STR 0003] has disallowed the said Cenvat credit whereas Hon'ble Tribunal in case of Birla Corporation Ltd. [2014 (35) STR977] followed the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Bombay and allowed the credit. Board may be requested by the conference to issue necessary clarification on the subject to avoid further litigation and to achieve uniformity in the practice of assessment.

Discussion & Decision

The conference discussed the issue in detail and the facts of both the cases where apparently conflicting judgments have been delivered. It was noted that the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Gujarat was in a very specific set of circumstances where the sales commission agent seemed to be only trading in the goods i.e. buying and selling the goods without undertaking any sales promotion or advertising. In the said judgment, Hon'ble court noted that "there is nothing to indicate that such commission agents were actually involved in any sales promotion activities as envisaged under the said expression. Obviously, commission paid to the various agents would not be covered in this expression since it cannot be stated to be a service used directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products or clearance of final products from the place of removal". Board Circular No. 943/4/2011-CX., dated 29-4-2011 at point No. 5 on the other hand has explained the situation where the commission agent renders the service of sales promotion in following words -"....... Moreover the activity of sale promotion is specifically allowed and on many occasions the remuneration for same is linked to actual sale.......". Board circular directs that input service credit would be available when there is a element of sales promotion as sales promotion is a service. Thus, the conflict between the judgment and the circular is not as large as is perceived. Both the Board circular and case laws on the subject allow credit of input services, when the activity of the sales commission agent involves an element of sales promotion.

Impact of decision of Gujarat High Court - Assessees and Tribunal benches within jurisdiction of Gujarat High Court were bound by decision of Gujarat High Court. However, even these assessees could take Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission, if there agreement is properly worded to establish that the agent is not simply trading but is also doing additional work of sales promotion and advertising.

Assessees outside jurisdiction of Gujarat High Court could take a stand that in view of contrary decision of Punjab and Haryana High Court, they are not bound by decision of Gujarat High Court.

For the sake of uniformity in practice and removal of doubts, following clarifications are issued in respect of queries received in this regard :

|  | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. | Whether an assessee availing option (i) or option (ii) under rule 6(3) is allowed to take CENVAT Credit of duty paid on inputs and input services which are used for both dutiable and exempted goods or services? | Yes, credit on such inputs and input services is allowed. However, an assessee following option (i) or (ii) under rule 6(3) shall not be allowed to take CENVAT credit of duty paid on those inputs and input services which are used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services [refer Explanation II of rule 6(3)]. For the purpose of the calculation of amount under formula given under rule 6(3A), the total CENVAT credit taken on inputs and input services does not include excise duty paid on inputs or service tax paid on input services which are used exclusively for the manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services. |
| 2. | Whether an assessee availing option (i) in respect of certain exempted goods/services can also avail option (ii) in respect of other exempted goods or services simultaneously ? | An assessee opting for either of the option is required to avail the said option for all the exempted goods manufactured by him and all the exempted services provided by him and the option once exercised during a financial year (F.Y.) cannot be withdrawn during the remaining part of the FY. Therefore, the same assessee cannot avail both option (i) and option (ii) simultaneously during a financial year. [Explanation I to Rule 6(3)]. |
| 3. | Assessee opting for option (i) is required to pay an amount equivalent to 10% of value of exempted goods or 8% of value of exempted services. What is the scope of term "value" for the said purpose? | Value of the exempted goods is the transaction value as determined in terms of section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 or value determined under section 4A. However, in case of goods chargeable to specific rate of duty, the value, shall be the transaction value to be determined under section 4. Value of the exempted service is the gross amount charged for providing the exempted service [without abatement]. |
| 4. | What is the accounting code to be followed by the assessee who is required to pay 8% or other amount for the exempted service under rule 6(3)? | For the present, the assessee can pay the said amount under the accounting code applicable for service tax i.e., 0044. |
| 5. | Whether input services distributor can also opt for option (i) or option (ii) ? | As ISD does not provide any service, and is like a trader, the question of availing either of the options would not arise. |
| 6. | Whether export of service without payment of service tax under Export of Service Rules shall be treated as exempted service for the purpose of rule 6(3) ? | No, export of services without payment of service tax are not to be treated exempted services. |
| 7. | What is the manner for calculation of CENVAT Credit amount attributable to inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods. | It is required to be done on the basis of actual consumption of inputs used and the quantification may be made based upon the stores/production records maintained by the manufacturer. Further, a certificate from Cost Accountant/Chartered Accountant giving details of quantity of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods, value thereof and CENVAT credit taken on these inputs may be submitted at the end of the year. |
| 8. | Whether credit in respect of input services covered by rule 6(5) would be required to be taken into account for determination of amount payable as per formula provide in rule 6(3A)? | No, the credit attributable to services mentioned in sub-rule (5), shall not be taken into account for determination of amount under rule 6(3A). |

INSTRUCTION F. NO. 137/72/2008-CX.4, DATED 21-11-2008

UTILIZATION OF ACCUMULATED CENVAT CREDIT RESTRICTED IN TERMS OF ERSTWHILE RULE 6(3)(c) OF CENVAT CREDIT RULES, 2004

Kindly refer to your letter C.No. 715/Hqrs/Audit/08 dated 20-11-2008 on the subject mentioned above wherein the issue of utilization of accumulated Cenvat credit has been raised.

The matter has been examined and the following points emerged during its consideration,—

Prior to 1-4-2008 [before the amendment in rule 6(3)] the option available to the taxpayer, under rule 6(3), was that, he was allowed to utilize credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output service. However, there was no restriction in taking Cenvat credit and also there was no provision about the periodic lapse of balance credit. This resulted in accumulation of credit in many cases.

W.e.f. 1-4-2008, under the amended rule 6(3), the following options are available to the taxpayers not maintaining separate accounts :

(i)

Option No. 1 - In respect of exempted goods, he may pay an amount equal to 10% of the value of exempted goods; and in respect of exempted/non-taxable services, he may pay an amount equal to 8% of the value of such exempted/non-taxable service.

OR

(ii)

Option No. 2 - He may pay an amount equivalent to Cenvat credit attributable to inputs and input services attributable to exempted goods and non-taxable/exempted services.

As stated earlier, many taxpayers had accumulated Cenvat credit balance as on 1-4-2008. The matter to be considered was whether this credit balance should be allowed to be utilized for payment of service tax after 1-4-2008.

As no lapsing provision was incorporated and that the existing rule 6(3) of the Cenvat Credit Rules does not explicitly bar the utilization of the accumulated credit, the department should not deny the utilization of such accumulated Cenvat credit by the taxpayer after 1-4-2008. Further, it must be kept in mind that taking of credit and its utilization is a substantive right of a taxpayer under value added taxation scheme. Therefore, in the absence of a clear legal prohibition, this right cannot be denied.

Pending issues may be decided accordingly.

16.17 Importation of service is 'supply'

As per section 7(1)(b) of CGST Act, importation of service, for a consideration whether or not in the course or furtherance of business, is 'supply' and subject to GST.

Thus, import of service from HO or branch outside India will be subject to GST even if no payment was made to HO or branch outside India.

Import of service from related person taxable even if without consideration - Import of services by a (*) person from a related person or from any of his other establishments outside India, in the course or furtherance of business is taxable even if without consideration - paragraph 4 of Schedule I of CGST Act [ * - The word was 'taxable'. This word has been omitted vide CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 w.e.f. 1-2-2019. Thus, import by any person from a related person outside India shall be 'import', but it should be in the course or furtherance of business.

Valuation of supply of import of services by a related person where recipient is eligible to full input tax credit - CBI&C, vide circular No. 210/4/2024-GST dated 26-6-2024 has clarified as follows -

In case of import of services by a registered person in India from a related person located outside India, the tax is required to be paid by the registered person in India under reverse charge mechanism. In such cases, the registered person in India is required to issue self-invoice under Section 31(3)(f) of CGST Act and pay tax on reverse charge basis.

Where the foreign affiliate is providing certain services to the related domestic entity, and where full input tax credit is available to the said related domestic entity, the value of such supply of services declared in the invoice by the said related domestic entity may be deemed as open market value in terms of second proviso to rule 28(1) of CGST Rules. Further, in cases where full input tax credit is available to the recipient, if the invoice is not issued by the related domestic entity with respect to any service provided by the foreign affiliate to it, the value of such services may be deemed to be declared as Nil, and may be deemed as open market value in terms of second proviso to rule 28(1) of CGST Rules.

Thus, value of supply of import of services by a related person where recipient is eligible to full input tax credit is Nil and hence GST is not payable under reverse charge.

Apparently, the intention is to provide that in computing income in the nature of commission or brokerage being a business of an assessee, the section would not apply. 4.9.3 Agency Business

Sub-section (6)(iii) provides that the section will not apply to 'a person carrying on any agency business'.

Agency business is described as follows (http://business.yourdictionary. com/agency):

"The relationship between an agent and a principal in which the agent acts for and represents the principal on the basis of the principal's instructions".

As discussed earlier, sub-section (6)(ii) covers any income earned by a commission agent. Prima facie, it would cover transactions where a person acts as an agent to carry out certain transactions incidental to his business. Thus, clause (iii) overlaps clause (ii).

Sub-section (6)(iii) covers the case where a person is carrying on agency business. In the light of the above discussions about an agent and agency business, it could be said that a person who is dealing in the goods of one or more principals, without carrying on trading activity of his own, is engaged in the agency business. Although, he is engaged in trading, the activity is in the nature of service rendered to someone else for effecting his sales. Normally, such person would purchase directly from or from a source identified by the person (principal) for whom he is acting as an agent. Also, he would have some contractual relationship with the Principal which would specify the limits to which he can bind the Principal as also specify assistance which the Principal would provide in the business of selling. The intention is not to permit such person to avail of the option of presumptive tax under the section.

Agency business could cover both: in respect of goods and/or services. Hence, the provision would not apply, say, to an insurance agent or an agent of Post Office or an agent rendering services for marketing of securities, etc.

Further, as discussed above, if a person apart from carrying on trading activities of his own e.g. of dealing in plastic furniture, also, carries on some agency business e.g. of representing a specified manufacturer of plastic furniture, the section would not apply to such person.

Thus, it appears that non-applicability of the section is fixed qua person and not qua business. In other words, if a person carries on any of the activities specified in sub-section (6), he/it cannot opt for presumptive taxation.

4.9.4 Increase in threshold limit to Rs. 1 crore

The second amendment is in definition of 'eligible business' contained in Explanation (b)(ii) providing for the threshold limit. Presently, it is: turnover or gross receipt should not exceed Rs. 60 lacs. If, it is less than that the business is considered as eligible business.

The amendment raises the threshold limit to Rs. 1 crore effective from 1-4-2013. Thus, any person engaged in business having a turnover or gross receipts of less than Rs. 1 crore, from and after assessment year 2013-14, would qualify for presumptive tax payable under the section.

Service Provider eligible for Cenvat credit

20.3-5 As per rule 3(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules, provider of output service shall be allowed to take Cenvat credit of specified duties and taxes. Thus, only a person who is providing taxable output service will be eligible to take Cenvat credit.

Output Service - "Output service" means any service provided by a provider of service located in the taxable territory but shall not include a service - (1) specified in section 66D of the Finance Act, 1994; or (2) where the whole of service tax is liable to be paid by the recipient of service [Rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules, as inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012] [Section 66D of Finance Act, 1994 covers list of services in negative list].

Rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules (as existing upto 1-7-2012 and from 29-2-2008) was reading as follows - "output service" means any taxable service, excluding the taxable service referred in section 65(105)(zzp) of Finance Act, 1994 (This is GTA service) provided by the provider of taxable service, to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder or any other person, as the case may be, and the expressions 'provider' and 'provided' shall be construed accordingly.

Till 29-2-2008, rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules stated that "output service" means any taxable service provided by the provider of taxable service, to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder or any other person, as the case may be, and the expressions 'provider' and 'provided' shall be construed accordingly.

Sale of food is deemed sale of goods, as per Constitution - Article 366(29A) of Constitution, as amended by Constitution (46th Amendment) Act, 1982, w.e.f. 2-2-1983 states as follows- 'Tax on the sale or purchase of goods' includes - - (f) a tax on supply, by way of or as part of any service or in any manner whatsoever, of goods, being food or any other article for human consumption or any drink (whether or not intoxicating), where such supply or service, is for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration - - And such transfer, delivery or supply of any goods shall be deemed to be a sale of those goods by the person making the transfer, delivery or supply and a purchase of those goods by the person to whom such transfer, delivery or supply is made.

Thus this is 'deemed sale of goods'.

Value in case of trading - As per Explanation I(c) to rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules, in case of trading, 'Value' for purpose of rule 6(3) and 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules shall be the difference between the sale price and the cost of goods sold (determined as per the generally accepted accounting principles without including the expenses incurred towards their purchase) or 10% of cost of goods sold, whichever is more.

Common input services - It is a fact that common input services are used both for deemed sale of goods and provision of output (taxable) service.

How to apply rule 6 in case of common input services ? - There are three possible views :

(a)

The 60% (in case of restaurant service)/40% (in case of outdoor catering service)/30% (in case of food service with mandap/shamiana/convention service) of value (on which service tax is not paid) shall be deemed to be value of 'exempted goods' . In effect, assessee can avail only 40% (in case of restaurant service)/60% (in case of outdoor catering service)/70% (in case of food service with mandap/shamiana/convention service) of Cenvat credit of input services and balance Cenvat credit is required to be reversed.

(b)

The sale of food is to be treated as sale of goods as per Constitutional provisions. Thus, difference between sale price of goods and purchase price of inputs should be taken as value of 'exempted services' as per Explanation I(c) to rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules. For example, in case of restaurant services, service tax is payable on 40% of value. Thus, 60% is to be taken as value of sale of food. If total value is 100 and value of purchase of goods is (say) 40, the value of 'exempted service' will be 20 (60 - 40). Thus, total value of service = taxable service + Exempt service = 40 + 20 = 60. Thus, the assessee can avail Cenvat credit of common input services in the ratio of 40/60 i.e. 66.67% of common input services and balance 33.33% should be reversed.

(iv) for the provision of output services excluding exempted services; and

(b) the receipt and use of input services—

(i) in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods and their clearance upto the place of removal;

(ii) in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products, excluding exempted goods, and their clearance upto the place of removal;

(iii) for the provision of exempted services; and

(iv) for the provision of output services excluding exempted services,

and shall take CENVAT credit only on inputs under sub-clauses (ii) and (iv) of clause (a) and input services under sub-clauses (ii) and (iv) of clause (b).]

1[(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rules (1) and (2), the manufacturer of goods or the provider of output service, opting not to maintain separate accounts, shall follow 2[any one] of the following options, as applicable to him, namely:—

3[(i) pay an amount equal to 4[six] per cent of value of the exempted goods and exempted services; or

(ii) pay an amount as determined under sub-rule (3A); or

(iii) maintain separate accounts for the receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs as provided for in clause (a) of sub-rule (2), take CENVAT credit only on inputs under sub-clauses (ii) and (iv) of said clause (a) and pay an amount as determined under sub-rule (3A) in respect of input services. The provisions of sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of clause (b) and sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of clause (c) of sub-rule (3A) shall not apply for such payment:

Provided that if any duty of excise is paid on the exempted goods, the same shall be reduced from the amount payable under clause (i):

Provided further that if any part of the value of a taxable service has been exempted on the condition that no CENVAT credit of inputs and input services, used for providing such taxable service, shall be taken then the amount specified in clause (i) shall be 1[six] per cent of the value so exempted:]

2[Provided *also that in case of transportation of goods or passengers by rail the amount required to be paid under clause (i) shall be an amount equal to 2 per cent of value of the exempted services.]

Explanation I.—If the manufacturer of goods or the provider of output service, avails any of the option under this sub-rule, he shall exercise such option for all exempted goods manufactured by him or, as the case may be, all exempted services provided by him, and such option shall not be withdrawn during the remaining part of the financial year.

3[Explanation II.—For removal of doubt, it is hereby clarified that the credit shall not be allowed on inputs used exclusively in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods or for provision of exempted services and on input services used exclusively in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods and their clearance upto the place of removal or for provision of exempted services.

and input services, then 7% 'amount' is payable on value so exempted - second proviso to rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

For example, if service tax is payable on 40% of value subject to non-availment of Cenvat credit on inputs and input services, then 7% is payable on 60% of value, if assessee opts for this option. 9.1-2 General provisions applicable in both the cases

Rule 6 mandatory to assessees who are manufacturers/service providers of taxable as well as exempted goods/services- The way new rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules w.e.f. 1-4-2016 is worded, Rule 6 is mandatory to assessees who are manufacturers/service providers of taxable as well as exempted goods/services. Such assessees must take entire Cenvat Credit and follow one of the options. They cannot just take eligible direct Cenvat credit and ignore the rest.

Option to be exercised for all exempted goods and service - The option has to be exercised in respect of all exempted goods manufactured and all exempted output services provided. The option once exercised shall not be changed in remaining part of financial year - Explanation I to Rule 6(3) substituted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Education cess not payable on 'amount' - Education cess and SAH education cess is payable only on 'duties of excise'. 'Amount' is not 'duty'. Hence, education cess or SAH education cess is not payable on such 'amount'.

Cenvat credit only of eligible inputs and input services - Cenvat credit can be taken only of eligible inputs and input services - Explanation 2 to Rule 6(3) inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016. [This is any way clear]

- Section 14A does not provide that if income is liable to tax at a lower rate, then also proportionate expenditure should not be allowed as deduction against other business income. Therefore, expenses incurred by assessee in respect of income liable to tax at special rate under section 115A can be allowed as deduction against income chargeable to tax at normal rate—JCIT v. American Express Bank Ltd. [2012] 24 taxmann.com 50 (Mum. - Trib.). 8D.1.4-6 HELD AS STOCK-IN-TRADE - Where shares were held by assessee-bank as stock-in-trade and not as investment—PCIT v. Punjab National Bank [2022] 140 taxmann.com 131/288 Taxman 127 (Delhi).

8D.1-5 AO's power to determine amount of expenditure incurred pre-AY 2007-08 - Up to AY 2006-07, no method has been provided for computing the expenditure incurred by the assessee in relation to exempt income. Even though no such method has been prescribed by the 1961 Act, the Assessing Officer has, first of all, to ascertain the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of the expenditure incurred in relation to income which does not form part of the total income under the Act. Even where the assessee claims that no expenditure has been incurred in relation to income which does not form part of total income, he will have to verify the correctness of such claim.

In case, he is satisfied with the claim of the assessee with regard to the expenditure or no expenditure, as the case may be, he is to accept the claim of the assessee insofar as the quantum of disallowance under section 14A is concerned. In such eventuality, the AO cannot embark upon a determination of the amount of expenditure for the purposes of section 14A(1). In case, he is not, on the basis of objective criteria and after giving the assessee a reasonable opportunity, satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee, he shall have to reject the claim and state the reasons for doing so.

Having done so, the AO will have to determine the amount of expenditure incurred in relation to income which does not form part of the total income under the said Act. He is required to do so on the basis of a reasonable and acceptable method of apportionment— Maxopp Investment Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 15 taxmann.com 390/203 Taxman 364 (Delhi), affirmed in Maxopp Investment Ltd. v. CIT [2018] 91 taxmann.com 154/254 Taxman 325 (SC). Thus, AO was free to adopt any reasonable and acceptable method.

But since there has been considerable dispute between the taxpayers and the Department on the method of determining such expenditure, therefore, the provisions of section 14A(2) [along with section 14A(3)] have been introduced.

8D.1-6 AO's power to determine amount of expenditure incurred for and from 1-4-2007 [section 14A(2) & 14A(3)] - Since, as discussed above, there has been considerable dispute between the taxpayers and the Department on the method of determining such expenditure, therefore, the provisions of section 14A(2) [alongwith section 14A(3)] have been introduced which applies prospectively for and from AY 2007-08 with the requirement of adopting a specific method of determining amount of such expenditure that has been incurred in relation to exempt income.

Section 14A(2) provides the manner in which the Assessing Officer is to determine the amount of expenditure incurred in relation to exempt income. However, the Assessing Officer is required to determine the amount of such expenditure only if he, having regard to the accounts of the assessee, is not satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of such expenditure. In other words, the requirement of the Assessing Officer embarking upon a determination of the amount of expenditure incurred in relation to exempt income would be triggered only if he returns a finding that he is not satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of such expenditure. Therefore, the condition precedent for the Assessing Officer entering upon a determination of the amount of the expenditure incurred in relation to exempt income is that he must record that he is not satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of such expenditure. This part of section 14A(2), which explicitly requires the fulfilment of a condition precedent, is also implicit in section 14A(1). It is only the prescription with regard to the method of determining such expenditure which is new and which will operate prospectively.

Section 14A(3) stipulates that the above provisions of section 14A(2) shall also apply where an assessee claims that no expenditure has been incurred by him in relation to exempt income. Thus, section 14A(3) is nothing but an offshoot of section 14A(2).

sale of goods manufactured by subsidiary in Singapore. Assessee received commission from its Singapore subsidiary. It was held that service was delivered to subsidiary. It cannot be said that service is delivered in India.

In K. Narsimhiah v. H. C. Singri Gowda AIR 1966 SC 330, in a different context, it was held that 'giving' of notice is not complete unless it has reached the hands of the person to whom it has been given. In K Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan (1999) 7 SCC 510 = AIR 1999 SC 3762 = 1999 AIR SCW 3809 = 99 Comp Cas 268 (SC), it was held that 'giving' notice is not same as 'receipt' of notice. Giving is a process of which receipt is the accomplishment - quoted with approval in C C Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Mohammed (2007) 77 SCL 117 (SC 3 member bench).

It should be noted that the words used are 'provided in taxable territory' and not 'performed in taxable territory'. Thus, actual (physical) performance is not the criteria whether or not the service is provided in taxable territory.

Hence, it can be argued that definition of 'intermediary' in rules is contrary to charging section 66B of Finance Act, 1994 and hence void. If someone challenges, we have to see what would be final outcome.

14.8-4 Ironical situation - receiving foreign exchange is taxed

The new provision has created an ironical situation. If Indian commission agent or stock broker provides service to principal outside India, he is required to pay service tax, though he is receiving payment in foreign exchange. On the other hand, if a foreign commission agent or foreign stock broker provides service to Indian Principal, the Indian Principal has to pay him in foreign exchange but no service tax is payable.

Thus, a transaction where actually India received foreign exchange is subjected to service tax, while transaction where there is outflow of foreign exchange from India is not subject to service tax.

14.8-5 No service tax on services provided by foreign Commission Agents or foreign stock broker to Indian Principals w.e.f. 1-10-2014

The aforesaid provision is working in reverse direction in case of foreign commission agents providing service to Indian Principal or foreign stock brokers. So far, rule 3 of POPS was applicable and place of provision of service was India. Hence, the Indian Principal was liable to pay service tax under reverse charge mechanism, in respect of commission paid by them to foreign commission agent or foreign stock broker.

Now, w.e.f. 1-10-2014, the place of provision of service is out of India as per rule 9(c) of POPS Rules. Hence, there is no service tax on commission paid to foreign commission agents or foreign stock brokers w.e.f. 1-10-2014. Since there is no service tax, any question of reverse charge cannot arise.

No declaration under EXP3 and EXP4 for services of foreign agent after 1-10-2014 - Now, notification No. 42/2012-ST is not relevant as no service tax is payable after 1-10-2014 under reverse charge on services provided by foreign commission agent to Indian manufacturers/service providers. Any declaration under EXP3 and EXP4 is not required in respect of foreign agency commission paid on or after 1-10-2014.

[Though the above is correct legal position, I agree assessees are going to face very tough time in convincing excise auditors. Hence, it is advisable to inform them in writing, to avoid charge of suppression of facts].

14.8-6 Hiring of aircrafts and vessels upto one month exempt

In case of hiring of all means of transport upto one month, other than aircrafts and vessels except yachts, the place of provision of service is the location of service provider [rule 9(d) of POPS Rules as amended w.e.f. 1-10-2014].

The words 'other than aircrafts and vessels except yachts' has been inserted w.e.f. 1-10-2014. Thus, hiring of vessels or aircrafts, irrespective of whether short term or long term, will be covered by the general rule, i.e. place of location of service receiver. Hiring of yachts would continue to be covered by rule 9(d) - para 4.1.3(iii) of MF(DR) letter No. 334/15/2014-TRU dated 10-7-2014

The effect is that if Indian service provider of renting of aircraft or vessel gives the aircraft or vessel (other than yacht) to a foreign customer for any period (less than one month or more than one month), the place of provision of service will be out of India, if it relates to goods (and service tax will not apply).

On the other hand, if service provider from outside India of renting of aircraft or vessel gives the aircraft or vessel (other than yacht) to an Indian customer for any period (less than one month or more than one month), the place of provision of service will be India, if it relates to goods (and service tax will not apply).

55.19

Clearing and Forwarding Agent's Services

Date of imposition of service tax - 16-7-1997

What was liable to tax upto 30-6-2012

Any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a clearing and forwarding agent in relation to clearing and forwarding operations in any manner [Section 65(105)(j)].

"Clearing and forwarding agent" means any person who is engaged in providing any service, either directly or indirectly, connected with clearing and forwarding operations in any manner to any other person and includes a consignment agent [Section 65(25)].

What was covered

Both clearing and forwarding operations required. Only clearing or only forwarding service is not sufficient.

Receiving goods, warehousing and dispatch, preparing invoices on behalf of Principal.

Services of coal merchants, who are acting as buyer's agents

Providing marketing and product support services.

What was not covered

Consignment Agent, who has right to sale goods on behalf of Principal, is not C&F Agent (even if definition of C&F Agent includes 'consignment agent') [He may get covered under BAS]

Simple buying and selling of goods.

Service of ICD and CFS taxable under 'storage and warehousing' services.

Simple storage service taxable under 'storage and warehousing' services.

Mere procuring or booking orders for the Principal by an agent on commission basis would not be 'Clearing and forwarding Agent service'. It will go under BAS.

Service of commission agent taxable under Business Auxiliary Service.

Valuation

Tax on commission and also on reimbursable expenses like godown rent, loading/unloading, freight, telephone, rent, salary etc.

Other issues

Accounting Code - Service Tax : 00440045.Payment of interest, penalty, etc. : 00440046.

Rule for determining export or import of service : 3(ii)

6.9

Other exemptions

Other exemptions are summarised below.

Services by performing artists - Services by a performing artist in folk or classical art forms of (i) music, or (ii) dance, or (iii) theatre, if the consideration charged for such performance is not more than one and half lakh rupees. The exemption will not apply to service provided by such artist as brand ambassador - Sr No. 16 of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 as amended w.e.f. 1-4-2015. The words in italics have been inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2015. The limit of Rs. one lakh has been increased to Rs. 1.50 lakhs w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Exemption is to performing artists and not to film actors. In Siddharth Suryanarayan v. UOI (2015) 51 GST 507 = 58 taxmann.com 194 (Mad HC DB), it was held that the two categories are entirely different. There is no discrimination.

Brand ambassador services not exempt - "Brand ambassador" means a person engaged for promotion or marketing of a brand of goods, service, property or actionable claim, event or endorsement of name, including a trade name, logo or house mark of any person - Definition clause 2(h) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012.

Brand ambassadors are subject to service tax - Para 7.11.2 of CBE&C's Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

Services by journalists - Services by way of collecting or providing news by an independent journalist, Press Trust of India or United News of India are exempt - Sr No. 17 of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012.

Parking to general public is taxable w.e.f. 1-4-2013 - Services by way of motor vehicle parking to general public was exempt upto 1-4-2013. This exemption has been withdrawn w.e.f. 1-4-2013. Leasing of space to an entity for providing such parking facility was not exempt even prior to 1-4-2013 - Sr. No. 24 of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012 as existing upto 1-4-2013. Now this entry stands omitted w.e.f. 1-4-2013.

Meaning of 'general public' - "General public" means the body of people at large sufficiently defined by some common quality of public or impersonal nature - Definition clause 2(q) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012.

Trade Union services - Service by an unincorporated body or a non-profit entity registered under any law for the time being in force, to its own members by way of reimbursement of charges or share of contribution as a trade union are exempt - Sr No. 28(a) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012.

"Trade union" has the meaning assigned to it in clause (h) of section 2 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 - Definition clause 2(zj) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 changed w.e.f. 1-4-2015 [earlier, the clause was 2(zi). However, the definition was same].

Services of mutual fund agent and distributor taxable w.e.f. 1-4-2015 - Service by a mutual fund agent to mutual fund or asset management company were exempt - Sr No. 29(c) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012 and existing upto 1-4-2015.

Service by a mutual fund distributor to mutual fund or asset management company were exempt - Sr No. 29(d) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012 and existing upto 1-4-2015.

This exemption has been withdrawn w.e.f. 1-4-2015.
