HEADNOTE: Section 16 of the Central Goods And Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit - Period April 2006 to 2008 - Whether it could not be contended that since definition of Rule 2(e) underwent amendment with effect from 1-4-2011, whereby, it was indicated that trading activity would fall in category of services, therefore rule 6(3)(c) could apply to trading activity only after 1.4.2011 - Held, yes - During relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax - Appellant company acted as a commission agent was also engaged in trading activities - Whether since appellant was not paying service tax on trading activity, credit of tax paid on services vis-a-vis input services could only be taken on a pro-rata basis as per formula stipulated in Rule 6(3)(c) - Held, yes - Whether however, since no separate accounts were maintained by appellant with regard to taxable and non-taxable services, apportionment as provided in Rule 6(3)(c) would triggered - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in denying credit of service tax - Held, yes [Para 12][In favour of revenue]GST/Cenvat Credit: Where during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax, if appellant engaged in activities of trading and commission agency did not maintain separate accounts regarding taxable and non-taxable services, it would not be entitled to credit of service tax

FACT: The appellant was engaged in trading activities as well as in commission business. The appellant obtained centralized registration with the service tax department under the category "Business Ancillary Services".

Evidently, the appellant's records were examined by the internal audit party of the department. The audit carried out revealed that the appellant had been claiming credit of service tax on various common input services which were used both for its trading activity and its business of commission agent.

As far as the commission agency business was concerned, service tax was paid by the appellant, while no service tax was paid for trading activity. Thus, the audit party came to the conclusion that excess credit of service tax had been claimed by the assessee.

The stand taken by the appellant was that during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax. It was alleged that due to an incorrect audit objection to the alleged utilization of cenvat credit qua the exempted services, the appellant had paid up the purportedly excess amount, which was, otherwise not payable.

The Adjudicating Authority, however, was not impressed with the stand taken by the appellant and, therefore, proceeded to reject its claim for refund.

The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order passed by Adjudicating Authority.

On appeal to the High Court:

HELD: Clearly, during the period in issue, i.e., 2006-07 and 2007-08, trading activity, which was one of the businesses, carried out by the appellant was not amenable to service tax. The amendment to rule 2(e), stated that there was no liability to pay service tax of trading activity, during the relevant period. [Para 9]

In this context, it may also be relevant to note, how exempted services was defined in rule 2(e) of the 2004 rules till 31-3-2011 and thereafter.

Both before and after amendment, 'exempted services' meant those taxable services, which were exempt from whole of service tax and, included those services on which service tax was not leviable, under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.2]

Therefore, given the rule position, what would govern the matter would be the determination of the issue as to whether or not, a particular service is amenable to service tax under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.3]

Since, the trading activity was not amenable service tax at the relevant period, surely, the apportionment as provided in rule 6(3)(c) would get triggered. [Para 10.4]

Having regard to the rule position and given the admitted fact that no separate accounts were maintained by the appellant, with regard to the taxable and non-taxable services, clause (c) of sub-rule 3 of rule 6 of 2004 rules would apply. [Para 11]

For the foregoing reasons, there was interference is called for with the order of the Tribunal. Accordingly, the questions of law framed are answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. [Para 12]

Section 16 of the Central Goods And Services Tax Act, 2017/Rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit - Period April 2006 to 2008 - Whether it could not be contended that since definition of Rule 2(e) underwent amendment with effect from 1-4-2011, whereby, it was indicated that trading activity would fall in category of services, therefore rule 6(3)(c) could apply to trading activity only after 1.4.2011 - Held, yes - During relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax - Appellant company acted as a commission agent was also engaged in trading activities - Whether since appellant was not paying service tax on trading activity, credit of tax paid on services vis-a-vis input services could only be taken on a pro-rata basis as per formula stipulated in Rule 6(3)(c) - Held, yes - Whether however, since no separate accounts were maintained by appellant with regard to taxable and non-taxable services, apportionment as provided in Rule 6(3)(c) would triggered - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in denying credit of service tax - Held, yes [Para 12][In favour of revenue]GST/Cenvat Credit: Where during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax, if appellant engaged in activities of trading and commission agency did not maintain separate accounts regarding taxable and non-taxable services, it would not be entitled to credit of service tax

; therefore, allegation of suppression was invalid.

Revenue argued that activity of trading could be considered as services and since during material time, it was not a taxable service, it should be construed as 'exempted service'. Since assessee has not maintained any separate account in respect of the dutiable/taxable goods/services and exempted goods/services, payment at 10 per cent/ 5 per cent of the value of the exempted services was to be made under rule 6(3). Assessee argued that trading was deemed as exempted service only from 1-4-2011; hence, demand for period prior thereto cannot be made on that count.

HELD: The goods which the assessee had traded are imported goods. As per the definition of exempted goods under rule 2(d) of CCR exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-C.E., dated 1-3-2011 is availed.

Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods. By no stretch of imagination imported goods which are traded can be considered as exempted goods. If that be so, the question of invoking the provisions of rule 6(2) and 6(3) for payment of a sum at the rate of 10 per cent/5 per cent on the value of the exempted goods would not arise at all. On this ground alone the impugned notice and the order is not sustainable in law. [Para 5.2]

Secondly, as per rule 6(2) maintenance of separate accounts is envisaged only when a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT credit. In the present case, the assessee has not availed any CENVAT credit at all in respect of input services relating to the traded goods. Therefore, question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise at all. Consequently provision of sub-rule (3) of the said rule 6 mandating payment of an amount equal to 10 per cent/5 per cent of the value of the exempted goods and exempted service would also not apply.

Even assuming but not admitting that the assessee has availed input service credit on both dutiable/exempted goods and taxable/exempted service, rule 6(3A) which came into force w.e.f. 1-4-2008 provides for reversal of credit on the input service attributable to exempted goods/services on a proportionate basis based on the turnover. In the present case, the assessee has precisely done that ab initio and has not taken any credit in respect of input services attributable to the traded goods. Calculation done by the assessee has not been disputed by the revenue and the revenue has not shown that the credit taken by the assessee in respect of input services in relation to manufactured goods was in excess of what was eligible to be taken. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence led by Revenue proving that the assessee has taken ineligible credit, the question of assessee violating the provisions of Rule 6 of the CCR, 2004 would not arise at all. [Para 5.3]

If the assessee reversed input service tax credit attributable to trading activities according to standard accounting principles, the same would suffice for satisfying the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 6. [Para 5.4]

As regards the wrong availment of credit during the period 2005-08, another show-cause notice has already been issued to the assessee which has been adjudicated and pending before Tribunal. Thus, the department was fully aware of the practices followed by the assessee and has also approved of the same. In view of the above, invocation of the extended period of time to demand service tax is also not sustainable in law. [Para 5.5]

I. Trading an exempted service only from 1-4-2011

Provisions of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, which came into force with effect from 16-08-2002 govern the entitlement to availment and utilization of cenvat credit up to 9-09-2004, on which date the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force. The 2004 Rules govern the field since 10-09-2004. [Para 5]

Under the Credit Rules, 2002 input service is defined in rule 2(c) as any taxable service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service. Rule 3(1) provided that an output service provider shall be allowed to take credit (service tax credit) of the service tax paid on input service, in the enumerated manner. Sub-clause (a) of this Rule provides that where an input service falls in the same category of taxable service as the output service, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 16-08-2002; sub-clause (b) stipulates that in any other case, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 14-05-2003. Sub rule (2) of Rule 3 provides that for the purpose of these rules, two services shall be deemed to be falling in the same category of taxable service, if the input service or output service fall in the same sub-clause of clause (105) of Section 65 of the Act.

Sub-rule (4) of rule 3 states that where a service provider avails credit on any input service and renders output services which are chargeable to service tax as well as exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be, he shall maintain separate accounts for receipt and consumption of input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of taxable output services and input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be. Sub-rule (5) of rule 3 enacts that where a service provider opts not to maintain separate accounts, as stipulated in sub-rule (4), he shall be allowed to utilize service tax credit for payment of service tax on any output service only to an extent of an amount not exceeding 35 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on such output services. [Para 6]

On a true and fair construction of the relevant provisions of the Credit Rules, 2002, it is apparent that credit could be taken on an input service falling in the same category of taxable service as the output service in respect of which the service tax liability arises and discharged from the available credit. It is axiomatic that trading in goods is neither a taxable service and could not, in the absence of a legislative/statutory fiction provided, capable of being construed as an exempted service. [Para 7]

Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, 2004 sets out the obligations of a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) provides that no cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or exempted services except in circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). Sub-rule (2) enjoins maintenance of separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input or input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service; and the quantity of input spent for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and authorizes taking of cenvat credit only on that quantity of input or input services which are intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing taxable output services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 carves out specified exclusions to the requirements set out in sub-rule (2). Sub-clause (c) of rule 6(3) stipulates that the provider of an output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

The goods which the assessee had traded are imported goods. As per the definition of exempted goods under rule 2(d) of CCR exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-C.E., dated 1-3-2011 is availed.

Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods. By no stretch of imagination imported goods which are traded can be considered as exempted goods. If that be so, the question of invoking the provisions of rule 6(2) and 6(3) for payment of a sum at the rate of 10 per cent/5 per cent on the value of the exempted goods would not arise at all. On this ground alone the impugned notice and the order is not sustainable in law. [Para 5.2]

Secondly, as per rule 6(2) maintenance of separate accounts is envisaged only when a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT credit. In the present case, the assessee has not availed any CENVAT credit at all in respect of input services relating to the traded goods. Therefore, question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise at all. Consequently provision of sub-rule (3) of the said rule 6 mandating payment of an amount equal to 10 per cent/5 per cent of the value of the exempted goods and exempted service would also not apply.

Even assuming but not admitting that the assessee has availed input service credit on both dutiable/exempted goods and taxable/exempted service, rule 6(3A) which came into force w.e.f. 1-4-2008 provides for reversal of credit on the input service attributable to exempted goods/services on a proportionate basis based on the turnover. In the present case, the assessee has precisely done that ab initio and has not taken any credit in respect of input services attributable to the traded goods. Calculation done by the assessee has not been disputed by the revenue and the revenue has not shown that the credit taken by the assessee in respect of input services in relation to manufactured goods was in excess of what was eligible to be taken. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence led by Revenue proving that the assessee has taken ineligible credit, the question of assessee violating the provisions of Rule 6 of the CCR, 2004 would not arise at all. In such a situation the only correct legal position appears to be that it is for the appellant to choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what would be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to service tax. The only obvious solution which would be legally correct appears to be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles is deducted and the balance only availed of for the purpose of payment of service tax of output service. This proposition is not against the law in view of the fact that there are several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal wherein a view has been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit."

Trading activity - Whether a service

As regards the issue as to whether trading activity can be called a service, it is quite clear that since trading activity is nothing but purchase and sales and is covered under Sales Tax Law, it may not be appropriate to call it a service. Trading activity cannot be called a service and, therefore, it cannot be considered as an exempted service also. [Para 5]

Applicability of Cenvat Credit Rules (and Service Tax Credit Rules) on trading activity

Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 provides that where output service provider does not maintain separate account, he is to follow the procedure or avail the options available under that rule. Rule 6 is applicable only when the output service provider is providing services which are chargeable to service tax and as well as exempted services. Similar is the situation in rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. Both these rules clearly speak of exempted services. Rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules also covers non-taxable services. Since trading activity was not at all a service, it is not correct to apply these provisions. [Para 7]

Eligibility for availing input service tax credit

In cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994. Therefore, there arises a situation where an assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable goods. There is no provision to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture. In such a situation the only correct legal position appears to be that the appellant choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what will be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to service tax. The only obvious solution which would be legally correct appeared to be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles was deducted and the balance only will be availed for the purpose of payment of service tax of output service. This proposition was not against the law in view of the fact the there were several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal, wherein a view had been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit. 5.3 The next question for consideration is whether CENVAT Credit can be taken in respect of trading prior to 1-4-2011. Though the CCR 2004 was amended to deem trading as an exempted service, the question is whether prior to 1-4-2011, trading can be considered as an exempted service. It is not in dispute that trading was not a taxable service prior to 1-4-2011 or after 1-4-2011. This matter was examined at length by this Tribunal in the Mercedez Benz case cited supra. In the said decision, it was held by this tribunal that trading was not a service and therefore, cannot be considered as an exempted service prior to 1-4-2011 and the amended provisions with effect from 1-4-2011 will not have retrospective effect. In the said decision, it was further held that the credit of service tax paid on common input services should be apportioned in the same ratio as the turnover of the manufactured goods and traded goods. It was further held that the input service definition under rule 2(l) of CCR in respect of business activity of the assessee covered only the business of manufacturing and not any other business. The reliance placed by the appellant on the decisions in the case of Badrika Motors (P) Ltd., Shariff Motors, Faber Heatcraft Industries Ltd. and Ghatge Patil Autofarm Machinization does not help for two reasons. These are single member decisions while the Mercedes Benz decision is a Division Bench decision and therefore, it prevails over the other decisions. Secondly, in these 4 cases, the appellants therein were rendering output services of Business Auxiliary and Authorized Service station services and therefore, in the facts of those cases, it was held that the service tax paid on GTA service could be availed as credit as the same can be considered as an input service in respect of the output service rendered. Thus the facts involved in those 4 cases relied upon by the appellant are completely different and distinguishable. In the case before us, the appellant is not an output service provider in respect of all the traded goods and no evidence has been placed before us in this regard. In such a situation, the question of taking credit on input service and its utilization thereof cannot be permitted at all prior to 1-4-2011 and we hold accordingly.

5.4 The CENVAT Credit scheme envisages nexus between input/input services and the output/output services which are taxable. Credit of input/input service tax is not permissible when the output or output service is not taxable. This implies that the cost of input/input services should form part of the value of the output/output service. This is the Essence of CENVAT credit scheme based on invoice based tax credit method. A plain reading of Rule 3 of CCR, 2004 makes this position abundantly clear. The hon'ble Apex Court considered the scope of CENVAT credit scheme in the Maruti Suzuki Ltd. v. CCE [2009] 22 STT 54 (SC) and held that unless there is a nexus between the input on which credit is taken and the out manufactured, CENVAT credit cannot be taken. The same ratio would apply in respect of input services also. In view of this position, the appellant could not have taken any credit on common input services used in the manufacture of excisable goods and traded goods prior to 1-4-2011 when trading was not a taxable service to the extent it is attributable to the traded goods. In the present case, from the records it is seen that the appellant has availed CENVAT credit on a host of inputs services without any evidence whatsoever with regard to its nexus and therefore, the entire credit attributable to the traded goods is not available to the appellant for taking or availment. The fact that the adjudicating authority, instead of denying the entire credit attributable to the traded goods, has allowed part of the input service tax credit based on a formula prescribed for the first time with effect from 1-4-2011, will not make any difference at all to the proposition that the appellant was not eligible for the credit ab-initio.

Therefore, it has to be held that trading activity cannot be called a service and, therefore, it cannot be considered as an exempted service also.

6. The next question that arises is whether Cenvat Credit Rules and Service Tax Credit Rules would be applicable. Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules is reproduced below :

"Where a manufacturer or provider of output service avails of CENVAT CREDIT in respect of any inputs or input services, [***], and manufactures such final products or provides such output service which are chargeable to duty or tax as well as exempted goods or services, then, the manufacturer or provider of output service shall maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input and input service meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service and the quantity of input meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and take CENVAT credit only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing output service on which service tax is payable."

7. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 provides that where output service provider does not maintain separate account, he has to follow the procedure or avail the options available under that Rule. But this rule is applicable only when the output service provider is providing services which are chargeable to service tax and as well as exempted services. Similar is the situation when we examine rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. Both these rules clearly speak of exempted services. Rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules also covers non-taxable services. Since trading activity is not at all a service, it is not correct to apply these provisions.

8. Then the question arises as to whether the appellant would be eligible for the full amount of service tax credit taken by them on input services can be used for payment of service on output service provided the input services have been used for providing the output services. No doubt there is no one to one correlation required. This is the reason why provisions have been made in Cenvat Credit Rules and Service Tax Credit Rules to cover such situations where an assessee is providing both exempted and taxable services. In cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both Central Excise Act as well as Finance Act, 1994. Therefore, we have a situation where an assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable goods and at the same time there is no provision to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture. In such a situation the only correct legal position appears to be that it is for the appellant to choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what would be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to service tax. The only obvious solution which would be legally correct appears to be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles is deducted and the balance only availed for the purpose of payment of service tax of output service. This proposition is not against the law in view of the fact that there are several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal wherein a view has been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit.

The scrutiny of the documents by Excise Auditor was made from October 2004 and notice was issued as follows – As per Rule 6(3) (b) & (c) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002, "the provider of output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding twenty percent of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services. However, if company has utilised more than this limit, then the excess credit utilised needs to be recovered with interest as provided in Rule 14 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002."

In view of the above, you are requested to guide on the solution to save taxes and interest if (A) The above matter relates exclusively to Capital Goods, (B) The above matter relates exclusively to Inputs/input Services (C) The above matter has combine problem of Capital Goods as well as Inputs/Input Services. Please arrange to reply at the earliest as AC (Audit) has given only two days to make payment.

Firstly, note that the ‘two day time for making payment’ is a pressure tactic. You should not fall prey to such pressures.

Secondly, the provision of 20% does not apply to Cenvat credit of capital goods. Thus, you can avail full Cenvat credit of capital goods plus 20% of credit of inputs and input services.

Thirdly, in case of 16 specified input services, restriction of 20% does not apply. See if some of input services fall in that category.

Finally, find what is the ratio of exempt services and taxable services. If (say) exempt services are 20% and if you forego 20% of credit of inputs and input services, what situation emerges? Of course, here is no provision to reverse credit on proportionate basis; but in Ballarpur Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2006 (201) ELT 146 [2007] 11 STT 321 Mumbai CESTAT, it was held that if Cenvat credit is reversed on pro rata basis, it means Cenvat credit has not been availed – relying upon Mayur Colours Ltd. v. CCE 2001(136) ELT 1111 (Tri-Mumbai). System of taking credit on proportionate basis has been accepted by the department in case of textile manufacturers/processors, where maintenance of separate account is not practically possible – CBE&C Circular No. 845/03/2006-CX dated 1-2-2007. Rule 6(3)(d) of the Cenvat Credit Rules also accepts principle of proportionate reversal in case of general insurance companies.

It can be argued that this principle should apply in all the cases.

In addition, we are also claiming Cenvat credit in total on common services like Telephone, Insurance, Bank charges, etc., since we are of the opinion that own trading is not a service and we are only providing taxable service of stock broker. According to our interpretation, restriction given in rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 is not applicable in our case.

During the course of Service Tax audit of our company, officials are considering own trading as a service and, therefore, they are forcing us to claim whole Cenvat credit restricted up to 20% of total liability and to pay the balance amount in cash. My query is

1.Whether own trading can be considered as non-taxable service

Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods. By no stretch of imagination imported goods which are traded can be considered as exempted goods. If that be so, the question of invoking the provisions of Rule 6(2) and 6(3) for payment of a sum @ 10 per cent/5 per cent on the value of the exempted goods would not arise at all. On this ground alone the impugned notice and the order is not sustainable in law. 5.3 Secondly, as per Rule 6(2) maintenance of separate accounts is envisaged only when a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT credit. In the present case, the appellant has not availed any CENVAT credit at all in respect of input services relating to the traded goods. Therefore, question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise at all. Consequently provision of sub-rule (3) of the said Rule 6 mandating payment of an amount equal to 10 per cent/5 per cent of the value of the exempted goods and exempted service would also not apply. Even assuming but not admitting that the appellant has availed input service credit on both dutiable/exempted goods and taxable/exempted service, Rule 3A which came into force w.e.f. 1-4-2008 provides for reversal of credit on the input service attributable to exempted goods/services on a proportionate basis based on the turnover. In the present case, the appellant has precisely done that ab initio and has not taken any credit in respect of input services attributable to the traded goods. Calculation done by the appellant has not been disputed by the Revenue and the Revenue has not shown that the credit taken by the appellant in respect of input services in relation to manufactured goods was in excess of what was eligible to be taken. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence led by Revenue proving that the appellant has taken ineligible credit, the question of appellant violating the provisions of Rule 6 of the CCR, 2004 would not arise at all.

5.4 The decision of the Tribunal in the case of Orion Appliances Ltd., cited (supra), also shows that if the assessee reversed input service tax credit attributable to trading activities according to standard accounting principles, the same would suffice for satisfying the provisions of sub-rule (3) of Rule 6.

Thus, the department was fully aware of the practices followed by the appellant and has also approved of the same. In view of the above, invocation of the extended period of time to demand service tax is also not sustainable in law.

Facts

The assessee is a trader in personal computers, photocopiers, telecom products and mobile phones etc. and had provided taxable services like Maintenance and Repair; Commissioning and Installation; Leased Circuit; Online Information and Data Processing and Business Auxiliary Services.

Assessee -

availed credit on service tax paid on input services utilized for its trading activities;

utilized credit to an extent not exceeding 35 per cent up to 09-09-2004 and to an extent of 20 per cent thereafter, of the Service tax payable on its taxable output services,

in terms of Rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 and Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004,

treating trading as an exempted service.

The show-cause notice dated 11-10-2006 alleged that as trading of goods is not a service, this cannot be considered as an exempted service and provisions of the Act and rules thereunder do not apply to trading activities.

The assessee reversed credit availed on service tax incurred by the assessee on sales commission, brokerage, travel agent service, warehouse charges, freight and courier charges, being input services for its trading activities.

The assessee neither responded to the show-cause notice nor attended personal hearing. Hence, the impugned order was passed ex parte.

Revenue's Arguments

Services utilized for trading of computers etc. would not amount to services utilized/consumed in the rendition of output services, since output services were provided after culmination of trading activities i.e. sale and delivery of computers etc. to customers. Input services in respect of which cenvat credit was taken stood utilized prior to delivery of computers and cannot be said to have been consumed/used in relation to rendition of output services;

Since trading is neither a service nor amounts to an exempted service, cenvat credit earned on an input services of trading-cannot be considered as credit earned on exempted service;

Consequently, cenvat credit taken in respect of input services of trading is liable to be reversed in toto and the inadmissible cenvat credit utilized for payment of service tax on taxable output services liable to be recovered, along with interest and penalty;

Since the assessee deliberately availed to disclose availment of cenvat credit on services which were not an input services for its output services, assessee contravened Rules 3 and 4 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 and the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, with an intent to evade payment of Service tax and therefore the extended period is invocable and interest and penalty also leviable.

Assessee's Arguments

The assessee submitted that -

all taxable services were provided by the assessee only in relation to computers, photocopiers etc. sold to various customers;

commissioning, installation, maintenance and repair services etc. were also services provided in relation to these traded goods;

Rule 2(b) of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 defines 'Input Services' as any service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service;

transportation of goods and the other services utilized for despatching goods to customers premises, is integral to the post-trading rendition of taxable services such as installation, commissioning, repair, maintenance etc.; and

thus, credit taken is unexceptionable.

The assessee alternatively claimed that since credit was utilized only to the extent of 35 per cent or 20 per cent of the payable service tax, as the case may be, interest should be calculated only on amount of credit actually utilized; that there is a distinction between taking of credit and utilization of credit and it is utilization alone that results in lesser remittance of tax in cash to Government and not taking of credit in assessee's books. Therefore, interest should be calculated only on the amount actually utilized, if wrongly utilized, but not on the gross credit wrongly availed.

No penalty should be imposed since availment of credit on the assumption that trading is an exempted activity was on account of interpretation and penalty is leviable only for wilful and deliberate conduct and not where availment of credit is on the basis of a mistaken but plausible interpretation of relevant provisions.

Issue Involved

Whether credit was rightly claimed and reversed ?

FACT: The revenue issued on the assessee a show cause notice alleging that it was utilizing the input service for providing output taxable service of clearing and forwarding agent service as well as for trading and proposed to raise demand upon it.

The Adjudicating Authority dropped the demand proposed in the show cause notice. He held that to be an exempted service, it must be a taxable service under the Finance Act, 1994. He further held that the trading activity was a non-taxable service. Therefore, it could not be an exempted service.

HELD: To be an exempted service, the activity should be a service. Without any statute categorizing the trading as a service, it cannot be held that it is an 'exempted service'. Therefore, the order-in-revision was not sustainable. [Para 2b]

. It is further submitted that trading activity has ever been an "exempted service" for purposes of the CENVAT Credit Rules 2004 as clarified by the explanation to Rule 2(e). IV. Interest not leviable, if credit availed not utilized

Where credit was taken or utilised and the mistake is brought to assessee's notice; an assessee corrects the mistake and immediately reverses the entry, the assessee cannot be said to have been taken benefit of the wrong entry in the account books; and if the assessee had not taken the benefit of Cenvat credit it would be not liable to pay interest i.e. when credit taken is reversed before utilisation of the credit; once the entry was reversed it is as if that Cenvat credit was not available. A few changes were further effected vide Notification No. 13/2011-CE (NT), dated 31-3-2011. On a few issues trade has requested for clarity. | Sl. No. | Issue | Clarification |

| 1. | Can credit of capital goods be availed of when used in manufacture of dutiable goods on which benefit under Notification No. 1/2011-CE is availed or in provision of a service whose part of value is exempted on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services is taken? | As per rule 6(4) no credit can be availed on capital goods used exclusively in manufacture of exempted goods or in providing exempted service. Goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-CE, dated the 1st March, 2011 is availed are exempted goods [Rule 2(d)]. Taxable services whose part of value is exempted on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services, used for providing such taxable service, shall be taken, are exempted services [Rule 2(e)]. Hence credit of capital goods used exclusively in manufacture of such goods or in providing such service is not allowed. |
| 2. | Is the credit of only specified goods and services listed in the definition of inputs and input services not allowed such as goods used in a club, outdoor catering etc., or is the list only illustrative? | The list is only illustrative. The principle is that Cenvat credit is not allowed when any goods and services are used primarily for personal use or consumption of employees. |
| 3. | How is the "no relationship whatsoever with the manufacture of a final product" to be determined? | Credit of all goods used in the factory is allowed except insofar as it is specifically denied. The expression "no relationship whatsoever with the manufacture of a final pro-duct" must be interpreted and applied strictly and not loosely. The expression does not include any goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. Only credit of goods used in the factory but having absolutely no relationship with the manufacture of final product is not allowed. While the law does not intend to allow any undue benefit to a service provider in terms of cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in providing non-taxable output activity, cenvat credit is a vested right. Once it is legally and validly availed, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific provisions exist for the same. [Para 13]

It has been a consistent judicial view that credit entitlement is on the date of receipt of inputs when the output activity was wholly dutiable. Merely because the finished goods eventually became exempt later on, the credit availed on inputs which were contained in semi-finished/finished goods form was held as not deniable. [Para 14]

In fact, in order to overcome such legal position, transitional provisions were introduced in the Cenvat Credit Rules. Rule 11, as it existed during the material period, provides that where any inputs are contained in semi-finished or finished goods form, as on date when the finished goods become exempt or output services become exempt, such credit will have to be reversed. As clarified vide Clarification No.334/1/2007-TRU, dated 28-2-2007 and also taken note of by the Madras High Court in the case of Tractor And Farm Equipment Ltd. v. Admittedly, in the instant case, the dispute is limited to credits availed on input services during a time when output service was wholly taxable. However, portion thereof became non-taxable on account of receipt of Completion Certificate later on. [Para 15]

This being the case, a harmonious reading of rule 3 read with rules 6 and 11 will suggest that eligibility/entitlement to credit has to be examined only at the time of receipt of input service and once it is found to be availed at a time when output service is wholly taxable and the said credit is availed legitimately, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific machinery provisions are made in this regard. As per TRU Clarification dated 28-2-2007, even if one assumed sale of immovable property after completion certificate to be 'exempt service', there is no legal requirement to reverse any credit availed on 'input services' in the past (prior to obtaining Completion Certificate) at all. [Para 16]

In the instant case, before obtaining the Completion Certificate, the service of the assessee was very much taxable during which period the assessee received input service.

CREDIT OF INPUT SERVICE TAX USED AS COMMON SERVICES

A manufacturing company manufactures twisted and texturising yarn. It pays excise duty on such yarn. It is also appointed dealer of POY/PFY of a Ltd. Co. Some quantity of above yarn (raw-material yarn) is consumed in manufacture of excisable yarn and he does trading for rest of the quantity. He receives commission on whole quantity of yarn purchased as a dealer. Service tax is paid on commission received on whole lot of yarn received as a dealer. The same company also manufactures machines for own use and for public sale. Excise duty is paid on manufacturing of final machines. It pays service tax on job charges paid in manufacture of making machines and also on repairs and maintenance on machines. The company is registered under excise and service tax provisions. Query - (a) Whether service tax paid on (input services) relating to job work and R and M can be set-off against service tax payable by company on output service tax on yarn commission? (b) It is said that with Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, across the board sectorial credit can be enjoyed by manufacturer-cum-service provider? (c) What are restrictions for a manufacturer-cum-service tax provider in Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004?

Basically, Cenvat provisions do not require one to one relationship. Cenvat is a common pool of credit of all duties as specified in rule 3(1). This credit can be utilised for payment of any duty or tax, as specified in rule 3(4), subject to restrictions as specified in rule 3(7). Thus, except restrictions under rule 3(7), the credit is completely inter-changeable.

Moreover, definition of input service is very wide. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’. Any relation with manufacture or provision of service is not required. Hence, in my view, Cenvat credit of any input service is available for payment of service tax on any output service.

Of course, department may not easily agree to this but I think legal position is quite clear.

A manufacturer engaged in manufacture of plastic bottles is also rendering services of a commission agent (sales agent) which is taxable as ‘business auxiliary service’. He avails credit of duties paid on various ‘inputs’ used exclusively for manufacture of excisable goods, ‘Capital Goods’ used exclusively for manufacture of excisable goods, ‘Input Services’ used for manufacture as well as for providing the service. Is he entitled to utilise Credit of the duties paid on ‘inputs’ or ‘capital goods’ for paying the service tax?

The question is raised only in light of the fact that the inputs/capital goods have no relationship at all with rendering of the service of Commission Agent.

5.1 As regards the contention that the service tax credit should have been recovered under the provisions of section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 and not under section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944, this contention is totally devoid of merits. Recovery of wrongly availed credit is provided for under Rule 14 of CCR, 2004. In the present case, the appellant is a manufacture of excisable goods and the credit taken on input services has been utilized for payment of duty on excisable goods. for the mechanism for availment of Cenvat credit by a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and providers of taxable and exempted services. Let us try to analyse and see whether traded goods can be considered as exempted goods or exempted services.

Rule 2(d) defines ‘exempted goods’, as excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to ‘nil’ rate of duty. In order to get classified as ‘exempted goods’, the goods should be first excisable goods, i.e., excise duty should be leviable on the same and then there should be an exemption from payment of excise duty or it should be chargeable at nil rate of duty. Obviously, the excise duty is not leviable on the traded goods and, hence, traded goods would not fall under the category of ‘Exempted goods’.

Rule 2(e) defines ‘exempted service’ as taxable service which is exempt from whole of the service tax leviable thereon, and includes services on which no service tax is leviable under section 66 of the Finance Act.

Bare reading of the above definition shows that the definition is wide and even covers all the services on which service tax is not leviable. However, trading activity on which VAT/CST is charged cannot be called service and, therefore, cannot be considered as an exempted service also.

On a perusal of above definition, it is clear that traded goods would neither fall under the category of dutiable/exempted goods or taxable/exempt services and, hence, rule 6 would not apply in determining the eligibility of Cenvat credit in respect of common input services used in providing dutiable goods/taxable services and traded goods.

Hon’ble CESTAT in the case of ABB Ltd. v. CCE&ST [2009] 21 STT 77 (Bang. - CESTAT)(LB) has held that the term ‘activities relating to business’ in the inclusive part of the definition of input service is a term of wide import and credit would be available in respect of all ‘Input services’ related to the business activities. Hence, based on this, one view can be taken that Cenvat credit in respect of common input services used in providing dutiable goods/taxable services and traded goods, would be available by treating them as services related to business activities.

However, such an interpretation would not be fair on account of the following reasons :

(i)Services referred to in the inclusive definition of ‘Input services’ under rule 2(l ) are required to be used in or in relation to the manufacture of final product or provision of taxable services and inclusive definition only suggests that some services which may seemingly not appear to be used in relation to the manufacture of final product would nevertheless be deemed to be so used [Prima facie view in the case of Colgate Palmolive (I) Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 12 STT 269 (Mum. - CESTAT)].

(ii)In case the assessee undertakes an activity, which cannot be called service or cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the scope/purview of the Excise Act as well as the Finance Act and, hence, to interpret that service tax credit will be allowed in respect of common input services utilized for providing one activity covered under the Act and another outside the ambit of the Act would not be fair.

(iii)Even on the grounds of equity, in case an assessee undertakes 100 per cent of this business activity as trading, he would not be entitled to credit of any input services. Hence, merely because the assessee also provides dutiable goods/taxable services, in addition to trading activity, he should not be entitled to full credit of service tax credit in respect of common inputs without the express authority of law.

Hon’ble CESTAT in the case of Orion Appliances Ltd. v. CST [2010] 27 STT 319 (Ahd. - CESTAT), while dealing with this issue, has held as under :

(i)Trading activity is nothing but purchase and sales and is covered under sales tax law; it cannot be called a service and, hence, cannot be considered as an exempted service also.

(ii)Since trading activity is not an exempted service, it is not correct to apply rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules as well as rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules.

(iii)In cases where an assessee is undertaking activity which cannot be called a service or manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both the Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994.

(iv)An assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable good.

(v)There are no provisions in the law to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture.

(vi)In such a situation, the only correct legal position appears to be that it is for the appellant to choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit.

CENVAT CREDIT – OPTION TO MAINTAIN SEPARATE ACCOUNTS

1. We are providing works contract services and job-work services where both services are liable for service tax one is at full rate and another is at abatement rate with reverse charge. We are taking Input of all input service and capital goods. Now we are doing some trading activity in same firm. Since we cannot separate common service like audit fees, accounting consultancy, bank charges etc. so we will be maintaining separate accounts. Whether this would be sufficient and if not, then, whether we have to give reverse 7% on trading turnover ?

Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, as it stood before 1-4-2016, mandated maintenance of separate books of account for taxable and exempted activities, failing which credit was liable to be reversed as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 (viz. 6 or 7 per cent; or pro rata).

Now, the requirement to maintain separate accounts has been done away within. In case of exempted as well as taxable activities, the credit cannot be taken for exempted activities and said credit is to be computed as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The said rule provides for percentage-based payment or pro rata reversal, as opted for by the assessee.

Hence, you have options :

Do not take credit of common inputs and input services

If credit is taken of common inputs and input services, then, —

either opt for percentage-based reversal or

opt for pro rata reversal.

CENVAT CREDIT – REVERSAL ON DISCOUNT RECEIVED ON INPUT SERVICES

2. One of my client has availed CENVAT credit on input service on the entire amount of the bill. Subsequently service provider has given the discount on the bill. Whether proportionate CENVAT credit to be reversed on the portion of the amount of discount received ?

Assuming no reverse charge case, credit can be taken on receipt of invoice. Further, payment of value of service and service tax should be made to the service provider within 3 months of date of invoice, failing which credit has to be reversed and can be re-taken only after full such payment.

As regards Part/Discounted Payment, it is provided in Circular No. 122/3/2010-S.T., dated 30-4-2010 that, in cases where receiver of service makes part/discounted payment only after 3 months, then, he is entitled to take full or pro rata credit provided he has also paid the amount of service tax, (whether proportionately reduced or the original amount) to the service provider.

Going by the Circular, if original amount of service tax is paid to the service provider, then, credit would not be touched. Accordingly, we opine as under :

[a]

If service tax amount is not changed and only value is reduced/negotiated, then, full credit may be taken [full and final settlement towards value would amount to 'payment of value' and would suffice requirements of rule 4(7)].

[b]

Alternatively, if service tax amount is also changed [say, original service tax is Rs. 14 and service tax as per revised value is Rs. 9.8], then, service provider may take benefit of rule 6(3) [credit of Rs. 4.2 may be taken by service provider] and service receiver may take credit of Rs. 9.8.

SERVICE TAX – GOVERNMENT/LOCAL AUTHORITY CAN BE BUSINESS ENTITY

3. Can Government/Local Authority be Business Entity for the purpose of section 65B of the Finance Act, 1994 ?

All services by government or local authority to any business entity are liable to service tax. Business Entity [Section 65B(17)]means any person ordinarily carrying out any activity relating to industry, commerce or any other business or profession. Since even government or local authority can be carrying out any activity relating to industry, commerce or any other business or profession, hence, they can also be business entity. Accordingly, the services might be liable to service tax.

However, by virtue of Entry 54 of Mega Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012, services provided —

by Government or a local authority

to another Government or local authority

falling under section 66D(a)(iv),

are exempt from service tax.

Hence, even if government or local authority is business entity, services availed by it from another government or local authority falling under section 66D(a)(iv) are exempt.

SERVICE TAX - SMALL SERVICE PROVIDER EXEMPTION - CLUBBING OF PARTNER'S RECEIPTS WITH THAT OF FIRM

1. Our partnership is registered under service tax and has been paying service tax under commercial coaching services. Now, the partners are also individually providing the same services however their receipts are less then Rs. 9 Lakhs. Please clarify whether partners are liable to pay service tax on the basis of their relation with firm and whether partners' receipts can be clubbed with that of the firm ?

As per definition of 'person' under section 65B(37), person is defined to include firm as a separate category of persons. Therefore, for purpose of service tax, firm is a separate person from its partners and same view would apply in respect of claim of small service provider's exemption.

However, creation of bogus entities or bogus separation of receipts in order to claim SSI-exemption has been held to be impermissible under Central Excise and same attracts clubbing of turnover.

In short, if resources are same (i.e., infrastructure, finance, staff, management, branding, control are same), then, clubbing would get attracted.

SERVICE TAX - COMMISSION FROM FOREIGN COMPANIES - LIABILITY TO SERVICE TAX

2. We are providing services of commission agent to Singapore based foreign company for the sale of iron ore. The commission is received in foreign exchange. Please clarify whether this would be liable to service tax ? Can there be any tax planning ?

As per rule 2(f) of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012, intermediary is defined to mean "intermediary" means a broker, an agent or any other person, by whatever name called, who arranges or facilitates a provision of a service (hereinafter called the 'main' service) or a supply of goods, between two or more persons, but does not include a person who provides the main service or supplies the goods on his account. As per rule 9(c), the Place of Provision of services of an intermediary would be location of such intermediary (w.e.f. 1-10-2014).

In view of definition under Rule 2(f), commission agents and other agents, or the like would be liable to service tax on their location basis. Accordingly, Indian commission agents of foreign companies are liable to service tax w.e.f. 1-10-2014, even if the commission is earned by them in the foreign exchange.

Hence, it appears that your services are liable to service tax. We would suggest of any tax planning in view of very wide words used.

Nevertheless, if it can be shown that the services being provided are consultancy services, not relatable to supply/sale of goods, then only, rule 9(c) read with rule 2(f) would not apply.

CENVAT CREDIT - WORKS CONTRACT SERVICES v. TRADING SERVICE

3. We are having 2 divisions : trading division and service division (works contract services). Can we take credit of input services received from sub-contractor which is used exclusively to provide works contract service ?

Since trading activity is also an exempted service under rule 2(e) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004; hence, you become provided for taxable as well as exempt service and have to comply with the provisions of rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Therefore, you should either maintain separate accounts and, if not, pay 7% (6% up to 18-5-2015) of the value of exempted services of trading as per rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

The provisions of rule 6 override provisions of all other rules.

SERVICE TAX - DISTRIBUTORS v. COMMISSION AGENTS

4. We are distributors of products of Johnson & Johnson. The following is the procedure :

J&J supplies to us @ Rs. 100 (invoiced) ;

We sells to our customer @ Rs. 100 ;

Bad debts, if any, are borne by us ;

We raise a debit note of Rs. 10 towards profit margin on sales ;

On confirmation J & J raises credit note of Rs. 10 on us.

Thus, we end up paying Rs. 90 to J&J.

Whether we are liable to pay service tax ? Whether our practice needs amends ?

In our considered view, your practice is very well in order. There is no service tax liability, as you are not an agent of J&J; in fact, you buy from J&J and sell to the customers. The fact that J&J invoices you first and title apparent gets transferred would show that there is pure sale of goods to you and by you to your customers.

It appears that this practice is being adopted by J&J to control your profit margin.

However, for the period prior to 1-4-2016, does this mean that a service provider can take and retain full credit on input services received even after receipt of Completion Certificate. The situation will be governed by rule 3 till such time, i.e., till the time rule 6 was specifically made applicable by virtue of the deeming fiction created. [Para 7] It is trite law and in terms of rule 3, cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used to provide output service is eligible. In fact, the Bombay High Court in the case of Mercedes Benz India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2016] 66 taxmann.com 332/54 GST 367 held, qua 'trading activity' vis-à-vis rule 6 mechanism, that it could not have been the intention of the Government to encourage trading by allowing full credit prior to 1-4-2011 and that the 'value' of exempt supply in nature of trading as provided after 1-4-2011 in law for complying with proportionate credit requirements should be made applicable to the period prior to 1-4-2011 as well. [Para 8]

In the instant case, it is evident that the assessee had started taking only proportionate credit after receipt of Completion Certificate which was after due intimation to the revenue and also certified by independent CA. It is the case of the assessee that rule 6 in toto cannot apply prior to 1-4-2016 to the instant case, since sale of immovable property is not exempt service at all. In the light of the provisions of rule 3, the assessee cannot avail full cenvat credit on input services received after obtaining Completion Certificate. However, the assessee cannot be expected to pay an amount equal to 8%/10% of sale price of immovable property after obtaining such Completion Certificate where no service tax is paid as if it is sale of immovable property, since rule 6 per se does not apply to the instant case until 1-4-2016 at all. Even after 1-4-2016, since the assessee had availed only proportionate credit, it is not legally required to pay 8%/10% amount under rule 6(3), since it can be said to have maintained separate accounts as required under rule 6(2). [Para 9]

Having taken only proportionate credit of service tax paid on input services after receipt of Completion Certificate, duly backed by CA certificate and certified work sheets for the proportionate credits availed after Completion Certificate and also demonstrated on sample basis during the course of hearing, the assessee has fulfilled its obligation under rule 3 read with rule 6 and as such it is not liable to pay an amount equal to 8%/10% of the 'sale price of immovable property' after receipt of completion certificate under rule 6. [Para 11]

The next question for consideration would arise as to whether the assessee was also required to reverse proportionate credit, out of the valid input service credits availed by it during the period 2010 till obtaining Completion Certificate, i.e., availing during the time when whole of output service of construction of residential complex was taxable. [Para 12]

While the law does not intend to allow any undue benefit to a service provider in terms of cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in providing non-taxable output activity, cenvat credit is a vested right. Once it is legally and validly availed, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific provisions exist for the same. [Para 13]

It has been a consistent judicial view that credit entitlement is on the date of receipt of inputs when the output activity was wholly dutiable. Merely because the finished goods eventually became exempt later on, the credit availed on inputs which were contained in semi-finished/finished goods form was held as not deniable. [Para 14]

In fact, in order to overcome such legal position, transitional provisions were introduced in the Cenvat Credit Rules. Rule 11, as it existed during the material period, provides that where any inputs are contained in semi-finished or finished goods form, as on date when the finished goods become exempt or output services become exempt, such credit will have to be reversed. As clarified vide Clarification No.334/1/2007-TRU, dated 28-2-2007 and also taken note of by the Madras High Court in the case of Tractor And Farm Equipment Ltd. v. CCE [2015] 54 taxmann.com 122/50 GST 68 and eventually upheld by the Apex Court, such embargo applies only to inputs and not to input services at all. Admittedly, in the instant case, the dispute is limited to credits availed on input services during a time when output service was wholly taxable. However, portion thereof became non-taxable on account of receipt of Completion Certificate later on. [Para 15]

(v)There are no provisions in the law to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture.

(vi)In such a situation, the only correct legal position appears to be that it is for the appellant to choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. (vii)Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what would be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to excise duty/service tax. The only obvious legally correct solution would be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles is deducted and the balance only availed for the purpose of payment of service tax on output service.

(viii)There are several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal wherein a view has been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit.

Further, while appreciating that the decision reached by the Hon’ble CESTAT was not as proposed in the show-cause notice or in the appeal, the bench also stated that the procedure adopted by the department was also not correct and at the same time, as per the law the assessee is not eligible for service tax paid on input service attributable to trading activity and, hence, the only solution that can be thought of has been discussed above.

Conclusion

4. The above judgment really deserves kudos because the Hon’ble CESTAT has preferred a very well reasoned and fair judgment on an issue, which has wide ramifications to majority of the assessees across the country as well as for the department. Also it needs to be appreciated that the members of the Bench have also prescribed the way and the periodicity for reversal of credit, taking into consideration practical difficulties faced for working out the same.

This issue has been discussed and litigated over a period of time since the introduction of Cenvat credit in respect of service tax. It is high time that CBEC realizes the need for providing a clarification on this issue so as to ensure that the litigation on the same is put to rest.

CENVAT CREDIT

We are providing both taxable and exempt services. Taxable services are to the tune of Rs. 45 lakhs and exempt services are Rs. 30 lakhs. Total input service tax paid is Rs. 3,00,000 which includes Rs. 1,00,000 which is directly related to taxable services. Balance Rs. two lakhs relates to common input services like telephone, rent, etc. We would like to know whether provision of proportionate credit under rule 6(3) applies to entire input credit of Rs. three lakhs or whether we can take full credit of Rs. one lakh and apply ratio to balance credit of Rs. two lakhs ?

Basic issue is whether rule 6(2) and 6(3) are mutually exclusive or whether they are complimentary. Of course, applying the ratio to entire credit is a safer option and in second case, some litigation is possible and, hence, it should be taken only after disclosing all details to the Department and after considering possible cost of litigation (after making full disclosure). However, my views are as follows—

Rule 6(2) and 6(3) should be taken as complimentary and not mutually exclusive. The words used in rule 6(3) are ‘notwithstanding anything contained in rule 6(1) and 6(2), the manufacturer of goods or provider of output service, opting not to maintain separate accounts, shall follow either of the following options as applicable to him’.

This sub-rule can be interpreted to mean that the assessee can follow rule 6(2) for inputs and input services for which he can maintain separate records and accounts and follow rule 6(3) in respect of inputs and input services for which the assessees opts not to maintain separate accounts.

In my view, fair interpretation is that rule 6(3) should apply to cases of common inputs and common input services where the assessee is not in a position to maintain separate accounts. Thus, rule 6(2) and 6(3) are complimentary.

In costing, there are concepts of ‘allocation’ and ‘apportionment’. The costs which can be allocated directly to a particular product should be so allocated, while costs which cannot be directly allocated to any particular product/service, should be apportioned on a reasonable basis. This principle can be applied here.

The input goods/services which can be directly allocated to taxable goods/services and exempt goods/services should be allocated under rule 6(2). Full credit should be allowed of the Cenvat credit allocable to taxable goods/services and no credit should be allowed for the Cenvat credit allocable to exempt goods/services. The remaining input credit/input services should be apportioned between taxable goods/services and exempt goods/services on the basis of formulae given in rule 6(3A). This should give best possible and most fair results. Of course, this should be done after making full disclosure to the Department, to avoid charge of suppression of facts.

INPUT SERVICES USED FOR SELF-MANUFACTURED AS WELL AS TRADED GOODS

We are manufacturers of engineering products. We also are traders of those products, i.e., we procure these goods under our brand name and sale. We have appointed selling agents for sale of our products (both self-manufactured and traded). We pay selling commission to our indenting agents. The selling agents charge service tax on the commission. We avail Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission paid by us on traded goods as well as self-manufactured goods, and utilise the same for payment of excise duty on our self-manufactured products. Department has issued a show-cause notice to us, informing that we are not eligible for service tax paid by us on commission attributable to traded goods. Please advise.

You are eligible for Cenvat credit of service tax paid both on self-manufactured goods and traded goods, for the following reasons -

(1)Definition of ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is very wide. As per inclusive part of the definition, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’, since the words used are ‘such as’ and not ‘viz.’.

(2)The inclusive part of definition clearly covers ‘sales promotion’. The inclusive part of definition does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’.

(3)Cenvat Credit Rules do not require any one to one relation between input and output.

(4)Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not require distribution of Cenvat credit in any particular ratio. Entire credit of service tax at HO or depot or branch offices can be transferred to any unit without any restriction. The rule makes no distinction between services used for manufacture and services used for other activities like trading, financing, etc.

(5)The Finance Minister in para 148 of his Budget Speech on 8-7-2004 has stated as follows, "I propose to take a major step towards integrating tax on goods and services. Accordingly, I propose to extend credit of service tax and excise duty across goods and services".

(6)Thus, the Cenvat Credit Rules have to be interpreted keeping this goal in mind and, hence, cannot be interpreted narrowly. As per doctrine of purposive interpretation, an interpretation which advances purpose of the Statute should be preferred over an interpretation which defeats the purpose.

(7)It is clear that after introduction of the Cenvat Credit Rules, the whole company is treated as one single entity for Cenvat credit. The definition of ‘input service’ and ‘input service distributor’ has abolished distinction between ‘goods’, ‘manufacture’ and ‘services’. Entire company is treated as one unit for purpose of Cenvat credit, as is the position under ‘Goods and Service Tax’ (GST) which has been set as the goal. Even concept of ‘LTU’ (Large Taxpayer Unit) is a step in that direction.

(8)Even assuming that there is some ambiguity (though really there is none), it is well-settled principle that the benefit of doubt goes to assessee.

Thus, Cenvat credit availed by you is legally correct.

However, you must keep in mind that current decisions of Tribunal are highly conservative and, hence, ultimate result is uncertain. You should be mentally prepared to pay interest @ 13%, if final decision goes against you.

9.11 Provisions upto 31-3-2008

Rule 6(3) has been radically changed w.e.f. 1-4-2008. Provisions upto 31-3-2008 are summarised below.

If assessee opts not to maintain separate accounts in respect of inputs and input services utilised for exempted goods/exempted output services as required under rule 6(2), he has to pay ‘amount’ of 10% of total price (excluding taxes) of exempted final product [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

In case of output services, he could utilise credit only upto 20% of service tax on output services. [He could ‘take’ full credit of service tax on input services, but utilise only upto 20% of tax payable on output services].

The third option i.e. proportionate reversal of Cenvat credit was not available upto 31-3-2008.

Partial manufacture/provision of exempted products/services — Cenvat credit of inputs and input services is not available if final product/output service is exempt from excise duty/service tax. In case of manufacturer manufacturing both exempt and dutiable goods (or service provider providing taxable as well as exempt services), it may happen that same inputs/input services are used partly for manufacture of dutiable goods/output services and partly for exempted goods/services. In such cases, the manufacturer/service provider has two options — (a) Maintain separate inventory and accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services. In such cases, he should not avail Cenvat credit of the inputs and input services which are used in exempted final services at all — Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules (b) Pay 10% ‘amount’ if he does not maintain separate inventory and records, if he is a manufacturer — Rule 6(3)(b) [If he is service provider, his credit is restricted to 20% of tax payable, as explained later] [provision upto 31-3-2008]

‘Amount’ if separate inventory and records not maintained - If the manufacturer opts not to maintain such separate accounts, he has to pay an amount equal to 10% of the ‘price’ of such exempted goods. Such payment can be made by debit to Cenvat credit account or PLA [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

Reversal of Cenvat credit in case of some exempted goods - In case of some specified exempted goods, the manufacturer of these final products only has to reverse Cenvat credit they had taken on inputs and input services, which were used for manufacture of exempted final product. - Rule 6(3)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Cenvat credit on capital goods — If capital goods are partly used for exempted goods and party for dutiable final products, entire Cenvat credit of duty paid on capital goods is available. Cenvat credit of duty on capital goods is not allowable only when it is exclusively used for manufacture of final products [rule 6(4)] — confirmed in Idea Cellular v. CCE (2009) 19 STT 423 = 36 VST 217 (CESTAT).

No reversal or payment of amount in certain cases — If excisable goods are removed to SEZ unit, SEZ developer, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting, payment of 10% ‘amount’ is not required [rule 6(6)].

Cenvat credit of service tax in case of supplies made by DTA to EOU - Supplies from DTA to EOU are entitled to Cenvat credit of service tax paid — para 6.11(v) of FTP.

Proportional Cenvat in case of general insurance companies providing taxable as well as exempt services - Rule 6(3)(d) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2007 provided an option to general insurance service providers providing taxable as well as exempted insurance schemes and who do not maintain separate input/input services credit accounts, to utilise Cenvat credit proportionate to the inputs and input services used in providing output services. The scheme was applicable only to general insurance services referred to in section 65(105)(d) and is optional - para 11.1 of D.O. F. No. 334/1/2007-TRU dated 28-2-2007 issued by Shri R Sekar, Joint Secretary (TRU). Now this specific provision has been deleted w.e.f. 1-4-2008.
