On a plain reading of the provisions of section 80HHC, it is evident that it applies to the assessee engaged in the business of export out of India including trading of goods. The expression 'business of export' must be given its due meaning. It not only speaks of export out of India, but also includes 'trading of goods'. [Para 7]

Indisputably, the CBDT issued a Circular No. 621, dated 19-12-1991 by way of explanatory notes to the provisions of section 80HHC. Said circular provided for modification of provisions relating to exemption of income from exports. The amendment by inserting sub-section (3) in the said provision was carried out so as to compensate the exporter from the comparative disadvantages faced by him in the international market. The formula, as was existing prior to 1991 as stated in the circular, often used to provide a distorted figure of export profits when receipts like interest commission, etc., which did not have an element of turnover were included in the profit and loss account and, thus, it was clarified that 'profits of the business' for the said provision would not include receipt by way of brokerage, commission, interest or any other receipt of a similar nature. It was, however, categorically stated that as some expenditure might be incurred in earning these incomes, which in the generality of cases is part of common expenses, ad hoc 10 per cent deduction from such incomes is provided to account for these expenses. The amendments in no uncertain terms were to take effect from 1-4-1992, i.e., for the assessment year 1992-93, and subsequent assessment years.

The aforementioned circular dated 19-12-1991 issued by the CBDT was binding on the Department. [Para 8]

Once it was held that the amendment carried out in 1991 by reason of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1991 was prospective in nature, ex facie the High Court committed a serious error in opining that the same being clarificatory in character would apply to the assessment year 1990-91. By reason of the purported clarification issued by the CBDT in terms of the said Circular, the area of exemption had not been widened, it has in effect and substance been curtailed.

By reason of such amendment, the Parliament did not intend that the income derived by way of brokerage/commission by the assessee should not be reckoned for the purpose of computing profit or loss earned by a person engaged in the business of export but by reason thereof the deduction to the extent of 10 per cent was held to be allowable thereby. [Para 9]

Section 80HHC was incorporated in the Act for providing incentive to export houses. It is now a well-settled principle of law that although the exemption provisions are to be construed strictly as regards the applicability thereof to the case of the assessee, but once it is found that the same is applicable, the same are required to be interpreted liberally. [Para 10]

It is also trite law that an exemption is to be granted unless it is expressly taken away. [Para 11]

The expression 'income arising out of business of export' brings within its sweep not only the export of any goods or merchandise manufactured or possessed by the assessee but also of trading goods. The Parliament, therefore, intended to provide incentive when a positive profit is earned by an exporter. [Para 12]

Resultantly, the judgment of the High Court could not be sustained and it was to be held that income derived by the assessee towards commission/brokerage for procuring orders of export for other exporters would be eligible to exemption from tax under section 80HHC.[Para 16]

Service of commission agent

The services of commission agent were taxable under Business Auxiliary Services till 1-7-2012. The services are taxable after 1-7-2012 also.

Commission, in common parlance, has duly been understood to mean a fixed charge payable to an agent or a broker for providing services for facilitating a transaction - Bangalore Turf Club v. Regional Director, ESIC (2014) 9 SCC 657 [SC 3 member bench].

Trade discount is not a commission and not liable to service tax - In Ahmedabad Stamp Vendors Association v. UOI (2002) 124 taxman 628 = 257 ITR 202 (Guj HC), the stamp vendors were purchasing stamps from Government in bulk and selling in retail, for which they were getting stamps at a discount of 0.5% to 4%. The relations between Government and stamp vendors were on Principal to Principal basis. It was held that this is a discount and not commission - view confirmed in CIT v. Ahmedabad Stamp Vendors Association (2012) 25 taxmann.com 201 = 210 Taxman 269 (SC) [The issue related to TDS under section 194H of Income Tax Act but principle applies to all sales] – followed in Roorkee Stamp Vendors Association v. State of Uttarakhand (2014) 227 Taxman 81 (Mag) = 42 taxmann.com 271 (Uttarakhand HC).

Sale and purchase of stamp paper is not commission - Discount (of 1%) given to stamp vendors who purchase and sale stamp paper is not a commission. Sale by Treasury Officer to stamp vendors is on principal to principal basis - Chief Treasury Officer v. UOI (2014) 220 Taxman 403 = 37 taxmann.com 391 (All HC DB). [The issue related to TDS under section 194H of Income Tax Act but principle applies to all sales]

Sale of SIM cards to distributors at discounted rate is not commission - Sale of SIM cards to distributors at discounted rate is not commission (and hence income tax TDS is not applicable), as the relationship is principal to principal and not principal and agent – Bharti Airtel v. Dy CIT (2014) 52 taxmann.com 31 (Karn HC).

This would be so even if payment is received in free foreign exchange. See discussions under Place of Provision of Service Rules.

In the instant case, the assessee had availed cenvat credit in the course of constructing the real estate projects developed by it, in terms of rule 3. The assessee, however, was paying service tax in case of properties which were not yet sold by way of sale deed even after obtaining Completion Certificate, where advances were received for such properties prior to the date of obtaining such Completion Certificate. The assessee submitted that it availed only proportionate cenvat credit determined on scientific basis by it (considering square foot area where service tax was paid and balance area where service tax will not be paid after completion certificate). It had not only given due intimation in this regard at the time of obtaining Completion Certificate but also produced CA certificate to support its case in this regard.

The instant appeal involves the following legal questions:

(a)

Whether receipt of consideration for residential units sold as immovable property after receipt of Completion Certificate amounts to providing exempted service and rule 6 is applicable in such case and as such whether the assessee is liable to pay 8%/10% amount of exempted value under rule 6.

(b)

Whether credit can be allowed to the assessee under rule 3 in such circumstances.

(c)

Whether the assessee can be said to have 'maintained proper separate accounts' as required under rule 6.

(d)

Whether the assessee is required to reverse cenvat credit availed during the period when output service was taxable before receipt of completion certificate, since such services were availed to construct entire property and portion of such property did not attract service tax after receipt of completion certificate.

(e)

Connected to the question (d), whether the assessee is eligible to seek refund of the amount paid under protest towards credit availed from 2010 till receipt of Completion Certificate based on CERA audit objection, wherein such credit was sought to be reversed based on considering square foot area where service tax was paid and balance area where service tax will not be paid after Completion Certificate. [Para 5]

There is merit in the submission of the assessee that for the purpose of invoking provisions of rule 6, in the present set of facts and circumstances, the output service must first be exempt service. Upon receipt of Completion Certificate for the projects, the output activity of sale of residential units becomes 'non-service' as per provisions of section 65B of the Finance Act, 1994 read with definition of the term 'exempt service' under rule 2(e). This is further supported by specific amendment carried out in rule 6(1), whereby with effect from 1-4-2016, Explanation 3 was inserted specifically dealing with a situation as in the instant case, where a deeming fiction was created that for the purposes of rule 6 exempted services as defined in clause (e) of rule 2 shall include an activity, which is not a 'service' as defined in section 65B(44) provided that such activity has used inputs or input services. There was no such stipulation prior to 1-4-2016 in law and prima facie such situation was not to be treated as exempt service and did not attract the mischief created under rule 6. [Para 6]

However, for the period prior to 1-4-2016, does this mean that a service provider can take and retain full credit on input services received even after receipt of Completion Certificate. The situation will be governed by rule 3 till such time, i.e., till the time rule 6 was specifically made applicable by virtue of the deeming fiction created. [Para 7]

It is trite law and in terms of rule 3, cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used to provide output service is eligible. In fact, the Bombay High Court in the case of Mercedes Benz India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2016] 66 taxmann.com 332/54 GST 367 held, qua 'trading activity' vis-à-vis rule 6 mechanism, that it could not have been the intention of the Government to encourage trading by allowing full credit prior to 1-4-2011 and that the 'value' of exempt supply in nature of trading as provided after 1-4-2011 in law for complying with proportionate credit requirements should be made applicable to the period prior to 1-4-2011 as well. [Para 8]

There is also no dispute that during the period of dispute, this service was fully and unconditionally exempt from service tax under Notification No. 8/2003-S.T.

As regards the BPO service, the same involved processing of mediclaims and transaction processing for the assessee's clients. These activities are specifically covered by the definition of Business Support Service as given in section 65(105)(zzzq) read with section 65(104c) of the Finance Act, 1994 which came into force with effect from 1-5-2006. It is well settled law that when a new service is brought within tax net by introducing a new clause in section 65(105) of the Finance Act, 1994, it has to be presumed that that service was not covered by any other clauses of section 65(105). Therefore, BPO service involving transaction processing and processing of mediclaims etc. became taxable with effect from 1-5-2006 and as such, the same was not taxable during the period of dispute. [Para 7]

So far as the Call Centre Service (Business Auxiliary Service) provided to overseas clients is concerned, there is no dispute that this is taxable service under section 65(105)(zzb) read with section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 and the same was fully exempt from service tax during the period of dispute in terms of exemption Notification no. 8/2003-S.T., If the assessee is providing a taxable service, although exempt by way of notification, but which had been exported, the assessee would be entitled to take Cenvat input credit in terms of rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Para 8]

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. It also imported finished goods on payment of duty. During the course of the business, it availed a number of services which were used in relation to the manufacture of final products as well as in relation to selling and marketing of final products, etc. As the assessee was having its head office situated in Mumbai which was registered as ‘Input service distributor’, the assessee received various services which it distributed to various factories as an input service distributor by issue of invoice in terms of rule 4A(2). The credit so distributed and availed by the assessee at various factories was utilized to discharge the excise duty liability of various factories on various final products manufactured by them. The revenue, however, denied said input service credit taken by the assessee on ground that said credit was availed for duty paid final products as well as exempted final products and, hence, it was not entitled to input service credit as per rule 6(2), as it was not maintaining separate account of input service for dutiable as well as exempted goods. Accordingly, demand was confirmed on assessee along with penalties.

Admittedly, in the instant case, the dispute is limited to credits availed on input services during a time when output service was wholly taxable. However, portion thereof became non-taxable on account of receipt of Completion Certificate later on. [Para 15] This being the case, a harmonious reading of rule 3 read with rules 6 and 11 will suggest that eligibility/entitlement to credit has to be examined only at the time of receipt of input service and once it is found to be availed at a time when output service is wholly taxable and the said credit is availed legitimately, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific machinery provisions are made in this regard. As per TRU Clarification dated 28-2-2007, even if one assumed sale of immovable property after completion certificate to be 'exempt service', there is no legal requirement to reverse any credit availed on 'input services' in the past (prior to obtaining Completion Certificate) at all. [Para 16]

In the instant case, before obtaining the Completion Certificate, the service of the assessee was very much taxable during which period the assessee received input service.

From a bare reading of rule 4(7), it is clear that the assessee is not required to wait till output service is sold to the service recipient. The assessee can take the credit immediately after the day on which bill/challan of input service is received. In the instant case, there is no dispute that the assessee has availed the credit after receipt of bill, challan in respect of input service. Therefore, the assessee was legally entitled to take the credit on the date after the receipt of service bills/challans. Therefore, the availment of cenvat credit by the assessee is absolutely legal and correct in accordance with rule 4(7). At the time of taking credit, there is no existence of any exempted service. Therefore, there is no application of rule 6. The part of the service was exempted only after obtaining completion certificate. Thereafter the assessee was not required to avail the cenvat credit on the input service, if any, received after obtaining the Completion Certificate. In the instant case, the assessee has either not availed the cenvat credit in respect of the services received after obtaining the Completion Certificate in respect of exempted service or availed proportionate credit attributed to the taxable output service. For this reason also rule 6 has no application for the period after obtaining the Completion Certificate.

In case of service becomes exempted at a later stage, unlike the provision for manufactured goods provided under rule 11(1)(2) and (3), there is no such provision in respect of the service. The only provision for the service is provided under sub-rule (4) of rule 11. From a reading of sub-rule(4) of rule 11, it can be seen that even if an output service provider avail the credit and output service becomes exempted; in such case the credit only in respect of inputs lying in stock or is contained in taxable service is required to be paid, whereas there is no provision for payment of cenvat credit equivalent to the input services used in respect of exempted service. Therefore, the cenvat credit availed in respect of input service is not required to be paid back under any circumstances. [Para 18]

Therefore, the assessee was not legally required to reverse any credit which was availed by it during the period 2010 till obtaining Completion Certificate, i.e., during the period when output service was wholly taxable in its hands, merely because later on some portion of the property was converted into immovable property on account of receipt of Completion Certificate and on which no service tax would be paid in future. [Para 19]

It is the case of the revenue that by demanding 8%/10% amount of sale of immovable property after obtaining Completion Certificate, the credits availed in the past are ipso facto regularized. It should, however, be appreciated that payment of 8%/10% is only an option or rather a mechanism to seek credit reversal on lump sum basis, where the assessee cannot maintain separate accounts/reverse proportionate credit on turnover basis or in cases where the assessee himself so chooses to follow such option. In other words, it is a substitute to regularise credit instead of accepting proportionate credit availed during the time when output service was exempt. Since the credits availed when output service was wholly taxable cannot be called into question, it cannot be said that such 8%/10% amount of sale of immovable property is to regularise not only credits availed after completion certificate but also availed during 2010 till the time completion certificate was obtained. In that sense, rule 6, if invoked, can deal with only prospective credits availed after output activity becoming exempt and not credits availed before the output activity become exempt. [Para 21]

The Larger Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE [2006] 4 STT 231 (New Delhi - CESTAT) had examined a similar issue and held that an agent engaged only for procuring purchase orders for the vendors on commission basis does not engage in any of the activities enumerated in the para 2.2 of Trade Notice No. 87/97 of Madurai Commissionerate (Equivalent to CBEC Circular, dated 11-7-1997), directly or indirectly. The commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with the work of clearing and forwarding of the goods would be a person, who in the ordinary course of business, makes contract for sale or purchase of the goods for others. The definition of ‘Commission Agent’ under section 2(aaa ) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 would apply in or in relation to service tax as it applies to duty of excise by virtue of clause (2) of section 65. Services of commission agents were included in the definition of ‘Business auxiliary service’ under clause (19) of section 65 with effect from 2003, which included service of the commission agent. The activity of mere procurement of purchase order for the principal on commission basis of a commission agent was treated separately by the Parliament from the activities of the C&F agent. In the instant case, the Commissioner (Appeals) found that the marketing agents appointed by the assessee did not carry out any activity other than procuring orders for the assessee’s goods. This activity was brought under the tax net with effect from 1-7-2003 when business auxiliary service was introduced. Business auxiliary service, inter alia, covers promotion of marketing or sale of goods. Therefore, the service involved was correctly classifiable under business auxiliary service with effect from 1-7-2003. Same services could not be classified under ‘Clearing & forward agent’s service’ for any previous period as the scope of clearing and forwarding agent’s service was not modified when business auxiliary service was introduced in the Act. Prabhat Zarda Factory (India) Ltd.’s case (supra) relied on by the revenue was overruled by the Larger Bench decision of the Tribunal in Larsen & Toubro Ltd.’s case (supra). In the circumstances, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be sustained and the appeal filed by the revenue was liable to be rejected.

The judgment of Gujarat High Court in case of Cadila was discussed at the Central Excise Tariff Conference on Tariff Matters organized by CBE&C on 28 and 29 October 2015. Minutes of the conference and decisions taken have been circulated vide CBE&C instruction F No. 96/85/2015-CX.1 dated 7-12-2015.

As per Para B.30 of aforesaid instruction dated 7-12-2015, the conference noted that in case of Cadila, the sales commission agent was only trading in goods i.e. buying and selling the goods without undertaking any sales promotion or advertising. If activity of sales commission agent involves an element of sales promotion, Cenvat credit of service tax paid on commission agent is available.

Full extract of para B.30 of the CBE&C instruction dated 7-12-2015 is given below.

B.30 Meerut Zone - Cenvat Credit - Admissibility of Cenvat Credit on Service Tax Paid on Sales Agency Commission Service:

Issue - CBEC vide its Circular No. 943/4/2011-CX dated 29.04.2011 at point No.5 has clarified that credit of service tax paid on sales commission services (Business auxiliary services) used in 28 relation to manufacture/sale of finished goods is admissible under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. However, there are conflicting judgments of Hon'ble High Courts in this regard. Hon'ble High Court of Gujarat in case of Cadila Health Care [2013 (30) STR 0003] has disallowed the said Cenvat credit whereas Hon'ble Tribunal in case of Birla Corporation Ltd. [2014 (35) STR977] followed the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Bombay and allowed the credit. Board may be requested by the conference to issue necessary clarification on the subject to avoid further litigation and to achieve uniformity in the practice of assessment.

Discussion & Decision

The conference discussed the issue in detail and the facts of both the cases where apparently conflicting judgments have been delivered. It was noted that the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Gujarat was in a very specific set of circumstances where the sales commission agent seemed to be only trading in the goods i.e. buying and selling the goods without undertaking any sales promotion or advertising. In the said judgment, Hon'ble court noted that "there is nothing to indicate that such commission agents were actually involved in any sales promotion activities as envisaged under the said expression. Obviously, commission paid to the various agents would not be covered in this expression since it cannot be stated to be a service used directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of final products or clearance of final products from the place of removal". Board Circular No. 943/4/2011-CX., dated 29-4-2011 at point No. 5 on the other hand has explained the situation where the commission agent renders the service of sales promotion in following words -"....... Moreover the activity of sale promotion is specifically allowed and on many occasions the remuneration for same is linked to actual sale.......". Board circular directs that input service credit would be available when there is a element of sales promotion as sales promotion is a service. Thus, the conflict between the judgment and the circular is not as large as is perceived. Both the Board circular and case laws on the subject allow credit of input services, when the activity of the sales commission agent involves an element of sales promotion.

Impact of decision of Gujarat High Court - Assessees and Tribunal benches within jurisdiction of Gujarat High Court were bound by decision of Gujarat High Court. However, even these assessees could take Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission, if there agreement is properly worded to establish that the agent is not simply trading but is also doing additional work of sales promotion and advertising.

Assessees outside jurisdiction of Gujarat High Court could take a stand that in view of contrary decision of Punjab and Haryana High Court, they are not bound by decision of Gujarat High Court.

FACT: The assessee, a commission agent, claimed deduction on account of dharmada, gaushala and pathshala expenses. He also claimed deduction on account of messing expenses for his constituents. The ITO disallowed the first claim in toto but allowed the claim in respect of messing expenses to the extent of half. On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the assessee's claim in respect of dharmada, etc. In regard to the claim for messing expenses for the constituents it held, it did not involve any element of entertainment. These expenses were necessitated by the nature of the trade carried on by the assessee. The constituents, who came from outlying agencies, had to stay on for lunch or dinner and for that purpose the assessee provided them with meals. It accordingly allowed the claim of the assessee in full.

On reference :

HELD: Following the decision in Thakur Das Shyam Sunder v. Addl. CIT [1974] 93 ITR 27 (All.), the Tribunal was justified in holding that the receipts on account of dharmada, gaushala and pathshala could not be treated as part of the trading receipts of the assessee.

As regards the allowability of messing expenses in the case of Brij Raman Dass & Sons v. CIT [1976] 104 ITR 541 (All.), it was held that the phrase 'entertainment expenses' occurring in section 37(2A) includes all expenses incurred in connection with the business of the entertainment of customers and constituents and the entertainment may consist of providing refreshments or it may consist of providing some other form of entertainment. For the assessment year 1972-73, the relevant provisions of section 37(2A) were amended and no amount was admissible under the head 'Entertainment expenses'. In this view normally the entire amount claimed by the assessee would be disallowed but it was found that half of the amount was allowed by the ITO. The department had not gone in appeal either to the Commissioner or to the Tribunal. This part of the allowance could not be touched. The half which had been allowed by the ITO was outside the purview of the appeal in the Tribunal. The result would be that ultimately the ITO's order stood restored.

Note : The decision was partly in favour of assessee and partly in favour of revenue.

INSTRUCTION F. NO. 137/72/2008-CX.4, DATED 21-11-2008

UTILIZATION OF ACCUMULATED CENVAT CREDIT RESTRICTED IN TERMS OF ERSTWHILE RULE 6(3)(c) OF CENVAT CREDIT RULES, 2004

Kindly refer to your letter C.No. 715/Hqrs/Audit/08 dated 20-11-2008 on the subject mentioned above wherein the issue of utilization of accumulated Cenvat credit has been raised.

The matter has been examined and the following points emerged during its consideration,—

Prior to 1-4-2008 [before the amendment in rule 6(3)] the option available to the taxpayer, under rule 6(3), was that, he was allowed to utilize credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output service. However, there was no restriction in taking Cenvat credit and also there was no provision about the periodic lapse of balance credit. This resulted in accumulation of credit in many cases.

W.e.f. 1-4-2008, under the amended rule 6(3), the following options are available to the taxpayers not maintaining separate accounts :

(i)

Option No. 1 - In respect of exempted goods, he may pay an amount equal to 10% of the value of exempted goods; and in respect of exempted/non-taxable services, he may pay an amount equal to 8% of the value of such exempted/non-taxable service.

OR

(ii)

Option No. 2 - He may pay an amount equivalent to Cenvat credit attributable to inputs and input services attributable to exempted goods and non-taxable/exempted services.

As stated earlier, many taxpayers had accumulated Cenvat credit balance as on 1-4-2008. The matter to be considered was whether this credit balance should be allowed to be utilized for payment of service tax after 1-4-2008.

As no lapsing provision was incorporated and that the existing rule 6(3) of the Cenvat Credit Rules does not explicitly bar the utilization of the accumulated credit, the department should not deny the utilization of such accumulated Cenvat credit by the taxpayer after 1-4-2008. Further, it must be kept in mind that taking of credit and its utilization is a substantive right of a taxpayer under value added taxation scheme. Therefore, in the absence of a clear legal prohibition, this right cannot be denied.

Pending issues may be decided accordingly.

FACT: The assessees, namely, FA and FW, were sourcing agents of two foreign companies, ‘DSI’ and ‘B’ which were importers of readymade garments. The assessees identified vendors (garment manufacturers) in India for procurement and supply of garments to said companies. They also provided operational assistance to vendors to ensure supply of goods to foreign companies as per terms and conditions of purchase orders and ensured payment by foreign companies to them. Besides that the assessees also engaged services of foreign commission agents for identifying customers and rendering marketing services on their behalf. For the above activities, namely, (i) service provided to foreign companies, (ii) operational assistance provided to Indian vendors and (iii) services received from foreign commission agents, the Commissioner confirmed demand of service tax under the category of ‘Business auxiliary service’ and also imposed penalties.

On appeal :

HELD: The assessees rendered services of the same description to the vendors. The assessee-FA rendered services to DSI by identifying the vendors in India for procurement and supply of garments. These services were rendered without a contract with the vendors and were incidental to services rendered to DSI. Similarly the assessee-FW had rendered services to the foreign company-B by monitoring production and export of garments by the vendors as per B’s orders. ‘B’ was the recipient of the service. FW had Research & Development facilities and assisted ‘B’ to decide the designs of the garments. The services rendered to ‘B’ and ‘DSI’ were correctly treated by the Commissioner as not exempt as exports during the material period. Only on 1-3-2007, such services when delivered and used outside India by a recipient located outside India, were extended the exemption. [Para 4]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Assessee used to receive goods from principal, store them in its godown, clear them to buyers, collect payment for sale and transmit sale proceeds to principal after taking commission - Whether services of appellant were of a consignment agent which was included in definition of ‘clearing and forwarding agent’s service’ - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, appellant had no prima facie case against demand of service tax - Held, yes [Para 3]

FACT: In instant appeal, the dispute arose as to whether the assessee could be said to have rendered services of ‘consignment agent’ or ‘commission agent’ to their customers.

HELD: In case of the first assessee, the assessee identified buyers for their principals, collected purchase orders, completed the sale transactions, collected payments and transmitted thereof to the principal. Thus, it had functioned as commission agent. The service of a commission agent was expressly covered under ‘Business auxiliary service’ which was introduced into the statute book only on 1-7-2003. The period of dispute in the appeal was prior to that date. The assessee had made out a prima facie case against the demand of service tax and, accordingly, waiver of pre-deposit and stay of recovery in respect of the amount of tax and penalties were to be granted. [Para 2]

In case of other two assessees the assessees were, admittedly, physically dealing with excisable goods. It used to receive such goods from its principal, store them in their godown, clear them to buyers, collect payments for the sale and transmit the same to the principal after taking commission. That activity would attract the definition of ‘clearing and forwarding agent’, which includes consignment agent. Apparently, therefore, the assessees seemed to have rendered service of a consignment agent to it customers during the respective periods. Such service was taxable during the period of dispute. Hence, there seemed to be no prima facie case for the assessees against the demand of service tax. Accordingly, it was directed to pre-deposit the tax amounts. [Para 3]

Rule 5 is applicable when any input or input service has been used in providing output service which is exported. The term 'output service' as defined in rule 2(p) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2005 during the period of dispute, means any taxable service provided by the provider of taxable service to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder or any other person, as the case may be, and the expression 'provider' and 'provided' shall be construed accordingly. In terms of Explanation to rule 2(p), if a person liable for paying service tax does not provide any taxable service or does not manufacture final products, the service tax for which he is liable to pay service tax shall be deemed to be the output service. Thus, in terms of definition of 'output service' in rule 2(p) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the 'output service' has to be a 'taxable service'. A 'taxable service' is the one in respect of which, in terms of the provisions of section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994, the tax at the prescribed rate is required to be paid and these services are those services which are specified in various clauses of section 65(105). A service which is not specified in any of the clauses of section 65(105) of the Finance Act, 1994, could not be treated as a 'taxable service' during the period of dispute. Since BPO service which was provided by the assessee to their offshore client and which involved transaction processing and the processing of mediclaims, etc. was not a taxable service during the period of dispute and it became taxable as "Support Service for business of Commerce" with effect from 1-5-2006 under section 65(105)(zzzq) read with section 65(104c) ibid, during the period of dispute, this service would not be covered by the provisions of rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 and accordingly, the Cenvat credit would not be available in respect of inputs or input services used in or in relation to providing of this service, whether for offshore clients or for domestic clients. Therefore, the assessee were not entitled for Cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in or in relation to providing of the BPO service during the period of dispute, even if the same had been exported. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 read with rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Charge of service tax on services rendered from outside India - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee, a manufacturer of excisable goods, exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it - It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A - Whether as per reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and it had wrongly taken cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods - Held, yes [Paras 2 and 6] [In favour of revenue]Service Tax : Where assessee exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it and availed credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, it was not eligible to avail cenvat of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services for trading of imported goods

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. During the year 2011-12, it had exported final products manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it. It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on import of services received from one 'C' under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A.

The Adjudicating Authority having discovered that the assessee had availed service tax credit on marketing consultancy services for traded goods (exempted goods) rendered by 'C' opined that the assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and the cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods was erroneous and recoverable in terms of rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

Thereupon the assessee reversed the cenvat credit to the extent of service tax attributable to trading of imported goods and also paid interest. It asserted that it was eligible for the cenvat credit in respect of market consultancy services.

The Adjudicating Authority confirmed the demand of service tax and interest and also imposed equal penalty on the assessee under rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 11AC of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order-in-original.

On second appeal:

HELD: The Adjudicating Authority discovered that the assessee has availed service tax credit on marketing consultancy service on traded goods rendered by 'C' and as per the reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, the assessee has wrongly taken the proportionate cenvat credit to the extent of service tax attributable to trading activity. Further the cenvat credit has been reversed on being pointed out by the Adjudicating Authority. In the impugned order, the Commissioner (Appeals) has discussed the whole issue with cogent reasoning and has rightly rejected the appeal of the assessee. Therefore, as far as confirmation of demand and interest is concerned, there is no infirmity in the impugned order.

As far as the levy of penalty is concerned, unless and until there is a finding that there was suppression of fact and irregular availement of credit, the question of levying penalty under rule 15(2) does not arise. Moreover, in the instant case, the assessee reversed the duty along with interest on being pointed out by the Adjudicating Authority and there was no intention to evade payment of duty as is required under rule 15 read with section 11AC. Therefore, the penalty levied upon the assessee was liable to be set aside. [Para 6]

In case of Third Country Shipments (TCS), if the Indian party buys and sales the goods, there is no issue of GST. However, if the Indian party gets only commission, he becomes intermediary and liability of GST arises. Hence, exemption from GST has been provided on such commission w.e.f. 1-10-2019, as stated below.

Services provided by an intermediary when location of both supplier and recipient of goods is outside the taxable territory have been exempted w.e.f. 1-10-2019 - Sr No. 12AA of Notification No. 9/2017-IT(R) dated 28-6-2017, inserted w.e.f. 1-10-2019.

16.17 Importation of service is 'supply'

As per section 7(1)(b) of CGST Act, importation of service, for a consideration whether or not in the course or furtherance of business, is 'supply' and subject to GST.

Thus, import of service from HO or branch outside India will be subject to GST even if no payment was made to HO or branch outside India.

Import of service from related person taxable even if without consideration - Import of services by a (*) person from a related person or from any of his other establishments outside India, in the course or furtherance of business is taxable even if without consideration - paragraph 4 of Schedule I of CGST Act [ * - The word was 'taxable'. This word has been omitted vide CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 w.e.f. 1-2-2019. Thus, import by any person from a related person outside India shall be 'import', but it should be in the course or furtherance of business.

Valuation of supply of import of services by a related person where recipient is eligible to full input tax credit - CBI&C, vide circular No. 210/4/2024-GST dated 26-6-2024 has clarified as follows -

In case of import of services by a registered person in India from a related person located outside India, the tax is required to be paid by the registered person in India under reverse charge mechanism. In such cases, the registered person in India is required to issue self-invoice under Section 31(3)(f) of CGST Act and pay tax on reverse charge basis.

Where the foreign affiliate is providing certain services to the related domestic entity, and where full input tax credit is available to the said related domestic entity, the value of such supply of services declared in the invoice by the said related domestic entity may be deemed as open market value in terms of second proviso to rule 28(1) of CGST Rules. Further, in cases where full input tax credit is available to the recipient, if the invoice is not issued by the related domestic entity with respect to any service provided by the foreign affiliate to it, the value of such services may be deemed to be declared as Nil, and may be deemed as open market value in terms of second proviso to rule 28(1) of CGST Rules.

Thus, value of supply of import of services by a related person where recipient is eligible to full input tax credit is Nil and hence GST is not payable under reverse charge.

Sub-section (6)(ii) provides that if any person carrying on eligible business, to which the section can apply, earns commission or brokerage (as explained above), such a person will not be able to pay tax on presumptive basis in respect of the eligible business.

Apparently, the intention is to provide that in computing income in the nature of commission or brokerage being a business of an assessee, the section would not apply. However, the language of the provision suggests that even if an assessee is carrying on, say, trading business, being eligible business and also derives commission or brokerage income, then also the presumptive tax provision will not apply to him in respect of both the businesses, that is, trading and the commission or brokerage business.

4.9.3 Agency Business

Sub-section (6)(iii) provides that the section will not apply to 'a person carrying on any agency business'.

Agency business is described as follows (http://business.yourdictionary. com/agency):

"The relationship between an agent and a principal in which the agent acts for and represents the principal on the basis of the principal's instructions".

As discussed earlier, sub-section (6)(ii) covers any income earned by a commission agent. Prima facie, it would cover transactions where a person acts as an agent to carry out certain transactions incidental to his business. Thus, clause (iii) overlaps clause (ii).

Sub-section (6)(iii) covers the case where a person is carrying on agency business. In the light of the above discussions about an agent and agency business, it could be said that a person who is dealing in the goods of one or more principals, without carrying on trading activity of his own, is engaged in the agency business. Although, he is engaged in trading, the activity is in the nature of service rendered to someone else for effecting his sales. Normally, such person would purchase directly from or from a source identified by the person (principal) for whom he is acting as an agent. Also, he would have some contractual relationship with the Principal which would specify the limits to which he can bind the Principal as also specify assistance which the Principal would provide in the business of selling. The intention is not to permit such person to avail of the option of presumptive tax under the section.

Agency business could cover both: in respect of goods and/or services. Hence, the provision would not apply, say, to an insurance agent or an agent of Post Office or an agent rendering services for marketing of securities, etc.

Further, as discussed above, if a person apart from carrying on trading activities of his own e.g. of dealing in plastic furniture, also, carries on some agency business e.g. of representing a specified manufacturer of plastic furniture, the section would not apply to such person.

Thus, it appears that non-applicability of the section is fixed qua person and not qua business. In other words, if a person carries on any of the activities specified in sub-section (6), he/it cannot opt for presumptive taxation.

4.9.4 Increase in threshold limit to Rs. 1 crore

The second amendment is in definition of 'eligible business' contained in Explanation (b)(ii) providing for the threshold limit. Presently, it is: turnover or gross receipt should not exceed Rs. 60 lacs. If, it is less than that the business is considered as eligible business.

The amendment raises the threshold limit to Rs. 1 crore effective from 1-4-2013. Thus, any person engaged in business having a turnover or gross receipts of less than Rs. 1 crore, from and after assessment year 2013-14, would qualify for presumptive tax payable under the section.

Rule 6 speaks about obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) of rule 6 states that cenvat credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input or input services which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or for providing exempted services. Sub-rule (2) of rule 6 states that in case the manufacture or service provider uses common inputs/input services, then such manufacturer or service provider has to maintain separate accounts and credit is to be taken only on that quantity of input or input service which is intended for manufacture of dutiable goods or providing taxable services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 speaks about the situation when such manufacturer or service provider does not maintain separate accounts. It provides for two options. It was amended vide Notification No. 10/2008-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2008 with effect from 1-4-2008. As per the new sub-rule (3) of rule 6, the manufacturer/service provider opting not to maintain separate account has to follow either of the following two options:-

A manufacturer shall pay 10 per cent (5 per cent with effect from 7-7-2009) of sale price of the exempted goods and an output service provider shall pay 8 per cent (6 per cent with effect from 7-7-2009) of the value of the exempted services; or

Reverse the credit on inputs and input services pertaining to exempted goods and exempted services as per the procedure and conditions prescribed in rule 6(3A). [Para 5]

The rule 6(3A) states that while exercising the option, the manufacturer of goods or the provider of output service shall intimate in writing the department regarding the option exercised. In the instant case, admittedly there is no intimation given by the assessee informing its exercise of option. The contention of the department is that when the assessee has not intimated its option in writing then the assessee is bound to pay the duty amount calculated under the first option. The said rule does not say that on failure to intimate, the manufacturer/service provider would lose his choice to avail second option of reversing the proportionate credit. Rule 6(3A) is nothing but a procedure contemplated for application of rule 6(3). Therefore, the argument of the revenue that the requirement to intimate the department about the option exercised is mandatory and on failure the assessee has no other option but to accept and comply rule 6(3)(i) and make payment of 5 per cent/10 per cent of sale price of exempted goods/value of exempted services is not acceptable or convincing. The rule 6(3A) does not lay down any such restriction. The procedure and conditions laid in rule 6(3A) is intended to make rule 6(3)workable and not to take away the option available to the assessee. In any case, at no stretch of imagination can it be said that on failure to intimate the department, rule 6(3)(i) would automatically come into application. [Para 6]

Therefore, the impugned demand raised against the assessee was not legal and proper. [Para 7]

The appellant-bank was an agent of the Reserve Bank of India. Under an arrangement, it undertook the Government transactions, namely, collection of direct tax/indirect tax, payment of pension, human resource department transactions under various departments, the Government deposits like RBI Bonds, PPF, Senior Citizen Savings Scheme etc. and it charged commission on the Government transactions. The Commissioner found that the entire tax had escaped assessment due to suppression by the bank. He rejected the argument of the appellant that it undertook the impugned activity as an agent of the RBI. It was under statutory obligation to conduct the Government business which was not exigible to service tax. This statutory function could not be termed as service. The impugned activities were normally undertaken by the treasury of the Government. The statutory function performed by the Government could not be treated as taxable service. The Commissioner observed that as per Notification No. 22/06-ST, dated 31-5-2006, taxable services provided or to be provided to any person by the RBI was exempted from service tax liability during the period 10-9-2004 to 30-9-2007. The assessees rendered services of the same description to the vendors. The assessee-FA rendered services to DSI by identifying the vendors in India for procurement and supply of garments. They co-ordinated with vendors for production, logistics and shipment of goods ordered, to DSI. FA rendered services to vendors by attending to the processing of purchase orders placed by DSI, by giving necessary operational assistance in the execution and ensuring the receipt of sale proceeds. These services were rendered without a contract with the vendors and were incidental to services rendered to DSI. Similarly the assessee-FW had rendered services to the foreign company-B by monitoring production and export of garments by the vendors as per B’s orders. ‘B’ was the recipient of the service. FW had Research & Development facilities and assisted ‘B’ to decide the designs of the garments. The services rendered to ‘B’ and ‘DSI’ were correctly treated by the Commissioner as not exempt as exports during the material period. Only on 1-3-2007, such services when delivered and used outside India by a recipient located outside India, were extended the exemption. [Para 4]

The assessees, had rendered services to the companies in terms of their contracts with them. They assisted in procurring of purchase orders by the vendors. They monitored progress and timely execution of the export orders placed by the companies. There was no contract between the assessees and their respective vendors. The assessees admittedly rendered the services described in the show-cause notices as evaluation of prospective customers for the companies, processing of purchase orders, customer management, processing of transactions, information and tracking of delivery schedules, operational assistance for marketing, formulation of customer service and pricing policies, managing distribution and logistics. The services rendered to the vendors and the foreign companies by the assessees, conformed to the statutory definition of ‘Support service of business or commerce’ (SSBC). The services rendered to the foreign companies and vendors were, therefore, classifiable under ‘SSBC’ and not under ‘BAS’. Levy on SSBC was introduced with effect from 1-5-2006. Therefore, the demands of service tax on those services, categorizing them as BAS for the period prior to 1-5-2006, from the assessees were not sustainable. [Para 4.1]

As regards BAS received by the assessees from foreign agents, the CBEC had clarified the jurisdiction where the Act operated in the territory of India in its Circular F.No. 36/4/2001, dated 8-10-2001. [Para 4.2]

As clarified by the Bombay High Court, in the case of Indian National Shipowners Association v. Union of India [2009] 18 STT 212, it was only after enactment of section 66A on 18-4-2006 that taxable services received from abroad by a person belonging to India are taxed in the hands of the Indian residents. The assessees, in the instant case, had received BAS from commission agents based abroad mostly prior to 18-4-2006. There is no provision in the Act to tax the assessees for these services. Therefore, demands on this account for the period prior to 18-4-2006 had to fail. [Para 4.3]

As the demands failed, no penalty could be imposed. In the circumstances, demand of tax, interest and penalties imposed in the impugned orders was liable to be set aside except for an amount paid by the assessee-FA for the period from April, 2006 to September, 2006, under reverse charge method as Indian recipient of services of foreign commission agents. In fact, in such case, there is no duty liability at all and hence question of Cenvat really should not arise.

However, in various cases, it has been held that if assessee still pays duty, Cenvat credit is not required to be reversed and receiver of goods can avail Cenvat credit (case law discussed in another chapter).

In case of service provider, question of 'manufacture' does not arise.

Service Provider eligible for Cenvat credit

20.3-5 As per rule 3(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules, provider of output service shall be allowed to take Cenvat credit of specified duties and taxes. Thus, only a person who is providing taxable output service will be eligible to take Cenvat credit.

Output Service - "Output service" means any service provided by a provider of service located in the taxable territory but shall not include a service - (1) specified in section 66D of the Finance Act, 1994; or (2) where the whole of service tax is liable to be paid by the recipient of service [Rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules, as inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012] [Section 66D of Finance Act, 1994 covers list of services in negative list].

Rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules (as existing upto 1-7-2012 and from 29-2-2008) was reading as follows - "output service" means any taxable service, excluding the taxable service referred in section 65(105)(zzp) of Finance Act, 1994 (This is GTA service) provided by the provider of taxable service, to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder or any other person, as the case may be, and the expressions 'provider' and 'provided' shall be construed accordingly.

Till 29-2-2008, rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules stated that "output service" means any taxable service provided by the provider of taxable service, to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder or any other person, as the case may be, and the expressions 'provider' and 'provided' shall be construed accordingly.

The reference to Goods Transport Agency Service (falling under section 65(105)(zzp) of Finance Act, 1994 of Finance Act, 1994) has been inserted to clarify that GTA service will not be treated as 'output service' where consignor/consignee is liable to make payment of service tax. Thus, service tax on GTA service will have to be paid by consignor/consignee only by cash and not through Cenvat credit.

HEADNOTE: Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Period June 2005 to October 2006 - Assessee, a manufacturer, was registered as an ‘input service distributor’ - It received various services and distributed same to various factories - It utilized input service credit availed at various factories for payment of excise duty liability of various factories on final products manufactured by them - Revenue denied said credit on ground that though input service credit was availed by assessee for duty paid as well as exempted final products, but it had not maintained separate records for inputs used in manufacture of dutiable and exempted goods - Whether since assessee had not maintained, separate accounts of input service separately for dutiable as well as non-dutiable exempted goods, in view of rule 6 only option left with assessee was either to reverse proportionate input service credit or to reverse 10 per cent of value of exempted final product at time of clearance - Held, yes - Whether assessee was not entitled to avail input service credit in full but it had to reverse input service credit proportionately availed for exempted final product - Held, yes [Paras 15 &16]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. It also imported finished goods on payment of duty. During the course of the business, it availed a number of services which were used in relation to the manufacture of final products as well as in relation to selling and marketing of final products, etc. As the assessee was having its head office situated in Mumbai which was registered as ‘Input service distributor’, the assessee received various services which it distributed to various factories as an input service distributor by issue of invoice in terms of rule 4A(2). The credit so distributed and availed by the assessee at various factories was utilized to discharge the excise duty liability of various factories on various final products manufactured by them. The revenue, however, denied said input service credit taken by the assessee on ground that said credit was availed for duty paid final products as well as exempted final products and, hence, it was not entitled to input service credit as per rule 6(2), as it was not maintaining separate account of input service for dutiable as well as exempted goods. Accordingly, demand was confirmed on assessee along with penalties.

On appeal :

HELD: As per the provisions of rule 6, the assessee has to maintain separate accounts of input/input services for both dutiable as well as non-dutiable exempted goods. In case assessee fails to maintain separate accounts for input/output services, then he shall pay an amount equal to 10 per cent of total price excluding sale tax and other taxes, if any, paid on such goods of the exempted final product charged by the manufacturer for sale of such goods at the time of such clearances from the factory. [Para 13]

In the instant case, undoubtedly the assessee had not maintained separate accounts of input service credit separately for dutiable as well as non-dutiable exempted goods. The only option left with the assessee was either to reverse proportionate input service credit or to reverse 10 per cent of the value of the exempted final product at the time of clearance. [Para 14]

In assessee’s own case, the Commissioner vide order No. 15/MI/2008, dated 31-7-2008 had held that assessee had to reverse the input service credit proportionately. The same view would be taken and it was to be held that assessee was not entitled to avail input service credit in full but it had to reverse input service credit proportionately, which is the intent of the law. [Para 15]

In view of the above discussion, requantification of the amount of reversal was required to be made to ascertain the proportionate inadmissible input service credit availed by the assessee for exempted final product. For the said purpose, the matter was sent back to the adjudicating authority to requantify the amount of inadmissible input service credit as discussed above. As issue involved in this case was a matter of interpretation of the admissibility of input service credit, no penalty was warranted in these appeals. Hence the penalties were dropped. [Para 16]

First of all considering the issue of trading income of the assessee. There is no dispute that the assessee is engaged in the import and export of the goods which is in the nature of trading activities. As per the Income-tax Act, the trading activity is not entitled for the exemption under section 10AA. However, the SEZ Rules have been framed by Central Government by virtue of the delegated Rule making power given to it by the Special Economic Zone Act 2005. As per rule 76 the term "service" includes trading activities if it relates to the import of the goods for the purposes of export in terms of its explanation to Rule 76 of 2006. [Para 7]

As per the first explanation of rule 76 trading will be treated as "service" if it is related to the import of the goods for the purpose of the export. In this case there is no dispute that goods imported by the assessee are in fact exported to other countries from its unit at Special Economic Zone. [Para 8]

The provisions as specified under The Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 would have overriding effect on the Income Tax Act because Special Economic Zone Act, 2005 is a Special Act and a later Act of the Parliament. [Para 10]

Since the Defortment is not able to point out any change in law or facts, therefore, respectfully following the order of Tribunal in earlier assessment year 2008-09, the claim of assessee was allowed in respect to its income from trading activity. [Para 11]

Secondly coming to the issue of denial of exemption in respect of warehousing. It is noted that the assessee has received Rs.23,06,539/- as warehouse charges. For corroborating this fact, the assessee has produced FIRC, ledgers, invoices for consultancy and warehousing charges. On perusal of the records including the remand report of Assessing Officer it is noted that the Assessing Officer disallowed the exemption on warehousing charges by observing that the assessee initially had shown the import of the goods as purchases and thereafter showed it as purchase return. According to Assessing Officer, on such transaction of purchase, and thereafter purchase return the assessee has shown warehouse income for Rs. 23,06,539. As per the Assessing Officer, the assessee cannot earn warehousing charges on such transaction and, therefore, such income is not entitled for exemption under section 10AA. It is noted the Rule 76 of SEZ Rules 2006 defines "Services" includes warehouse activity also, so income from the said activity qualify for exemption under section 10AA on the same reasoning as that given for trading activity. As a matter of fact, the assessee has raised the bill for the warehousing charges and the payment was also received for the same by foreign exchange. The FIRC is also placed in support of the payment. Indeed the assessee has recorded the transaction as purchase and purchase return along with quantitative details of the goods in the books of account. So, the question arises as to whether the accounting entries can change the character of the transaction. It is noted that the assessee has raised the invoice for the warehousing and handling charges. The Assessing Officer /Commissioner (Appeals) has not pointed out any defect in the bill, payment of the bill and the FIRC in support of the income. Hence, it is considered that the accounting entries cannot form the sole basis for denying the exemptions on account of warehousing charges to the assessee. As stated earlier, when warehousing activity has been included in the definition of 'service' as per Rule 76, therefore, the income from warehousing qualifies for exemption under section 10AA and, thus, the claim of the assessee is to be allowed. The service provider can avail Cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services and excise duty paid on capital goods, but not of excise duty paid on food items.

Composite contract of material plus service - The contract is composite contract of material plus services. Hence, rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules should be applicable.

Departmental clarification that food served in restaurants is 'exempted goods' - Para 8.4.3 of CBE&C's education Guide released on 20-6-2012 states that sale of food in restaurant would amount to clearance of exempt goods and thus, provisions of Rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules will be applicable.

Sale of food is deemed sale of goods, as per Constitution - Article 366(29A) of Constitution, as amended by Constitution (46th Amendment) Act, 1982, w.e.f. 2-2-1983 states as follows- 'Tax on the sale or purchase of goods' includes - - (f) a tax on supply, by way of or as part of any service or in any manner whatsoever, of goods, being food or any other article for human consumption or any drink (whether or not intoxicating), where such supply or service, is for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration - - And such transfer, delivery or supply of any goods shall be deemed to be a sale of those goods by the person making the transfer, delivery or supply and a purchase of those goods by the person to whom such transfer, delivery or supply is made.

Thus this is 'deemed sale of goods'.

Value in case of trading - As per Explanation I(c) to rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules, in case of trading, 'Value' for purpose of rule 6(3) and 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules shall be the difference between the sale price and the cost of goods sold (determined as per the generally accepted accounting principles without including the expenses incurred towards their purchase) or 10% of cost of goods sold, whichever is more.

Common input services - It is a fact that common input services are used both for deemed sale of goods and provision of output (taxable) service.

How to apply rule 6 in case of common input services ? - There are three possible views :

(a)

The 60% (in case of restaurant service)/40% (in case of outdoor catering service)/30% (in case of food service with mandap/shamiana/convention service) of value (on which service tax is not paid) shall be deemed to be value of 'exempted goods' . In effect, assessee can avail only 40% (in case of restaurant service)/60% (in case of outdoor catering service)/70% (in case of food service with mandap/shamiana/convention service) of Cenvat credit of input services and balance Cenvat credit is required to be reversed.

(b)

The sale of food is to be treated as sale of goods as per Constitutional provisions. Thus, difference between sale price of goods and purchase price of inputs should be taken as value of 'exempted services' as per Explanation I(c) to rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules. For example, in case of restaurant services, service tax is payable on 40% of value. Thus, 60% is to be taken as value of sale of food. If total value is 100 and value of purchase of goods is (say) 40, the value of 'exempted service' will be 20 (60 - 40). Thus, total value of service = taxable service + Exempt service = 40 + 20 = 60. Thus, the assessee can avail Cenvat credit of common input services in the ratio of 40/60 i.e. 66.67% of common input services and balance 33.33% should be reversed.

HEADNOTE: Section 65(25), read with section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Taxable services - Clearing and Forwarding Agent's Services - Period from April 2001 to March 2004 - Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with work of clearing and forwarding of goods, service would not be a taxable service under Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services - Said service is appropriately classifiable under Business Auxiliary Services and is exempt for period from 1-7-2003 to 9-7-2004 under Notification No. 13/2003-ST [Paras 2 to 8] [In favour of assessee]Service Tax : Where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with work of clearing and forwarding of goods, service would not be a taxable service under Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services

FACT: Facts

The assessee gets TV sets manufactured by three manufacturers.

Three manufacturers of TV sets place orders on manufacturers of picture tubes.

The picture tubes are directly supplied by the picture tube manufacturers and payments are received from the manufacturers of TV sets directly.

The rates of picture tubes are however settled by the assessee with the supplier/manufacturers of picture tubes.

After receiving payment from the manufacturers of TV sets, manufacturers/suppliers of picture tubes pay agreed amounts as commission, to the assessee.

Department sought levy of service tax on this commission under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services'.

Issue Involved

Whether commission earned by assessee was liable to service tax under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' ?

HELD: Commission on purchase not covered under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' :

The conjunctive 'and' between the words 'clearing' and 'forwarding' indicate and mean that where clearing operations are separate from forwarding operations, levy of tax would not be attracted i.e. there would be no charge of tax if the transaction involved only one of the two components of the conjuncted service namely 'clearing' and 'forwarding'. The expression a clearing and forwarding agent in relation to clearing and forwarding operations, in any manner' contemplates only one person operating both as the clearing and the forwarding agent; and if a person has rendered service as forwarding agent without rendering any service as 'clearing agent' he could not be considered to have rendered both services as a 'clearing and forwarding agent'. [Para 2]

'Clearing and forwarding operations' would be various activities having a bearing on clearance of goods and would normally involve documentary processes and arrangements for transfer of goods to their destination; and may also involve clearance at subsequent stages during forwarding operations. A clearing and forwarding agent normally undertakes the following activities :-

(a)

Receiving goods from the factories or premises of the principal or his agents;

(b)

Warehousing these goods;

(c)

Receiving despatch orders from the principal;

(d)

Arranging despatch of goods as per the directions of the principal by engaging transport on his own or through the authorised transporters of the principal;

(e)

Maintaining records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; and

(f)

Preparing invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 3]

Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for the vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of the enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with the work of clearing and forwarding of goods, the service would not be a taxable service as defined in section 65(105)(j) read with section 65(25) which defines a clearing and forwarding agent. [Para 4]

In this case, assessee neither receives goods from the factory premises of the principal; warehouses such goods; receives despatch orders from the principal; arranges despatch of goods as per directions of the principal by engaging a transport on its own or through authorised transporters of the principal; nor maintains records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; nor even prepares invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 5]

8D.1-5 AO's power to determine amount of expenditure incurred pre-AY 2007-08 - Up to AY 2006-07, no method has been provided for computing the expenditure incurred by the assessee in relation to exempt income. Even though no such method has been prescribed by the 1961 Act, the Assessing Officer has, first of all, to ascertain the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of the expenditure incurred in relation to income which does not form part of the total income under the Act. Even where the assessee claims that no expenditure has been incurred in relation to income which does not form part of total income, he will have to verify the correctness of such claim.

In case, he is satisfied with the claim of the assessee with regard to the expenditure or no expenditure, as the case may be, he is to accept the claim of the assessee insofar as the quantum of disallowance under section 14A is concerned. In such eventuality, the AO cannot embark upon a determination of the amount of expenditure for the purposes of section 14A(1). In case, he is not, on the basis of objective criteria and after giving the assessee a reasonable opportunity, satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee, he shall have to reject the claim and state the reasons for doing so.

Having done so, the AO will have to determine the amount of expenditure incurred in relation to income which does not form part of the total income under the said Act. He is required to do so on the basis of a reasonable and acceptable method of apportionment— Maxopp Investment Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 15 taxmann.com 390/203 Taxman 364 (Delhi), affirmed in Maxopp Investment Ltd. v. CIT [2018] 91 taxmann.com 154/254 Taxman 325 (SC). Thus, AO was free to adopt any reasonable and acceptable method.

But since there has been considerable dispute between the taxpayers and the Department on the method of determining such expenditure, therefore, the provisions of section 14A(2) [along with section 14A(3)] have been introduced.

8D.1-6 AO's power to determine amount of expenditure incurred for and from 1-4-2007 [section 14A(2) & 14A(3)] - Since, as discussed above, there has been considerable dispute between the taxpayers and the Department on the method of determining such expenditure, therefore, the provisions of section 14A(2) [alongwith section 14A(3)] have been introduced which applies prospectively for and from AY 2007-08 with the requirement of adopting a specific method of determining amount of such expenditure that has been incurred in relation to exempt income.

Section 14A(2) provides the manner in which the Assessing Officer is to determine the amount of expenditure incurred in relation to exempt income. However, the Assessing Officer is required to determine the amount of such expenditure only if he, having regard to the accounts of the assessee, is not satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of such expenditure. In other words, the requirement of the Assessing Officer embarking upon a determination of the amount of expenditure incurred in relation to exempt income would be triggered only if he returns a finding that he is not satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of such expenditure. Therefore, the condition precedent for the Assessing Officer entering upon a determination of the amount of the expenditure incurred in relation to exempt income is that he must record that he is not satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of such expenditure. This part of section 14A(2), which explicitly requires the fulfilment of a condition precedent, is also implicit in section 14A(1). It is only the prescription with regard to the method of determining such expenditure which is new and which will operate prospectively.

Section 14A(3) stipulates that the above provisions of section 14A(2) shall also apply where an assessee claims that no expenditure has been incurred by him in relation to exempt income. Thus, section 14A(3) is nothing but an offshoot of section 14A(2).

14.8-4 Ironical situation - receiving foreign exchange is taxed

The new provision has created an ironical situation. If Indian commission agent or stock broker provides service to principal outside India, he is required to pay service tax, though he is receiving payment in foreign exchange. On the other hand, if a foreign commission agent or foreign stock broker provides service to Indian Principal, the Indian Principal has to pay him in foreign exchange but no service tax is payable.

Thus, a transaction where actually India received foreign exchange is subjected to service tax, while transaction where there is outflow of foreign exchange from India is not subject to service tax.

14.8-5 No service tax on services provided by foreign Commission Agents or foreign stock broker to Indian Principals w.e.f. 1-10-2014

The aforesaid provision is working in reverse direction in case of foreign commission agents providing service to Indian Principal or foreign stock brokers. So far, rule 3 of POPS was applicable and place of provision of service was India. Hence, the Indian Principal was liable to pay service tax under reverse charge mechanism, in respect of commission paid by them to foreign commission agent or foreign stock broker.

Now, w.e.f. 1-10-2014, the place of provision of service is out of India as per rule 9(c) of POPS Rules. Hence, there is no service tax on commission paid to foreign commission agents or foreign stock brokers w.e.f. 1-10-2014. Since there is no service tax, any question of reverse charge cannot arise.

Any declaration under EXP3 and EXP4 is not required in respect of foreign agency commission paid on or after 1-10-2014.

14.8-6 Hiring of aircrafts and vessels upto one month exempt

In case of hiring of all means of transport upto one month, other than aircrafts and vessels except yachts, the place of provision of service is the location of service provider [rule 9(d) of POPS Rules as amended w.e.f. 1-10-2014].

The words 'other than aircrafts and vessels except yachts' has been inserted w.e.f. 1-10-2014. Thus, hiring of vessels or aircrafts, irrespective of whether short term or long term, will be covered by the general rule, i.e. place of location of service receiver. Hiring of yachts would continue to be covered by rule 9(d) - para 4.1.3(iii) of MF(DR) letter No. 334/15/2014-TRU dated 10-7-2014

The effect is that if Indian service provider of renting of aircraft or vessel gives the aircraft or vessel (other than yacht) to a foreign customer for any period (less than one month or more than one month), the place of provision of service will be out of India, if it relates to goods (and service tax will not apply).

On the other hand, if service provider from outside India of renting of aircraft or vessel gives the aircraft or vessel (other than yacht) to an Indian customer for any period (less than one month or more than one month), the place of provision of service will be India, if it relates to goods (and service tax will not apply).
