Scope of definition of input service under rule 2(l) is very wide :

As per rule 2(l)(ii), the expression "input service" is defined in broad terms. In order to be an input service, the following requirements must be satisfied -

(i)

Firstly, the expression requires the utilisation of "any service";

(ii)

secondly, the service must be used by the manufacturer; and

(iii)

thirdly, the service may be used, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products up to the place of removal.

The expression "directly or indirectly" has a wide import. The service, in other words, need not be a service which is directly used by the manufacturer in the manufacture of a final product. The definition of "input service" comprehends within its sweep a service which is used by the manufacturer even indirectly, and in or in relation to the manufacture of a final product.

Where the legislature or its delegate uses the expression "in or in relation to", its object and purpose is to widen the scope and purview of the entitlement.

When the words "directly or indirectly" and "in or in relation to the manufacture of final products" are used in conjunction that is indicative of the comprehensive sweep and ambit of the statutory provision. [Para 13]

Effect of rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 :

Rule 6(1) stipulates that no Cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or for provision of exempted services, save in the circumstances which are mentioned in rule 6(2).

Rule 6(2) deals with a situation where inter alia a manufacturer manufactures both dutiable final products as well as exempted goods. In such a situation, in order to avail of Cenvat credit, the manufacturer is required to maintain separate accounts for the receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs and input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products and the quantity of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods. Rule 6(2) stipulates that a manufacturer can take Cenvat credit only on that quantity of input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. In other words, Cenvat credit is not admissible on that quantity of input or input service which is not intended for use and is not used in the manufacture of dutiable goods.

Rule 6(5) confers an option to follow one of two courses of action to a manufacturer not opting to maintain separate accounts. Under rule 6(5), which has a non obstante provision overriding sub-rules (1), (2) and (3) credit of the whole of the service tax paid on taxable services of a specified description is allowable unless such a service is used exclusively in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services. In other words, where a service is of the description which is specified in rule 6(5), the manufacturer is entitled to credit of the whole of the service tax unless the service is used exclusively, that is to say solely in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods or any provision of exempted services. [Para 13]

Services used in manufacture of exempted intermediate product are eligible for credit if such intermediate product is used in dutiable final product :

Merely because the assessee manufactures exempted goods, that would be no justification to disallow to it the benefit of availing of Cenvat credit on that quantity of input service which is utilised in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products.

The definition of the expression "input service" is cast in broad terms. The expression "input service" means any service used by the manufacture, whether directly or indirectly or in or in relation to the manufacture of final products.

It is impossible to accept the hypothesis that would assert, that input services that are utilized by the assessee in or in relation to the process of manufacture that takes place at Mumbai Offshore is not a service that is used by the manufacturer in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products. The dutiable final products that are manufactured by the assessee at its Uran plant are fundamentally premised upon the manufacturing process which commences at Mumbai Offshore.

There can be no manner of doubt that the input services which go into the process of production at Mumbai Offshore meet the description of services that are utilized by the manufacturer directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products. The manufacture of the dutiable final products cannot take place without the process in question.

A banking company enters into an agreement with borrower for financing vehicle. It has tied up with a particular dealer where the banking company receives some amount from the dealer in reciprocal arrangement. The company accounts it as discount and contends that no service tax is applicable as there is no client relationship and no contract as such. Please advise (i) Whether it can be treated as a part of taxable service income under Banking & Financial services? (ii) Otherwise will it taxable under Business Auxiliary services as in the nature of commission (iii) Whether any contract is required for it? Whether oral contracts are also liable for service tax ?

9. Usually, the dealer gets commission for arranging a customer for the banking company. Here the arrangement seems to be in reverse. In any case, our view is as follows – (a) Discount is given directly to customer. If amount is paid to third person, it is not a ‘discount’. (b) Here, the money is paid by dealer to the hire purchase company. (c) The banking company cannot be said to be ‘commission agent’ of the dealer since it is not acting on behalf of agent. (c) The banking company is promoting its own business and not that of the dealer (d) Hence, in our view, the so-called ‘service’ given to the dealer cannot come under ‘Business Auxiliary Service’.

If amount is paid to dealer, really it is nothing but ‘commission’ though you may call it discount.

However, your last point is not valid. Contract need not be in writing. Under the Contract Act, oral contract is valid and binding. In fact, the Contract Act makes no distinction between oral contract and written contract. The arrangement between dealer and banking company is nothing but ‘contract’.

FACT: • During the course of the audit of the records, it was found that the assessee had availed credit of service tax paid on manpower supply service and security service during the period 2005-06 and 2006-07 up to January 2007.

• It was found that even though the invoices issued by the service providers charged service tax but no service tax was paid to the Government.

• Subsequent investigations revealed that the premises given in the invoice and the registration number were found to be wrong and no service tax had been paid by the service providers.

• The assessee pleaded that it was not aware that the firms were non-existent and they were not paying the service tax.

• The assessee objected to invocation of extended period of limitation and imposition of personal penalty on its employee.

• The assessee had also availed credit of telephone services and not made reversal required under rule 6 though it was engaged in trading activity and manufacture of exempted goods.

Assessee's contentions

• They had received the service during the relevant period.

• Since the registration number and the address were available and service was being received, they had a bona fide belief that service tax paid by them to the service providers was in turn paid to the Government of India.

• They had taken all reasonable steps that an ordinary person could have taken.

Revenue's contentions

• The employee of the assessee had clearly stated that they were receiving the services from the two service providers and the service provider suddenly disappeared in January 2007.

• He also admitted that the company had not verified the existence of the service providers and service providers had come to the factory and collected the cheques.

• Thus, it cannot be said that the assessee were not aware of the fraud played by the two service providers.

• Thus, credit was deniable invoking extended period of limitation.

Issue involved

• Whether credit was available ?

Brief Background

1. Airlines sell tickets to IATA agent, IATA agent sells tickets to sub-agent, sub-agent sells the tickets to the ultimate customer.

Sub-agent is having two source of income- (i) Commission income which he gets from the IATA agent; & (ii) Profit charged from the customers by selling tickets at the amount higher than at what he gets tickets from the IATA agent.

The question that arises here for consideration is whether service tax is chargeable on the commission income only or on the amount of profit earned from the customers also ?

Analysis of Air Travel Agent's Service and commission under old law

2. In the regime to 1-7-2012 only those services where taxable which were prescribed in the list of 119 services. The service by way of booking of air tickets was taxed under the head 'Air Travel Agent's Service. According to this service only those persons were liable to be taxed who were receiving income directly from the airlines. The sub-agents who were not receiving the income from airlines were not liable to pay service tax in the earlier regime under this head of service. This contention was confirmed by the trade notice, Letter No. CE/20/ST/Air Travel/97, dated 27-8-1997 in which department had clarified that - sub-agents were not liable to pay service tax under the head of 'Air travel agent's service'. However, the commission income received by sub-agents fell under the head of 'Business Auxiliary Service'. The Business Auxiliary Service was introduced vide Notification No. 7/2003-ST, dated 20-6-2003. The clause (vii) of said service covered the services of 'commission agent' in it. The commission agent for the said service meant as under—

"Commission Agent" means any person who acts on behalf of another person and causes sale or purchase of goods, or provision or receipt of services, for a consideration, and includes any person who, while acting on behalf of another person—

(i)

deals with goods or services or documents of title to such goods or services; or

(ii)

collects payment of sale price of such goods or services; or

(iii)

guarantees for collection or payment for such goods or services; or

(iv)

undertakes any activities relating to such sale or purchase of such goods or services;

Therefore, in the earlier regime the commission income earned by the sub-agents was liable to be taxed under the head of 'Business Auxiliary Service'.

Analysis of air travel agent's service and commission under new law

3. In the new regime, when the definition of service (section 65B(44)) was introduced under the Finance Act, 1994 each and every activity done or agreed to be done for a consideration from one person to another is a service and thereby, liable to service tax. Therefore, in the new regime also the commission income is liable to be taxed under the head of 'Business Auxiliary Service'.

Another important question which is to be answered is whether the profit earned on sale of such tickets is liable to service tax?

The definition of good is given under section 65B(25) of the Finance Act, 1994 as per which goods mean - every kind of movable property other than actionable claim and money; and includes securities, growing crops, grass, and things attached to or forming part of the land which are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale;

From the perusal of above definition it becomes amply clear that any movable property is goods. The ticket is 'goods'1 as it is a movable property. Now, the question which is to be determined is whether such profit is trading income or commission income?

There is very thin line of difference between the commission income and trading income. In the case of commission income, the commission agent gets the possession of goods but he does not get the ownership to those goods. He is entitled to sell those goods but he cannot claim those goods himself. On contrary, in the case of trading the title to goods is transferred. Where there is transfer of title in goods it is not liable to service tax as clause (e) of section 66D exempts the activity by way of - 'trading of goods'.

Conclusion

4. From the above discussion it can be concluded that where the title of goods is transferred in the name of sub-agent then the profit earned shall not be liable to service tax as it falls within the ambit of section 66D. Where the title to goods is not transferred, the profit earned shall be treated as commission income and shall be made liable to service tax under the head of 'Business Auxiliary Service'.

HEADNOTE: Section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Power to grant exemption from service tax -  Period prior to 7-12-2008 - In view of clarification by Director (Drawback) that service tax on foreign commission agency had not factored in All Industry Rates of Drawback and, further because, foreign commission agent's services were not input services so as to be eligible for drawback, assessee could not be denied refund in respect of said services under Notification No. 41/2007-ST - Refund could not be denied even if assessee had made exports under drawback shipping bills and clause (e) of proviso to said notification had barred exemption by way of refund in cases where drawback had been claimed - Moreover, since rate of refund thereunder had increased from 2 per cent to 10 per cent of FOB with effect from 7-12-2008, said increased rate was eligible to assessee filing claim of refund on or after 7-12-2008 [Paras 5.4  5.5] [Partly in favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee had claimed exemption by way of refund under Notification No. 41/2007-ST in respect of service tax on commission paid to foreign commission agent for causing sale of export goods.

The assessee had also claimed drawback under drawback rules.

Department denied exemption as exemption was subject to condition of non-availment of drawback of service tax (as per clause (e) of proviso to Notification).

Moreover, refund in other cases was restricted to 2 per cent of FOB value of exports, despite fact that rate had been increased to 10 per cent with effect from 7-12-2008 and refund claim was filed after such date.

HELD: Director (Drawback), in his letter dated 9-11-2009 in response to query under RTI Act, had stated that service tax paid on foreign agency commission was not factored in All Industry Rates of Drawback prior to 2007 or after 2007. In view of said clarification and also in view of fact that said services were not input services (and not eligible for drawback) but were linked to exports, Department's rejection of refund on ground that assessee had availed drawback and thereby enjoyed double benefit was contradictory and was not sustainable. [Para 5.4]

Further, Notification 33/2008, dated 7-12-2008, removed such condition of availing of drawback on Service tax paid on the specified services under the Customs, Central Excise Duties and Service Tax Drawback Rules, 1995. [Para 5.4]

Therefore, assessee was eligible for the refund amounts claimed on the export made under drawback shipping bills. [Para 5.4]

In respect of other claims, refund at rate of 2 per cent of FOB value was increased to 10 per cent of FOB value as per amended Notification 33/2008 dated 7-12-2008. In respect of refund claims filed before the date of said amendment, restriction of 2 per cent of FOB value by the Lower Adjudicating Authority needed no interference. However, in other cases, since refund claims were filed after the date of amended Notification 33/2008, dated 7-12-2008, assessee was entitled to 10 per cent of FOB value as refund. [Paras 5.4 & 5.5]

Service by a stock-broker to any person in connection with the sale or purchase of securities listed on recognised stock exchange.

Jobbing and arbitrance taxable.

22.4 Some case law relating to definition of 'input service' has become inapplicable after amendment to definition of 'input service' w.e.f. 1-4-2011. However, major part of case law is still relevant. The case law, which in my view is still relevant, is given below.

Services of Commission agent

22.4-1 There were disputes about eligibility of Cenvat credit on servicers provided by commission agent. Hence, following explanation has been added to rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, w.e.f. 3-2-2016 after sub-clause (C) -

Explanation - For the purpose of this clause, sales promotion includes services by way of sale of dutiable goods on commission basis.

The drafting of the explanation is faulty. Firstly, it is not clear what is meant by 'this clause', since firstly, any of sub-clauses (A), (B) and (C) of definition of 'input service' has no relation with 'sales commission'. Secondly, commission agent really never sales the goods. He only 'facilitates' sales. Thirdly, the explanation only refers to sale of dutiable goods. What about commission agents of services like hotels, travel of passengers, food etc.?

Be as it may, at least issue of eligibility of input service of commission agent of goods has been sorted out.

The explanation has retrospective effect - In Essar Steel India v. CCE (2016) 335 ELT 660 (CESTAT), it has been rightly held that this explanation is clarificatory in nature and has retrospective effect.

In my view, this decision is correct, for reasons stated below.

Right from beginning, department has consistently held (as per circulars/instructions discussed below) that input service of service tax paid by commission agents is eligible 'input service'. Tribunal and one High Court (Punjab and Haryana HC) have also consistently held the same view. Problems were created only because one adverse decision of Gujarat High Court in case of Cadila Healthcare delivered in year 2013.

Departmental circular - Para 5 of CBE&C circular No. 943/04/2011-CX, dated 29-4-2011 has specifically clarified that even under new definition of input service, service tax on sales commission is eligible as input service.

Canteen services as input service

22.4-2 There is some dispute relating to canteen services.

As per exclusion clause (C) of Rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, services in relation to outdoor catering is not eligible for Cenvat credit if such service is primarily used for personal use or consumption of employee.

The issue is whether the canteen is primarily for personal use or consumption of employee.

In Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages v. CCE (2015) 51 GST 126 = 56 taxmann.com 378 (CESTAT), it has been held that if cost is borne by company and if canteen service is used by all employees in general, it is not 'primarily for personal use or consumption of employee' and is eligible for Cenvat credit (even after 1-4-2011).

However, this view has not been accepted in Applied Micro Circuits v. CCE (2016) 54 GST 159 = 66 taxmann.com 103 (CESTAT SMB). In this case, it was held that Cenvat credit of service tax paid on outdoor catering and insurance of employees is not available.

It can be argued that canteen is not 'outdoor catering' as per trade parlance, even if run by outside contractor.

The question does not arise if (a) canteen is as per statutory requirements under Factories Act, as that service is exempt from service and hence no question of Cenvat credit (b) Canteen is not air conditioned.

In that case, service tax is not payable at all.

During the relevant period i.e. prior to 10-9-2004, as per Rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, credit could have been taken on the Service Tax paid on input services which fall under the same category of taxable service as that of output service and, therefore, the CENVAT Credit of duty paid on capital goods was not available prior to 10-9-2004. Separate proceedings were not required for denial of credit, as it was a part of assessment :

The submissions that separate proceedings should have been initiated for rejection of CENVAT Credit availment, especially because the original adjudicating authority has appropriated the amount debited from the CENVAT Credit account, were incorrect. Even in the cases of clandestine removal and in the cases where the assessee has not taken the registration from the Department and whole activity of the assessee was not known to the Department, it has been the practice to allow admissible CENVAT Credit to the assessee, if the assessee is able to show that capital goods are received, documents are available and used by the assessee for manufacture of finished goods even if procedure for availment of CENVAT Credit would not have been followed by the assessee. Just because the returns were filed subsequent to issue of show-cause notice, the requirement under the law for the adjudicating authority to consider availability of CENVAT Credit and allow the benefit of admissible CENVAT Credit while confirming the duty demand does not undergo a change. Role of C&F Agent :

Ordinarily, a C & F agent receives goods from the factory or premises of the manufacturer (the Principal) or his agents and stores these goods, dispatches these goods as per orders received from the Principal, arranges transport, etc. for the purpose and prepares invoices on behalf of the Principal. In respect of such service, the C&F agent receives commission on the basis of agreed terms. Therefore, an essential characteristic of any service, to fall in the category of C & F agent, is that the relationship between the service provider and receiver should be in the nature of principal (owner) and agent. The C & F Agent carries out all activities in respect of goods right from the stage of their clearances from the premises of the principal to its storage and delivery to the customers. [Para 5.4(iv)]

Premises of C&F Agent is Place of Removal under section 4(3)(c) of Central Excise Act, 1944 :

The clearing and forwarding agent is an agent of the principal. The goods stored by him after clearance from the factory would therefore, be stored on behalf of the principal, and as such the place where such goods are stored by the C&F agent would fall within the purview of sub-clause (iii) of clause (c) of section 4(3) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and as such would be the place of removal. [Para 5.4(vi)]

Services eligible for input service credit prior to 1-4-2008 :

Viewed from that light the services rendered by the C&F agent of clearing the goods from the factory premises, storing the same and delivering the same to the customer would fall within the ambit of rule 2(l) of the Rules as it stood prior to its amendment with effect from 1-4-2008, namely clearance of final products from the place of removal.

However, such services would not amount to sales promotion and would not be eligible for input service in that sense. [Para 5.4(vi)]

HEADNOTE: Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Business auxiliary service - Assessee rendered commission agent’s service for period prior to 1-7-2003 - Service tax was demanded - However, commission agent’s service was covered in ‘Business auxiliary service’ only on 1-7-2003 - Whether assessee had made out a prima facie case against demand of service tax - Held, yes [Para 2]

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Clearing and forwarding agent - Assessee used to receive goods from principal, store them in its godown, clear them to buyers, collect payment for sale and transmit sale proceeds to principal after taking commission - Whether services of appellant were of a consignment agent which was included in definition of ‘clearing and forwarding agent’s service’ - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, appellant had no prima facie case against demand of service tax - Held, yes [Para 3]

FACT: In instant appeal, the dispute arose as to whether the assessee could be said to have rendered services of ‘consignment agent’ or ‘commission agent’ to their customers.

HELD: In case of the first assessee, the assessee identified buyers for their principals, collected purchase orders, completed the sale transactions, collected payments and transmitted thereof to the principal. Thus, it had functioned as commission agent. The service of a commission agent was expressly covered under ‘Business auxiliary service’ which was introduced into the statute book only on 1-7-2003. The period of dispute in the appeal was prior to that date. The assessee had made out a prima facie case against the demand of service tax and, accordingly, waiver of pre-deposit and stay of recovery in respect of the amount of tax and penalties were to be granted. [Para 2]

In case of other two assessees the assessees were, admittedly, physically dealing with excisable goods. It used to receive such goods from its principal, store them in their godown, clear them to buyers, collect payments for the sale and transmit the same to the principal after taking commission. That activity would attract the definition of ‘clearing and forwarding agent’, which includes consignment agent. Apparently, therefore, the assessees seemed to have rendered service of a consignment agent to it customers during the respective periods. Such service was taxable during the period of dispute. Hence, there seemed to be no prima facie case for the assessees against the demand of service tax. Accordingly, it was directed to pre-deposit the tax amounts. [Para 3]

• It was strange that appellants received, services from a service provider whose existence they knew only because he used to come to collect the cheque and they did not even bother to verify whether the office premises in the invoice was in existence or not.

• Since the service provider was located in Vapi itself (place of assessee) would also go against the assessee since it cannot even be their case that ascertaining the existence or otherwise of the service provider was a difficult task.

• The fact that appellant did not make any efforts to locate the service provider nor did they make any effort to intimate the department nor did they debit the amount of credit taken goes against the appellants and therefore it has to be held that the invocation of extended time-limit for demand in this case is sustainable.

• Further, for the same reasons, the assessee is liable to penalty also. [Para 9]

Credit was reversible as assessee was engaged in trading activity/ exempted goods

• The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of animal feed which is exempted and was also engaged in trading activity.

• If that is the case in respect of trading activity, the credit attributable to trading activity, is not admissible and is required to be reversed.

• The principle of self assessment and submission of only the results of self assessment in the form of return would show that it is the responsibility of the assessee to assess the goods correctly and pay the taxes correctly.

• In this case it cannot be said that the assessee was not aware that for trading activity credit is not admissible.

• Once the assessee is considered to be aware of statutory provisions relating to availment of credit and his activities, the normal conclusion of a ordinary prudent person is that the assessee had deliberately avoided reversing the credit attributable to trading activity and thereby suppressing/misdeclaring the fact of availment of credit to the department.

• Therefore the demand with interest and imposition of penalty has to be upheld. [Para 10]

Personal penalty not leviable on employee

• It cannot be said that the employee derived any extra benefit because of the lapses.

• It has not been shown that there was any motive on his part.

• Since penalty has been imposed on the assessee, penalty imposed employee has to be set aside. [Para 12]

Assessee's arguments

Its chairman became the chairman of the three subsidiaries. It provided services to those subsidiaries against payment.

It merely relates to its ownership of shares and receipt of dividends, which fall outside the scope of VAT.

There is some dispute relating to canteen services.

As per exclusion clause (C) of Rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, services in relation to outdoor catering is not eligible for Cenvat credit if such service is primarily used for personal use or consumption of employee.

The issue is whether the canteen is primarily for personal use or consumption of employee.

In Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages v. CCE (2015) 51 GST 126 = 56 taxmann.com 378 (CESTAT), it has been held that if cost is borne by company and if canteen service is used by all employees in general, it is not 'primarily for personal use or consumption of employee' and is eligible for Cenvat credit (even after 1-4-2011).

The Larger Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE [2006] 4 STT 231 (New Delhi - CESTAT) had examined a similar issue and held that an agent engaged only for procuring purchase orders for the vendors on commission basis does not engage in any of the activities enumerated in the para 2.2 of Trade Notice No. 87/97 of Madurai Commissionerate (Equivalent to CBEC Circular, dated 11-7-1997), directly or indirectly. The commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with the work of clearing and forwarding of the goods would be a person, who in the ordinary course of business, makes contract for sale or purchase of the goods for others. The definition of ‘Commission Agent’ under section 2(aaa ) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 would apply in or in relation to service tax as it applies to duty of excise by virtue of clause (2) of section 65. Services of commission agents were included in the definition of ‘Business auxiliary service’ under clause (19) of section 65 with effect from 2003, which included service of the commission agent. The activity of mere procurement of purchase order for the principal on commission basis of a commission agent was treated separately by the Parliament from the activities of the C&F agent. In the instant case, the Commissioner (Appeals) found that the marketing agents appointed by the assessee did not carry out any activity other than procuring orders for the assessee’s goods. This activity was brought under the tax net with effect from 1-7-2003 when business auxiliary service was introduced. Business auxiliary service, inter alia, covers promotion of marketing or sale of goods. Therefore, the service involved was correctly classifiable under business auxiliary service with effect from 1-7-2003. Same services could not be classified under ‘Clearing & forward agent’s service’ for any previous period as the scope of clearing and forwarding agent’s service was not modified when business auxiliary service was introduced in the Act. Prabhat Zarda Factory (India) Ltd.’s case (supra) relied on by the revenue was overruled by the Larger Bench decision of the Tribunal in Larsen & Toubro Ltd.’s case (supra). In the circumstances, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be sustained and the appeal filed by the revenue was liable to be rejected.

While the Cenvat credit demand is for the period from 1-4-2005 to 28-2-2006, the show cause notice had been issued on 23-10-2009. Assessee's submission is that while in the service tax return for the six monthly period ending September, 2006 submitted by them on 25-10-2006, they had not disclosed the information pertaining to export of services and availment of Cenvat credit in respect of input services but in a subsequent letter dated 9-3-2007 addressed to the concerned Superintendent, the information regarding export of service and Cenvat credit in respect of the input services for the same had been furnished. The fact of the assessee intimating the department in respect of their return for the six monthly Period ending September, regarding export of services and availment of Cenvat credit in respect of the same under their letter dated 9-3-2007 has been accepted by the department but the Commissioner has observed that the same cannot be accepted as voluntary disclosure, as there is no provision for filing of revised return. When the department accepts that the assessee under their letter dated 9-3-2007 had submitted the required information about export of service and availment of Cenvat credit in respect of the input service during the period of dispute, they cannot be accused of having suppressed this information from the department with intent to evade service tax by wrongly availing the Cenvat credit. The ST-3 returns filed by an assessee are, after all, required to be scrutinized by the concerned range officers/Asstt. Commissioner. Hence, longer limitation period would not be applicable to the department and as such, the entire demand for wrongly availed Cenvat credit would be time-barred. [Para 11]

There was no dispute by either side that when an application is made by a person for registration as a sub-broker or a person registered as such under the SEBI Act, 1992 read with the regulations made thereunder, he shall be called as a stock broker. So also, there is no dispute that in terms of section 65(105)(a) services provided to any person by a sub-broker or stock broker in connection with the sale or purchase of securities listed on a recognized stock exchange shall be taxable services from 10-9-2004. So also, a sub-broker who is registered or has made an application for registration as such under the SEBI Act, 1992, is permitted to provide similar service as provided by a stock broker. The service so provided becomes taxable service under the Act with effect from 10-9-2004. [Para 8]

It is true that there is no provision under the Act for double taxation. The scheme of service tax law suggests that it is a single point tax law without being a multiple taxation legislation. In the absence of any statutory provision to the contrary, providing of service being event of levy, self-same service provided shall not be doubly taxable. If service tax is paid by a sub-broker in respect of same taxable service provided by the stock broker, the stock broker is entitled to the credit of the tax so paid on such service if entire chain of identity of sub-broker and stock broker is established and transactions are provided to be one and the same. In other words, if the main stock broker is subjected to levy of service tax on the self-same taxable service provided by sub-broker to the stock broker and the sub-broker has paid service tax on such service, the stock broker shall be entitled to the credit of service tax. Such a proposition finds support from the basic rule of Cenvat credit and service of a sub-broker may be input service provided for a stock broker if there is an integrity between the services. Tax paid by a sub-broker may not be denied to be set off against ultimate service tax liability of the stock broker if the stock broker is made liable to pay service tax for the self-same transaction. Such set off depends on the facts and circumstances of each case and subject to verification of evidence as well as rules made under the law with effect from 10-9-2004. No set off is permissible prior to this date when a sub-broker was not within the fold of law during that period. [Para 9]

Therefore, the matter was sent back to the original authority to verify as to whether the stock brokers had paid service tax on behalf of the sub-brokers and, if so, reduce the demand on sub-brokers to that extent and pass fresh orders. All the appeals were allowed by way of remand. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 65(25), read with section 65(19) of the Finance Act, 1994 - Taxable services - Clearing and Forwarding Agent's Services - Period from April 2001 to March 2004 - Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with work of clearing and forwarding of goods, service would not be a taxable service under Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services - Said service is appropriately classifiable under Business Auxiliary Services and is exempt for period from 1-7-2003 to 9-7-2004 under Notification No. 13/2003-ST [Paras 2 to 8] [In favour of assessee]Service Tax : Where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with work of clearing and forwarding of goods, service would not be a taxable service under Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services

FACT: Facts

The assessee gets TV sets manufactured by three manufacturers.

Three manufacturers of TV sets place orders on manufacturers of picture tubes.

The picture tubes are directly supplied by the picture tube manufacturers and payments are received from the manufacturers of TV sets directly.

The rates of picture tubes are however settled by the assessee with the supplier/manufacturers of picture tubes.

After receiving payment from the manufacturers of TV sets, manufacturers/suppliers of picture tubes pay agreed amounts as commission, to the assessee.

Department sought levy of service tax on this commission under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services'.

Issue Involved

Whether commission earned by assessee was liable to service tax under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' ?

HELD: Commission on purchase not covered under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' :

The conjunctive 'and' between the words 'clearing' and 'forwarding' indicate and mean that where clearing operations are separate from forwarding operations, levy of tax would not be attracted i.e. there would be no charge of tax if the transaction involved only one of the two components of the conjuncted service namely 'clearing' and 'forwarding'. The expression a clearing and forwarding agent in relation to clearing and forwarding operations, in any manner' contemplates only one person operating both as the clearing and the forwarding agent; and if a person has rendered service as forwarding agent without rendering any service as 'clearing agent' he could not be considered to have rendered both services as a 'clearing and forwarding agent'. [Para 2]

'Clearing and forwarding operations' would be various activities having a bearing on clearance of goods and would normally involve documentary processes and arrangements for transfer of goods to their destination; and may also involve clearance at subsequent stages during forwarding operations. A clearing and forwarding agent normally undertakes the following activities :-

(a)

Receiving goods from the factories or premises of the principal or his agents;

(b)

Warehousing these goods;

(c)

Receiving despatch orders from the principal;

(d)

Arranging despatch of goods as per the directions of the principal by engaging transport on his own or through the authorised transporters of the principal;

(e)

Maintaining records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; and

(f)

Preparing invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 3]

Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for the vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of the enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with the work of clearing and forwarding of goods, the service would not be a taxable service as defined in section 65(105)(j) read with section 65(25) which defines a clearing and forwarding agent. [Para 4]

In this case, assessee neither receives goods from the factory premises of the principal; warehouses such goods; receives despatch orders from the principal; arranges despatch of goods as per directions of the principal by engaging a transport on its own or through authorised transporters of the principal; nor maintains records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; nor even prepares invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 5]

16.3-11 On-going contracts as on 1-6-2007

Service tax on works contract was introduced w.e.f. 1-6-2007. Prior to 1-6-2007, services were covered under construction service, erection and commissioning service etc., where service tax could be paid on 33% value without Cenvat credit. After introduction of works contract service, a composition scheme was introduced where service tax was payable on 40% value but with Cenvat credit. Rule 3(3) of Composition Scheme provided that assessee who wants to pay service tax under composition scheme shall avail such option before payment of service tax.

CBE&C issued circular No. 98/1/2008-ST dated 4-1-2008 that composition scheme would not be available in case of on-going contracts as on 1-6-2007 (as they could not have exercised option to pay service tax under new composition scheme before payment of service tax).

Validity of this circular has been upheld in Nagarjuna Construction Co. Ltd. v. GOI (2012) 38 STT 60 = 27 taxmann.com 331 = 59 VST 119 = (2013) 1 SCC 721 (SC).

This decision will not apply in case of changes in composition scheme made w.e.f. 1-7-2012 as under new provisions, there is no requirement of submitting any option to department. Further, the 33% scheme has been omitted altogether (as notification No. 1/2006-ST which provided this scheme has been rescinded w.e.f. 1-7-2012 without any saving clause).

There is no dispute with regard to the fact that, the assessee is a licensed commission agent operating in the Agricultural Market Committee Yard in Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, with a valid certificate of license, as a commission agent, under rule 49 and section 7(1)(b) of the Andhra Pradesh Agricultural Produce and Livestock Market Act, 1966. As per AMC regulations, the assessee receives 2 per cent commission from farmers on sales to purchasers/traders/exporters, and the same has been offered as income in the financial statements and paid relevant taxes. The buyers/traders/exporters deducted TDS under section 194Q in respect of sales on the total sale value and reported in the PAN number of the assessee. Similarly, the buyers/traders/exporters had deducted TDS under section 194A in respect of interest payment on delayed payments and reported in the PAN number of the assessee. [Para 7]

Since the assessee has considered only commission income as its income and, after relevant expenditure, offered net profit for taxation, it claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders in terms of sections 194Q and 194A. In total, the Assessing Officer allowed proportionate credit for TDS on the ground that the assessee has offered only the part of the income, whereas it claimed TDS on the entire sales value. It is found that, once the assessee is operating as a commission agent, then the income of the assessee is net commission income received from the farmers, but not the total sales value of the farmers. Since the law provides for TDS under section 194Q on total sales value, and further, the assessee has raised sales invoices in its name, the traders have deducted TDS on the entire sales value, but the fact remains that, the assessee has considered the total income accrued on the total sales value being commission received from the farmers, as its income. Therefore, the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A, has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee and thus, the provisions of section 199 read with rule 37BA(2) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 are complied with. Therefore, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) that Assessing Officer has rightly allowed proportionate credit as per section 199 read with rule 37BA(2), is incorrect, going by the facts, because, there is no finding from the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) that, the income on which TDS has been deducted under sections 194Q and 194A has not suffered tax in the hands of the assessee. Since the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194A and 194Q has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee, the assessee has righty claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders and reported in Form 26AS. The Assessing Officer, without appreciating relevant facts, allowed proportionate credit for TDS, even though the assessee is entitled for credit for the entire TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A. The Commissioner (Appeals), without appreciating relevant facts, simply sustained additions made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 8]

16.17 Importation of service is 'supply'

As per section 7(1)(b) of CGST Act, importation of service, for a consideration whether or not in the course or furtherance of business, is 'supply' and subject to GST.

Thus, import of service from HO or branch outside India will be subject to GST even if no payment was made to HO or branch outside India.

Import of service from related person taxable even if without consideration - Import of services by a (*) person from a related person or from any of his other establishments outside India, in the course or furtherance of business is taxable even if without consideration - paragraph 4 of Schedule I of CGST Act [ * - The word was 'taxable'. This word has been omitted vide CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 w.e.f. 1-2-2019. Thus, import by any person from a related person outside India shall be 'import', but it should be in the course or furtherance of business.

Valuation of supply of import of services by a related person where recipient is eligible to full input tax credit - CBI&C, vide circular No. 210/4/2024-GST dated 26-6-2024 has clarified as follows -

In case of import of services by a registered person in India from a related person located outside India, the tax is required to be paid by the registered person in India under reverse charge mechanism. In such cases, the registered person in India is required to issue self-invoice under Section 31(3)(f) of CGST Act and pay tax on reverse charge basis.

Where the foreign affiliate is providing certain services to the related domestic entity, and where full input tax credit is available to the said related domestic entity, the value of such supply of services declared in the invoice by the said related domestic entity may be deemed as open market value in terms of second proviso to rule 28(1) of CGST Rules. Further, in cases where full input tax credit is available to the recipient, if the invoice is not issued by the related domestic entity with respect to any service provided by the foreign affiliate to it, the value of such services may be deemed to be declared as Nil, and may be deemed as open market value in terms of second proviso to rule 28(1) of CGST Rules.

Thus, value of supply of import of services by a related person where recipient is eligible to full input tax credit is Nil and hence GST is not payable under reverse charge.

■ Since the assessee has considered only commission income as its income and, after relevant expenditure, offered net profit for taxation, it claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders in terms of sections 194Q and 194A. In total, the Assessing Officer allowed proportionate credit for TDS on the ground that the assessee has offered only the part of the income, whereas it claimed TDS on the entire sales value. It is found that, once the assessee is operating as a commission agent, then the income of the assessee is net commission income received from the farmers, but not the total sales value of the farmers. Since the law provides for TDS under section 194Q on total sales value, and further, the assessee has raised sales invoices in its name, the traders have deducted TDS on the entire sales value, but the fact remains that, the assessee has considered the total income accrued on the total sales value being commission received from the farmers, as its income. Therefore, the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A, has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee and thus, the provisions of section 199 read with rule 37BA(2) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 are complied with. Therefore, the reasons given by the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner (Appeals) that Assessing Officer has rightly allowed proportionate credit as per section 199 read with rule 37BA(2), is incorrect, going by the facts, because, there is no finding from the Assessing Officer or the Commissioner (Appeals) that, the income on which TDS has been deducted under sections 194Q and 194A has not suffered tax in the hands of the assessee. Since the entire income pertains to TDS deducted under sections 194A and 194Q has suffered tax in the hands of the assessee, the assessee has righty claimed credit for TDS as deducted by the traders and reported in Form 26AS. The Assessing Officer, without appreciating relevant facts, allowed proportionate credit for TDS, even though the assessee is entitled for credit for the entire TDS deducted under sections 194Q and 194A. The Commissioner (Appeals), without appreciating relevant facts, simply sustained additions made by the Assessing Officer. [Para 8]

Commission agent means person acting 'on behalf of' another :

• During period prior to 16-5-2005, the expression "commission agent" was defined in Exemption Notification No. 13/03-ST, dated 20-6-2003 to mean "a person who causes sale or purchase of goods, on behalf of another person for a consideration which is based on the quantum of such sale or purchase". [Para 8.4]

• The definition of 'commission agent' as given in section 65(19) for period on or after 16-5-2005 emphasizes on the 'commission agent' acting 'on behalf of' another person. Thus, a 'commission agent' acts on behalf of a principal and sells or buys the goods or provides or receives the services on behalf of his principal for some commission. The commission agent as agent of the principal can also deal with the goods or services, collect payment for sale price of goods or services sold or provide guarantee for the payment or undertake any activity relating to such sale or purchase of such goods or service. But all this activity must be as an agent acting on behalf of principal. [Para 9]

'On behalf of' connotes agency :

• The words, 'on behalf of' in the statute connote an agency when one person acts on behalf of the other. The former acts as the agent of the latter. An agency is the relationship of principal and agent in terms of a contract express or implied while an agency may also be created by a statute. [Para 8.5]

'Broker' is different from 'commission agent' :

• The broker by the nature of the role played by him is different from a commission agent. The distinction between a broker and a commission agent is that a commission agent, having control over the goods sells them to others. Though he may act for a disclosed principal at either end, he negotiates the sale with the purchaser on his own behalf. The broker does not sell the goods on his own behalf, but merely brings the vendor and the vendee together and settles the price. [Para 8.5]

• Brokers are those that contrive, make and conclude bargain and contracts between merchants and tradesmen, in matter of money and merchandise, for which they have a fee or reward. [Para 11]

• The authority given to a broker to negotiate a sale and find a purchaser, without furnishing him with all the terms, means "to find a man willing to become a purchaser and not to find him and make him a purchaser". [Para 8.5]

Assessee was a shipbroker and not a commission agent :

• A shipbroker is essentially a broker. Shipbrokers are specialist intermediaries for negotiations between shipowner and charterers who use the ship to transport some cargo or between the buyers and sellers of the ship. A shipbroker bring together a shipowner who wants employment/fixture for his ship located at a particular Port and ship charterer who requires a particular type of ship at or around a particular Port to transport some cargo. They help in negotiating the terms of the charter and finalisation of charter-party agreement and also assist both the parties in compliance of the charter - party terms and full and final settlement of all the dues and claims. The shipbroker also acts as an intermediary for bringing together a shipowner who wants to sell his ship and the prospective buyer and assisting in sale of the ship. For providing these services, the shipbrokers have to maintain database of shipowners, the class of ships owned by them and their location. [Para 10]

• It was not the case of the Department that the assessee had agreements with shipping companies etc. for representing them in negotiations. [Para 10]

• The essential ingredient of a 'Commission agents' service is acting on behalf of a principal which was missing in the case of the assessee. From the nature of their activity it was clear that brokers were purely intermediaries who did not act on behalf of either shipowner or the charterer and, therefore, they could not be said to be commission agents. [Para 10]

Conclusion

• The assessee while acting as shipbrokers could not be called commission agents of the shipowner or ship charterer and, thus, were not covered by the definition of 'Business Auxiliary Service". [Para 11.1]

Period only up to 16-6-2005

In their memorandum, the assessee has admitted that they are not disputing the payment of service tax under BAS as a "commission agent" with effect from 16-6-2005 and has paid the tax along with interest which has been appropriated in the impugned order. They dispute their liability to pay service tax before 16-6-2005 as customer management service on various grounds. [Para 5.2]

Notice need not specify particular sub-clause of section 65(19)

As regards the first ground that the show cause notice does not mention the clause of 65 (19) under which their liability arose —

-

in the show cause notice, the various activities undertaken by the assessee has been enumerated under 11 heads ;

-

later, the notice clearly describe how and why the activities undertaken by the assessee would fall under BAS as defined in law.

-

Thus the assessee has been put to notice in clear terms about their liability to pay service tax. Merely because the particular sub-clause of section 65(19) has not been specifically mentioned in the show cause does not vitiate the show cause notice or the proceedings initiated thereunder and this is the settled position in law. If the exercise of a power can be traced to a legitimate source, the fact that the same was purported to have been exercised under a different power does not vitiate the exercise of the power in question. [Para 5.3]

Services taxable under BAS from 10-9-2004

The activities undertaken by the assessee for which they were collecting service charges were in respect of cargo imported or exported by their customers and this fact is evident from the nature of service charges collected, namely,

(1)

Bill of lading fees;

(2)

LCL consolidation charges;

(3)

Amendment charges for amendments in bill of lading;

(4)

Facilitation/processing charges;

(5)

Administration charges for stamp duty;

(6)

Delivery Order fees for taking delivery of cargo;

(7)

Documentation fees for export to USA;

(8)

Hazardous Documentation charges for taking special care of hazardous cargo;

(9)

Bill of lading surrender charges;

(10)

Manifest correction charges; and

(11)

Detention waiver/refund processing charges.

Thus, these services were in relation to procurement of goods or services, which are inputs for the client and such services clearly fell under sub-clause (iv) of section 65(19) as it stood with effect from 10-9-2004.

Even if it is held that these activities did not fall under sub-clause (iv), they would certainly fall under sub-clause (vii) as any service incidental or auxiliary to any activity specified in sub-clauses (i) to (vi).

Even if the appellant had acted as a commission agent as claimed by them, they would fall under sub-clause (vii) of clause (19) of section 65 as the entry covered the services rendered as a commission agent.

Thus, the assessee was liable to pay service tax prior to 16-6-2005. [Para 5.4]

The contention of the assessee that to come under BAS, there should be 3 parties and the service should have been rendered "on behalf of the client", is also incorrect for the following reason. Rendering of service on behalf of the client applies only to sub-clauses (iii), (v) and (vi) which relate to customer care management, production of goods and provision of services. The said condition does not apply to sub-clause (iv) which deals services rendered to the client and consequently to sub-clause (vii) which is incidental or auxiliary to the service under sub-clause (iv). Similarly the condition "on behalf of" also does not apply to services specified in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) of section 65 (19) apart from sub-clause (iv). Therefore, this contention of the assessee has to be rejected outright. [Para 5.5]

From the statutory definition of BAS as it stood prior to 10-9-2004, the services rendered by the assessee would not come under any of the activities specified under various sub-clauses, namely, (i) promotion or marketing or sale of goods produced or provided by or belonging to the client; (ii) promotion or marketing of service provided by the client; (iii) any customer care service provided on behalf of the client; or (iv) any incidental or auxiliary support service in respect of (i) to (iii). Therefore, there would not be any liability to pay service tax prior to 10-9-2004 on the assessee. [Para 5.6]

Sub-section (6)(ii) provides that if any person carrying on eligible business, to which the section can apply, earns commission or brokerage (as explained above), such a person will not be able to pay tax on presumptive basis in respect of the eligible business.

Apparently, the intention is to provide that in computing income in the nature of commission or brokerage being a business of an assessee, the section would not apply. However, the language of the provision suggests that even if an assessee is carrying on, say, trading business, being eligible business and also derives commission or brokerage income, then also the presumptive tax provision will not apply to him in respect of both the businesses, that is, trading and the commission or brokerage business.

4.9.3 Agency Business

Sub-section (6)(iii) provides that the section will not apply to 'a person carrying on any agency business'.

Agency business is described as follows (http://business.yourdictionary. com/agency):

"The relationship between an agent and a principal in which the agent acts for and represents the principal on the basis of the principal's instructions".

As discussed earlier, sub-section (6)(ii) covers any income earned by a commission agent. Prima facie, it would cover transactions where a person acts as an agent to carry out certain transactions incidental to his business. Thus, clause (iii) overlaps clause (ii).

Sub-section (6)(iii) covers the case where a person is carrying on agency business. In the light of the above discussions about an agent and agency business, it could be said that a person who is dealing in the goods of one or more principals, without carrying on trading activity of his own, is engaged in the agency business. Although, he is engaged in trading, the activity is in the nature of service rendered to someone else for effecting his sales. Normally, such person would purchase directly from or from a source identified by the person (principal) for whom he is acting as an agent. Also, he would have some contractual relationship with the Principal which would specify the limits to which he can bind the Principal as also specify assistance which the Principal would provide in the business of selling. The intention is not to permit such person to avail of the option of presumptive tax under the section.

Agency business could cover both: in respect of goods and/or services. Hence, the provision would not apply, say, to an insurance agent or an agent of Post Office or an agent rendering services for marketing of securities, etc.

Further, as discussed above, if a person apart from carrying on trading activities of his own e.g. of dealing in plastic furniture, also, carries on some agency business e.g. of representing a specified manufacturer of plastic furniture, the section would not apply to such person.

Thus, it appears that non-applicability of the section is fixed qua person and not qua business. In other words, if a person carries on any of the activities specified in sub-section (6), he/it cannot opt for presumptive taxation.

4.9.4 Increase in threshold limit to Rs. 1 crore

The second amendment is in definition of 'eligible business' contained in Explanation (b)(ii) providing for the threshold limit. Presently, it is: turnover or gross receipt should not exceed Rs. 60 lacs. If, it is less than that the business is considered as eligible business.

The amendment raises the threshold limit to Rs. 1 crore effective from 1-4-2013. Thus, any person engaged in business having a turnover or gross receipts of less than Rs. 1 crore, from and after assessment year 2013-14, would qualify for presumptive tax payable under the section.

(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, the Commissioner may, in such circumstances and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, permit a Commission Agent engaged in the business of agricultural produce, to pay at his option in lieu of the amount of tax leviable from him under this Act, a lump sum tax by way of composition at such rate as may be fixed by the State Government by notification in the Official Gazette.

(2) The permission to pay lump sum tax under sub-section (1) shall be granted by the Commissioner to a Commission Agent who,—

(a)

exclusively carries on a business of agricultural produce, and

(b)

is licensed as general commission agent with a market committee established under the Gujarat Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1963.

(3) The Commissioner shall not grant permission to pay lump sum tax under sub-section (1) to a Commission agent who,—

(a)

sells the goods in the course of inter-State trade and commerce or exports goods out of the territory of India,

(b)

purchases the goods in the course of inter-State trade and commerce or imports goods from a place out of the territory of India,

(c)

dispatches the goods to his branch or his consigning agent outside the State or receives the goods from his branch situated outside the State or from consigning agent outside the State,

(d)

sells the goods to a person who is not a registered dealer, or

(e)

sells the goods to a dealer who is permitted to pay lump sum tax under section 14.

(4) The commission agent who is permitted under sub-section (1) to pay lump sum tax shall not,—

(a)

be entitled to claim tax credit in respect of tax paid by him on his purchases,

(b)

charge any tax under this Act in his sales bill or sales invoices in respect of the sales on which lump sum tax is payable, and

(c)

issue tax invoice to any dealer who has purchased the goods from him.

(5) The commission agent who is permitted to pay lump sum tax under sub-section (1) shall be liable to pay purchase tax leviable under 2[sub-sections (1), (3), (4) and (6)] of section 9 in addition to the lump-sum tax under this section.

(6) The permission granted under sub- section (1) shall remain valid so long as the provisions of this section and rules made in this behalf are complied with; and in case of breach of any of the provisions of this section or rules, the commission agent shall be liable to pay tax under sections 7 and 9 for such tax period as may be prescribed.

As is clear from Board Circular No. 59/8/2003 dated 20-6-2003, there is difference between commission agent and consignment agent. Consignment agent actually deals with the goods, when he receives the same from the principal and dispatches them on the direction of the principal to the ultimate customer. Consignment agent may not even be associated with the procurement of orders or does not directly deal with the self-purchase. He is acting on behalf of the principal and deals with the movement of the goods as per the direction of the principal. On the other hand, commission agent is only concerned with the procurement of orders, for which he may receive the fixed amount along with some percentage amount. In the instant case, as per the terms of the agreement, the appellants were hired for canvassing and advancing the sale of the principal products and also to procure orders for the same. In such a scenario, they had to be held as commission agent rather than consignment agent. The services as commission agent were levied to tax under the category of business auxiliary service with effect from 1-7-2003 and period in instant appeal was prior to the said date. As such, they were not liable to pay any tax during the said period. [Para 3]

In the case of CIT v. Ramsarup [1962] 45 ITR 248 , the Full Bench held that on atrue interpretation of section 10 and sub-section (1) of section 24 and the first proviso thereto, an assessee is not entitled to claim a set-off of the loss suffered by him in speculation business against the profits of the assessee in a business other than a business consisting of speculative transactions. Following the above decision, if the speculation transactions were separate and distinct from the commission agency business, the losses arising from speculative transactions had been properly disallowed and carried forward. There was such material, on which the Tribunal had based its finding that the two business of speculative transactions and commission agency, were separate and distinct business.

Further, the Tribunal was right in its conclusion that the true profit and loss of a transaction could only be worked out after allowing the commission paid in that transaction and, therefore, the speculative profits and losses could only be worked out after debiting the commission paid. Therefore the commission payment made on the assessee's speculative transactions, formed a direct charge and, therefore, rightly loaded against speculative transactions.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

The petitioners-companies were engaged in ship broking and other activities. As ship brokers the petitioners assisted, guided and supported the ship owners and the ship charterers to negotiate deals and conclude fixtures. Brokerage was paid by the ship owners and sometimes through charterers. The petitioners also undertook distinct activities like ship agency’s services to clients for loading/unloading of cargo, to act as port agents, facilitate and procure berth hiring, etc. The petitioners were registered with the service tax department under the category of ‘Steamer agent’s service’ and had been filing returns and paying service tax. The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004, with effect from 10-9-2004, expanded the scope of ‘Business auxiliary services’ by including activities relating to procurement of inputs, processing of good (not amounting to manufacture), or provisions of services on behalf of the clients by including them in the definition of ‘Business auxiliary services’. The Finance Act, 2005, with effect from 16-6-2005, made further amendments and expanded the scope of ‘Business auxiliary service’ by including commission agents. Show-cause notices were issued to the petitioners on ground that they were covered and liable to pay service tax under the head of ‘Business auxiliary services’. The petitioners filed the instant writ petitions contending that they were not acting as commission agents and that their activities and earnings could not be categorized as activities and earnings of a ‘Commission agent’. It was also contended that they were providing services by way of exports within meaning of the Export of Services Rules, 2005 and, therefore, could not be subjected to service tax.

On reading the provisions of the Krishi Utpadan Mandi Rules framed under the UP Krishi Utpadan Mandi Adhiniyam, 1964, it is apparent that the commission agent is accountable for that recovery which he makes from the seller in sale voucher in Form No. 6 and he is not liable to deposit any other amount with the market committee. Again, he is also not liable to deposit the amount of market fee on the total sales which he makes. Market fee only on those sales which have been recorded in sale voucher in Form No. 6 is payable to the market committee. Thus, the market fee realised by the commission agent does not form part of his trading receipt and he holds this amount only as a trustee for and on behalf of the market committee.

Accordingly, the sum of Rs. 29,028 was not liable to tax as trading receipt of the assessee.

"... It is also not possible to accept the contention of Mr. Naik for the Revenue that the definition of 'commission or brokerage' as contained in the Explanation to section 194H is so wide that it would include any payment receivable, directly or indirectly, for services in the course of buying or selling of goods and that, therefore, the discount availed of by the stamp vendors constitutes commission or brokerage within the meaning of section 194H. If this contention were to be accepted, all transactions of sale from a manufacturer to a wholesaler or from a wholesaler to a semi wholesaler or from a semi-wholesaler to a retailer would be covered by section 194H. To fall within the aforesaid Explanation, the payment received or receivable, directly or indirectly, is by a person acting on behalf of another person (i) for services rendered (not being professional services), or (ii) for any services in the course of buying or selling of goods, or (iii) in relation to any transaction relating to any asset, valuable article or thing. The element of agency is to be there in case of all services or transactions contemplated by Explanation (i) to section 194H. If a car dealer purchases cars from the manufacturer by paying price less discount, he would be the purchaser and not the agent of the company, but in the course of selling cars, he may enter into a contract of maintenance during the warranty period, with the customer (purchaser of the car) on behalf of the company. However, such services rendered by the dealer in the course of selling cars does not make the activity of selling cars itself an act of agent of the manufacturer when the dealings between the company and the dealer in the matter of sale of cars are on 'principal to principal' basis. This is just an illustration to clarify that a service in the course of buying or selling of goods has to be something more than the act of buying or selling of goods. When the licensed stamp vendors take delivery of stamp papers on payment of full price less discount and they sell such stamp papers to retail customers, neither of the two activities (buying from the Government and selling to the customers) can be termed as the service in the course of buying or selling of goods " (emphasis supplied)

In the light of the above, it can be said that:

♦ When a person acts on behalf of and under the directions and control of another person and sells the goods of the other person not as its own but as that of the other person, he acts as an agent.

♦ The remuneration received for the above service can be considered as commission1.

♦ When a person acts as an intermediary between two persons for negotiating a deal in relation to purchase or sale of any property or goods enabling the two persons to reach a contract, he acts as a broker.

♦ The remuneration received for the above service can be considered as brokerage.

♦ Discount/Rebate cannot be considered as commission or brokerage.

Commission on purchase not covered under 'Clearing and Forwarding Agent's services' :

The conjunctive 'and' between the words 'clearing' and 'forwarding' indicate and mean that where clearing operations are separate from forwarding operations, levy of tax would not be attracted i.e. there would be no charge of tax if the transaction involved only one of the two components of the conjuncted service namely 'clearing' and 'forwarding'. The expression a clearing and forwarding agent in relation to clearing and forwarding operations, in any manner' contemplates only one person operating both as the clearing and the forwarding agent; and if a person has rendered service as forwarding agent without rendering any service as 'clearing agent' he could not be considered to have rendered both services as a 'clearing and forwarding agent'. [Para 2]

'Clearing and forwarding operations' would be various activities having a bearing on clearance of goods and would normally involve documentary processes and arrangements for transfer of goods to their destination; and may also involve clearance at subsequent stages during forwarding operations. A clearing and forwarding agent normally undertakes the following activities :-

(a)

Receiving goods from the factories or premises of the principal or his agents;

(b)

Warehousing these goods;

(c)

Receiving despatch orders from the principal;

(d)

Arranging despatch of goods as per the directions of the principal by engaging transport on his own or through the authorised transporters of the principal;

(e)

Maintaining records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; and

(f)

Preparing invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 3]

Where a person is engaged only for procuring purchase orders for the vendor on a commission basis but does not engage in any of the enumerated activities (of a clearing and forwarding agent), directly or indirectly; or where services are provided by a commission agent engaged to procure orders and not entrusted with the work of clearing and forwarding of goods, the service would not be a taxable service as defined in section 65(105)(j) read with section 65(25) which defines a clearing and forwarding agent. [Para 4]

In this case, assessee neither receives goods from the factory premises of the principal; warehouses such goods; receives despatch orders from the principal; arranges despatch of goods as per directions of the principal by engaging a transport on its own or through authorised transporters of the principal; nor maintains records of the receipt and despatch of goods and the stock available at the warehouse; nor even prepares invoices on behalf of the principal. [Para 5]

Hence, assessee, in no manner, engages in any of the six enumerated activities which constitute clearing and forwarding operations. It never has custody of the picture tubes; does not receive them from manufacturers of the tubes; does not warehouse the picture tubes; does not receive despatch orders from manufacturers of picture tubes which are directly forwarded to manufacturers of the TV sets; does not arrange despatch of goods as per directions either of the manufacturers of picture tubes or manufacturers of TV sets; nor engages transport on its own or through authorised transporters of manufacturers of picture tubes or manufacturers of TV sets; and does not maintain records of the receipt and despatch of picture tubes and the stock available at the warehouse; nor prepares invoices either on behalf of the principal manufacturers or manufacturers of TV sets. [Para 6]

There is neither the conjunctive service of clearing and forwarding provided by the assessee nor either of the services of clearing or forwarding. As the assessee has not provided any of the core enumerated activities of clearing and forwarding operations, it has not directly or indirectly provided any service connected with clearing and forwarding operations in any manner to any other person. That the assessee was not a consignment agent is also not in dispute. [Para 7]

Therefore, assessee is not liable to Service Tax under the taxable head 'clearing and forwarding agency'. Even otherwise, commission agents were exempt from service tax vide Notification No. 13/2003 dated 20-5-2003 from 1-7-2003 upto 9-9-2004. Revenue proceeded on the basis that the assessee had provided 'clearing and forwarding agency' service, contrary to the distinct classification w.e.f. 1-7-2003; the services provided by it constituted Business Auxiliary Service. [Para 8]

The question that is raised in such cases is whether the service provided is regarded as having been exported out of India in accordance with the Export of Service Rules, 2005. In Blue Star Ltd. v. (b) Market development activity - The activity of holding of investors meeting and making arrangements for collection of money from investors and issuing them deposit certificates can also be regarded to be liable under Business auxiliary service as per the decision of the Tribunal in Shri Ram Overseas Finance Ltd. v. (c) Information technology service - Information technology service has been exempted. These can be understood to be software development activities, testing the codes as it is developed, support and consultancy in software customisation. These services would be appropriately classified under Consulting engineering services. This exemption would not apply to maintenance of software. Thus, the customer care services provided on behalf of a client involving maintenance of software would be liable under this category. Here, the activity would have to be distinguished from maintenance of software done for a client, as, in such cases, the liability would be under management, maintenance and repair category.

(d) Commission agent v. Clearing and forwarding agent - This category also seeks to tax services of a commission agent. ‘Commission agent’ as per the Explanation to section 65(19) means any person who acts on behalf of another person and causes sale or purchase of goods, or provision or receipt of services, for a consideration, and includes any person who, while acting on behalf of another person—

(i )deals with goods or services or documents of title to such goods or services; or

(ii )collects payment of sale price of such goods or services; or

(iii )guarantees for collection or payment for such goods or services; or

(iv )undertakes any activity relating to such sale or purchase of such goods or services. It should be noted that commission agent is one who has to be differentiated from a clearing and forwarding agent (including a consignment agent) whose services would be taxed under the clearing and forwarding agent’s service. Just because a commission agent stores and forwards the goods to customers, he cannot be taxed as a clearing and forwarding agent as per the decision of the Tribunal in CCE v. Chandan Chemicals [Final Order No. 125/2007-ST, dated April 24, 2007].

The distinction between the two was also brought out in Marigold Paints (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 14 STT 342 (Bang. - CESTAT).
