20.3-5 As per rule 3(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules, provider of output service shall be allowed to take Cenvat credit of specified duties and taxes. Thus, only a person who is providing taxable output service will be eligible to take Cenvat credit.

Output Service - "Output service" means any service provided by a provider of service located in the taxable territory but shall not include a service - (1) specified in section 66D of the Finance Act, 1994; or (2) where the whole of service tax is liable to be paid by the recipient of service [Rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules, as inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012] [Section 66D of Finance Act, 1994 covers list of services in negative list].

Rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules (as existing upto 1-7-2012 and from 29-2-2008) was reading as follows - "output service" means any taxable service, excluding the taxable service referred in section 65(105)(zzp) of Finance Act, 1994 (This is GTA service) provided by the provider of taxable service, to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder or any other person, as the case may be, and the expressions 'provider' and 'provided' shall be construed accordingly.

Till 29-2-2008, rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules stated that "output service" means any taxable service provided by the provider of taxable service, to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder or any other person, as the case may be, and the expressions 'provider' and 'provided' shall be construed accordingly.

The reference to Goods Transport Agency Service (falling under section 65(105)(zzp) of Finance Act, 1994 of Finance Act, 1994) has been inserted to clarify that GTA service will not be treated as 'output service' where consignor/consignee is liable to make payment of service tax. Thus, service tax on GTA service will have to be paid by consignor/consignee only by cash and not through Cenvat credit.

BPL Mobile Cellular Ltd.[2012] 37 STT 365/26 taxmann.com 216.

Further, this issue had lost relevance for the future because of exemption under Notification 25/2012-ST-S. No. 29 for this type of service. [Para 26]

Issue : Whether the following transaction amounts to taxable service subject to service tax ?

(A) Jobbing : Transaction entered on principal-to-principal basis between member brokers of the same Stock Exchange.

(B) Own Trading : Transactions entered on their own account by the brokers.

(C) Arbitrage : Transactions entered into by two brokers of different stock exchanges in order to get profit from price difference between two markets. Clarification : (A) When the transaction is on principal-to-principal basis between brokers, no investor is involved and as such no taxable service is provided and, therefore, no service tax is chargeable. It will attract service tax with effect from September 10, 2004 in view of the changed definition of ‘taxable service’ under section 65(105)(a). This is because from such date, service provision to any person has been made taxable.

(B) Where a broker enters into a transaction on his own account with an investor who is non-member of the stock exchange, the service provided will be taxable service and subject to service tax.

(C) In case of arbitrage transaction, i.e., the transaction between two brokers of different stock exchanges, the service is provided by a broker, i.e., the member of a stock exchange to a non-member of that stock exchange even though the investor may be a member of another stock exchange. There being an investor involved in the transaction, the service so provided to the investor will be a taxable service subject to service tax.

Issue : Whether service tax is chargeable at both the ends, when an investor is provided with taxable service by two brokers of different stock exchanges by various quarters :

Example , if a Calcutta based investor buys a security quoted on the Bombay stock exchange through his broker in Calcutta, he ends up paying service tax twice first to the Bombay stock exchange broker and then to the Calcutta stock exchange broker through whom the initial order was placed. In a situation like this, it has been represented that, it amounts to double taxation on a transaction of one single security.

Clarification : In the situation pointed out above, the investor is provided with taxable service by two brokers. First by the Bombay stock exchange broker through the Calcutta stock exchange broker and then by the Calcutta stock exchange broker.

Since the commission/brokerage is charged at both the ends, the charge of service tax at both the ends is both conceptually and legally correct. The investor placed his order for buying a security quoted at the Bombay stock exchange for the reason that either it is not available at the Calcutta stock exchange or the price is more beneficial at the Bombay stock exchange. It is open to the investor to either place his order on the Bombay stock exchange broker or through his Calcutta stock exchange broker. In the former case, he would have to pay service tax only on the service provided by the Bombay stock exchange broker. In the latter case, he pays higher commission paid to him by the Calcutta stock exchange broker, which includes the brokerage of the Bombay stock exchange broker. It cannot, therefore, be said that the investor is paying service tax twice.

The investor, in fact, pays double commission for avoiding the hassles involved in going to the Bombay stock exchange broker direct.

The service tax being the percentage of the brokerage charged from the investor, there is no double taxation involved. Service tax charged is only incidental to the charging of the commission/brokerage charged by the brokers.

It is, therefore, clarified that charging of service tax from an investor who is provided with taxable service by two brokers of different stock exchanges does not amount to double taxation.

First of all considering the issue of trading income of the assessee. There is no dispute that the assessee is engaged in the import and export of the goods which is in the nature of trading activities. As per the Income-tax Act, the trading activity is not entitled for the exemption under section 10AA. However, the SEZ Rules have been framed by Central Government by virtue of the delegated Rule making power given to it by the Special Economic Zone Act 2005. As per rule 76 the term "service" includes trading activities if it relates to the import of the goods for the purposes of export in terms of its explanation to Rule 76 of 2006. [Para 7]

As per the first explanation of rule 76 trading will be treated as "service" if it is related to the import of the goods for the purpose of the export. In this case there is no dispute that goods imported by the assessee are in fact exported to other countries from its unit at Special Economic Zone. [Para 8]

Since the Defortment is not able to point out any change in law or facts, therefore, respectfully following the order of Tribunal in earlier assessment year 2008-09, the claim of assessee was allowed in respect to its income from trading activity. [Para 11]

Secondly coming to the issue of denial of exemption in respect of warehousing. It is noted that the assessee has received Rs.23,06,539/- as warehouse charges. For corroborating this fact, the assessee has produced FIRC, ledgers, invoices for consultancy and warehousing charges. On perusal of the records including the remand report of Assessing Officer it is noted that the Assessing Officer disallowed the exemption on warehousing charges by observing that the assessee initially had shown the import of the goods as purchases and thereafter showed it as purchase return. According to Assessing Officer, on such transaction of purchase, and thereafter purchase return the assessee has shown warehouse income for Rs. 23,06,539. As per the Assessing Officer, the assessee cannot earn warehousing charges on such transaction and, therefore, such income is not entitled for exemption under section 10AA. It is noted the Rule 76 of SEZ Rules 2006 defines "Services" includes warehouse activity also, so income from the said activity qualify for exemption under section 10AA on the same reasoning as that given for trading activity. As a matter of fact, the assessee has raised the bill for the warehousing charges and the payment was also received for the same by foreign exchange. The FIRC is also placed in support of the payment. Indeed the assessee has recorded the transaction as purchase and purchase return along with quantitative details of the goods in the books of account. So, the question arises as to whether the accounting entries can change the character of the transaction. It is noted that the assessee has raised the invoice for the warehousing and handling charges. The Assessing Officer /Commissioner (Appeals) has not pointed out any defect in the bill, payment of the bill and the FIRC in support of the income. Hence, it is considered that the accounting entries cannot form the sole basis for denying the exemptions on account of warehousing charges to the assessee. As stated earlier, when warehousing activity has been included in the definition of 'service' as per Rule 76, therefore, the income from warehousing qualifies for exemption under section 10AA and, thus, the claim of the assessee is to be allowed. FACT: The assessee, a commission agent, claimed deduction on account of dharmada, gaushala and pathshala expenses. He also claimed deduction on account of messing expenses for his constituents. The ITO disallowed the first claim in toto but allowed the claim in respect of messing expenses to the extent of half. On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the assessee's claim in respect of dharmada, etc. In regard to the claim for messing expenses for the constituents it held, it did not involve any element of entertainment. These expenses were necessitated by the nature of the trade carried on by the assessee. The constituents, who came from outlying agencies, had to stay on for lunch or dinner and for that purpose the assessee provided them with meals. It accordingly allowed the claim of the assessee in full.

On reference :

HELD: Following the decision in Thakur Das Shyam Sunder v. Addl. CIT [1974] 93 ITR 27 (All.), the Tribunal was justified in holding that the receipts on account of dharmada, gaushala and pathshala could not be treated as part of the trading receipts of the assessee.

As regards the allowability of messing expenses in the case of Brij Raman Dass & Sons v. CIT [1976] 104 ITR 541 (All.), it was held that the phrase 'entertainment expenses' occurring in section 37(2A) includes all expenses incurred in connection with the business of the entertainment of customers and constituents and the entertainment may consist of providing refreshments or it may consist of providing some other form of entertainment. For the assessment year 1972-73, the relevant provisions of section 37(2A) were amended and no amount was admissible under the head 'Entertainment expenses'. In this view normally the entire amount claimed by the assessee would be disallowed but it was found that half of the amount was allowed by the ITO. The department had not gone in appeal either to the Commissioner or to the Tribunal. This part of the allowance could not be touched. The half which had been allowed by the ITO was outside the purview of the appeal in the Tribunal. The result would be that ultimately the ITO's order stood restored.

Note : The decision was partly in favour of assessee and partly in favour of revenue.

Suppose, BSNL issues SIM cards costing Rs. 500 plus service tax of Rs. 50/- to the distributor as per terms of an agreement against appropriate security. Distributor sells the card to the customer, collects Rs. 550 from customer by cheque in the name of BSNL and deposits it with BSNL. BSNL pays service tax of Rs. 50 to Govt. Out of the remaining Rs. 500 constituting the value of service rendered by BSNL, Rs. 15 is paid to the distributor. Revenue is asking service tax on this Rs. 15 from the distributor considering it as consideration for business auxiliary service rendered by distributor to BSNL in marketing the service of BSNL. Thus, BSNL was paying service tax on MRP of the cards and paying commission to distributors out of MRP realized. In such a situation, collecting service tax on MRP of SIM card from BSNL and collecting service tax again on that part of the amount paid by BSNL to the distributor out of MRP realized, puts the parties to these transactions at a doubly disadvantageous position as compared to service tax actually payable on the discounted price of the card. Double taxation plea not permissible in case of VAT chain :

The argument that tax should not be demanded in situations where somebody else has paid tax on the taxable value of a service is not an argument that can be accepted normally. If this argument is adopted, a taxpayer "X" in a VAT chain can argue that the next person "Y" who uses the service as input will be paying tax and X need not pay tax. In a VAT chain it is difficult to identify who is the ultimate consumer who is not paying further tax.

Taking the case of telecommunication service if the customer is a person who does not pay service tax on any of his activities, a telecom operator cannot adopt this argument. But if the customer is an industrialist he is eligible for credit of service tax to be paid by him. So a telecom operator can adopt the argument in respect of services rendered to such customers. Such logic will make any VAT system for collecting tax unworkable. [Para 21]

amendment carried out in 1991 by reason of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1991 was prospective in nature, ex facie the High Court committed a serious error in opining that the same being clarificatory in character would apply to the assessment year 1990-91. By reason of the purported clarification issued by the CBDT in terms of the said Circular, the area of exemption had not been widened, it has in effect and substance been curtailed. By reason of such amendment, the Parliament did not intend that the income derived by way of brokerage/commission by the assessee should not be reckoned for the purpose of computing profit or loss earned by a person engaged in the business of export but by reason thereof the deduction to the extent of 10 per cent was held to be allowable thereby. [Para 9]

Section 80HHC was incorporated in the Act for providing incentive to export houses. It is now a well-settled principle of law that although the exemption provisions are to be construed strictly as regards the applicability thereof to the case of the assessee, but once it is found that the same is applicable, the same are required to be interpreted liberally. [Para 10]

It is also trite law that an exemption is to be granted unless it is expressly taken away. [Para 11]

The expression 'income arising out of business of export' brings within its sweep not only the export of any goods or merchandise manufactured or possessed by the assessee but also of trading goods. The Parliament, therefore, intended to provide incentive when a positive profit is earned by an exporter. [Para 12]

Resultantly, the judgment of the High Court could not be sustained and it was to be held that income derived by the assessee towards commission/brokerage for procuring orders of export for other exporters would be eligible to exemption from tax under section 80HHC.[Para 16]

All these services were rendered in India. As such the services rendered by the assessee to the foreign enterprises did not qualify for exemption under section 80-O and the payments received were not entitled to exemption under section 80-O. However, the inclusion of the above income in the impugned block assessment under section 158BC, was not proper and justified. The assessee had filed its return for the assessment year 1994-95 on 31-1-1995, i.e., before the date of the search. It had also filed return for the assessment year 1995-96 on 25-1-1996, i.e., before passing of the impugned block assessment order on 27-12-1996, though after the date of the search. For the assessment year 1995-96 also the assessee had furnished the particulars of the commission received from the foreign enterprises. Thus, it was not a case where receipt of commission from the foreign enterprises had been detected as a result of the search and seizure operation. So far as the disallowance of the claim of exemption under section 80-O was concerned, it also could not be termed as detection as a result of the search and seizure operation. The disallowance is a matter of law in which there can be difference in the stand of the assessee and the revenue. Such disallowance cannot be brought within the purview of Chapter XIV-B. The disallowance of the claim of exemption under section 80-O as in the instant case would not come within category of undisclosed income as provided in section 158B(b).

Regarding inclusion of income of the assessment year 1996-97, as the assessee had recorded receipt of gross commission from the foreign enterprises in the books of account and as the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1996-97 had not ended, the commission from the foreign enterprises was not includible in the block period. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in including the income pertaining to the assessment years 1994-95, 1995-96 and 1996-97 (broken period) in the impugned block assessment under section 158BC. The income should be considered in the respective assessment under section 143(3). The prior period expenses on travelling and telephone was not similarly liable to be included in the impugned block assessment.

The income received in March, 1993 was, however, includible in the assessment year 1994-95 as shown by the assessee because the accounting period was from 2-3-1993 to 31-3-1994.

Hence, the assessee's appeal was partly allowed.

On a combined reading of the definition of ‘Clearing and Forwarding Agent’ under section 65(25) and the meaning of ‘Del Credere Agent’ and the amendment brought about in the year 2005, whereby a del credere agent is included in the category of ‘Business auxiliary service’, it is clear that the service rendered by a del credere agent prior to the said amendment could not have been brought within the scope of the definition of ‘Clearing and forwarding agent’ under the Act. [Para 4]

Therefore, in the instant case, the assessee was not a clearing and forwarding agent for RIL and he was a del credere agent and he was not liable to pay any service tax as had been ordered by the Asstt. Commissioner. The agreement with RIL, inter alia, included condition that the assessee would sell the products of its principal in the area as assigned; that the assessee would indemnify its principal from all losses caused by the customer’s failure to make payment of any products sold to them and; that the assessee would get a commission at a specified rate per Metric Tonne of the products sold by it. These conditions established that the assessee was a del credere agent which was covered under the nomenclature of ‘Business auxiliary service’ in clause (19 ) of section 65. [Para 5]

The period in question in this appeal was from 1-10-1999 to 30-9-2004 which was prior to the amendment of ‘Business auxiliary service’ which is with effect from 16-6-2005. Therefore, the assessee could not be brought within the scope of taxable service, viz., ‘Clearing and Forwarding Agent’s Services’. [Para 6]

The assessees rendered services of the same description to the vendors. The assessee-FA rendered services to DSI by identifying the vendors in India for procurement and supply of garments. They co-ordinated with vendors for production, logistics and shipment of goods ordered, to DSI. FA rendered services to vendors by attending to the processing of purchase orders placed by DSI, by giving necessary operational assistance in the execution and ensuring the receipt of sale proceeds. These services were rendered without a contract with the vendors and were incidental to services rendered to DSI. Similarly the assessee-FW had rendered services to the foreign company-B by monitoring production and export of garments by the vendors as per B’s orders. ‘B’ was the recipient of the service. FW had Research & Development facilities and assisted ‘B’ to decide the designs of the garments. The services rendered to ‘B’ and ‘DSI’ were correctly treated by the Commissioner as not exempt as exports during the material period. Only on 1-3-2007, such services when delivered and used outside India by a recipient located outside India, were extended the exemption. [Para 4]

The assessees, had rendered services to the companies in terms of their contracts with them. They assisted in procurring of purchase orders by the vendors. They monitored progress and timely execution of the export orders placed by the companies. There was no contract between the assessees and their respective vendors. The assessees admittedly rendered the services described in the show-cause notices as evaluation of prospective customers for the companies, processing of purchase orders, customer management, processing of transactions, information and tracking of delivery schedules, operational assistance for marketing, formulation of customer service and pricing policies, managing distribution and logistics. The services rendered to the vendors and the foreign companies by the assessees, conformed to the statutory definition of ‘Support service of business or commerce’ (SSBC). The services rendered to the foreign companies and vendors were, therefore, classifiable under ‘SSBC’ and not under ‘BAS’. Levy on SSBC was introduced with effect from 1-5-2006. Therefore, the demands of service tax on those services, categorizing them as BAS for the period prior to 1-5-2006, from the assessees were not sustainable. [Para 4.1]

As regards BAS received by the assessees from foreign agents, the CBEC had clarified the jurisdiction where the Act operated in the territory of India in its Circular F.No. 36/4/2001, dated 8-10-2001. [Para 4.2]

As clarified by the Bombay High Court, in the case of Indian National Shipowners Association v. Union of India [2009] 18 STT 212, it was only after enactment of section 66A on 18-4-2006 that taxable services received from abroad by a person belonging to India are taxed in the hands of the Indian residents. The assessees, in the instant case, had received BAS from commission agents based abroad mostly prior to 18-4-2006. There is no provision in the Act to tax the assessees for these services. Therefore, demands on this account for the period prior to 18-4-2006 had to fail. [Para 4.3]

As the demands failed, no penalty could be imposed. In the circumstances, demand of tax, interest and penalties imposed in the impugned orders was liable to be set aside except for an amount paid by the assessee-FA for the period from April, 2006 to September, 2006, under reverse charge method as Indian recipient of services of foreign commission agents. [Para 5]

The assessee for export of its finished product, availed the services of middlemen abroad who helped it in procuring the export orders for which they were paid commission. Since the said foreign middlemen did not have any office or business establishment in India, the revenue was of the view that during the period from July, 2004 to November, 2005, during which the service was received the assessee would be liable to pay service tax in terms of the provisions of rule 2(1)(d)( iv). Accordingly, service tax demand was confirmed on the assessee under the category of ‘Business auxiliary service’. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the demand. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that service received by it had not been rendered in India but had been rendered by persons outside India from off-shore locations and such import of taxable service became taxable only with effect from 18-4-2006 when section 66A was added to the Act and the Taxation of Services (Provided from Outside India and Received in India) Rules, 2006 were issued. It was also contended that before demanding service tax under the category of ‘Business auxiliary service’ (commission agent), there must be shown to exist a legal contractual relationship of principal and agent between it and the foreign middlemen, which had neither been alleged nor established as a fact.

The new provision has created an ironical situation. If Indian commission agent or stock broker provides service to principal outside India, he is required to pay service tax, though he is receiving payment in foreign exchange. On the other hand, if a foreign commission agent or foreign stock broker provides service to Indian Principal, the Indian Principal has to pay him in foreign exchange but no service tax is payable.

Thus, a transaction where actually India received foreign exchange is subjected to service tax, while transaction where there is outflow of foreign exchange from India is not subject to service tax.

14.8-5 No service tax on services provided by foreign Commission Agents or foreign stock broker to Indian Principals w.e.f. 1-10-2014

The aforesaid provision is working in reverse direction in case of foreign commission agents providing service to Indian Principal or foreign stock brokers. So far, rule 3 of POPS was applicable and place of provision of service was India. Hence, the Indian Principal was liable to pay service tax under reverse charge mechanism, in respect of commission paid by them to foreign commission agent or foreign stock broker.

Now, w.e.f. 1-10-2014, the place of provision of service is out of India as per rule 9(c) of POPS Rules. Hence, there is no service tax on commission paid to foreign commission agents or foreign stock brokers w.e.f. 1-10-2014. Since there is no service tax, any question of reverse charge cannot arise.

No declaration under EXP3 and EXP4 for services of foreign agent after 1-10-2014 - Now, notification No. 42/2012-ST is not relevant as no service tax is payable after 1-10-2014 under reverse charge on services provided by foreign commission agent to Indian manufacturers/service providers. Any declaration under EXP3 and EXP4 is not required in respect of foreign agency commission paid on or after 1-10-2014.

[Though the above is correct legal position, I agree assessees are going to face very tough time in convincing excise auditors. Hence, it is advisable to inform them in writing, to avoid charge of suppression of facts].

14.8-6 Hiring of aircrafts and vessels upto one month exempt

In case of hiring of all means of transport upto one month, other than aircrafts and vessels except yachts, the place of provision of service is the location of service provider [rule 9(d) of POPS Rules as amended w.e.f. 1-10-2014].

The words 'other than aircrafts and vessels except yachts' has been inserted w.e.f. 1-10-2014. Thus, hiring of vessels or aircrafts, irrespective of whether short term or long term, will be covered by the general rule, i.e. place of location of service receiver. Hiring of yachts would continue to be covered by rule 9(d) - para 4.1.3(iii) of MF(DR) letter No. 334/15/2014-TRU dated 10-7-2014

The effect is that if Indian service provider of renting of aircraft or vessel gives the aircraft or vessel (other than yacht) to a foreign customer for any period (less than one month or more than one month), the place of provision of service will be out of India, if it relates to goods (and service tax will not apply).

On the other hand, if service provider from outside India of renting of aircraft or vessel gives the aircraft or vessel (other than yacht) to an Indian customer for any period (less than one month or more than one month), the place of provision of service will be India, if it relates to goods (and service tax will not apply).

A. Emergence of concept of service tax :

While on the manufacture of goods, tax is levied in the name of excise duty and on sale of goods tax is levied in the name of sales tax, there are number of activities, falling in the category of 'service sector' which constitute 40 per cent of National GDP, which are not subjected to tax. This has kept a number of activities, which in fact are an important part of the national economy, outside the tax net. It is of course true that the persons rendering such services are subjected to income-tax covered by Entry 83 in List I of Schedule VII of the Constitution, but that by itself is not sufficient as the persons manufacturing goods pay excise duty on the manufacture of goods and pay sales tax on sale of goods and are also liable to pay income-tax on the income earned by them. The professionals rendering services for remuneration and similarly other persons rendering service in a larger number of fields for remuneration can only be subjected to professional tax by the State Legislature by virtue of Entry 60 in List II but subject to the maximum limit of Rs. 2,500 per annum in view of the provisions of article 276(2) of the Constitution of India. Such tax is on profession/trade/calling/employment irrespective of the fact whether they were earning any income or not. In these circumstances, the Parliament decided to tax the services being rendered by the professionals and by other trades and callings. Thus, the service tax is absolutely distinct and separate from the tax on profession/trade/calling/employment. [Para 4]

B. Legislative history :

The Government of India has notified service tax on 12 new services added in the service tax net by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998, vide notification dated 7-10-1998. The liability has been made effective from 16-10-1998. Further, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 93, the Central Government had exempted in the public interest the taxable services other than that of auditing and accounting provided by a practising chartered accountant in his professional capacity to a client. Vide notification dated 16-10-1998 certain exemptions have been given to the Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost and Works Accountants. Thus, the net result was that the service tax was leviable on chartered accountants in relation to accounting, auditing and certification services provided by them, in their professional capacity. As section 12B of Central Excise Act, 1944 has been made applicable in relation to the impugned service tax, the direct legal consequence is that there is a presumption that service tax has been passed on to the customer, who is the beneficiary of the service, and that is the reason why the service tax is levied on the service provider himself. It is open to the service provider to pass on the tax to the beneficiary of the service and reimburse himself. Thus, it is evident that the service provider does not pay the tax and the tax falls on the service receiver. [Para 6]

C. Legislative competence :

The subject-matter of taxation available to the Parliament is enumerated in Entries 80 to 97 of List I. Entries 45 to 66 of List II are available to the State Legislature. Under article 246(1), the Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters and that includes the power to impose tax enumerated in List I. Where the case does not fall either in the State List or the Concurrent List, the Parliament has residuary power under Entry 97 of List I. [Para 7]

The Parliament has power to levy tax on the manufacture of goods as per Entry 84 in the Union List, and also to levy tax on the services being rendered by a professional. Thus, if the tax on a trade or calling would also include the power to tax the transactions being entered into by a person carrying on any trade or calling, there would not have been a separate entry to confer the power to levy tax on sale of goods. A trader carrying on his business of buying and selling goods and subjected to tax under Entry 60 in the State List is also liable to pay taxes on the sale or purchase of goods under Entry 54 in the State List. Thus, it is evident that the two taxes are separate and distinct and they cannot be merged merely because a person liable to pay tax under Entry 60 in the State List and also liable to collect and pay tax on sale of goods under entry 54 in the said list is one and the same person in both the cases. [Para 8]

A chartered accountant or an architect who is paying professional tax but not providing any service though he chooses to be on the roll of Architects or the chartered accountants, would not be required to pay the service tax. [Para 11]

On a plain reading of the provisions of section 80HHC, it is evident that it applies to the assessee engaged in the business of export out of India including trading of goods. The expression 'business of export' must be given its due meaning. It not only speaks of export out of India, but also includes 'trading of goods'. [Para 7]

Indisputably, the CBDT issued a Circular No. 621, dated 19-12-1991 by way of explanatory notes to the provisions of section 80HHC. Said circular provided for modification of provisions relating to exemption of income from exports. The amendment by inserting sub-section (3) in the said provision was carried out so as to compensate the exporter from the comparative disadvantages faced by him in the international market. The formula, as was existing prior to 1991 as stated in the circular, often used to provide a distorted figure of export profits when receipts like interest commission, etc., which did not have an element of turnover were included in the profit and loss account and, thus, it was clarified that 'profits of the business' for the said provision would not include receipt by way of brokerage, commission, interest or any other receipt of a similar nature. It was, however, categorically stated that as some expenditure might be incurred in earning these incomes, which in the generality of cases is part of common expenses, ad hoc 10 per cent deduction from such incomes is provided to account for these expenses. The amendments in no uncertain terms were to take effect from 1-4-1992, i.e., for the assessment year 1992-93, and subsequent assessment years.

The aforementioned circular dated 19-12-1991 issued by the CBDT was binding on the Department. [Para 8]

Once it was held that the amendment carried out in 1991 by reason of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1991 was prospective in nature, ex facie the High Court committed a serious error in opining that the same being clarificatory in character would apply to the assessment year 1990-91. By reason of the purported clarification issued by the CBDT in terms of the said Circular, the area of exemption had not been widened, it has in effect and substance been curtailed.

By reason of such amendment, the Parliament did not intend that the income derived by way of brokerage/commission by the assessee should not be reckoned for the purpose of computing profit or loss earned by a person engaged in the business of export but by reason thereof the deduction to the extent of 10 per cent was held to be allowable thereby. [Para 9]

Section 80HHC was incorporated in the Act for providing incentive to export houses. It is now a well-settled principle of law that although the exemption provisions are to be construed strictly as regards the applicability thereof to the case of the assessee, but once it is found that the same is applicable, the same are required to be interpreted liberally. [Para 10]

It is also trite law that an exemption is to be granted unless it is expressly taken away. [Para 11]

The expression 'income arising out of business of export' brings within its sweep not only the export of any goods or merchandise manufactured or possessed by the assessee but also of trading goods. The Parliament, therefore, intended to provide incentive when a positive profit is earned by an exporter. [Para 12]

Resultantly, the judgment of the High Court could not be sustained and it was to be held that income derived by the assessee towards commission/brokerage for procuring orders of export for other exporters would be eligible to exemption from tax under section 80HHC.[Para 16]

8D.1-5 AO's power to determine amount of expenditure incurred pre-AY 2007-08 - Up to AY 2006-07, no method has been provided for computing the expenditure incurred by the assessee in relation to exempt income. Even though no such method has been prescribed by the 1961 Act, the Assessing Officer has, first of all, to ascertain the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of the expenditure incurred in relation to income which does not form part of the total income under the Act. Even where the assessee claims that no expenditure has been incurred in relation to income which does not form part of total income, he will have to verify the correctness of such claim.

In case, he is satisfied with the claim of the assessee with regard to the expenditure or no expenditure, as the case may be, he is to accept the claim of the assessee insofar as the quantum of disallowance under section 14A is concerned. In such eventuality, the AO cannot embark upon a determination of the amount of expenditure for the purposes of section 14A(1). In case, he is not, on the basis of objective criteria and after giving the assessee a reasonable opportunity, satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee, he shall have to reject the claim and state the reasons for doing so.

Having done so, the AO will have to determine the amount of expenditure incurred in relation to income which does not form part of the total income under the said Act. He is required to do so on the basis of a reasonable and acceptable method of apportionment— Maxopp Investment Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 15 taxmann.com 390/203 Taxman 364 (Delhi), affirmed in Maxopp Investment Ltd. v. CIT [2018] 91 taxmann.com 154/254 Taxman 325 (SC). Thus, AO was free to adopt any reasonable and acceptable method.

But since there has been considerable dispute between the taxpayers and the Department on the method of determining such expenditure, therefore, the provisions of section 14A(2) [along with section 14A(3)] have been introduced.

8D.1-6 AO's power to determine amount of expenditure incurred for and from 1-4-2007 [section 14A(2) & 14A(3)] - Since, as discussed above, there has been considerable dispute between the taxpayers and the Department on the method of determining such expenditure, therefore, the provisions of section 14A(2) [alongwith section 14A(3)] have been introduced which applies prospectively for and from AY 2007-08 with the requirement of adopting a specific method of determining amount of such expenditure that has been incurred in relation to exempt income.

Section 14A(2) provides the manner in which the Assessing Officer is to determine the amount of expenditure incurred in relation to exempt income. However, the Assessing Officer is required to determine the amount of such expenditure only if he, having regard to the accounts of the assessee, is not satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of such expenditure. In other words, the requirement of the Assessing Officer embarking upon a determination of the amount of expenditure incurred in relation to exempt income would be triggered only if he returns a finding that he is not satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of such expenditure. Therefore, the condition precedent for the Assessing Officer entering upon a determination of the amount of the expenditure incurred in relation to exempt income is that he must record that he is not satisfied with the correctness of the claim of the assessee in respect of such expenditure. This part of section 14A(2), which explicitly requires the fulfilment of a condition precedent, is also implicit in section 14A(1). It is only the prescription with regard to the method of determining such expenditure which is new and which will operate prospectively.

Section 14A(3) stipulates that the above provisions of section 14A(2) shall also apply where an assessee claims that no expenditure has been incurred by him in relation to exempt income. Thus, section 14A(3) is nothing but an offshoot of section 14A(2).
